body:
An enterprise giving thousands of employees a personal, persistent OpenClaw workspace needs six things proven at once: warm-pool claims with batch image acceleration, deletion that releases everything, sleep/wake with recorded durations, fleet-wide image/config/resize rollouts, NAS-backed 20 GB per-employee storage that scales past per-user-PV attach limits, and a stable per-employee URL. No existing example demonstrates that combination end to end; this one does, with an asserting test script (`run-test-gke.sh`) and measured results from a live GKE validation (warm claim adoption p50 174 ms; suspend ~1.7 s; disk-tier wake 22.3 s; rebuild downtime 5.2 s; deletion residue-free).

The central design rule: a warm claim is only sub-second because it changes nothing about the running pod except metadata — so everything per-employee arrives without touching the pod spec, via a Filestore subdirectory late-bound into the already-running warm pod (pattern adapted from `latebind-storage-gke-sandbox`). One unified `SandboxTemplate` serves every employee.

The README leads with the customer requirements (P0 test checklist) and keeps the main path strictly inside that bar; alternatives that trade a P0 away (multishares/per-user PVCs, Autopilot paths, HDD tier) live in an explicit appendix with their conflicts named. A Known Gaps section records what live validation and a platform gap review surfaced honestly: the unresolved Autopilot trilemma, the convention-only unbind invariant, Pod Snapshots' sharp edges, no in-platform idle detection, no per-claim sizing, grow-only storage without quota enforcement, and the example-grade portal/daemon glue.

Components: provisioning/teardown scripts, storage + late-bind daemon, unified template + warm pool, a small lifecycle portal, sandbox-router + Gateway API wiring (optional IAP), Pod Snapshots runbooks for memory-tier sleep, a rate-limited rolling-update script, and latency/fio measurement tools.

title: Decouple sandbox provisioning from PodSpec

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

body:
## Intro

Just thought I'd put it a few words above the generated content; my main goal is to get the discussion going and it's totally fine if this is way off. Obviously I am coming from the KubeVirt world so a bit biased, but I think this totally deserves a thorough discussion.

## Summary

The current Sandbox API requires `corev1.PodSpec` via `SandboxBlueprint.podTemplate`, coupling every sandbox to a Pod. As non-pod workloads emerge — KubeVirt VMs ([Issue #1157](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1157)), off-node runtimes ([lambda-microvm-sandbox-shim](https://github.com/jicowan/lambda-microvm-sandbox-shim)), Windows environments — the API needs a pluggable provisioning layer that decouples the user-facing Sandbox from any specific runtime backend.

This proposal outlines the motivation and the design space. It does not commit to a specific approach — the goal is to align on direction before designing the interface.

## Motivation

- **`SandboxBlueprint.podTemplate` is a required `corev1.PodSpec`.** Every Sandbox is, by definition, a Pod. The status surface confirms this (`PodIPs`, `NodeName`, `PodScheduled` condition). A sandbox consumer needs compute, network, storage, exec, and lifecycle management — not a PodSpec.

- **Issue #1157 proves the PodSpec reinterpretation problem.** To add KubeVirt support, #1157 reinterprets `containers[0].image` as a containerDisk source, `env` as a metadata Secret, and `volumeMounts` as virtio disks. This can't express UEFI firmware, TPM, machine type, CPU topology, GPU passthrough, live migration, SEV/TDX, or any VM-specific configuration. These aren't edge cases — they're the reason to choose a VM.

- **[lambda-microvm-sandbox-shim](https://github.com/jicowan/lambda-microvm-sandbox-shim) proves the pattern is emerging ad-hoc.** This PoC bridges Lambda MicroVMs with agent-sandbox on EKS 1.36. Because there's no driver interface, it had to: (1) fork the SDK, (2) replace the Pod reconciler with a custom provider, (3) re-map PodSpec fields to MicroVM config, (4) use an annotation as a poor man's routing mechanism. The project explicitly notes *"off-node MicroVMs can't conform to CRI semantics."*

- **Windows workloads are ruled out entirely.** Kata runs a Linux guest kernel. KubeVirt can run Windows Server 2022, Windows 11, or any OS with virtio/WHQL drivers. If AI agents need Windows environments, the current API has no answer.

- **Node-level sandbox preparation is coming.** Confidential computing (SEV-SNP, TDX) needs node-level attestation and key provisioning. Cybersecurity providers may need to inject eBPF monitoring, load security profiles, or set up audit pipelines on the node before a sandbox starts — and scrub the node after termination. These are "NodePrepareSandbox / NodeCleanupSandbox" operations — the same pattern as CSI's `NodeStageVolume`/`NodePublishVolume` and DRA's `NodePrepareResources`/`NodeUnprepareResources`.

- **KEP-539.2 is complementary, not competing.** [KEP-539.2](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/docs/keps/539.2-runtime-standardization/README.md) standardizes the *data plane* — how SDKs talk to `sandboxd` inside a running sandbox (exec, filesystem, Jupyter). It doesn't address how sandboxes are provisioned, what backs them, or how lifecycle maps to infrastructure. It activates after you already have a running environment.

## Design

### Possible approaches

Kubernetes has solved similar problems several times, each with different trade-offs:

**CSI / DRA pattern.** A gRPC driver interface with controller and node services. Driver-specific config passed as opaque `runtime.RawExtension` (following DRA's `OpaqueDeviceConfiguration` model). Each driver defines its own config CRD, validates it with its own webhooks.
- Pro: fully extensible, consistent interface for both control plane and node operations, proven at scale
- Con: operational overhead (sidecar/deployment per driver, socket registration), heavier to implement

**Gateway API pattern.** `SandboxClass` names a `controllerName`. Each backing type provides its own controller that watches Sandbox CRs. Common lifecycle logic provided as a Go library.
- Pro: maximally extensible, no gRPC infrastructure, each team owns their controller
- Con: common logic (warm pools, claims, templates) must be a consumable library, coordination between controllers

**Compiled-in adapter pattern.** The Sandbox controller ships with Go adapter implementations for known types (Pod, KubeVirt VM). Third parties contribute adapters.
- Pro: simple, testable, no operational overhead
- Con: adding a new backing type means recompiling, doesn't scale to many types

These aren't mutually exclusive — the project could start with one and graduate to another. The key architectural question is whether node-level operations are a near-term requirement (which argues for a gRPC interface from the start) or a future extension (which allows starting simpler).

## What I'd like feedback on

1. **Is decoupling from PodSpec a goal for this project?** The roadmap lists "Decouple API from Runtime" (KEP #597, #747) as in-progress, but those KEPs address the data-plane protocol (`sandboxd`), not control-plane provisioning. Is control-plane decoupling on the radar?

2. **How should the project handle #1157?** The KubeVirt proposal reinterprets PodSpec fields for VM semantics. Should this be accepted as a pragmatic first step, or should the project design a pluggable backend model first and implement #1157 on top of it?

3. **Which pattern fits best?** CSI/DRA-style gRPC drivers, Gateway API-style per-class controllers, or compiled-in adapters? Does the project have a preference, or should this be explored in a follow-up KEP?

4. **Are node-level operations a near-term concern?** If sandboxes need node-level preparation (security providers, confidential computing), that argues for designing the interface now. If those use cases are far out, a simpler approach can work initially (wild future speculation - cybersecurity provider for sandbox?)

/kind api-change

title: examples: cluster-wide egress control with the Network Policy API

labels.name: size/XXL

labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

body:
The template-managed `NetworkPolicy` cannot deny egress cluster-wide or allow destinations by domain name, and any template author can relax it. Users keep asking for both.

This adds `examples/network-policy-api-sandbox`: a walkthrough that layers `ClusterNetworkPolicy` from the SIG Network [Network Policy API](https://network-policy-api.sigs.k8s.io/) on top of the `NetworkPolicy` agent-sandbox already manages per template:

- Admin tier: deny-all egress for every sandbox pod, then DNS, GitHub FQDNs and a per-tenant PyPI allowlist at higher precedence.
- `Pass` to the NetworkPolicy tier for an in-cluster service, so each template decides through `spec.networkPolicy.egress`.
- Baseline tier as the floor for sandboxes no `NetworkPolicy` selects.

Templates stay `Managed`: the API is designed to work with `NetworkPolicy`, not replace it, and the controller's defaults keep applying. The network policy management guide is updated to point here for FQDN and cluster-wide defaults instead of recommending `Unmanaged`.

Enforcement uses [kube-network-policies](https://kube-network-policies.sigs.k8s.io/), the SIG Network reference implementation, which runs alongside any CNI; any conformant implementation works with the same manifests. Verified on a conformant Kubernetes cluster with agent-sandbox v1.0.2: `scripts/test.sh` passes 22/22.

title: examples: execution-scoped credentials for a reused Sandbox

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: needs-ok-to-test
labels.description: Indicates a PR that requires an org member to verify it is safe to test.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Supersedes #1639, which I opened from the wrong GitHub account by mistake —
same author, different identity, and the CNCF CLA is only signed under this
one. Content and history are otherwise unchanged except for the
review-response fixes listed below, made in response to the review already
left on #1639. Closing #1639 in favor of this one.

Adds `examples/containarium-execution-scoped-token`: a runnable reference for
**execution-scoped credentials in a reused Sandbox** — the
authorization–execution lifetime mismatch from #1580 — for one credential
class, model provider API keys.

A credential provisioned into a reusable Sandbox lives as long as the Sandbox,
not as long as the execution that justified it. Two runs in one box end up with
the union of both runs' authority, and a credential from a finished run stays
usable by whatever runs next. This is the second of the two contributions
[@janetkuo invited on #1580](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1580#issuecomment-5593702590)
— "expanding documentation or reference examples demonstrating short-lived token
projection or credential-proxy sidecars".

One long-lived `Sandbox` runs two executions back to back. Each gets its own
short-lived token, and the example holds three properties together, because any
two of them still leave a hole:

1. **The real key is never in the box.** It lives in a credential proxy
   (Containarium's standalone model gateway, published image, pinned by
   digest) that verifies the caller's scoped token, injects the real key, and
   proxies upstream. What the box holds is worthless anywhere else.
2. **The token reaches one process, not the pod.** It goes in
   `ProcessConfig.env_vars` on `ProcessService.Start` — not the `Sandbox` spec,
   not the `SandboxClaim`, not a `Secret`, not the workspace volume. It is not
   readable via `get pod`, and the next run does not inherit it.
3. **The token is revoked at `ExitEvent`, not left to expire.** Removing a
   variable from a process's environment does not invalidate a copy that already
   left the process. This is the specific gap #1580 describes, and the check
   below replays a copy that never went back into the sandbox.

The `Sandbox` is never destroyed to end a credential — preserving reuse is the
point of #1580.

**On fresh sandboxes.** The README is explicit that claiming a fresh instance
from a `SandboxWarmPool` is the intended pattern and that reuse leaks more than
credentials. This example is for the cases where reuse is deliberate, and it
addresses only the credential dimension; it says plainly that it does **not**
reset the filesystem, kill leftover processes, reset the environment block, or
restart language kernels — those are `Setup()` / `Clean()` in
[KEP-539.2](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/docs/keps/539.2-runtime-standardization#reusable-sandboxes-setup--cleanup),
not this example's job. It does suggest one addition to `Clean()`'s
implementation considerations, beside "Environment Variables": **revoke** every
credential issued for the run, not only remove it from the environment block.

##### Why the generated `processv1` stubs and not `clients/go/sandbox`

For the run itself, the runner uses
`packages/sandboxd/spec/process/v1` directly. The high-level client's only hook
for environment variables is `Options.Env`, which injects them into the
`SandboxClaim` — putting the token in the pod spec for the life of the sandbox,
which is exactly the anti-pattern the example exists to replace. The README says
so, and suggests a small follow-up: a per-call
`WithEnv(map[string]string)` option on `Commands.Run` landing in
`ProcessConfig.env_vars`, which would let the high-level client express this
pattern and make the drop to the generated stubs unnecessary. Happy to send that
as a separate PR if you want it.

##### Why Cilium

kind's default CNI (kindnet) does not enforce `NetworkPolicy` — it accepts the
object and drops nothing. On a default kind cluster the "direct egress is
blocked" check would pass with the policy having no effect, i.e. a check that
cannot fail. So `kind-config.yaml` sets `disableDefaultCNI: true` and
`run-test-kind.sh` installs Cilium, following
[`examples/demo-cilium-egress`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/examples/demo-cilium-egress).

The egress probe is also hardened against passing for the wrong reason: it dials
the provider **by IP** (resolved on the host, never inside the box) so a DNS
failure cannot look like enforcement, and it runs the *identical* probe against
the allowed gateway immediately before. The runner requires that positive
control to succeed before it calls the check a pass. During development the
probe did pass for the wrong reason once — a malformed `/dev/tcp` path — which is
why the control is there.

##### `sandboxd` image: built locally, not pulled

`sandboxd` has no released image: `v1.0.2` ships manifests only, and
`registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/sandboxd` has no `v1.0.2` tag. The only published
builds are on the k8s staging registry. #1639 pinned a per-commit staging tag by
digest there; review correctly flagged that as not durable — that registry is
periodically garbage-collected, so even a digest-pinned reference eventually
404s, which a digest pin alone does not protect against.

`run-test-kind.sh` now builds `sandboxd` from `packages/sandboxd/Dockerfile` at
the checked-out commit and `kind load`s it under a fixed local tag;
`sandbox.yaml` references that tag with `imagePullPolicy: Never`, so it is
never pulled from any registry. The README documents the trade-off (one extra
`docker build` in the happy path, in exchange for the example not rotting when
the staging registry is swept) and flags this as the one piece expected to
change once a release image exists.

##### Notes for review

- `runner/` has no `go.mod` and adds **no dependency to the root module**: it
  imports the repo's own generated stubs, so it lives in the root module like
  [`examples/sandboxd-sandbox/client`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/examples/sandboxd-sandbox/client).
  The gateway token is therefore minted with the standard library only
  (`runner/token.go`) rather than pulling a JWT library into the module for one
  example — which also has the side benefit of making the claims, and the fact
  that `run_id` + `jti` are all that bind the credential to a run, legible in
  the diff.
- No provider API key is needed to run the test. Check 1 asserts the **gateway**
  accepted the token, discriminating on the body against the gateway's finite
  list of plain-text refusals, not on the status code — because without a key
  the provider itself answers 401 and a status-only assertion would confuse
  "gateway refused the credential" with "provider refused the key". The runner
  prints the refusal list beside the observed body so a reader can check the
  distinction rather than trust it. `PROVIDER_API_KEY=<real key>` makes it a 200.
- `go build`, `go vet`, and `gofmt -l` are clean on the changed package;
  `shellcheck` is clean on `run-test-kind.sh`; both manifests parse as valid
  YAML. I could not re-run the full `run-test-kind.sh` end-to-end after this
  round's changes — this environment has no `docker`/`kind` — so the "Test
  output" below is unchanged from #1639's original run and predates the three
  fixes in this PR. None of those three touch the runtime behavior the test
  output demonstrates (revoke-on-exit, egress blocking, per-run tokens); happy
  to post a fresh run, or have a reviewer/CI trigger one, before merge.

##### Changes since #1639 (review response)

Addressing review already left on #1639:

- **Pin the model-gateway image by digest**, not a mutable tag — it is the one
  pod holding the real provider key.
- **Stop depending on the k8s-staging-images registry for `sandboxd`** — see
  "`sandboxd` image: built locally, not pulled" above.
- **Propagate a deferred revoke failure into `doRun`'s returned error** instead
  of only logging it to stderr, per the CodeRabbit finding aditya-shantanu
  endorsed — a run whose credential silently failed to revoke now fails the
  test instead of being reported as a pass.

Not addressed here, left as open, non-blocking hardening notes per the
original review (both already called out in the README's "Hardening notes" —
happy to act on either if you'd rather they were code, not prose):

- A leftover same-UID process from run 1 can still read run 2's token out of
  `/proc/<pid>/environ` — per-process delivery isolates runs only if no
  process survives the run, which is `Clean()`'s job, not this example's.
- The gateway's admin revoke route shares the port the `NetworkPolicy` opens
  to the sandbox, guarded only by a static bearer token.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1580

Not "Fixes": #1580 asks for an execution-scoped authorization abstraction and
this PR is a reference example for one credential class, so the issue should
stay open for the `Clean()` / lifecycle-hook work.

title: feat(sdks): support streaming file downloads

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: ok-to-test
labels.description: Indicates a non-member PR verified by an org member that is safe to test.

labels.name: size/XL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 500-999 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The existing Go and Python file download APIs return the complete file as
`[]byte` or `bytes`. This makes client memory usage proportional to file size,
even though both supported runtimes can deliver response bodies incrementally.

This PR adds streaming download APIs that copy response data directly into a
caller-owned destination:

- Go:
  - Add `Files.ReadTo(ctx, path, io.Writer)` and the corresponding
    `Sandbox.ReadTo` convenience method.
  - Preserve `Read()` and its existing `[]byte` behavior by implementing it on
    top of the shared streaming path.
- Python:
  - Add synchronous `Filesystem.read_to()` for binary file-like destinations.
  - Add asynchronous `AsyncFilesystem.read_to()` for asynchronous binary sinks.
  - Extend the sync and async connectors to return unbuffered streaming
    responses when requested.

The implementation supports both the legacy python-runtime and sandboxd where
the corresponding SDK transport is available. Existing byte-returning APIs
remain backward compatible.

Download limits are enforced without buffering the complete response. A
declared oversized response is rejected before writing, while unknown-length
responses are limited as they stream. Responses are closed on success, failure,
retry, and cancellation.

Destinations remain caller-owned and are never closed by the SDK. If a network,
cancellation, size-limit, or destination-write error occurs, bytes already
written remain in the destination and the returned byte count describes the
completed portion.

For example, callers can stream a Sandbox file directly to local storage:

```go
download, err := os.Create("model-copy.bin")
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
defer download.Close()

written, err := sb.ReadTo(ctx, "model.bin", download)
if err != nil {
    log.Fatal(err)
}
fmt.Printf("downloaded %d bytes\n", written)
```

The PR also adds documentation and coverage for chunked responses, partial
destination writes, known and unknown response lengths, limit violations,
cancellation, destination failures, response cleanup, and legacy/sandboxd
endpoint selection.

This is the download-side counterpart to the streaming upload work in #1634
and does not depend on that PR.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1637

#### Testing

- `go build ./clients/go/sandbox/...`
- `go vet ./clients/go/sandbox/...`
- `go test -race ./clients/go/sandbox/...`
- `python -m pytest -q k8s_agent_sandbox/test/unit` (`384 passed`, `1 skipped`, `14 subtests passed`)
- `make toc-verify`
- `git diff --check upstream/main...HEAD`

#### Release Note

```release-note
Added streaming file download APIs to the Go and Python SDKs so callers can write Sandbox file contents incrementally to caller-owned destinations without buffering the complete response.
```


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **New Features**
  - Added streaming file downloads to caller-provided destinations with `ReadTo` in the Go SDK and `read_to` in the Python SDK.
  - Streaming downloads report bytes written, support partial writes, and avoid buffering entire files.
  - Added asynchronous streaming download support in Python.

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Download-size limits are consistently enforced during streaming.
  - Improved cleanup after errors, retries, cancellation, or destination failures.
  - Added validation for invalid destinations and download-size limits.

- **Documentation**
  - Updated SDK documentation with streaming download usage, limits, and destination-handling behavior.

title: docs: review and synchronize roadmap statuses with the current implementation

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be updated?

The roadmap was last comprehensively updated in #871, which was merged on May 28, 2026.

Since then, the project has evolved rapidly and has reached the v1.0 release. Several roadmap entries still appear as `Planned` or `In Progress`, although their original core functionality has already been implemented on `main`.

Some clear examples are:

- **Smart WarmPool Selection** is marked `In Progress`, but #491 has been closed and the selection strategy was implemented in #878.
- **Agent Sandbox MCP Server** is marked `Planned`, but a complete MCP server was added in #1141.
- **Storage Customization at Claim Time** is marked `Planned`, but claim-level `volumeClaimTemplates` and the corresponding template policies were implemented in #960.
- **Strict Sandbox-to-Pod Mapping** is marked `In Progress`, but #127 has been closed and the controller now has deterministic pod association, ownership checks, and regression tests.
- **1st Class Router** is marked `Planned`, although the Go router was added in #838 and is now built, tested, packaged, and shipped with deployment manifests.
- Benchmarking infrastructure, performance documentation, SDK functionality, and integration examples have also progressed significantly since the last comprehensive roadmap update.

Some entries may intentionally describe a broader goal than the functionality already merged. Therefore, maintainer confirmation would be helpful before simply marking them as complete.

### Why is this needed?

The roadmap is an important entry point for contributors looking for available work.

When completed or partially completed functionality is still marked as `Planned`, contributors may:

- spend time investigating work that has already been implemented;
- propose duplicate issues or implementations;
- have difficulty understanding which parts of a larger initiative are still genuinely available;
- miss smaller follow-up tasks hidden behind a broad roadmap entry.

Keeping the roadmap aligned with the implementation would make it easier for contributors to identify useful work and understand the remaining scope of each initiative.

### Suggested outcome

- Review each roadmap entry against the current implementation.
- Move clearly completed initiatives into the `Completed` section.
- For partially completed initiatives, clarify what remains before they can be considered complete.
- Link unfinished roadmap entries to active tracking issues or KEPs where possible.
- Consider recording the last review date or reviewing the roadmap during each release cycle.

This issue's purpose is to confirm the current status and remaining scope with the maintainers.

title: examples: execution-scoped credentials for a reused Sandbox

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: needs-ok-to-test
labels.description: Indicates a PR that requires an org member to verify it is safe to test.

labels.name: cncf-cla: no
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has not signed the CNCF CLA.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds `examples/containarium-execution-scoped-token`: a runnable reference for
**execution-scoped credentials in a reused Sandbox** — the
authorization–execution lifetime mismatch from #1580 — for one credential
class, model provider API keys.

A credential provisioned into a reusable Sandbox lives as long as the Sandbox,
not as long as the execution that justified it. Two runs in one box end up with
the union of both runs' authority, and a credential from a finished run stays
usable by whatever runs next. This is the second of the two contributions
[@janetkuo invited on #1580](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1580#issuecomment-5593702590)
— "expanding documentation or reference examples demonstrating short-lived token
projection or credential-proxy sidecars".

One long-lived `Sandbox` runs two executions back to back. Each gets its own
short-lived token, and the example holds three properties together, because any
two of them still leave a hole:

1. **The real key is never in the box.** It lives in a credential proxy
   (Containarium's standalone model gateway, published image, pinned tag) that
   verifies the caller's scoped token, injects the real key, and proxies
   upstream. What the box holds is worthless anywhere else.
2. **The token reaches one process, not the pod.** It goes in
   `ProcessConfig.env_vars` on `ProcessService.Start` — not the `Sandbox` spec,
   not the `SandboxClaim`, not a `Secret`, not the workspace volume. It is not
   readable via `get pod`, and the next run does not inherit it.
3. **The token is revoked at `ExitEvent`, not left to expire.** Removing a
   variable from a process's environment does not invalidate a copy that already
   left the process. This is the specific gap #1580 describes, and the check
   below replays a copy that never went back into the sandbox.

The `Sandbox` is never destroyed to end a credential — preserving reuse is the
point of #1580.

**On fresh sandboxes.** The README is explicit that claiming a fresh instance
from a `SandboxWarmPool` is the intended pattern and that reuse leaks more than
credentials. This example is for the cases where reuse is deliberate, and it
addresses only the credential dimension; it says plainly that it does **not**
reset the filesystem, kill leftover processes, reset the environment block, or
restart language kernels — those are `Setup()` / `Clean()` in
[KEP-539.2](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/docs/keps/539.2-runtime-standardization#reusable-sandboxes-setup--cleanup),
not this example's job. It does suggest one addition to `Clean()`'s
implementation considerations, beside "Environment Variables": **revoke** every
credential issued for the run, not only remove it from the environment block.

##### Why the generated `processv1` stubs and not `clients/go/sandbox`

For the run itself, the runner uses
`packages/sandboxd/spec/process/v1` directly. The high-level client's only hook
for environment variables is `Options.Env`, which injects them into the
`SandboxClaim` — putting the token in the pod spec for the life of the sandbox,
which is exactly the anti-pattern the example exists to replace. The README says
so, and suggests a small follow-up: a per-call
`WithEnv(map[string]string)` option on `Commands.Run` landing in
`ProcessConfig.env_vars`, which would let the high-level client express this
pattern and make the drop to the generated stubs unnecessary. Happy to send that
as a separate PR if you want it.

##### Why Cilium

kind's default CNI (kindnet) does not enforce `NetworkPolicy` — it accepts the
object and drops nothing. On a default kind cluster the "direct egress is
blocked" check would pass with the policy having no effect, i.e. a check that
cannot fail. So `kind-config.yaml` sets `disableDefaultCNI: true` and
`run-test-kind.sh` installs Cilium, following
[`examples/demo-cilium-egress`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/examples/demo-cilium-egress).

The egress probe is also hardened against passing for the wrong reason: it dials
the provider **by IP** (resolved on the host, never inside the box) so a DNS
failure cannot look like enforcement, and it runs the *identical* probe against
the allowed gateway immediately before. The runner requires that positive
control to succeed before it calls the check a pass. During development the
probe did pass for the wrong reason once — a malformed `/dev/tcp` path — which is
why the control is there.

##### `sandboxd` image pin

`sandboxd` has no released image: `v1.0.2` ships manifests only, and
`registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox/sandboxd` has no `v1.0.2` tag. The only published
builds are on the k8s staging registry. `sandbox.yaml` pins the **per-commit
staging tag plus its digest**:

```
us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/k8s-staging-images/agent-sandbox/sandboxd:v20260912-v1.0.2-17-g3565f96@sha256:0cf52cfc…
```

so a reader can see which commit built it *and* cannot get different bytes next
month, which `latest-main` alone does not give. Building from
`packages/sandboxd/Dockerfile` at a tagged commit was the alternative; it would
make the happy path depend on a local build plus `kind load`, and the digest pin
keeps `run-test-kind.sh` one command. The README says which and why, and flags
this as the one line expected to change once a release image exists — glad to
switch it to a release tag in this PR if one is imminent.

##### Notes for review

- `runner/` has no `go.mod` and adds **no dependency to the root module**: it
  imports the repo's own generated stubs, so it lives in the root module like
  [`examples/sandboxd-sandbox/client`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/examples/sandboxd-sandbox/client).
  The gateway token is therefore minted with the standard library only
  (`runner/token.go`) rather than pulling a JWT library into the module for one
  example — which also has the side benefit of making the claims, and the fact
  that `run_id` + `jti` are all that bind the credential to a run, legible in
  the diff.
- No provider API key is needed to run the test. Check 1 asserts the **gateway**
  accepted the token, discriminating on the body against the gateway's finite
  list of plain-text refusals, not on the status code — because without a key
  the provider itself answers 401 and a status-only assertion would confuse
  "gateway refused the credential" with "provider refused the key". The runner
  prints the refusal list beside the observed body so a reader can check the
  distinction rather than trust it. `PROVIDER_API_KEY=<real key>` makes it a 200.
- `go vet` and `golangci-lint run --config=dev/tools/.golangci.yaml` are clean on
  the new package; `shellcheck run-test-kind.sh` is clean.

Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1580

title: docs: align KEP-539.2 sandboxd connectivity and security model with the implementation

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What is inconsistent?

The current KEP and implementation describe different sandboxd connectivity and security contracts.

[KEP-539.2 currently says](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/3565f96b5cbe6a426a3cb6a6ab52ba2bc5cc82ce/docs/keps/539.2-runtime-standardization/README.md#L141-L156) that both sandboxd ports bind strictly to localhost and are not exposed without explicit proxying through sandbox-router. It also says the SDK discovers the endpoints through `SANDBOXD_GRPC_ADDR` and `SANDBOXD_REST_ADDR`.

The implemented and documented behavior is different:

- [sandboxd defaults to `0.0.0.0`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/3565f96b5cbe6a426a3cb6a6ab52ba2bc5cc82ce/packages/sandboxd/cmd/sandboxd/main.go#L21-L25), with containment provided by pod isolation and NetworkPolicy.
- [The default is also encoded in `defaultListenHost`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/3565f96b5cbe6a426a3cb6a6ab52ba2bc5cc82ce/packages/sandboxd/cmd/sandboxd/main.go#L64-L69).
- [The sandboxd User Guide](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/3565f96b5cbe6a426a3cb6a6ab52ba2bc5cc82ce/packages/sandboxd/USER_GUIDE.md#L20-L24) documents pod-network reachability via a Service, sandbox-router, or port-forward.
- The Go SDK also supports direct in-cluster Service and Pod IP connectivity after #1576.
- [An E2E test comment](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/3565f96b5cbe6a426a3cb6a6ab52ba2bc5cc82ce/test/e2e/extensions/sandboxd_test.go#L86-L90) still calls the daemon loopback-bound even though the test manifest and daemon default use `0.0.0.0`.

The `0.0.0.0` behavior was introduced deliberately in #1347, so this appears to be documentation drift rather than an unresolved choice of bind address. #1526 identified part of the same mismatch, but it was closed by #1576 after direct in-cluster transport was added; the KEP mismatch remains.

### What would you like to be changed?

- Update KEP-539.2 to reflect the implemented default listener and supported connectivity paths.
- Clearly state that sandboxd does not provide its own authentication and that deployments exposing it on the pod network must enforce the intended trust boundary, for example with NetworkPolicy.
- Correct stale loopback-only comments in tests and related documentation.
- Clarify whether `SANDBOXD_GRPC_ADDR` and `SANDBOXD_REST_ADDR` are intended for workload-local clients/examples or for automatic SDK runtime discovery. The current SDKs select runtime and connectivity explicitly; #1347 also described auto-detection as out of scope.
- Keep the KEP, implementation comments, User Guide, examples, and tests consistent.

This issue does not necessarily require changing the runtime default; its purpose is to make the documented contract accurately describe the behavior that has already been implemented and reviewed.

title: SDKs: support streaming file downloads without buffering the entire response

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add a streaming download API to the supported SDKs so callers can copy a file into a destination without materializing the complete response in memory.

The existing APIs should remain available and backward compatible:

- Python: `Filesystem.read()` and `AsyncFilesystem.read()` should continue to return `bytes`.
- Go: `Files.Read()` should continue to return `[]byte`.

A new API could write incrementally to a caller-provided sink, for example a Python binary file-like object / async sink and a Go `io.Writer`. The exact public API names can be decided during implementation.

### Why is this needed?

The current download implementations buffer the whole response:

- [Python sync `read()`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/3565f96b5cbe6a426a3cb6a6ab52ba2bc5cc82ce/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/files/filesystem.py#L114-L139) accesses `response.content`.
- [Python async `read()`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/3565f96b5cbe6a426a3cb6a6ab52ba2bc5cc82ce/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/files/async_filesystem.py#L63-L85) also accesses `response.content`.
- [Go `Files.Read()`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/3565f96b5cbe6a426a3cb6a6ab52ba2bc5cc82ce/clients/go/sandbox/files.go#L349-L392) uses `io.ReadAll`.

This makes client memory usage proportional to file size even though both HTTP runtimes can deliver response bodies incrementally. It is especially limiting for agent workloads that need to retrieve large artifacts, datasets, archives, or logs.

This is the download-side counterpart to streaming uploads in #1376 and #1634.

### Expected behavior

- Existing byte-returning APIs remain unchanged.
- The new path transfers response chunks incrementally to the destination.
- Download-size limits, when configured, are enforced while streaming rather than after buffering.
- Responses and destination resources have clear ownership and are cleaned up correctly on success, failure, and cancellation.
- Legacy and sandboxd transports behave consistently where supported.
- Sync/async Python behavior remains aligned.
- Unit tests cover large responses, partial writes, limit violations, cancellation/errors, and response cleanup.

title: Fix toc-verify false positives on Windows CRLF checkouts

labels.name: size/XS
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 0-9 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: do-not-merge/invalid-commit-message
labels.description: Indicates that a PR should not merge because it has an invalid commit message.

labels.name: needs-ok-to-test
labels.description: Indicates a PR that requires an org member to verify it is safe to test.

labels.name: cncf-cla: no
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has not signed the CNCF CLA.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`mdtoc`, which `dev/tools/verify-toc` and `dev/tools/update-toc` use to validate KEP tables of contents, does not understand CRLF line endings. It treats the carriage return as part of a code fence, so fenced code blocks are never closed and headings inside them are added to the generated table of contents. On a Windows checkout with the default `core.autocrlf=true`, `make toc-verify` therefore fails on KEP READMEs that are actually correct, and `make toc-update` would rewrite them incorrectly.

This marks KEP markdown as `text eol=lf` in `.gitattributes` so those files are always checked out with LF, regardless of `core.autocrlf`. The TOC tooling then sees the same input on every platform.

Notes:

- I checked `mdtoc` v1.4.0 (the latest release); it has the same CRLF behavior, so bumping `TOOL_VERSION` does not fix this.
- Only `docs/keps/**/*.md` is affected, since that is the only tree the TOC tooling reads.
- Existing CRLF working trees need a re-checkout for the attribute to take effect (e.g. `git rm --cached -r . && git reset --hard` or a fresh clone).

Verification (Windows, Git Bash):

- Without this change, a clone with `core.autocrlf=true` produces 28 CRLF pairs in `docs/keps/119-sandbox-suspended-state/README.md` and `mdtoc --dryrun` exits 1.
- With this change, the same clone checks the file out with 0 CRLF pairs and `mdtoc --dryrun` exits 0.
- `./dev/tools/verify-toc` passes end-to-end.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1613

#### Release Note

```release-note
NONE
```

- **Chores**
  - Standardized line endings for KEP documentation files to ensure table-of-contents verification works consistently across platforms.

body:
### Summary

Incremental documentation clarification on top of #1106, which already covered the Sandbox-level defaults for `shutdownTime`/`shutdownPolicy` and the `status.podIPs` clearing-on-suspend semantics. This PR fills the gaps that remained afterwards (found while re-reading the API docs against the controllers; relates to the themes raised in #1104 but does not claim its checklist — those items were addressed by #1106):

**SandboxClaim lifecycle defaults:**
- `spec.lifecycle.shutdownPolicy` godoc now documents the default (`Retain`) and what each policy does to the claim object at expiry, and that the underlying Sandbox (and its Pod and Service) is released regardless of the policy (mirrors the existing `Sandbox` `Lifecycle` field docs from #1106).
- `spec.lifecycle.shutdownTime` godoc now states precisely what happens when it is unset: the claim never expires at a scheduled time and lives until explicitly deleted, unless `ttlSecondsAfterFinished` expires it after the sandbox has finished. The previous wording ("the SandboxClaim itself won't expire") was inaccurate when a TTL is set.

**podIPs resume semantics (Sandbox and mirrored SandboxClaim status):**
- `status.podIPs` godoc on both `Sandbox` and `SandboxClaim` now also documents that when a suspended Sandbox is resumed, a new pod is created and the field is repopulated from that pod's status (the clearing-on-absence behavior was already documented by #1106).

**Site docs:**
- Added a "Default Behavior" section to the lifecycle page (unset `shutdownTime` = no expiry; `Retain`/`Delete` retention behavior).
- Noted podIPs suspend/resume semantics on the snapshots (suspend/resume) page.

All statements are taken from controller behavior: core expiry handling and status reset on `Retain` (controllers/sandbox_controller.go), claim expiry paths including TTL (extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go + internal/lifecycle/expiry.go), and podIPs clear/repopulate logic.

### Verification
- `make generate-api-docs` (crd-ref-docs v0.3.0, Go 1.26): `docs/api.md` in this PR is the real regenerated output, not a hand edit.
- `go build ./api/... ./extensions/api/...` and `go vet` on the same packages: pass.
- KAL linter (`make lint-api` equivalent) on `./api/... ./extensions/api/...`: 0 issues.
- `toc-verify`: unaffected (no edited file carries a `<!-- toc -->` marker; docs/keps untouched).

  - Documented the effects of `Retain`, `Delete`, and `DeleteForeground` after expiration.
  - Explained default behavior when shutdown settings are omitted.
  - Clarified suspend and resume behavior, including Pod replacement, snapshot restoration, and refreshed Pod IP status.
  - Documented how suspended Sandboxes report readiness and live status fields.

title: feat(python-sdk): support streaming file uploads

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: ok-to-test
labels.description: Indicates a non-member PR verified by an org member that is safe to test.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Python SDK callers currently have to materialize large uploads as `bytes` because `Filesystem.write` and `AsyncFilesystem.write` do not accept file objects. This change lets both methods accept binary file objects and stream them from their current position in bounded chunks.

- streams legacy uploads with a single-file multipart body without buffering the payload
- streams sandboxd raw PUT uploads and disables replay for non-rewindable request bodies
- preserves the existing `bytes` and `str` behavior and omits unknown stream sizes from tracing
- documents stream ownership and current-position semantics, with unit and E2E coverage

Validation: the Python 3.11 unit suite passes with 381 passed, 1 skipped, and 8 subtests passed. A local HTTP smoke test also verified chunked sync and async multipart uploads.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1376

#### Release Note

```release-note
Python SDK file writes now accept binary file objects and stream uploads without buffering the entire payload in client memory.
```

body:
Fixes #1629.

A Sandbox name longer than 63 characters can cause the derived Service creation to fail when `spec.service` is enabled. The resulting `Invalid` error was previously returned from `Reconcile`, causing the controller to repeatedly retry the same permanent error.

### Changes

- Treat permanent `Invalid` errors as terminal.
- Report `Ready=False` with reason `InvalidConfiguration`.
- Avoid requeueing permanent errors.
- Add regression tests for the terminal error path.

### Verification

- Verified permanent `Invalid` errors are not returned from `Reconcile`.
- Verified transient errors continue to be retried.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Bug Fixes**
  - Permanent configuration validation errors now appear as `Ready=False` with a clear `InvalidConfiguration` reason.
  - Prevented repeated retries for unrecoverable resource validation failures, such as names exceeding platform limits.
  - Reduced unnecessary error logging for permanent validation failures.
  - Added coverage to verify invalid configurations are surfaced without requeueing.

title: Sandbox with a name longer than 63 chars and spec.service gets permanently stuck and hot-loops the controller

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What happened?

When `spec.service: true` and the Sandbox name is longer than 63 characters,the corresponding headless Service cannot be created.

The controller derives the Service name directly from the Sandbox name,but Kubernetes Service names are limited to 63 characters.

As a result, a 64+ character Sandbox name causes the Service creation tofail and the Sandbox can never become Ready.
63 characters works, while 64 characters reproduces the issue.

### Expected behavior

The invalid name should either be rejected up front, or the controller should report a clear terminal error instead of continuously retrying the failed Service creation.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?
Apply two Sandboxes that differ only in name length, both with spec.service: true:
```
NAME63="s$(printf 'b%.0s' {1..62})"   # 63 chars -> works
NAME64="s$(printf 'b%.0s' {1..63})"   # 64 chars -> wedges
for N in "$NAME63" "$NAME64"; do
cat <<EOF | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
metadata: {name: ${N}, namespace: default}
spec:
  service: true
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      containers:
      - {name: main, image: nginx:alpine, ports: [{containerPort: 80}]}
EOF
done
kubectl get sandbox "$NAME63" "$NAME64" \
  -o custom-columns='NAME:.metadata.name,READY:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].status,REASON:.status.conditions[?(@.type=="Ready")].reason'
kubectl get pod "$NAME64" -o wide          # Pod is Running
kubectl get svc "$NAME64"                  # NotFound — never created
kubectl logs -n agent-sandbox-system deploy/agent-sandbox-controller --tail=200 \
  | grep -c "must be no more than 63 characters"   # grows over time
```
Observed: the 63-char Sandbox is Ready=True/DependenciesReady; the 64-char one is Ready=False/ReconcilerError with message Service "…" is invalid: metadata.name: … must be no more than 63 characters, its Service is NotFound, and the controller log keeps accumulating Reconciler error stacktraces.

### Version

v1.0.2 (also reproduces on main)

### Anything else we need to know?
#### Possible fix

A candidate fix is available in #1630, which prevents permanent `Invalid`errors from being requeued and reports them as a terminal condition.

body:
Supersedes and closes #1506.

Dependabot's `python:3.14-bookworm` bump has failed `presubmit-agent-sandbox-test-e2e` on five consecutive heads for the same reason: `requirements.txt` pins **pydantic-core 2.33.2**, which ships no cp314 wheels (PyO3 caps at 3.13), so pip falls back to a maturin source build that aborts during the image build. Dependabot only edits the Dockerfile and cannot recompile the lockfile, so a manual PR is needed.

### Changes
- `requirements.in`: `pydantic==2.11.4` → `pydantic==2.12.0` — the first pydantic release supporting Python 3.14, and the exact pin used by [google-gemini/computer-use-preview](https://github.com/google-gemini/computer-use-preview) HEAD, so the two `pip install` steps in the Dockerfile agree.
- `requirements.txt`: recompiled with `pip-compile --generate-hashes` under Python 3.14. Version deltas are limited to pydantic 2.12.0, pydantic-core 2.41.1 (ships cp314 wheels), and typing-inspection 0.4.4; the rest of the diff is refreshed hash lists.
- `Dockerfile`: `python:3.13-bookworm` → `python:3.14-bookworm` (same bump as #1506).

### Verification
- Scripted check against PyPI: all 42 pins have a linux cp314-compatible (or pure-python) wheel, and every `--hash` matches an official PyPI digest.
- `pip install --require-hashes` into a clean Python 3.14 venv succeeds; `pytest test_main.py` passes (4/4).
- Full `docker build` of the example image on `python:3.14-bookworm` succeeds (both requirements installs, `playwright install`, chromium).
- Container runtime check: uvicorn starts, `GET /` returns `{"status":"ok","message":"Sandbox Runtime is active."}`, and `pytest test_main.py` passes inside the container (Python 3.14.7, pydantic-core 2.41.1).

* **Chores**
  * Updated the Gemini CU sandbox to use Python 3.14.
  * Updated Pydantic and related typing packages to newer versions.
  * Regenerated the sandbox’s pinned dependency requirements for Python 3.14.

title: fix(flake-report): stop counting aborted, clone-failed, and pre-test-broken runs as infra

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: size/XL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 500-999 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
## What was wrong

`analyze_tab()` in `dev/tools/flake-report` classified every red Overall column with no failing junit testcase as an infrastructure failure. Three benign run shapes produce that exact TestGrid signature and were all miscounted as infra:

1. **Aborted runs** — the trigger plugin cancels an in-flight job when a newer push to the PR supersedes it (`finished.json` says `"result": "ABORTED"`). Not a failure at all.
2. **Stale-PR clone failures** — the PR no longer merges onto main (`clone-records.json` has `"failed": true`). Author-actionable: rebase needed.
3. **Pre-test PR breakage** — junit exists with zero failing testcases, but a compile/vet/mypy gate broke: the PR's own bug.

## Evidence

Verified against the full Prow GCS history (see the analysis comments on the trackers this heuristic filed):

- #1566 (`presubmit-test-unit`): [analysis](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1566#issuecomment-5640228528) — the reported "49 infra runs" were 35 trigger-plugin ABORTED runs + 7 clonerefs merge conflicts + 7 PR-caused pre-test failures. Zero real infra failures.
- #1565 (kwok scalability lane): [analysis](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1565#issuecomment-5640229437) — mostly stale-PR clone conflicts, plus a perf gate that fails after junit is written (junit emission for that gate is handled in a separate PR).

## Changes

1. **Exclude aborted runs.** For each red Overall column, the run's `finished.json` is fetched from GCS over HTTPS (via the per-build pointer file for `pr-logs/directory` tabs); `"result": "ABORTED"` columns are dropped from infra counts. Their junit "errors" are also excluded from per-test flake tallies and the consistent-failure check, closing the KNOWN LIMITATION noted on 2026-09-04.
2. **Exclude clone failures.** A red run whose `clone-records.json` shows `"failed": true` **with a verified merge conflict in the git output** is counted separately and reported as "N red run(s) were stale-PR clone failures (rebase needed)". Clone failures without a conflict (network, ref-fetch) and junit-less red runs with no `clone-records.json` at all stay in the infra count — the cause cannot be proven benign, so the classifier is deliberately conservative (regression-tested).
3. **Reclassify junit-present/zero-failing/job-red as pre-test PR breakage**, reported under a new report section. Only "pod started, produced no junit, not aborted/clone-failed" remains infra.

Artifacts are fetched only for the red columns under consideration, so a mostly-green window stays cheap. The `--json` payload keeps the existing `flaky`/`consistent`/`infra` keys and adds `aborted_runs`, `clone_failures`, `pretest_failures` per tab for the daily pipeline.

## Testing

- Classification is factored into pure functions (`classify_red_run`, `column_build_id`, `make_artifact_fetcher`) and covered by a new network-free unit suite `dev/tools/flake_report_test.py` (17 tests), wired into the existing `dev/tools` pytest run under `make test-unit`. Full `dev/tools` suite: 105 tests pass.
- Live read-only run on `presubmit-test-unit` (window 100): 52 red runs → 37 aborted + 7 clone failures + 5 pre-test breakage + 1 infra (previously all 52 would have been infra candidates). Kwok lane: 24 red → 14 aborted + 7 clone failures + 1 pre-test + 2 infra.

Fixes #1566
Part of #1565

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Improvements**
  - Flake reports now distinguish aborted runs, test failures, pre-test failures, verified clone merge-conflict failures, and infrastructure failures.
  - Network and ref-fetch clone errors remain classified as infrastructure failures.
  - Missing clone records no longer trigger clone-failure classification.
  - Aborted runs and columns are excluded from flake counts and findings.
  - Build identifiers are resolved from the final segment of column IDs.
  - Flaky-status cells are treated as failing tests when classifying red runs.
<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

Updates `go.opentelemetry.io/otel` from 1.45.0 to 1.46.0
Release notes

Sourced from go.opentelemetry.io/otel's releases.

v1.46.0/v0.68.0/v0.22.0/v0.0.19

This release is the last to support Go 1.25. The next release will require at least Go 1.26.

Added

  • Support testing of Go 1.27. (#8811)
  • Support http/json protocol in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracehttp. (#8273, #8775, #8831)
  • Add Hasher struct and methods in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute to compute authoritative Distinct hashes incrementally for attribute filtering and deduplication. (#8598)

Changed

  • Lazily evaluate filtered and dropped attributes on measurement hot paths in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/metric to avoid unnecessary attribute set allocations. (#8598)
  • Add ErrExporterShutdown to go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log and return it from the go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/stdout/stdoutlog, go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploggrpc, and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploghttp exporters when Export is called after Shutdown. (#8773)
  • Clarify in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/log that calling Logger.Enabled is optional and that cached results can become stale. (#8764)

Fixed

  • Export dropped attribute counts in OTLP log records from go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploggrpc and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploghttp. (#8829)
  • Name span events created from OpenTracing logs after the event log field, falling back to log, instead of always using an empty name in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/bridge/opentracing. (#8648)
  • Count exception attributes omitted due to the attribute count limit as dropped in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log. (#8796)
  • Prevent log record and instrumentation scope attributes with empty keys from reaching processors and exporters in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log. (#8797)
  • Fix a data race when span attributes are read concurrently in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace. (#8706)
  • Prevent a panic in (*Set).Filter when called on a nil receiver in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute. (#8792)
  • The simple span and log processors record otel.sdk.processor.{span,log}.processed when the record is submitted to the exporter instead of after the export completes, and no longer set error.type from the export outcome, in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log. (#8705)
  • Prevent Resource.MarshalLog from panicking on nil resources in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/resource. (#8758)

title: Harden the kwok scalability presubmit against invisible gate failures and transient infra errors

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
## Motivation

RCA of all 25 real FAILURE runs on `presubmit-agent-sandbox-test-e2e-scalability-kwok` since Aug 3 (analysis: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1565#issuecomment-5640229437):

| Category | Count | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clone conflicts (PR not mergeable, not lane's fault) | 13 | No action needed in this repo |
| Perf-gate violations invisible in junit | 8 | ClusterLoader2 succeeds, junit says `failures=0`, then `scrape_controller_metrics.py` fails the job with the violation printed only to stdout (e.g. `P99: ~562.5 ms (Target: <= 500.0 ms) [VIOLATION]`) — Spyglass/TestGrid render these as "failed before tests ran" |
| Real infra flakes | 2 | GitHub 503 downloading etcd inside `kwokctl create cluster` (no retry, cold cache); proxy.golang.org stream error during the CL2 `go build` (no `\|direct` fallback) |
| Caused by the PR under test | 2 | Working as intended |

## What this PR changes

1. **Perf gate emits junit** — `scrape_controller_metrics.py` gains a `--junit-out` flag (wired to `${ARTIFACTS}/junit_controller-metrics.xml` by the presubmit script) and writes one testcase per validated percentile (`claim-adoption-latency-p50/p90/p99`); failures carry the measured value vs target, and the metrics-unavailable path emits a failing testcase too. Job exit behavior is unchanged — this is purely Spyglass/TestGrid visibility, so gate violations stop registering as "failed before tests ran".
2. **Retry `kwokctl create cluster`** — bounded 3-attempt loop, deleting the partial cluster between attempts, mirroring the `curl --retry 5` the script already uses for its own kwokctl binary download. Covers the cold-cache etcd/kubernetes binary downloads GitHub occasionally 503s.
3. **GOPROXY `|direct` fallback** — the Prow job env pins proxy-only; exporting `GOPROXY="https://proxy.golang.org|direct"` lets the CL2 build and `go run` survive proxy incidents.
4. **Real readiness wait** — the `sleep 3` after launching the controller with `go run ... &` is replaced with a bounded poll (up to 120s) of the controller's `:8082/readyz` endpoint, failing loudly (dumping `controller.log`) on timeout or early process death. A cold-pod compile can exceed 3s, and CL2 starting before the controller is ready inflates the adoption-latency samples the gate measures — a plausible contributor to marginal violations like 562ms vs the 500ms target.

## Verification

- `bash -n dev/ci/presubmits/test-e2e-scalability-kwok` passes.
- Exercised `scrape_controller_metrics.py` end-to-end against a synthetic metrics server: violating fixture → exit 1 + junit with `failures="1"` and message `P99: ~666.7 ms exceeded target <= 500.0 ms`; passing fixture → exit 0 + `failures="0"`; unreachable endpoint → exit 1 + failing testcase.
- Added unit tests for the junit writer to the existing `dev/ci/presubmits/shared` suite (already wired into `make test-unit`); all 6 tests in the suite pass.

Fixes #1565

title: presubmit-agent-sandbox-test-e2e is failing on every PR: envd-sandbox image build broken by e2b-dev/infra repo rename

labels.name: priority/critical-urgent
labels.description: Highest priority. Must be actively worked on as someone's top priority right now.

labels.name: kind/failing-test
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a consistently or frequently failing test.

body:
#### What happened

`presubmit-agent-sandbox-test-e2e` (a required presubmit) has been failing on **every PR** since 2026-09-11 06:02 UTC (last green run: 2026-09-10 23:59 UTC). The job dies during setup, before any test runs.

The e2e harness (`deploy-kind` → `push-images`) builds every Dockerfile in the repo, including `examples/envd-sandbox/Dockerfile`, which builds E2B's `envd` daemon from source. Stage 1 of that build fails:

```
> [builder 3/5] RUN git clone https://github.com/e2b-dev/infra.git /src/infra \
      && cd /src/infra && git checkout 411b63edf6dea8edd265d1c5e442f41a80b76b2a
fatal: unable to read tree (411b63edf6dea8edd265d1c5e442f41a80b76b2a)
ERROR: ... exit code: 128
```

Example failing run: https://prow.k8s.io/view/gs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1619/presubmit-agent-sandbox-test-e2e/2098473362517921792

#### Root cause

Upstream renamed `e2b-dev/infra` to `e2b-dev/runtime` and **restructured its history** in the process. The old clone URL still redirects, but the bare commit SHA pinned in `ENVD_VERSION` (`411b63ed…`) is no longer reachable from any branch or tag in the renamed repo, so `git checkout` fails. `push-images` aborts, `deploy-kind` never completes, and the whole e2e suite fails on every PR.

#### Impact

- All open PRs are blocked (e2e is required for merge).
- TestGrid `presubmit-test-e2e` per-test rows have dropped out (no junit produced), and the failed runs emit a `Pod` junit row, so flake-report's infra detector does not flag the lane (see also #1564).

#### Fix

Repin `ENVD_VERSION` to the upstream **release tag** `envd-v0.6.13` (= commit `2acf2d51bd1e`) — tags survive upstream rebases, unlike bare SHAs — and update the clone URL and doc links to the renamed repo. Verified: fresh clone + tag checkout succeeds, and `envd` compiles at that tag with the Dockerfile's exact build flags.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Consolidates the core Go sandbox router deployment manifests into a single multi-document `sandbox-router.yaml` file in `sandbox-router/deploy/`.

This PR:

2. Removes the individual core YAML files and keeps optional components (`rbac-tokenreview.yaml`, `networkpolicy.yaml`, `examples/gateway-gke.yaml`) separate.
3. Updates `sandbox-router/deploy/README.md` to document single-file apply commands (both remote raw GitHub URL and local clone) for core and optional components.
4. Updates `site/content/docs/getting_started/install_prerequisites/_index.md` to use `kubectl apply -f .../sandbox-router.yaml`, replacing the old Python router curl+sed pipeline and updating the rollout target name to `deployment/sandbox-router`.

title: perf(sandbox): requeue without error when namespace is terminating

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
### Motivation
When deleting a Kubernetes namespace containing large volumes of sandboxes (e.g. tens of thousands of sandboxes in stress or fleet scale runs), the namespace controller deletes Sandboxes and child Pods asynchronously.

When a child Pod is deleted first while the Sandbox still exists, the Sandbox reconciler attempts to re-create the child Pod. Because the namespace is terminating, `kube-apiserver` rejects the create request with `403 Forbidden` (`corev1.NamespaceTerminatingCause`). Returning this error directly pushes the Sandbox onto the exponential-backoff retry queue.

In fleet testing with 72,000 sandboxes per cluster, this produced **~670,000 errored reconciles** and an avalanche of `403 Forbidden` POST calls to the API server during namespace teardown, directly contending with the namespace controller's deletion pipeline.

### Changes
- Check `k8serrors.HasStatusCause(podErr, corev1.NamespaceTerminatingCause)` in `reconcileChildResources`.
- Return `ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: 30 * time.Second}, nil` when the namespace is terminating instead of returning an error.
- Re-checks after 30 seconds if the sandbox outlives the namespace, without polluting retry queues or spamming API servers.

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

## Bug Fixes

* Improved Sandbox reconciliation while its namespace is being deleted or terminated.
* Namespace-termination conditions encountered during status updates or child-resource creation now trigger an automatic retry after 30 seconds without surfacing an error.
* Prevented expected namespace-termination conditions from triggering standard error backoff, while continuing to surface unrelated errors normally.
* Improved handling of namespace-termination errors when they are wrapped or combined with other errors.

labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

A way to distribute requests across a group of already claimed Sandboxes running the same workload, through one application endpoint without the caller having to provide a Sandbox ID.

The consumer would prefer to use the native sandbox-router for this. Before proposing an implementation, I'd like to clarify whether this selection belongs in Agent Sandbox or whether the intended approach is to use Kubernetes networking or a higher level orchestrator.

### Why is this needed?

A user claims additional prewarmed Sandboxes as demand grows. They run the same workload from the same SandboxTemplate, and each can handle multiple requests and conversations concurrently.

Claiming is already handled. They need to distribute application traffic across those instances, not claim a new Sandbox for every request.

The current router expects the caller to identify a specific Sandbox. The consumer would therefore need to add selection logic on their side or use another routing path. They would prefer the platform to handle this without having to bypass the native router.

title: build: normalize line endings via .gitattributes to fix Windows TOC false positives

labels.name: lgtm

labels.name: size/S

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

On a clean Windows checkout with the default `core.autocrlf=true`, git converts the repository's LF line endings to CRLF on checkout. The `mdtoc` tool used by `make toc-verify` (`dev/tools/verify-toc`) is CRLF-sensitive: it misparses markdown headings and reports spurious table-of-contents diffs in the KEP README files, even though the content did not change. The same commit passes cleanly on a clean LF checkout.

This adds a `.gitattributes` file that normalizes text files to LF line endings on checkout (`* text=auto eol=lf`), regardless of the platform or the checkout's `core.autocrlf` setting, and explicitly marks the repo's `.png`/`.webp` binary assets so they are never subject to line-ending normalization. ### What happened?

On a clean Windows checkout with the default `core.autocrlf=true` setting, the repository's documented `make toc-verify` check (implemented by `./dev/tools/verify-toc`) reports table-of-contents changes in seven tracked KEP README files. The same frozen commit passes on a clean LF checkout, so this is a line-ending/tooling portability false positive rather than stale repository content.

Affected files:

- `docs/keps/119-sandbox-suspended-state/README.md`
- `docs/keps/174-metadata-propagation/README.md`
- `docs/keps/208-mutually-exclusive-field-in-sandboxclaim/README.md`
- `docs/keps/359-refactor-python-sdk/README.md`
- `docs/keps/539.2-runtime-standardization/README.md`
- `docs/keps/694-kep-for-suspend-and-resume-for-beta/README.md`
- `docs/keps/NNNN-template/README.md`

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. On Windows, clone `kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox` at the commit below with the default `core.autocrlf=true` checkout behavior.
2. From the clean checkout, run `make toc-verify` (or `./dev/tools/verify-toc`) using Git Bash.
3. Observe that `mdtoc` exits non-zero and reports changes in the seven files listed above.
4. Repeat from a clean checkout with `core.autocrlf=false`; the verifier reports no changes and exits zero.

The false-positive list includes headings that occur inside fenced shell/comment examples. Running `make toc-update` would rewrite tracked README files, including adding those parsed headings, even though the source content has not changed. Please confirm the intended CRLF/tooling behavior before accepting any generated documentation update.

### Version

`main` at `020634dfe575374d480e0f075e0d620744034f78` (2026-09-11).

### Anything else we need to know?

The failure is documentation/tooling portability only; no runtime or API behavior is involved. A clean LF checkout passes the same verifier at the same SHA. No existing open issue or PR covering this Windows false positive was found.

title: perf(sandbox): one status write per launch behind --sandbox-transitional-status-window

labels.name: needs-rebase
labels.description: Indicates a PR cannot be merged because it has merge conflicts with HEAD.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: size/XL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 500-999 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
## What

Adds `--sandbox-transitional-status-window=T` (default `0`, which keeps today's behavior). While a Sandbox is younger than `T`, the controller skips *transitional* status writes (reason/message churn, nodeName/podIPs fills, PodScheduled Unknown/True) and writes only *material* changes (condition value flips, terminal Ready reasons, PodScheduled=False). A launch that reaches Ready inside the window writes status exactly once, at the Ready flip. A stuck sandbox still flushes an explanatory status at age `T` via `RequeueAfter`. With the window enabled, a small `staleCacheGuard` also skips reconcile passes whose cached Sandbox predates the controller's own outstanding writes, which were only producing no-op PATCHes. With the window at its default of `0` the guard is inactive and the reconcile path is main's, unchanged.

Deferred writes are recomputed from informer state by whichever pass flushes them, so nothing is lost on crash or failover.

## Why

The controller writes Sandbox status two to four times per sandbox plus no-op re-PATCHes from reconciles racing its own informer. Nothing reads the pre-Ready writes; consumers wait on Ready. Under load those writes queue in the apiserver ahead of the Ready flips and pod status updates that readiness depends on.

## Evidence

20-cluster fleet benchmark (200 n2-standard-4 workers per cluster, 72k sandboxes per cluster created at 1,000/s, readiness taken from server-side `lastTransitionTime`). All comparisons are paired: same clusters, same day, controller swapped in place.

| clusters | controller | time to 72k Ready (s) | own fixed-60s Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| us-east1-b, europe-west4-c, asia-southeast1-b | main | 112 / 132 / 114 | 39k / 33k / 37k |
| same | this PR without the PodScheduled rule (2.0 PATCH/launch) | 91 / 96 / 93 | 44k / 41k / 43k |
| same | **this PR**, window=180s | **75 / 76 / 75** | **59k / 58k / 59k** |
| asia-south1-b, northamerica-northeast1-a, australia-southeast1-a | main | 189 / 134 / 132 | 22k / 34k / 34k |
| same | **this PR**, window=180s | **93 / 75 / 76** | **47k / 59k / 59k** |
| us-east1-c, asia-northeast1-b, southamerica-east1-a | **this PR**, window=180s | **74 / 77 / 81** | **59k / 57k / 54k** |

With the window the clusters ready sandboxes at the create rate (the create span is 72s). main issued 3.7 status PATCHes per launch on its fastest cluster and 7.8 on its slowest, where the stale-cache feedback loop was worst.

The PodScheduled rule mattered: main's PodScheduled condition mirroring made the Unknown→True flip a second material write per launch, which cost about half the gain.

## Notes

- The default stays off. The fleet and scaleup benchmark scenarios pass `--sandbox-transitional-status-window=180s`.

body:
One Go driver drives Sandbox creation across N pre-provisioned clusters at a
paced aggregate rate and measures how fast the fleet drives them to Ready,
over a fixed 60-second server-clock window.

Result: 1,037,564 Sandboxes Ready in the fixed window across 20 clusters on
pure upstream Kubernetes (one default kube-scheduler per cluster), 0 create
errors.

Driver (test/fleet):
- Per-cluster rate limiters and worker pools. A single shared limiter is
  unfair under wide-area latency - near clusters' workers win a
  disproportionate token share and starve far clusters, staggering the
  per-cluster readiness peaks so the fleet's single verdict window cannot
  capture them together.
- Sandbox-only watch (a pod firehose from N clusters would make the driver
  the bottleneck) with a reflector-style LIST resync on 410 Gone, so
  readiness transitions are never silently dropped.
- Verdict from server-side Ready timestamps over a FIXED [firstReady+10s,
  +70s) window, not a sliding max; raw per-cluster JSONL is the source of
  truth and a self-contained HTML report is recomputed from it.

kOps-on-GCE scenario (test/benchmarks/scenarios/fleet-kops-gcp):
- Idempotent up/run/down scripts. 100GB pd-ssd worker disks to fit the
  per-region SSD quota, maxPods=500 under the /23 pod CIDR, a tuned sandbox
  controller on a dedicated tainted node, image prepull, clusters named by
  zone.
- run pre-flights (stale-namespace drain, prepull verify, capacity check)
  and auto-generates the report.
- README covers prerequisites, the up/run/down flow, reading the report, and
  what actually moves the number (readiness-bound; ~54k/min per-cluster
  apiserver ceiling; linear scaling; feed ~1000/s per cluster).

Promotes golang.org/x/time to a direct dependency (the driver's rate
limiters).

## Summary

A handful of examples under `examples/` have real logic sitting behind an HTTP endpoint with zero test coverage — allowlists and path-traversal guards standing between untrusted input and a shell or the filesystem, a mutating webhook's patch generation, small state machines that are easy to get subtly wrong. This PR adds unit tests for eight of them, following the "test what's load-bearing" guidance in `AGENTS.md` rather than chasing coverage for its own sake.

- **`n8n-mcp/source/server.py`** — the `/execute` command allowlist + `shlex` parsing that's the only thing standing between an n8n-triggered request and shell injection.
- **`webhook-inject-timestamp/main.go`** — the mutating webhook's JSON-Patch generation and JSON-Pointer escaping (easy to get subtly wrong, previously untested).
- **`hermes-agents-as-a-service/gateway/gateway.py`** — bearer-token auth, the mode × conditions state machine, DNS-1123 user validation, and the idle-sweeper's suspend decision.
- **`firecracker-sandbox/main.py`** — the workspace-escape guard (`_safe_path`) and the exec timeout / process-group-kill path.
- **`gke-swap/python-density/parse_telemetry.py`** — the CSV → JSON telemetry aggregation math.
- **`kata-aks`** — the Go client's router HTTP handling and local claim-cache I/O, plus the Python agent's required-settings validation and bounded per-owner chat history.
- **`n8n-sandbox/bridge/main.py`** — request validation and the claim-sandbox-then-always-release guarantee (verified the sandbox is released even when the command or script write fails).
- **`sandboxed-tools/pkg/agent`** — `FindLatestBackup`/`PruneBackups`, the local backup retention logic (keeps the wrong files if the sort/prune logic is ever wrong).

Each new `dev/ci/presubmits/<name>` script for the Python examples follows the same install-then-pytest shape already used by `test-analytics-tool` and `test-langchain`. The two Go suites (`webhook-inject-timestamp`, `kata-aks/client`, `sandboxed-tools/pkg/agent`) don't need a presubmit script — they're picked up automatically by the existing `go.mod`/`test-unit` discovery.

I have a companion PR against `kubernetes/test-infra` adding the Prow job entries for the six new presubmit scripts.
