title: `latebind-storage-gke-sandbox` example doesn't work outside GKE

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/awaiting-more-evidence
labels.description: Lowest priority. Possibly useful, but not yet enough support to actually get it done.

body:
## Background

We're evaluating `SandboxWarmPool` for per-user persistent storage on warm-pool pods (which are pre-created before the user is known, so can't have a PVC attached up front). We followed [`examples/latebind-storage-gke-sandbox`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/examples/latebind-storage-gke-sandbox) as a template on our own (non-GKE) cluster, and could not get the core mechanic to work at all: a host-side `mount --bind` performed on a pod's `emptyDir` after the pod is already `Running` never becomes visible inside the sandbox.

## Environment

- Not GKE — plain k3s (v1.36.2+k3s1), reproduced on two separate clusters.
- `agent-sandbox` v0.4.3 and current `main`/v0.5.x — same result either way.
- `runsc release-20260721.0` and `release-20260608.0`.
- Non-GKE containerd setup applied per [gVisor's containerd doc](https://gvisor.dev/docs/user_guide/containerd/configuration/) (`pod_annotations = ["dev.gvisor.*"]`), since the guide's annotations require it outside GKE.

## What we found

1. Basic repro following the guide closely: bind mount genuinely takes effect on the host (`findmnt`/`ls` confirm it), but the sandbox still shows an empty directory and `cat` fails with "No such file or directory".
2. The lower-level annotations `force-shared` is supposed to set (`dev.gvisor.spec.mount.<vol>.{type,share,source}`) never apply consistently to the workload container itself — only to a separate "sandbox" container spec (two independent CRI `Create` calls). GKE apparently has an admission controller that pre-populates these on the Pod before either container is created; nothing does this outside GKE. We worked around it by manually patching in the correct values ourselves (using the pod's real UID). **Even with that fixed, late-bind still didn't work.**
3. `strace` on the workload's `runsc-gofer` process showed the root cause: the gofer opens a directory FD for the mount once, at container-creation time, and every later lookup (`Walk`/`Open` in `runsc/fsgofer/lisafs.go`) reuses that same cached FD — it never re-resolves the path, so a later `mount --bind` on that path stays invisible. (Standard Linux "an already-open FD doesn't follow a later bind mount" behavior.) Reproduced with `--directfs` both on and off.
4. To confirm, we patched `lisafs.go` to force a fresh re-open of the mount point's FD before each `Walk`/`Open`, rebuilt `runsc` + `containerd-shim-runsc-v1`. With that patch, late-bind works exactly as the guide describes. So the mechanism is sound in principle — open-source gVisor's gofer just doesn't do this re-resolution.

We found nothing in gVisor's docs connecting GKE's ["optimized, custom platform"](https://github.com/google/gvisor/blob/master/g3doc/user_guide/production.md) (which appears to be about syscall interception, not the gofer/filesystem layer) to this behavior, so we don't know whether GKE Sandbox genuinely differs here or this example was simply never validated outside GKE.

## Questions

1. Has anyone validated this example on non-GKE gVisor?
2. If this is a known GKE-only gap, could the guide say so explicitly? (It currently only gates on a minimum *GKE* version, which reads as a gVisor version requirement rather than "GKE-exclusive".)

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

TypeScript callers cannot currently set a controller-enforced lifetime for a sandbox. If the client exits before cleanup, its claim can remain indefinitely.

Add optional `shutdownAfterSeconds` to `CreateSandboxOptions`. It sets the claim's absolute `spec.lifecycle.shutdownTime` and `shutdownPolicy: "Delete"`, matching the Python SDK. The lifetime starts at the creation call, including provisioning time. Omitting the option preserves existing behavior.

Invalid durations, including timestamps outside RFC3339's year range, fail before Kubernetes requests. Tests cover the emitted claim, unchanged behavior without the option, and invalid inputs.

Validation:
- All 137 TypeScript unit tests pass; the 11 new tests failed before implementation.
- Type checking, Biome, and the TypeScript build pass.
- Repository builds, Go/API lint, Go/Python unit suites, TOC verification, and OLM verification pass. `make all` hit a local Go compiler/GOROOT mismatch in the nested OLM unit module; that module passed when rerun with `GOROOT` unset and `GOTOOLCHAIN=go1.26.4`, followed by the remaining verification targets.

title: Python SDK: wrap ProcessService.Start + SendSignal (streaming exec with cancellation)

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add Python SDK wrappers for two sandboxd ProcessService gRPC RPCs that aren't yet exposed:

- `Start`: server-streaming exec that yields stdout/stderr events in real time
- `SendSignal`: POSIX signal delivery for cancellation

Both methods should be available on the sync Sandbox and async AsyncSandbox handles.

Proposed public API - the `Start` wrapper returns a session handle that owns the `process_id`, and `SendSignal` is a method on that handle rather than a free-standing function.

### Why is this needed?

Today, `commands.run()` (wrapping Execute) is the only way to run a command from Python.
The sandboxd runtime already implements `Start` and `SendSignal`, and the generated Python stubs are vendored at `k8s_agent_sandbox/_proto/process/v1/`. This is purely a client-side wrapping gap.

Related: #1438  (async sandboxd support) — async wrapper depends on the grpc.aio channel plumbing landing there

title: feat(clients/ts,sandboxd): wire sandboxd proto codegen and verify gRPC-over-port-forward interop

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
<!-- Provide a clear and concise description of the changes in this PR. -->

#977 tracks the **sandboxd protocol layer** for the TypeScript SDK — the runtime connectivity (`Execute`, filesystem) that #976 deliberately left out so the resource layer could land on its own. 
The connect layer itself (pod port-forward tunnel, REST client, gRPC client, `Sandbox` integration, lifecycle state machine) is a sizeable change and will come as its own PR.

This PR is the groundwork for it: wire up TypeScript proto codegen, commit the generated stub, add the (optional) gRPC dependencies, and — before committing to the connect-layer implementation — prove one load-bearing assumption end to end.
That assumption: a Connect-ES client generated by `protoc-gen-es` can complete a real gRPC `Execute` call over **h2c** through a **WebSocket pod port-forward** from `@kubernetes/client-node`. 
sandboxd's gRPC port is a plain grpc-go server (not the Connect protocol), and `@connectrpc/connect-node`'s gRPC transport always dials HTTP/2 — so this path had to be exercised, not assumed. 
Keeping it separate means the follow-up PR can focus on the tunnel and client design without also re-litigating the gRPC stack choice.

No public SDK API changes here; the generated stub is not referenced by any exported type yet.

Changes:

- **`packages/sandboxd/spec/buf.gen.typescript.yaml`**
  new `buf` template that emits the `ProcessService` stub with `protoc-gen-es` v2 (`target=ts`), using the same `buf.build/bufbuild/es` remote-plugin + pinned-version pattern as `buf.gen.python.yaml`. 
  Wired into `spec/generate.go`'s `go:generate` chain alongside the existing Go/Python steps. 
  `protoc-gen-es` copies `process.proto`'s leading license header into its output, so `buf generate --template buf.gen.typescript.yaml` reproduces the committed stub byte-for-byte with no post-processing (verified by deleting the file and regenerating).
- **`clients/typescript/agentic-sandbox-client/src/_proto/process/v1/process_pb.ts`**
  the generated stub, committed (same convention as the Python SDK's `_proto/`). Regeneration instructions live in `src/_proto/README.md`.
- **Optional gRPC dependencies**
  `@bufbuild/protobuf`, `@connectrpc/connect`, `@connectrpc/connect-node` added as **optional `peerDependencies`** (`peerDependenciesMeta`), mirroring the existing OpenTelemetry pattern.
  #977's acceptance criteria call for optional gating so that files-only consumers do not pull in the gRPC runtime. The follow-up PR wires the `run()` path to `dynamic import` these.
- **Build/lint exclusions**
  `src/_proto` is excluded from the SDK's `tsc` build (`tsconfig.json`) and from Biome (`biome.json`). 
  Nothing in the public API references the stub yet; without the `tsc` exclusion it is compiled into `dist/`, leaking the `@bufbuild/protobuf` import into the published package for consumers who never touch the sandboxd layer.
- **Interop smoke test**
  `test/e2e/clients/typescript/test-e2e-sandboxd-interop.test.ts` deploys a sandboxd-backed `Sandbox` in kind, port-forwards to both `:8080` and `:9090`, and performs a real `Execute(["/bin/sh", "-c", "echo hello world"])`, asserting exit code `0` / stdout `"hello world\n"` / empty stderr. 
  It runs in the existing TS e2e job (`vitest run` picks up `*.test.ts`; `dev/tools/push-images` builds the `packages/sandboxd` image for that job, which the Go e2e suite's `test/e2e/extensions/sandboxd_test.go` already depends on). 
  `test/e2e/clients/typescript/framework/predicates.ts` gains one shared helper, `readyConditionIsTrue()`, matching the Go framework's `predicates.ReadyConditionIsTrue`; the port-forward plumbing stays in the test file only.

##### Result of the interop check

The full path works:

```
grpc-go sandboxd
  ↕ h2c  
client-node WebSocket port-forward
  ↕ local TCP  
createGrpcTransport
```

- `protoc-gen-es` v2 output + Connect-ES `createGrpcTransport()` + h2c + a local TCP listener + the Kubernetes WebSocket port-forward + real sandboxd completes `Execute` successfully. 
  No switch to `@grpc/grpc-js` + ts-proto is needed.
- `GrpcTransportOptions` has no `httpVersion` field — `createGrpcTransport` always uses `http2.connect()`, so there is nothing to configure there (unlike `createConnectTransport`, which can negotiate HTTP/1.1).
- `readMaxBytes` is set explicitly to 4 MiB (parity with grpc-go / grpc-python receive defaults); Connect-ES's own default is ~4 GiB and sandboxd buffers `Execute` output unboundedly server-side.

##### Notes for the reviewer

- **Scope.** No public SDK API changes. The generated stub is not referenced by any exported type or by `dist/`; it exists for the follow-up connect-layer PR to build on.
- **The interop test's port-forward plumbing is throwaway.** It uses `@kubernetes/client-node`'s `PortForward.portForward()` for the small call only. 
  The production tunnel in the follow-up PR does **not** reuse it (that helper does not propagate receive backpressure, ignores `output.write()`'s return value, and gives no pre-open WebSocket handle). 
  Only the single real-`Execute` smoke test is kept here, so CI carries one throwaway implementation rather than several.
- **Dependencies are `devDependencies` + optional `peerDependencies` only.** The package is still `private: true`; nothing is published from this PR.
  `test/e2e/clients/typescript/package-lock.json` also picked up transitive `postcss` / `nanoid` bumps from `npm install` — happy to drop those if you'd rather keep the lockfile change to the new deps.
- **Independent of #1535.** This branch is cut from `main` directly; it does not depend on the review-follow-ups PR.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Under high sustained claim rates (e.g. 10–20+ claims/sec) or large warm pools (>1,000 replicas), default controller deployments can encounter API server write spikes and warm-pool replenishment stalls due to HTTP/2 stream saturation and watch frame queueing behind write bursts (expectations gate timeout).

This PR updates `docs/configuration.md` and `site/content/docs/performance-assessment/_index.md` to document several flags and features added for high scale:
- **API transport & connection settings**: `--separate-watch-connection` (dedicates an isolated HTTP/2 connection for list/watch informer streams) and `--api-connections` (shards non-watch traffic across N connections to bypass `SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS`).
- **Warm pool replenishment shaping**: `--sandbox-warm-pool-max-refill-rate` (paces pool creates via token bucket) and `--sandbox-warm-pool-replenish-delay` (defers refill during claim bursts).
- **API write & cache optimizations**: `--disable-claim-events`, `--disable-claim-observability-annotations`, `--cache-label-selectors`, and `--sandbox-write-behind-window`.
- **High-throughput tuning guide & sample Deployment**: provides architecture rationale for the expectations gate fallback and a recommended Deployment configuration.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Ref #1240
Ref #1251

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Fixes two failures breaking presubmits on `main` after recent CI environment / Go toolchain updates:

1. **`presubmit-agent-sandbox-lint-olm`**: `olm/Makefile` pinned an older `golangci-lint` version (`v2.1.0`) and used a local download target. This failed under the updated Go toolchain in CI. We update `olm/Makefile` to use `go tool -modfile=$(REPO_ROOT)/dev/tools/go.mod golangci-lint`, aligning it with the rest of the repository and making `dev/tools/go.mod` the single source of truth.
2. **`presubmit-test-autogen-up-to-date`**: Regenerates `packages/sandboxd/spec/process/v1/process.pb.go` to remove redundant blank comment lines formatted away by newer `go/format`.

Release notes

Sourced from go.opentelemetry.io/otel's releases.

v1.46.0/v0.68.0/v0.22.0/v0.0.19

This release is the last to support Go 1.25. The next release will require at least Go 1.26.

Added

  • Support testing of Go 1.27. (#8811)
  • Support http/json protocol in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracehttp. (#8273, #8775, #8831)
  • Add Hasher struct and methods in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute to compute authoritative Distinct hashes incrementally for attribute filtering and deduplication. (#8598)

Changed

  • Lazily evaluate filtered and dropped attributes on measurement hot paths in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/metric to avoid unnecessary attribute set allocations. (#8598)
  • Add ErrExporterShutdown to go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log and return it from the go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/stdout/stdoutlog, go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploggrpc, and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploghttp exporters when Export is called after Shutdown. (#8773)
  • Clarify in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/log that calling Logger.Enabled is optional and that cached results can become stale. (#8764)

Fixed

  • Export dropped attribute counts in OTLP log records from go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploggrpc and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploghttp. (#8829)
  • Name span events created from OpenTracing logs after the event log field, falling back to log, instead of always using an empty name in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/bridge/opentracing. (#8648)
  • Count exception attributes omitted due to the attribute count limit as dropped in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log. (#8796)
  • Prevent log record and instrumentation scope attributes with empty keys from reaching processors and exporters in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log. (#8797)
  • Fix a data race when span attributes are read concurrently in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace. (#8706)
  • Prevent a panic in (*Set).Filter when called on a nil receiver in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute. (#8792)
  • The simple span and log processors record otel.sdk.processor.{span,log}.processed when the record is submitted to the exporter instead of after the export completes, and no longer set error.type from the export outcome, in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log. (#8705)
  • Prevent Resource.MarshalLog from panicking on nil resources in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/resource. (#8758)

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
## Motivation

The sandboxed-tools example demonstrates running the agent loop outside the sandbox while executing tools inside it — but the tools and system prompt were hardcoded, so trying a different agent profile meant editing the agent loop. This PR makes the tools + prompts pluggable, and adds a plug-in that reproduces the [gemini-cli](https://github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli) (Apache-2.0) tool surface so gemini-cli-style agents can run on the sandboxed-tools architecture.

## What's in the PR

**Pluggable toolsets** (`pkg/toolsets`): a `Toolset` bundles the system prompt, the LLM-callable tools, and the sandbox image they expect, selected with the new `-toolset` flag (or `TOOLSET` env var). The existing tools became the `basic` toolset and remain the default; behavior of the example is unchanged unless you opt in.

**`geminicli` toolset** (`pkg/toolsets/geminicli`): the gemini-cli tool names, parameter schemas, descriptions, result formats, and (non-interactive) system prompt, extracted from gemini-cli's tool manifest and prompt snippets with attribution, so model behavior tuned for gemini-cli transfers directly:

- `list_directory`, `read_file` (line ranges + truncation hints), `write_file`, `replace` (exact-literal edits that fail loudly on ambiguity), `glob` (`**`/`{a,b}`, newest first), `grep_search` (context lines, include globs, match caps), `read_many_files`, `run_shell_command` (background support via `is_background`).

**Tools implemented in Go, not Node**: the filesystem tools compile into a single static `geminicli-toolbox` binary that runs *inside* the sandbox (`geminicli-toolbox <tool>` with JSON args on stdin, result on stdout). `images/gemini-toolbox/Dockerfile` builds the image (debian-slim + bash/git + the binary)

**Known gaps are inventoried**: TODOs in `pkg/toolsets/geminicli` document every gemini-cli tool we don't implement (web_fetch, google_web_search, write_todos, ask_user, plan mode, skills, memory/GEMINI.md, MCP) and per-tool parity gaps (multimodal read_file, gitignore respect, background PID/PGID reporting), with notes on what implementing each would need.


<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Added configurable `basic` and `geminicli` toolsets for the sandboxed-tools example.
  * Added CLI selection through the `-toolset` option or `TOOLSET` environment variable.
  * Added Gemini CLI-style file, search, editing, directory, and shell tools.
  * Added automatic sandbox image selection, including a dedicated Gemini CLI toolset image.
  * Limited captured command output and indicate when it is truncated.

* **Documentation**
  * Updated setup instructions, tool descriptions, image configuration, and usage examples.

* **Tests**
  * Added coverage for toolset selection and sandbox tool behavior.

title: Fix stale olm lint pin and regenerate drifted protobuf file

labels.name: size/XS

labels.name: kind/failing-test
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a consistently or frequently failing test.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Two presubmit checks (`presubmit-agent-sandbox-lint-olm`, `presubmit-test-autogen-up-to-date`) are currently failing on `main` and on every PR rebased against it, unrelated to whatever those PRs actually change.

**`lint-olm`:** `olm/Makefile` pins `GOLANGCI_LINT_VERSION ?= v2.1.0`, which predates the repo's `go 1.26.0` requirement (toolchain `go1.26.4`). Elsewhere in the repo, golangci-lint is already managed via `dev/tools/go.mod`'s `tool` block and is on `v2.12.2`. The stale `olm`-local pin can't type-check code under Go 1.26, so every symbol pulled in through the ginkgo/gomega dot-imports in `olm/test/e2e/*.go` and `olm/test/utils/utils.go` shows up as `undefined: X (typecheck)` -- not a real code defect, just a version pin that never got bumped alongside the rest of the repo. Bumping it to `v2.12.2` for consistency fixes it.

**`test-autogen-up-to-date`:** `packages/sandboxd/spec/process/v1/process.pb.go` had drifted from what `dev/tools/fix-go-generate` produces under the current Go toolchain -- `gofmt` now drops a redundant blank `//` line immediately before two `oneof` type lists (`Types that are assignable to Event:` / `...to Payload:`). Regenerated and committed the up-to-date file.

Verified both failures reproduce identically on other open, unrelated PRs (#1579, #1572), confirming this is pre-existing drift on `main` and not specific to any one PR's changes.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
None

#### Release Note
```release-note
NONE
```

title: Feature Request: Execution-Scoped Authorization for Persistent and Reusable Sandboxes

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/awaiting-more-evidence
labels.description: Lowest priority. Possibly useful, but not yet enough support to actually get it done.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Agent Sandbox workloads often need credentials for external services, such as Git access tokens, cloud storage credentials (e.g., Amazon S3), API keys, or other service-specific tokens, in order to execute agent-generated code. In a persistent or reusable sandbox, these credentials are typically provisioned to the sandbox environment and therefore remain available for the lifetime of the sandbox rather than the lifetime of the individual execution that requires them. As the same sandbox is reused for multiple executions with different external-service requirements, credentials needed by an earlier execution may remain accessible to later executions that no longer require them. 

This creates an authorization–execution lifetime mismatch: the lifetime of external-service authorization exceeds the lifetime of the execution that justified it, leading to systematic excessive permission. We propose support for execution-scoped external-service authorization, so that credentials can be dynamically provisioned and revoked with each execution while preserving sandbox reuse.

### Why is this needed?

## Motivation

Agent Sandbox intentionally supports stateful and reusable sandbox environments. Features such as SandboxWarmPool, persistent Sandboxes, and suspend/resume can significantly reduce initialization and execution overhead for agent workloads.

However, the lifetime of a sandbox is not necessarily the same as the lifetime of an execution running inside it. A long-lived sandbox may sequentially execute multiple tasks, and different tasks may require different authorities,  such as access to external services, repositories, cloud storage, or other resources through credentials such as access tokens and API keys.

This creates a potential mismatch between execution lifetime and authorization lifetime.

For example, consider two executions in the same reusable sandbox:

Execution E1 requires authority A1
Execution E2 requires authority A2

Ideally:

```E1 -> A1```
```E2 -> A2```

However, if authorization is provisioned at sandbox creation time or otherwise tied to the lifetime of the reusable sandbox, the effective authorization may become:

```Sandbox -> A1 ∪ A2```

As a result, while executing E1, authority A2 may also be available even though it is not required, and vice versa. Authorities from completed executions may also remain accessible to later executions.

This is an authorization–execution lifetime mismatch: the authorization can outlive the execution for which it was required. From a least-privilege perspective, this may systematically introduce excessive permissions as sandboxes are reused across heterogeneous workloads.

For example, suppose E1 runs code that only needs access to an Amazon S3 bucket, while E2 needs a GitHub access token to access a private repository. If both credentials are retained in the same reusable Sandbox, then during E2 the S3 token may also be present even though E2 has no legitimate need for S3 access. Code running in E2 could therefore misuse the stale or over-provisioned S3 credential. The same problem applies in the opposite direction for credentials retained from later executions.

### Relationship to Workload Identity

Issue https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/78 discusses managing different workload identities across Sandboxes. This proposal considers a complementary problem: authorization requirements may also change between executions within the same persistent or reusable Sandbox.

Therefore, binding identity/authorization only to the Sandbox lifecycle may not always provide sufficiently fine-grained least privilege.

### Proposed Direction

It may be useful for Agent Sandbox to provide an abstraction for execution-scoped authorization, where authorization can be dynamically bound to the execution or task using a Sandbox and revoked when that execution completes, without requiring the underlying Sandbox itself to be destroyed.

Conceptually:

```Sandbox lifetime:```
```|----------------------------------------------------|```

```Execution E1:```
```|----------|```
```Granted Authorization A1:```
```|----------|```
```                 Execution E2:```
```                 |-------------|```
```                 Granted Authorization A2:```
```                 |-------------|```

The goal would be to preserve the performance benefits of persistent/reusable Sandboxes while allowing authorization lifetime to follow execution lifetime.

Possible mechanisms could include, but not limited to:
1. short-lived or dynamically projected workload credentials;
2. per-execution authorization token issuance and revocation;
3. lifecycle hooks for external credential managers to provision and revoke authorization at execution boundaries.

Ideally, Agent Sandbox could provide a unified mechanism for execution-scoped external-service authorization, including the provisioning, rotation, and revocation of credentials as executions begin and end. Alternatively, Agent Sandbox could expose a well-defined authorization lifecycle interface that allows external credential or identity-management systems to bind credential lifetime to individual executions.

In either case, the key requirement is that external-service authorization should follow the execution lifecycle rather than the lifetime of the reusable sandbox.

### Security Benefits

This would decouple authorization lifetime from sandbox lifetime and align it with execution lifetime:

Authorization lifetime != Sandbox lifetime
Authorization lifetime ~= Execution lifetime

Such a model could preserve sandbox reuse for efficiency while reducing excessive permissions caused by stale or over-provisioned authority.

### Questions for the Community
1. Is it a real issue/feature needed by Agent-sandbox?
2. If it is real, does the community consider execution-scoped authorization within a persistent Sandbox to be within the scope of Agent Sandbox?
3. If it is real, could any of my potential mechanisums adopted to the Agent-sandbox to fix this issue?
4. Is there already a lifecycle boundary/API that higher-level agent runtimes can use to dynamically provision and revoke workload authority?
5. If not, would an execution-level authorization/identity lifecycle be useful as part of the Sandbox API?

title: examples(irsa-simulation-localstack): verify the WebIdentityToken's trust boundary

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: ok-to-test
labels.description: Indicates a non-member PR verified by an org member that is safe to test.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
`irsa-simulation-localstack` (#1340) documents that LocalStack's STS mock accepts any `WebIdentityToken` without checking it, so on its own it only proves the sandbox pod *discovers and uses* IRSA-style credentials — not that the token would be trusted by a real relying party.

This adds `sts-trust-verifier`, a small proxy sitting in front of LocalStack that, for the one action this flow uses (`AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity`), fetches the cluster's own JWKS from its `/openid/v1/jwks` discovery endpoint and verifies the token's signature, issuer, and audience before forwarding to LocalStack — the same cryptographic check a real AWS IAM OIDC provider performs. The JWKS location is always a fixed, in-cluster constant, never derived from the token being verified, to avoid an SSRF vector.

This still doesn't validate a real AWS account's IAM OIDC provider registration or role trust policy (there is no real AWS account involved) — it proves the verification mechanics work correctly against the cluster's actual signing key, which is what the original example's caveat called out as unverified.

**Hardening baked into the verifier:**
- Verification is pinned to `algorithms=["RS256"]` rather than trusting the token's own header `alg` — closes the alg-confusion class of attack.
- A *known* `kid` is re-checked against the cluster's real JWKS every 300s, not trusted forever — otherwise a rotated/revoked key stays trusted indefinitely.
- Concurrent requests for the same not-yet-cached `kid` are serialized with a lock so they collapse into a single JWKS fetch instead of a thundering herd.
- Rejections return a generic error message to the caller; the real reason goes to server logs only.
- `Handler.timeout = 30` bounds how long a caller can hold a thread open with a stalled connection.
- `do_handshake_on_connect=False` + an explicit handshake in `Handler.setup()`: the TLS handshake used to happen inside the server's single-threaded accept loop, so a client that opens a connection and never sends a ClientHello could block *all* other connections. Now the handshake happens per-connection in that connection's own thread, bounded by the same timeout.
- Upstream request failures (LocalStack unreachable/timeout) now return a clean `502 InternalFailure` instead of leaving the caller hanging.
- The Deployment sets CPU/memory requests and limits.

**Transport encryption — both hops TLS, both genuinely certificate-verified (no `verify=False` anywhere):**
- **sandbox → sts-trust-verifier** (carries the real WebIdentityToken and the resulting AWS credentials): `trust-verifier-tls.yaml` issues a certificate via cert-manager's `selfsigned` `ClusterIssuer` (the one `amazon-eks-pod-identity-webhook`'s own install already creates), and the sandbox pod genuinely verifies it via `AWS_CA_BUNDLE`.
- **sts-trust-verifier → LocalStack**: LocalStack supports `CUSTOM_SSL_CERT_PATH` for a custom certificate. `localstack-tls.yaml` issues LocalStack its own certificate matching its real Service DNS name; `localstack.yaml`'s init container concatenates cert-manager's separate `tls.key`/`tls.crt` into the single combined PEM file LocalStack expects. The verifier verifies against it (`LOCALSTACK_CA_FILE`).

`run-test-kind.sh` automates the happy path (a real webhook-injected token) and four rejection cases against a live cluster:
- an unrecognized `kid`
- a real `kid` with a forged signature (exercises the RSA signature check itself, not just the key lookup)
- a genuinely cluster-signed token (minted via `kubectl create token`) with the wrong audience
- a genuinely cluster-signed, correct-audience token checked against a deliberately mismatched `EXPECTED_ISSUER`

The last two specifically exercise the audience/issuer checks in `jwt.decode()` — the first two are rejected earlier and wouldn't catch a regression that dropped those two checks. Expired-token rejection is verified separately via an isolated cryptographic test rather than the live script, since Kubernetes' TokenRequest API hard-rejects any token duration under 10 minutes, making a live already-expired cluster-signed token impractical to obtain quickly.

Verified live end-to-end against a kind cluster with cert-manager + `amazon-eks-pod-identity-webhook` installed: all five cases behave correctly over real, mutually-verified TLS on both hops. Also verified in isolation: a hand-built alg-confusion token is rejected purely because the algorithm is pinned server-side; 20 concurrent requests for the same unknown `kid` trigger exactly one JWKS fetch; a simulated key rotation causes a previously-cached, now-rotated-out `kid` to be rejected once the cache-age window elapses; a stalled/incomplete connection is dropped after ~30s instead of hanging forever; a stalled TLS handshake no longer blocks a second, legitimate connection; an unreachable upstream returns a clean 502; and an expired-but-correctly-signed token is rejected while an otherwise-identical non-expired one is accepted.

One test-harness bug found and fixed along the way: `kubectl rollout status` confirms the control plane's view of a rollout, but kube-proxy's dataplane converges asynchronously — a request made the instant `rollout status` returns can occasionally still race a just-terminated pod. Replaced ad hoc response checks with an `assert_rejected` helper that retries briefly; this caught the exact race live during testing.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Ref #818 (cites this example directly when discussing the static/unverified nature of IRSA-style credentials in agent-sandbox)

#### Release Note
```release-note
NONE
```

  * Added a trust-verifier proxy for the IRSA LocalStack simulation.
  * Added JWT signature and claim validation for issuer, audience, expiry, key rotation, and forged tokens.
  * Added HTTPS protection and certificate verification for both credential-bearing connections.
  * Added Kubernetes deployment, certificates, configuration, and sandbox integration.

* **Documentation**

title: docs: clarify restartPolicy interaction with claim lifecycle cleanup

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: kind/documentation
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to documentation.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
## What is the problem?

The relationship between `restartPolicy` and claim lifecycle cleanup is undocumented, leading to silent resource leaks in production configurations.

`agent-sandbox` serves two distinct workload patterns that require different restart and cleanup strategies:

| Workload Pattern | Examples | Recommended `restartPolicy` | Cleanup mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ephemeral batch / one-shot** | Single script execution, Playwright scrape, isolated shell command | `Never` | TTL fires on pod exit → claim GC'd immediately |
| **Interactive session / gateway** | MCP servers, Jupyter kernels, n8n workflows, persistent REPLs | `OnFailure` or `Always` | `ShutdownTime` / `maxLifetimeSeconds` (KEP-1306) |

The gap: when `restartPolicy` is omitted, Kubernetes defaults to `Always`, and pool operators who rely solely on `TTLSecondsAfterFinished` for cleanup get **no cleanup at all** — the sandbox never reaches a terminal state, so TTL never fires.

### Two concrete failure modes

1. **Zombie VMs from completed workloads.** The agent finishes its work, the container exits, but `Always` restarts it. The sandbox never reaches `Finished: True`. TTL never fires. The VM sits idle consuming CPU and memory until manually deleted. Validated empirically: `ShutdownPolicy: Delete + TTL=10` on a kata-qemu pool resulted in 11+ stuck VMs per node.

2. **Unbounded CrashLoopBackOff.** An interactive container that OOMs or panics on startup enters `CrashLoopBackOff` indefinitely under `Always`. The pod is never terminal, TTL never fires, and the sandbox actively consumes resources in a crash loop with no escape — unless `ShutdownTime` or `maxLifetimeSeconds` provides a hard deadline.

Current examples use a mix of `Never`, `OnFailure`, and implicit `Always` without explaining which cleanup mechanisms work with each.

## What should change?

### 1. SandboxTemplate documentation

Add a section explaining the `restartPolicy` × lifecycle interaction:

| `restartPolicy` | TTL fires? | ShutdownTime fires? | Risk if no lifecycle set |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Never` | Yes — pod reaches `Failed`/`Succeeded` | Yes | Low — TTL handles cleanup |
| `OnFailure` | Only on clean exit (exit 0) | Yes | Medium — crashes don't trigger TTL |
| `Always` (default) | Never — container restarts indefinitely | Yes | **High — no cleanup path without ShutdownTime** |

Recommend explicit `restartPolicy` in all templates — relying on the implicit `Always` default hides a cleanup gap.

### 2. Example templates

Audit examples to ensure every sample explicitly sets `restartPolicy` with a comment explaining the choice:

```yaml
# OnFailure: container restarts on crash but not on clean exit.
# TTL only fires on exit 0. Use maxLifetimeSeconds (KEP-1306) for
# hard deadline cleanup of long-running or crash-looping workloads.
restartPolicy: "OnFailure"
```

### 3. Controller warning event (stretch goal)

When a `SandboxWarmPool` has `claimDefaults` with TTL but no `ShutdownTime`/`maxLifetimeSeconds`, and the referenced template uses `restartPolicy: Always` or omits it, emit a warning event:

```
Warning IneffectiveCleanup pool/kata-agent-pool: template uses restartPolicy
Always but claimDefaults relies solely on TTLSecondsAfterFinished — TTL will
not fire because the sandbox never reaches a terminal state. Consider adding
maxLifetimeSeconds or setting restartPolicy: Never.
```

## What this is NOT proposing

- Mandating or defaulting `restartPolicy: Never` — that breaks long-running agent workloads (MCP servers, interactive sessions)
- CEL validation to reject `Always` — operators have legitimate reasons to use it
- Any API change — documentation + optional controller-side warning only

## Related

- #1306 — warm pool claim cleanup defaults
- KEP-1306 `maxLifetimeSeconds` addresses the cleanup gap for `Always`/`OnFailure` workloads

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

An existing strict runtime task cannot change claim ownership safely through labels and owner references alone. This adds an opt-in `SamePolicyFirstClaim` protocol with a durable claim attempt, an exclusive Sandbox reservation, authenticated runtime evidence, and two protected release-authorization writes. The claim becomes ready only after a confirmed successor commit and current verification for that exact claim and execution.

Admission enforces the companion, runtime controller, and bound node-agent writer identities. It protects the final metadata transition and recovery outcomes across controller retries, pool cleanup, deletion, and legacy adoption paths. Pool deletion uses UID/resourceVersion preconditions, and unresolved reservations continue to count toward pool capacity after ownership changes.

The integration is disabled by default. A pool must opt in, protected admission must be installed, and the paired runtime must advertise a qualified native hold/transfer profile. API and controller tests do not qualify the native runtime. The chart requires supplied TLS credentials and does not generate or install certificates.

Compatibility requires attention: legacy warm adoption and recovery now reject strict pool executions from the paired provider, including when the new opt-in is disabled. Drain and replace those legacy pool members and claims through their cold lifecycle before enabling the paired contract. Ordinary runtimes retain their existing adoption path. Please apply `release-note-action-required`.

Validation:

- Integration commit `c9678492cb65f08c45bf0e5b4e86c91da08ea531` passed `TMPDIR=/private/tmp npm_config_registry=https://registry.npmjs.org make all verify-olm-bundle`, including generation, builds, Go/API lint, Go race suites, Python suites, all 126 TypeScript tests, and documentation/OLM verification. The public npm registry supplied the unchanged locked dependencies; no dependency files changed.
- The v1.0.0 qualification checkout at `74cc799d424d0b480703c529222a9c2f61f3b63c`, based on `bb72f49d79f009a960eed2ae6c32e1cc082399c5`, passed `TMPDIR=/private/tmp npm_config_registry=https://registry.npmjs.org make all`. This PR integrates that implementation onto `e5e2831295a789299722a9f4d922250167b1e879` and regenerates the upstream OLM bundle. Both branches carry the same readiness, RuntimeClass recovery, and pool cleanup fixes.
- All 15 canonical wire and projection fixtures match the paired runtime implementation byte for byte. Focused regressions cover absent, expired, and mismatched readiness verification, expiry-driven reconciliation, authoritative strict-handler checks despite stale caches, concurrent reservations during pool cleanup, and preservation of reconcile-error and suspended-state reasons while adoption is pending. These regressions fail with the original production implementations and pass with the fixes.

- The `74cc799d424d0b480703c529222a9c2f61f3b63c` qualification build passed live cancellation, Claim metadata and policy mutation, agent replacement while held, cleanup rejection after commit, competing claims, and controller restart on Linux `6.17.7-300.fc43.aarch64`. An earlier build at `81aca1919f4235b9aa58cf9e3b0cdb5542c8743c` completed 30 cold and 30 warm samples with no rejection, fallback, or cleanup failures. Warm p50 was 15.879 seconds versus 7.437 seconds for cold; the measurements do not establish a speedup. Reports retain `qualifiedForAdoption=false`.

Native runtime conformance and performance qualification remain separate requirements before enabling the advertised runtime capability.

#### Release Note

The integration is disabled by default and requires a separately qualified native runtime plus protected admission. ACTION REQUIRED: legacy strict warm-pool adoption and recovery are rejected for the paired provider; drain and replace legacy strict pool members and claims through their cold lifecycle before enabling the paired contract. Ordinary runtimes retain their existing adoption behavior.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
<!-- Provide a clear and concise description of the changes in this PR. -->
The connector caught every RequestException, including a 404, and reset the resolved Pod IP and closed the port-forward tunnel. A 4xx is a successful round trip, so a normal missing-file read tore the tunnel down and forced the next call to rebuild it. Go SDK and async connector already handle this correctly.

### Repro
```python 
from k8s_agent_sandbox import SandboxClient
from k8s_agent_sandbox.models import SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig

WARMPOOL = "testing"
NAMESPACE = "default"

def main():
    client = SandboxClient(connection_config=SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig())
    sandbox = client.create_sandbox(warmpool=WARMPOOL, namespace=NAMESPACE)
    conn = sandbox.connector            # holds the resolved Pod IP
    strat = conn.strategy               # holds base_url + the port-forward subprocess
    try:
        sandbox.commands.run("true")
        old_proc = strat.port_forward_process
        print("before 404:")
        print(f"  pod_ip                = {conn._pod_ip}")
        print(f"  base_url              = {strat.base_url}")
        print(f"  port-forward pid      = {old_proc.pid} (alive={old_proc.poll() is None})")

        # A normal "file not found" read.
        try:
            sandbox.files.read("does-not-exist.txt")
        except Exception as exc:
            print(f"\nread() raised: {type(exc).__name__} status_code={getattr(exc, 'status_code', None)}\n")

        # The teardown has already run: state is cleared and the process killed.
        print("after 404 (no new call yet):")
        print(f"  pod_ip                = {conn._pod_ip}")
        print(f"  base_url              = {strat.base_url}")
        print(f"  port-forward process  = {strat.port_forward_process}")
        print(f"  pid {old_proc.pid} alive          = {old_proc.poll() is None}  <- killed")

        # The sandbox itself was never broken: this succeeds, but only after the connector rebuilds the tunnel.
        result = sandbox.commands.run("echo still-usable")
        new_proc = strat.port_forward_process
        print("\nafter follow-up run() (tunnel rebuilt):")
        print(f"  stdout                = {result.stdout.strip()!r}")
        print(f"  base_url              = {strat.base_url}")
        print(f"  port-forward pid      = {new_proc.pid}  <- new process")

        print(f"\nresult: a 404 killed pid {old_proc.pid} and forced a rebuild to pid {new_proc.pid} (bug)")
    finally:
        sandbox.terminate()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```sh
before 404:
  pod_ip                = 10.244.0.112
  base_url              = http://127.0.0.1:60568
  port-forward pid      = 23002 (alive=True)
ERROR:root:Request to sandbox failed: 404 Client Error: Not Found for url: http://127.0.0.1:60568/download/does-not-exist.txt

read() raised: SandboxRequestError status_code=404

after 404 (no new call yet):
  pod_ip                = None
  base_url              = None
  port-forward process  = None
  pid 23002 alive          = False  <- killed

after follow-up run() (tunnel rebuilt):
  stdout                = 'still-usable'
  base_url              = http://127.0.0.1:60580
  port-forward pid      = 23006  <- new process
```

### Proposed fix

Only reset the Pod IP and close the connection for genuine transport failures.

### After
```python
before 404:
  pod_ip                = 10.244.0.114
  base_url              = http://127.0.0.1:62800
  port-forward pid      = 61485 (alive=True)

read() raised: SandboxRequestError status_code=404

after 404 (no new call yet):
  pod_ip                = 10.244.0.114
  base_url              = http://127.0.0.1:62800
  port-forward process  = <Popen: returncode: None args: ['kubectl', 'port-forward', 'svc/sandbox-rout...>
  pid 61485 alive          = True  <- killed

after follow-up run() (tunnel rebuilt):
  stdout                = 'still-usable'
  base_url              = http://127.0.0.1:62800
  port-forward pid      = 61485  <- same process
```

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds retry-safe deterministic `SandboxClaim` creation to the Python SDK while preserving the existing random-name behavior by default.

- Adds optional keyword-only `claim_name` and `adopt_existing` parameters to both `SandboxClient.create_sandbox()` and `AsyncSandboxClient.create_sandbox()`.
- Adopts only an API `409 AlreadyExists`, and only when the caller explicitly opts in.
- Validates the existing Claim's identity and immutable request contract before adoption, including labels, warm pool, lifecycle, Workspace volume templates, Pod metadata, and environment.
- Pins the Claim UID and resourceVersion observed during explicit creation/adoption so a same-name replacement fails closed during readiness/watch recovery.
- Separates automatically managed random Claims from caller-owned explicit/adopted Claims, preventing timeout, cancellation, context-manager, and stale-handle paths from deleting caller-owned resources.
- Keeps sync and async behavior aligned and documents the ownership/cleanup contract.

This enables durable workflow engines with at-least-once execution semantics to retry sandbox creation without creating duplicate sandboxes or accidentally adopting a different request:

```python
sandbox = client.create_sandbox(
    warmpool="python-sandbox-pool",
    namespace="agents",
    claim_name=f"sandbox-{task_id}",
    adopt_existing=True,
)
```

##### Relationship to #1090

This PR intentionally supersedes #1090 and credits @brightsparc for the original API proposal and implementation. It preserves the `claim_name` / `adopt_existing` design and incorporates the review feedback already addressed there, then extends it with full contract validation, UID/resourceVersion lineage checks, concurrency-safe ownership transfer, and broader sync/async regression coverage.

The original branch has had no author updates since July 5 BRT (July 6 UTC), is currently conflicting with `main`, and is labeled `needs-rebase`. I offered the hardened fork lineage on #1090 before opening this alternative. I am opening this current-`main` version ready for review and will actively address CI, review feedback, and future rebases so maintainers have a maintained path to land the feature.

##### Verification

- `TMPDIR=/private/tmp make all` (exit 0) on `main` at `e5e2831295a789299722a9f4d922250167b1e879`; generated-code checks and the repository's Go, Python, and TypeScript suites passed

- TypeScript: 126 passed
- Hugo Extended 0.163.3 site build: 192 pages rendered successfully

Additional real-controller evidence for the same contract is recorded in #1090 using the immutable v0.5.6-compatible candidate and the official v0.5.6 controller. It covers concurrent creator/adopter races, process termination after persistence, readiness timeout overlap, mismatched contracts, UID-preconditioned deletion/recreation, and final resource cleanup.

Fixes #1089
Supersedes #1090

title: SandboxWarmPool silently reports nothing when SandboxTemplate does not exist

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### What happened?

A `SandboxWarmPool` whose `sandboxTemplateRef` points at a `SandboxTemplate` that does not exist never creates any sandboxes, and surfaces no signal about why. The pool sits at `READY` blank / `DESIRED N` indefinitely, which is identical to a healthy pool that is still warming up.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

### Repro
```sh
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxWarmPool
metadata:
  name: testing-pool
  namespace: default
spec:
  replicas: 1
  sandboxTemplateRef:
    name: does-not-exist
EOF

kubectl get sandboxwarmpool testing-pool
# NAME          READY   DESIRED   AGE
# testing-pool           1         10s      <- blank and no hint it's broken

kubectl get sandboxwarmpool testing-pool -o jsonpath='{.status}'
# {"observedGeneration":1,"selector":"..."}  <- no error

kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=testing-pool
# No resources found in default namespace.
```


### Version

v1.0.1

### Anything else we need to know?

### Expected behavior

The pool should surface the missing dependency similar to the claim path:

```sh
kubectl apply -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxClaim
metadata: {name: testing-claim, namespace: default}
spec:
  warmPoolRef: {name: no-such-pool}
EOF

kubectl get sandboxclaim testing-claim
# NAME         READY   SANDBOX   REASON             AGE
# testing-claim   False             WarmPoolNotFound   6s

kubectl get sandboxclaim testing-claim -o jsonpath='{.status}'
# {"conditions":[{"lastTransitionTime":"...","message":"SandboxWarmPool \"no-such-pool\" not found","observedGeneration":1,"reason":"WarmPoolNotFound","status":"False","type":"Ready"}],"sandbox":{}}%
```

## Proposed direction
`SandboxWarmPoolStatus` has no `conditions` field today, so the two options differ in scope:

1. Emit a Warning Event for missing template, reusing the existing `setNotProgressing` mechanism, without api change.
2. Add a `conditions` field and `Reason` column to match the claim path, api change

Feel free to assign to me if this should be fixed, thanks

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
`presubmit-test-e2e-scalability-kwok` frequently dies before any test runs, killed by
Prow's job timeout ("Entrypoint received interrupt: terminated"). Pulling TestGrid data
and the actual `build-log.txt` for ~9 recent red runs showed the timeout hitting at
different points in the script — during `go: downloading`, Docker-in-Docker startup,
`kwokctl create cluster`, and once mid-test — including one PR whose three consecutive
attempts were all killed by timeout at different stages. That pattern points at the
job's total setup cost being tight against its time budget, not a single broken step.

One clear, fixable contributor: the script builds the `clusterloader2` binary from
source on every run via a full `git clone` of `kubernetes/perf-tests` (~116 MiB,
GitHub-reported size, with a long history), even though only one pinned commit's tree
is ever used. The `CACHE_DIR` meant to cache the built binary does not survive across
runs since Prow presubmits run in fresh ephemeral pods, so this full clone happens on
effectively every single run. `kubernetes/perf-tests` has no published release
binaries for `clusterloader2` (checked `GET /repos/kubernetes/perf-tests/releases` —
empty), so building from source is unavoidable, but fetching only the pinned commit
is not: replacing the full clone with `git init` + `git fetch --depth 1 origin
<sha>` + `git checkout FETCH_HEAD` pulls only that commit's objects.

This reduces one source of setup-time cost in a job that is timeout-sensitive; it does
not, on its own, prove the flakiness is eliminated, since the actual Prow job timeout
value is configured in `kubernetes/test-infra`, outside this repository.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1565

#### Release Note
```release-note
NONE
```

Validation performed locally (no live Prow/kind/kwok access in this environment):
- `bash -n dev/ci/presubmits/test-e2e-scalability-kwok` — syntax OK.
- `shellcheck dev/ci/presubmits/test-e2e-scalability-kwok` — only a pre-existing,
  unrelated SC2329 info-level false positive on `cleanup()` (it's invoked via
  `trap cleanup EXIT`); no new warnings from this change.
- Ran the new fetch sequence against the real `kubernetes/perf-tests` repo with the
  actual pinned commit (`d14a402a9540e4c8ba34717e428bfd2cf31a41a8`): confirmed
  `git rev-parse HEAD` matches the pinned SHA exactly and `clusterloader2/` is present
  with the expected contents — behaviorally equivalent end state to the old
  `clone` + `checkout <sha>` sequence.
- Ran `go build -o ... ./cmd/clusterloader.go` against that shallow checkout: module
  resolution succeeded and 40+ k8s.io/client-go, k8s.io/api, k8s.io/apimachinery, etc.
  packages compiled correctly before the build failed due to the local sandbox
  machine running out of disk space (unrelated to this change; verified via `df -h`
  showing the whole host at ~100% full from unrelated data). I could not produce a
  finished `clusterloader2` binary in this environment, so I cannot claim the full
  build succeeded end-to-end here.
- Timed a full clone vs. the new shallow fetch locally: 175 MiB/~7.5s vs. 62 MiB/~1.8s.
  CI's Docker-in-Docker network is typically slower/more constrained, so the relative
  savings should be at least as large there, but this was not measured in CI itself.
- Did not and could not run the actual Prow job end-to-end (needs kwokctl,
  Docker-in-Docker, a live Prow pod, and the job timeout config that lives in
  kubernetes/test-infra, not this repo).
- `git log --branch main` shows `main` CI green at the branch tip this PR is based on.

CI on this repo requires a maintainer to add `ok-to-test` — happy to address anything
it surfaces.

title: fix(ci): retry Node.js download to reduce presubmit-test-unit infra flakes

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: ok-to-test
labels.description: Indicates a non-member PR verified by an org member that is safe to test.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
`presubmit-test-unit` has been failing before any test runs in 56 of 57 recent
red runs (per the auto-generated flake report). `dev/tools/test-unit` calls
`ensure_node()` to install Node.js for the TypeScript unit test suite, and
`install_node()` downloaded the Node.js tarball via a single, un-retried
`urllib.request.urlretrieve()` call. Any transient network drop against the
nodejs.org CDN fails the whole presubmit before a single test executes,
matching the issue's symptom exactly. `dev/ci/shared/runner.py` already
retries its own bring-up steps (kind cluster create, image push, deploy) for
the same class of transient CI failure; this applies the same idea to the
Node.js download.

This PR wraps the download in a bounded retry loop (3 attempts, 5s delay
between attempts), returning failure only once all attempts are exhausted.

Disclosure: I could not reproduce a live CDN network drop or run the actual
Prow `presubmit-test-unit` job. Validation is a mocked unit test that
demonstrates the code-level defect (no retry on a call that can transiently
fail): it fails without the fix and passes with it, plus a full run of the
existing `dev/tools` unit test suite with no regressions. Whether this
reduces the observed flake rate in Prow is not something I could confirm
directly, but the mechanism matches the reported symptom.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1566

#### Release Note
```release-note
NONE
```

title: rbac: trim over-granted controller verbs and add an e2e RBAC-denial guard

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

body:
Trims controller ClusterRole verbs that no reconciler ever issues, and adds an e2e guard so the trims stay honest. Split out of #1472 to keep one concern per PR. Every trim was verified by call-site audit against current `main` (independent of #1472's deletions — none of that dead code touches these verbs).

**Verb trims (kubebuilder markers; manifests under `k8s/`, `helm/`, `olm/` are regenerated output):**
- Sandbox controller: drop `create;update` on `sandboxes` (users create them; the controller writes only via the status/finalizers subresource rules) and `update;delete` on `persistentvolumeclaims` (create-only; owner-reference GC handles deletion).
- SandboxClaim controller: drop `create` on `sandboxclaims` (it never creates claims), the direct `pods` rule entirely (the claim controller performs no Pod reads or writes — readiness comes from the Sandbox's conditions; the warmpool controller is the only Pod reader and keeps `get;list;watch`), `update` on events, and `delete` on leases.
- SandboxTemplate controller: primary resource down to `get;list;watch;patch`; drop `patch` on NetworkPolicies; `update` on events.
- SandboxWarmPool controller: primary resource down to `get;list;watch` (status/finalizers via subresource rules); `update` on events.

**Guard:** `TestMain` in both e2e suites now scans controller logs after the run for `is forbidden: User` RBAC denials and fails the suite if any appear, so a future verb regression surfaces in presubmit instead of production.

Narrows the blast radius of a compromised controller ServiceAccount; no behavior change for correctly functioning controllers.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

- **Security**
  - Tightened controller permissions across sandbox resources, workloads, events, leases, network policies, and related Kubernetes objects.
  - Restricted several resources to read-only access where applicable and removed unnecessary write operations.
  - Added narrowly scoped permissions for persistent volume claims, sandbox templates, and sandbox warm pools.

- **Tests**
  - End-to-end tests now detect RBAC denial messages in controller logs and report them as test failures when appropriate.
  - Added coverage for RBAC access issues across both standard and extension test suites.

title: rl-sdk: allow adopting warm pools provisioned by the fleet layer

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The RL SDK hardcoded its warm-pool name to `pool-<template>` ([`fleet.py:476`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/examples/agent-sandbox-rl/agent_sandbox_rl/fleet.py)). The multi-cluster fleet layer names the same pools `<template>-pool`. So an RL harness pointed at a cluster whose pools were provisioned by someone else — the fleet layer, a platform team, a previous run — does not find the pools standing right in front of it. It falls through to `_ensure_pool`, builds a parallel size-1 pool per image, and reports a healthy run: working, orders of magnitude slower than the warm pods it ignored, and silent about it.

Two changes, matching items 1 and 2 of the issue.

**1. The pool name is derivable and configurable.** New `FleetConfig.pool_name_format`, default `"pool-{template}"` (unchanged behaviour), with placeholders `{template}` and `{image_hash}`. Pointing the SDK at fleet-provisioned pools is now a one-liner:

```python
FleetConfig(pool_name_format="{template}-pool")
```

The format is validated at config time, against a *rendered sample* rather than the string itself: it must produce a DNS-1123 subdomain, and it must vary per image. That second check matters — a format with no per-image placeholder maps every image onto one pool name, the second image upserts the first one's pool, and the only symptom is tasks claiming sandboxes that are running the wrong image. There is no later error to catch it, so it is rejected up front.

**2. An adopt-only mode.** `FleetConfig(adopt_existing=True)` plans against the warm pools already present in the namespace instead of creating any:

```python
fleet = SandboxFleet(
    FleetConfig(clusters=[...], namespace="rl", adopt_existing=True),
    tasks=tasks,
)
fleet.plan()   # raises PoolNotFoundError if any task image is unserved
```

Matching is **by image**, not by name: each pool's `spec.sandboxTemplateRef` is resolved to its `SandboxTemplate` and then to the runtime container's image. Adoption therefore does not require the provisioner and this SDK to agree on a naming convention at all — which is the whole problem — and item 1 becomes an optimization rather than a prerequisite.

A miss raises `PoolNotFoundError` listing the uncovered images (with the pool name this SDK looked for) and a per-cluster count of what it did find, because "wrong namespace", "wrong cluster" and "pool not filled yet" are indistinguishable from the exception type alone.

**Adopt mode is read-only end to end.** Blocking pool creation is the obvious half; the rest of the write paths were enumerated too, since each one corrupts a namespace this SDK does not own:

| Path | Under `adopt_existing` |
| --- | --- |
| `ensure_templates()` | skipped — `ensure_template` reconciles pod-template labels, which would stamp *our* run-id onto the provisioner's template and thereby onto every sandbox it goes on to create |
| `_ensure_pool` / pool create | never called |
| `set_pool_replicas` (`recycle(scale_on_hold=True)`) | no-ops with a warning — the depth belongs to the provisioner |
| `_unwarm_entry` (sliding-window sweeps) | no-ops — would delete pools out from under every other consumer of the fleet |
| `_teardown` | adopted pools and templates are filtered out of the delete set even if they carry our managed label; claims we created are still swept |
| `reserve_replicas` / `warm_add` | not called — the capacity counters track what this fleet created, and it created none of this |

Two consequences worth calling out for reviewers:

- **Readiness is `>= 1` ready replica, not `>= observed depth`.** The pool's depth moves under us as its provisioner replenishes or rescales, so waiting for the full observed depth would make readiness a race against someone else's controller. One warm replica is the claimable-now contract the SDK actually needs.
- **The overcommit breaker is explicitly disarmed** (`expected = 0`). It compares planned intent against `live_owned_count()`, which counts pods carrying this run's label — and adoption creates none. Leaving it wired would be a ceiling of (provisioner's depth × 1.5) against a count that is structurally zero: a breaker that cannot fire. An explicit `max_live_sandboxes` still applies. Better documented than accidental.

**The non-adopt path is no longer silent either.** The on-demand fallthrough now warns once per `(cluster, image)`, naming the pool name it looked for and pointing at both `pool_name_format` and `adopt_existing`. That silence is what made the original behaviour a bug rather than a gap.

**Deferred:** item 3 of the issue — a `TaskSource` that reads the hub's published assignment — depends on the fleet layer's Python package, which is still unmerged in #1394. Happy to follow up once that lands.

**Tests:** 24 new tests in `examples/agent-sandbox-rl/tests/test_adopt.py`, in five groups — pool-name config and its validators, `discover_pools` against a fake `custom_api` (including a template with no matching pool, and two pools serving one image), adopt planning and its miss message, the read-only warm/scale/teardown contract, and an end-to-end run over adopted pools plus a regression for the silent fallthrough. Full suite: 347 passed, up from a 323 baseline. A mutation pass over the four adopt guards confirmed each one is load-bearing (disabling them fails exactly the tests written for them).

No API, CRD, or controller changes — this is confined to `examples/agent-sandbox-rl/`. Default behaviour is unchanged: `pool_name_format` defaults to the previously hardcoded string and `adopt_existing` defaults to `False`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1533

#### Release Note

```release-note
The RL SDK example can now adopt warm pools provisioned by something else (such as the multi-cluster fleet layer) instead of building a parallel set of its own. `FleetConfig.pool_name_format` makes the generated pool name configurable, and `FleetConfig.adopt_existing=True` plans against the pools already present in the namespace — matching them by container image rather than by name — and raises `PoolNotFoundError` when a task image is unserved instead of silently falling back to slow on-demand provisioning.
```

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
kOps GCP benchmark presubmits occasionally fail during cluster validation with `dial tcp <external-ip>:443: i/o timeout`, indicating that the apiserver never became reachable through the external load balancer before the validation timeout expired. When validation fails, the exit cleanup handler immediately tears down the cluster VMs, destroying the console output needed to determine why the control plane node failed bootstrap or health checks. In addition, the cluster validation timeout was hardcoded in the runner script.

This PR:
1. **Captures control-plane serial port console logs on validation failure**: Extracts the control-plane VM's serial port output via `gcloud` and writes it to `$ARTIFACTS/control-plane-serial-port.log` before teardown, preserving critical boot and `nodeup` logs in Prow. The VM lookup is scoped to the cluster's managed instance group (`a-control-plane-${ZONE}-${CLUSTER_NAME}`) to prevent cross-contamination during concurrent runs.
2. **Unifies cluster validation handling**: Consolidates cluster validation into a `validate_cluster()` helper used by both initial cluster validation and the Cilium post-restart re-validation, ensuring failure diagnostic capture is applied consistently.
3. **Parameterizes validation timeout**: Replaces the hardcoded `15m` initial wait and `5m` Cilium re-validation wait with `"${STRESS_VALIDATE_WAIT:-15m}"` and `"${STRESS_CILIUM_VALIDATE_WAIT:-5m}"`, allowing manual or periodic runs to adjust timeouts without modifying code.

body:
Each node's pod CIDR is carved from the cluster pod CIDR (10.4.0.0/14 on kOps GCE), and the mask bounds the cluster along **two axes at once**:

- pods per node ≤ 2^(32−mask) − 2 (/24 → 254, /23 → 510)
- node count ≤ 2^(mask−14) (/24 → 1024, /23 → 512, /22 → 256)

Both cliffs fail hard, and the node-count one fails confusingly: GCE rejects instance creation with `IP_SPACE_EXHAUSTED` when the per-node alias range can't be allocated. A 300-node scale run with /22 stalled at exactly 253 workers + 3 support nodes = 256 slots.

/23 balances the axes for benchmark shapes: up to 510 pods/node **and** up to 512 nodes. Overridable via `STRESS_NODE_CIDR_MASK_SIZE`.

body:
etcd's default quota is 2GiB, and crossing it is a cliff rather than a slowdown: etcd raises the NOSPACE alarm and rejects **every** write with `mvcc: database space exceeded` until the alarm is cleared.

A 100k-pod benchmark launch writes ~2GB into etcd. Fast runs finished at ~1.7GB; a marginally slower run crossed the quota mid-fill and collapsed into a kubelet retry storm — 3.6M failed status PATCHes at ~3,200/s for 15 minutes — while etcd-manager never cleared the alarm.

8GiB puts the cliff far from any benchmark workload; etcd only uses the space it actually writes. Overridable via `STRESS_ETCD_QUOTA_BYTES`.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
 The router NetworkPolicy was deliberately excluded from the OLM bundle in #1425 because of three bugs identified during review. Now that #1537 is merged and #1539 (router label) is in flight, the policy can be fixed and included.

This fixes a couple of bugs in the network policy:

  - API server egress unreachable: used `namespaceSelector` targeting the `default` namespace, but the API server runs on host-network control plane nodes — not as in-cluster pods — so the rule never matched. With the OLM default `--cache-enabled=true`, cache sync would hang indefinitely. Fixed nodes — not as in-cluster pods — so the rule never matched. With the OLM default `--cache-enabled=true`, cache sync would hang indefinitely. Fixed with  a port-only rule (no `to` restriction) on 443/6443.
- Egress port too narrow: only TCP 8888 was allowed, but `X-Sandbox-Port` lets callers specify any port and the SDK exposes `ServerPort`. Removed the port restriction from the sandbox egress rule.
- Ingress lacked justification: `namespaceSelector: {}` on the proxy port is intentional — the router is the entry point and the authz layer (`--authz-mode`) is the security boundary, not L4. Added clear documentation.

Shipping *no* NetworkPolicy means zero network-level restrictions on the router.
This policy restricts egress to DNS + sandbox pods + API server + OTel, which is
strictly more secure than the status quo. Every objection from #1425 is addressed.


Depends on: #1539 (router `app: sandbox-router` label)
Refs: #1409, #1425, #1537 with a port-only rule (no `to` restriction) on 443/6443.

Follow-up to the four-part fleet series (#1394 and its parts 2–4). The `ClusterProfile` inventory backend itself already shipped there — the provider and publisher in part 1, the CRD, hub RBAC and setup scripts in part 2, the operator walkthrough in part 3, and the offline planner preflight in part 4.

What was missing is the tooling to tell you *why* a hub integration isn't working, which matters more here than usual: on GKE almost every failure in this path presents as an authentication error regardless of its actual cause. A 401 from the hub is IAM, not RBAC. A hub that times out while bucket writes keep succeeding is routing — a GKE control plane's public IP is not a Google API endpoint, so Private Google Access does not cover it. `kubernetes>=36` drops the `Bearer` prefix the older client sent. An ADC redirect produces a 403 that reaches the planner, not just the member. Without a way to see the wire, each of these reads as "the integration is broken."

**Two halves of a hub, each runnable on its own:**

- `demo/seed-clusterprofiles.sh` — plays the **cluster manager**: creates `ClusterProfile` objects and owns their identity and health conditions. Deliberately writes no capacity.
- `demo/publish-clusterprofile.py` — plays the **fleet member**: publishes capacity onto `ClusterProfile` status via server-side apply, using the same `ClusterProfilePublisher` the real member uses.

Splitting them is the point. The two halves are separate writers of the same object, and server-side apply is what keeps them from clobbering each other — so being able to run one without the other is how you confirm field ownership is actually working rather than merely that the values are present.

**Driving the read path:**

- `demo/cp-registry.py` — drives the `clusterprofile` inventory provider straight against a hub with no GCS in the loop, which separates "the hub is wrong" from "the bucket is wrong."
- `demo/fleet-spec-clusterprofile-e2e.yaml` — a spec with no `cluster_weights` at all, so both the cluster list and the weights must come from the hub or the plan cannot be produced. 40 sandboxes fleet-wide: enough for the weight split to be visible in the pool arithmetic, small enough to materialise in under a minute. Uses the `sb-tmpl-a..e` templates from `deploy/example-templates-xs.yaml`.

**Seeing the wire:**

- `deploy/hub-probe.sh` — raw-wire probe of the member→hub path with no Python client in the way.
- `deploy/auth-probe.sh` — prints the headers the Python client actually sends, which is how the missing-`Bearer` case is identified rather than guessed at.
- `deploy/hubcheck-job.yaml` — runs the existing `fleet-hubcheck` entrypoint as a Job, so the check runs from inside a member pod with that pod's real dentity instead of from a laptop with yours.

**Watching it under load:**

- `demo/watch-clusterprofile-drift.py` — samples, once per interval, the three numbers that should agree (what the cluster has, what the member publishes, what the hub serves) and measures how far apart they drift under density. Published capacity is eventually consistent by construction, so the useful question is not whether it drifts but how much, and whether it converges.

No Go code, no controller changes, no API changes. Nothing here runs unless an operator invokes it.

Ref #1394 (part 1/4 — the `ClusterProfile` provider and publisher this exercises)

There is deliberately no kind path. The fleet layer's subject is per-cluster capacity reporting and cross-cluster placement, and neither is meaningfully exercised by two single-node clusters on one laptop — a green kind run would mostly assert that the code doesn't crash.

**`fleet/demo/preflight-cp-plan.py`** — proves a spec plans to the totals you intended, offline. A spec with `cluster_weights: {}` moves the budget split out of the file and into whatever the members publish as `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-capacity`; that is the point of the `ClusterProfile` integration and also its failure mode, because nothing catches a wrong capacity until a multi-cluster run has already been spent. This runs the real
`ClusterProfileInventory.load()` and the real `planner.plan()` against synthetic profiles — only `list_profiles()` is substituted, so the Hamilton split, `compute_replicas`, the spread-first pre-pass and the `min_clusters` round-robin all execute as they will on the day. `--omit CLUSTER` covers the case that motivated it: a member that never publishes does **not** drop out, it gets weight 1.0 and takes a rounding-error share, so the plan succeeds, nothing errors, and the fleet lands short.

**`fleet/demo/observe.sh`** — per-cluster snapshot plus GCS state, and `--fail-modes`, which injects all three recovery cases: kill a member (its capacity report ages out and the next `apply` shifts assignments away), hand-delete a warm pool (recreated on the next reconcile), and corrupt `assignments.json` (members log the parse error and keep serving last-known-good).

**`fleet/demo/stress-e2e.py`** — the only thing here that exercises the full lifecycle including `SandboxClaim` adoption, and therefore the only thing that makes the capacity-aware selector respond to real load. Reads the live `assignments.json`, rotates through every pool weighted by size, refreshes kubeconfig contexts itself, cleans up after itself. Reports a warm-hit rate, which is the number to read: below ~50% the pool is draining faster than the `SandboxWarmPool` controller replenishes it, and every latency percentile in the summary is measuring cold sandbox creation rather than the fleet.

**`fleet/demo/run-xs-e2e.sh`** + **`fleet/demo/fleet-spec-xs.yaml`** + **`fleet/deploy/create-gke-standard-fleet.sh`** + **`fleet/deploy/example-templates-xs.yaml`** — the whole GKE walkthrough as one idempotent command across three XS Standard clusters with image streaming on. body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add Python SDK wrappers for the two sandboxd runtime REST endpoints defined in packages/sandboxd/spec/filesystem/v1/filesystem.yaml that aren't yet exposed to users:

`GET /health` — sandbox readiness / heartbeat probe
`GET /metadata`— non-sensitive workload environment metadata

Both should be available on the sync Sandbox and async AsyncSandbox handles, returning typed pydantic models.

Proposed public API (could also be under sandbox.runtime.* namespace if preferred):

```
# Sync
sandbox.health()      # -> HealthStatus(status="ok", uptime_seconds=3600)
sandbox.metadata()    # -> RuntimeMetadata(env={"WORKSPACE": "/workspace", ...})

# Async
await sandbox.health()
await sandbox.metadata()
```

### Why is this needed?

The runtime already serves both endpoints, but the Python SDK doesn't expose them. 

### Acceptance criteria
- sandbox.health() / await async_sandbox.health() returns a HealthStatus when sandboxd responds 200, and surfaces an error when sandboxd responds 503.
- sandbox.metadata() / await async_sandbox.metadata() returns a RuntimeMetadata populated from the env field of the response.
- Both methods raise a clear error when the connector is not sandboxd-backed.
- Sync/async behavior and error handling are covered by parity tests.
- README documents installation and usage.

Related : #1438 -- needs this change to be merged first to prevent duplicate code for the async path
