title: sandbox-router: browser clients (WebSocket) cannot address a sandbox at all — header-only routing has no path a browser can use

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
## Problem

`sandbox-router` routes exclusively by request headers (`X-Sandbox-ID` required,
`X-Sandbox-UID`/`-Namespace`/`-Port`/`-Pod-IP` optional). That's a fine contract for a
Go/Python SDK or `curl`, but it is unreachable for a browser in the specific case that
matters most for a browser: a WebSocket connection.

Concretely, two real use cases we hit trying to put browser-facing dev tooling behind
this router:

1. **A web IDE's terminal** (code-server / VS Code in the browser) — the whole editor
   UI loads fine over plain HTTP, but the terminal, extension host, and most of the
   interactive state ride over a single WebSocket the page's own JS opens.
2. **A dev server's hot-reload client** (Vite/webpack HMR) — same shape: the app loads
   fine, but live-reload depends on a WebSocket the dev-server's bundled client code
   opens.

In both cases, the browser (or the third-party JS the browser is running — code-server's
own bundle, the HMR client — which we don't author and can't modify) is the one opening
the connection, and:

- A top-level navigation, an `<iframe src>` load, and `new WebSocket(url, protocols)` all
  have **no browser API for attaching custom request headers**. `protocols` on the
  `WebSocket` constructor only negotiates a subprotocol (`Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`); it is
  not a headers map.
- This is **not** something a Service Worker can work around either — WebSocket
  handshakes are explicitly not exposed to the `fetch` event. This is why tools that need
  to intercept WebSocket traffic client-side (e.g. Mock Service Worker) have to patch the
  global `WebSocket` constructor instead of using a Service Worker at all, and it's the
  subject of a still-open spec issue: https://github.com/w3c/ServiceWorker/issues/947.

So today, putting a WebSocket-dependent tool behind this router from a browser requires
standing up a separate, bespoke header-injecting proxy in front of it whose only job is
translating a plain browser-reachable URL into the `X-Sandbox-*` headers this router
needs — and that proxy itself has to be WebSocket-capable, which is its own non-trivial
piece of infrastructure (we ended up needing a hand-rolled `HttpServletRequest.upgrade()`
+ raw-socket splice on our own Java control-plane, because the JDK's `HttpClient` cannot
represent a `101 Switching Protocols` upgrade at all). None of that would be necessary if
the router itself accepted routing information from something a browser *can* put in a
plain URL.

### This isn't hypothetical — it's already documented in-tree

[`examples/vscode-sandbox`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/examples/vscode-sandbox) hits exactly this. Its README's "Option A: Simple Access" avoids the router entirely (`kubectl port-forward` straight to the pod), specifically because that's the only way that currently just works from a browser. "Option B: Secure Access (gVisor / Kata / Production)" — the case where the router is actually required, because direct pod port-forwarding isn't compatible with those runtimes — instructs the user to:

> 1. Install a header-modifying extension (e.g. **ModHeader** for Chrome/Edge/Firefox).
> 2. Configure the extension to send `X-Sandbox-ID` / `X-Sandbox-Port`.
> 3. Navigate to `http://<GATEWAY_IP>`.

That's a real, currently-recommended workaround for exactly the "browser wants to reach a sandboxed web IDE through this router" case — and it only claims the VS Code *interface* loads, not that the terminal (the WebSocket) works. It also isn't something a product could ship to its own end users (you can't ask every user of your own web app to install and hand-configure a specific browser extension per session), and it's unclear it even fully solves the WebSocket half of the problem: browser extensions using `webRequest` *can* observe a WebSocket handshake (unlike a page-level Service Worker), but whether `onBeforeSendHeaders` modifications actually take effect on that handshake specifically is inconsistently documented even in Chromium's own docs — I haven't been able to confirm it either way, and wouldn't want to build on it regardless given the per-user manual setup problem above.

## Proposal

An **opt-in, additive** path-based routing mode: a request whose path starts with an
operator-configured prefix is routed by `<prefix>/<namespace>/<id>/<port>/<rest...>`
instead of headers. Header-based routing stays exactly as it is — default off, and any
request whose path doesn't match the prefix falls straight through to today's behavior
unchanged.

The reason this actually solves the WebSocket case (not just plain HTTP): once a page is
loaded at a URL under this prefix, a *relative* WebSocket URL that page's own JavaScript
opens — which is how code-server and typical dev-server HMR clients behave — carries the
same prefix along automatically. No client-side code, no Service Worker, nothing custom
on our side; it's just how browsers resolve relative URLs.

I've put together a draft implementation as a PR (opt-in flag, additive parsing path,
tests, README) — happy to adjust the design based on maintainer feedback before it goes
further: #1413

### Prior art: this is the industry-standard way of solving this

Every comparable browser-facing dev-environment platform I could check embeds the
routing identity in the URL itself rather than in a header, for exactly the reason
above — a browser can't set custom headers on the requests that matter. They differ on
*where* in the URL, but not on the underlying principle:

- **Coder** (the company behind `code-server`, the tool this issue is literally about)
  exposes forwarded ports both via a wildcard subdomain (`<port>.<subdomain>`) *and* via
  a plain **path**, `<url>/proxy/<port>` — i.e. the same shape as this PR, port encoded
  directly in the path, no special client support required.
- **GitHub Codespaces** forwards ports via a dedicated subdomain per
  workspace+port (`{codespace}-{port}.app.github.dev`).
- **Gitpod** does the same (subdomain per workspace+port).
- **OpenSandbox**, another ephemeral-sandbox platform in this space, does it path-based
  too: its SDK's `sandbox.get_endpoint(port)` mints a URL shaped as either
  `<host>/<sandbox-id>/<port>/` (ingress-gateway mode) or
  `<host>/v1/sandboxes/<sandbox-id>/proxy/<port>/` (server-proxy mode) — sandbox ID and
  port encoded directly in the path, essentially the same shape this PR proposes,
  consumed by a gateway/proxy that strips the prefix before forwarding to the pod.

Subdomain-based routing needs wildcard DNS and a wildcard/SAN TLS cert per environment,
which is heavier infra than a single path-routed hostname — that's the trade-off this PR
leans away from by choosing path over subdomain, but the core idea (identity travels in
the URL a browser can construct, not in a header it can't send) is the same one every
one of these platforms already converged on independently.

One thing worth flagging for anyone adopting this flag specifically for a dev-server
preview use case (Vite/webpack HMR, not just a static-file tool like code-server), since
it's exactly what OpenSandbox's path-based setup above also had to deal with: Vite/webpack
emit *absolute* `/@vite/`, `/@fs/` paths that break under any path prefix, so a plain
`vite`/`webpack-dev-server` can't sit behind a path-routed proxy unmodified — it needs its
own small reverse proxy in front of it (outside the scope of this router) that re-adds the
stripped prefix, rewrites `<base href>`, and tunnels the HMR WebSocket itself, told its own
public path prefix out-of-band before it starts. Not something this router needs to know
or do anything about, but a heads-up so "the editor works under `--path-routing-prefix`
but a Vite dev server's HMR doesn't" isn't mistaken for something this PR broke.

Deliberately **not** proposing:
- Any change to `X-Sandbox-Pod-IP` / `X-Sandbox-UID` handling — both stay header-only,
  since they're dial-target overrides for SDKs that already hold cluster-internal
  knowledge, never appropriate for a browser tab.
- Any change to the router's "no authentication by default" model — a path-derived
  identifier is no more or less protected than the same identifier in a header is today;
  the one real trade-off is that a path shows up in browser history / referrer / access
  logs in a way a header doesn't, which is exactly why this is opt-in rather than the
  default.

title: Default NetworkPolicy on SandboxTemplate doesn't match the project's own sandbox-router deploy manifests

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### What happened?

When `SandboxTemplate.spec.networkPolicyManagement` is left unset (defaults to `Managed`), the controller generates a default `NetworkPolicy` (`buildDefaultNetworkPolicySpec` in `extensions/controllers/sandboxtemplate_controller.go`) that only allows ingress from:
- namespace `agent-sandbox-system`
- pods labeled `app: sandbox-router`

But the project's own reference deployment (`sandbox-router/deploy/*.yaml`) ships the router to namespace `default`, labeled `app.kubernetes.io/name: sandbox-router`. Neither matches the hardcoded default. Following the project's own docs for both the controller and the router, with no misconfiguration of your own, still produces a silently dropped connection (`dial tcp ...: i/o timeout`) between the router and the Sandbox pod.

We also checked Google Cloud's own official GKE tutorial for this project: [Isolate AI code execution with Agent Sandbox](https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/how-to/agent-sandbox). Its `SandboxTemplate` manifest sets no `networkPolicyManagement`/`networkPolicy` field either, and its own `sandbox-router-svc`/`sandbox-router-deployment` are both deployed to `namespace: default`, the identical mismatch, in Google's own published, official example.


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy the controller with default settings (no custom `networkPolicy` on any `SandboxTemplate`)
2. Deploy `sandbox-router` per `sandbox-router/deploy/`
3. `CreateSandbox`/`Write`/`Run` via the Go SDK's default tunnel connection strategy: times out


### Version

v0.5.6

### Anything else we need to know?

**Workaround:** write a custom `spec.networkPolicy` on the `SandboxTemplate` matching wherever your router actually lives.

**Possibly related:** #1044 (default policy's `podSelector` also didn't match warm-pool pods; different label, same feature area) and #1057 (the Go SDK's own tunnel config hardcodes `agent-sandbox-system` as the router's namespace, same "assumed fixed namespace" root cause, client-side instead of controller-side).

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR makes the working directory of the python-runtime-sandbox configurable through a new `SANDBOX_BASE_DIR` env var.

Running the sandbox with `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` is not possible today: `/app` is both where the code lives and where `/execute` and the file endpoints work, so uploads fail on the read-only rootfs and mounting a writable volume at `/app` shadows `main.py`. With `SANDBOX_BASE_DIR` pointing at a writable mount (e.g. an emptyDir at `/workspace`) the code stays on the read-only image and the file API keeps working. It defaults to `/app`, so existing deployments are not affected. Same pattern already used for `SANDBOX_EXEC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`.

It also fixes `/upload` to create the parent directories, otherwise a filename like `data/input.csv` returns a 500 because `open()` does not create them. The path is already confined by `get_safe_path`.

Tested on a kind cluster with the pod locked down (restricted PSA, non-root, seccomp RuntimeDefault, caps dropped, read-only rootfs). 5 new tests added, full suite passes (26).

BR

NONE

title: router cache: fence stale Pod events by Pod UID

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
## Summary

The sandbox-router cache keys routing entries by Sandbox UID, but it does not retain the backing Pod UID. During Pod recreation, a delayed delete or NotReady event from the old Pod removes the cache entry for the replacement Pod.

## Reproduction

Using the current cache handlers with two Pods that have the same Sandbox owner UID and the same Pod name but different Pod UIDs:

1. Add old Pod `P1` for Sandbox UID `S`; cache stores its IP.
2. Add replacement Pod `P2` for the same Sandbox UID `S`; cache stores the replacement IP.
3. Deliver a delayed Delete event for `P1`, or a NotReady update for `P1`.
4. The current cache removes `S` entirely, including the entry for `P2`.

This reproduced deterministically in a temporary cache test, 20/20 runs for both Delete and NotReady events.

## Impact

Requests routed through the cache can temporarily fall back to DNS or fail with an upstream resolution or connection error even though the replacement Sandbox Pod is Ready. This is relevant to warm-pool rotation, Pod recreation, and informer relist or compaction ordering.

## Proposed fix

- Store the backing Pod UID in `cache.Entry`.
- Make Delete and NotReady removal conditional on both Sandbox UID and Pod UID.
- Preserve the existing name-index fencing behavior for recreated Pods.
- Add regression tests proving stale old-Pod events cannot evict the current replacement entry.

This is limited to the router cache and does not change the Sandbox API.

title: multi-cluster-fleet: add multi-cluster warm-pool planner, part 1/4

labels.name: size/XXL

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds the Python package for a new `fleet: a fleet planner that pre-warms `SandboxWarmPool` capacity across many clusters from a single spec, so an RL rollout or batch-eval workload can reach a scale no single cluster can hold.

**This is PR 1 of 4** It contains only the Python package and its unit tests — no deploy manifests, no Go library, no hub tooling. Those follow and are independently reviewable:

| PR | contents |
|---|---|
| **1 (this)** | `python/` package + tests, `ARCHITECTURE.md` |
| 2 | deploy manifests, kind quickstart, `README.md`, `TESTING.md` |
| 3 | ClusterProfile hub setup + scale/diagnostic tooling |

##### How it works

Placement is mediated entirely through object storage — there is no new control plane. A per-cluster `fleet-member` reads its slice of `assignments.json` from a shared bucket and reconciles local `SandboxWarmPool` objects; `SandboxTemplate` CRs stay operator-managed (kubectl or GitOps) and the member only verifies they exist.

Placement is capacity-aware: each member publishes warm-pool depth, ready count, in-flight claims and node pressure on an interval, and the planner weights the split by what clusters actually report. The split uses Hamilton largest-remainder so per-cluster totals sum exactly to the fleet target rather than drifting by rounding.

Inventory is pluggable. By default the planner discovers clusters from capacity reports in the bucket; it can instead read SIG-Multicluster [`ClusterProfile`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cluster-inventory-api) CRs from a hub, with each member publishing its own capacity into its own profile via server-side apply. The spec and `assignments.json` travel through the bucket either way.

##### What's in this PR

`python/agent_sandbox_fleet/`, 15 modules:

- `planner.py`, `budget.py`, `sizing.py`, `placement.py` — the plan behind `fleetctl apply`: cluster selection, replica sizing, Hamilton split
- `cli.py` — `fleetctl` (`apply`, `status`, `show-assignments`, `show-registry`, `route`)
- `fleet_member.py` — the per-cluster daemon: reconcile pools, publish capacity
- `inventory.py` — the two inventory sources (bucket capacity reports, ClusterProfile hub) behind one interface
- `publisher.py`, `hubauth.py`, `hubcheck.py` — ClusterProfile SSA publishing, hub credentials, preflight
- `objectstore.py`, `resolver.py`, `registry_rewrite.py`, `trainer.py` — GCS client, template→cluster routing, image-host rewriting, weight-manifest reference implementation

Entry points: `fleetctl`, `fleet-member`, `fleet-hubcheck`.


##### Testing

118 unit tests (`python/tests/`), pure Python — no cluster, bucket, or network required. Run with `pip install -e ./python[test] && pytest`.

The suite is **not yet wired into presubmit**: `dev/tools/test-unit` carries an explicit registry of example Python suites and this one isn't in it. Registering it needs the package's runtime deps installed (including `k8s-agent-sandbox` from the local sibling path, as `agent-sandbox-rl` already does), so I've left it out of this PR to keep it scoped. Happy to add it here instead if reviewers would rather it land together.

##### What this deliberately does not do

- **CRD-ify the fleet spec** — it ships as JSON in a bucket. A `SandboxFleet` CRD is future work.
- **Route user-facing `SandboxClaim`s across clusters** — this is fleet-driven pre-warming only; claim routing is a separate concern.
- **Distribute model weights** — `trainer.py` writes manifests and fake deltas for reference, but nothing consumes them.

title: Add Template printer column to SandboxWarmPool for -o wide

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

When managing multiple SandboxWarmPools backed by different SandboxTemplates, `kubectl get sandboxwarmpool` currently shows only Ready, Desired, and Age. There is no way to see which template backs which pool without inspecting each resource individually.

  Adding sandboxTemplateRef.name as a priority=1 printer column (visible with -o wide) would make the pool-to-template mapping immediately visible:
```
  $ kubectl get sandboxwarmpool -o wide
  NAME              READY   DESIRED   AGE   TEMPLATE
  python-warmpool   3       3         10m   python-sandbox-template
  node-warmpool     5       5         10m   node-sandbox-template
```
  
  PR #1002 previously proposed this (among other columns for all four CRDs) and received lgtm but was self-closed due to inactivity, not a design objection. PR #1053 later landed just the Desired column from that set. This issue is scoped to the single remaining Template column on SandboxWarmPool.

  The implementation is a one-line kubebuilder marker addition. I'm happy to send the PR if there's no objection.

### Why is this needed?

This came up during a demo where I had several warm pools running and lost track of which pool mapped to which template.

body:
## What

Two pieces, working toward launching 1M sandboxes/minute across 10 clusters (100k/cluster in 60s, ~1,667/s each):

1. **Controller: one status write per launch** (`--sandbox-transitional-status-window`, default off)
   - `materialStatusChange`: explicit material-vs-transitional classification of status changes (condition value flips, Finished add/removal, and terminal Ready reasons are material; reason/message churn and field fills are transitional).
   - Transitional writes on sandboxes younger than the window defer and ride the Ready flip; stuck sandboxes flush an explanatory status at age == window via RequeueAfter. Crash-safe: deferred writes are recomputed from informer state (same argument as #1252).
   - `staleCacheGuard`: skips reconcile passes running against an informer copy that predates the controller's own last write (rv-equality only; the write's own watch event guarantees a fresh pass) — these passes produced ~39k no-op PATCHes per 50k launches.

2. **`scaleup-kops-gcp` scenario + `scaleup` presubmit/periodic**: kindnet, maxPods=512, /22 node pod CIDRs, fill-phase launch with a rate-vs-target verdict; shared runner gains backward-compatible knobs (node size/zone, maxPods, node CIDR mask, scheduler QPS, APF inflight, validate wait, benchmark-suite skip).

## Measured (100 nodes × 500 sandboxes = 50k, n2-standard-64 CP, 6-run campaign)

| run | change | best-60s ready | all 50k Ready |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | baseline | 496/s | 164s |
| 2 | scheduler client QPS 500→4000 | 602/s | 146s |
| 3 | APF inflight 400/200→3200/1600 | 679/s | 114s |
| 6 | **this PR's controller change** | **757/s** | **99.5s** |

Run 6 mechanics: sandbox status PATCHes 107,333 → 48,446 (0.97/launch), stale no-ops eliminated, pod-ready p50 55.9s → 40.5s (freed APF seats accelerate the pod path), zero failed launches.

Negative results are encoded as comments where the knobs live: uncapping the controller client without this PR's write gating inflated transitional writes 76% and lost throughput in both APF lanes tried (runs 4–5); the controller-in-workload-high FlowSchema ships unapplied for experiments.

## WIP

- [ ] Rerun with controller client QPS uncapped now that transitional writes are structurally gated (expected to close the ~30s pod-ready→sandbox-Ready gap)
- [ ] 200-node full leg (needs ~1,700 vCPUs quota) and target-enforcement flip
- [ ] Possibly retire the pod-name annotation write (derivable pod names?)

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
In `examples/python-runtime-sandbox/main.py`, the `/execute` handler is `async def` but called blocking `subprocess.run(...)` directly on the event loop, with no timeout. Two consequences:

1. Any exec (even a legitimate 30s command) starved the event loop, so the health-check endpoint (`GET /`) and all file endpoints stopped answering for the duration of the exec.
2. A command that never exits (`sleep infinity`, a process waiting on stdin, a crashed-but-not-exited child) blocked the loop forever with no timeout to recover it — the sandbox stayed up but stopped responding to everything, indefinitely.

This PR wraps the `subprocess.run` call in `asyncio.to_thread(...)` so it runs off the event loop (health check and file endpoints keep responding while a command executes), and adds a `timeout=` argument sourced from a new `SANDBOX_EXEC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` env var (default `300`). `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` falls into the handler's existing `except Exception` clause and is reported as a normal failed execution (`exit_code=1`, descriptive `stderr`), matching the shape of every other error path in this handler — no new failure mode is introduced.

Note: this fixes the event loop being starved / the server becoming unresponsive to other endpoints — it does not change behavior around process crashes, and normal `/execute` responses for successful commands are unchanged.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1375

#### Release Note
```release-note
Fixed `/execute` in the python-runtime-sandbox example blocking the event loop (and the health check with it) for the duration of every command, and added a `SANDBOX_EXEC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` (default 300s) timeout so a runaway or hung command no longer wedges the sandbox indefinitely.
```

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`exec.CommandContext` only sends SIGKILL to the child PID on context cancellation, not its process group. Since Start/Execute use `Setpgid: true`, grandchildren survive as orphans when the parent is killed (e.g. client disconnect).

**Fix:** Replace `exec.CommandContext` with `exec.Command`, add `killProcessGroupOnContextDone` helper that signals `-PGID` (whole process group) on context cancellation. Also check context before forking to avoid starting commands we'd immediately kill.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
N/A

#### Release Note
```release-note
Fixed orphan process leak in sandboxd when clients disconnect from long-running commands with grandchildren.
```

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

In `reconcileChildResources`, the `err` variable was reused for both `reconcilePod` and `reconcileService` return values. By the time `computeConditions` was called, `err` held the service error, which was then passed as the `podErr` parameter.

Fix: capture pod and service errors in separate variables (`podErr`, `svcErr`) and pass the correct one to `computeConditions`.

title: Python client: Filesystem.write only accepts bytes/str, forcing whole payloads into memory — accept file-like objects and stream

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added

`Filesystem.write` / `AsyncFilesystem.write` (k8s-agent-sandbox 0.5.4) accept `content: bytes | str`, so a caller must materialize the entire payload in memory before uploading. For large workspace files (datasets, archives, model outputs) that is a transient memory spike on the client, and callers integrating the sandbox behind streaming-oriented interfaces (e.g. the OpenAI Agents SDK's sandbox session contract, which hands backends an `io.IOBase` precisely so they can stream) end up buffering or imposing artificial size caps.

The wall is thin, because both ends already stream:

- the transport (`httpx` / `requests`) natively streams file-like objects in multipart payloads — `files={"file": (path, fileobj)}` works today;
- the runtime server receives the upload through FastAPI's `UploadFile`, which spools to disk rather than holding memory.

Only the client signature forces the buffering.

### Proposed change

Widen the accepted type and pass file-like objects through:

```python
async def write(self, path: str, content: bytes | str | BinaryIO, ...):
    if isinstance(content, str):
        content = content.encode("utf-8")
    # bytes -> as today; file-like -> handed to the transport, which streams it
    files_payload = {"file": (path, content)}
```

The only wrinkle is the tracing attribute `sandbox.file.size`, which calls `len(content)` — for file-like objects it could be omitted or derived via `os.fstat` when available.

Happy to send this as a PR (CLA in progress on our side); filing the issue first per the contributor guide.

/kind feature

title: python-runtime example: /execute blocks the event loop and has no timeout — one hung command wedges the sandbox permanently

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### What happened

In `examples/python-runtime-sandbox/main.py`, the `/execute` handler is `async def` but calls blocking `subprocess.run(...)` directly on the event loop, with no timeout:

```python
@app.post("/execute", ...)
async def execute_command(request: ExecuteRequest):
    ...
    process = subprocess.run(args, capture_output=True, text=True, cwd="/app")
```

Two consequences:

1. **Every exec freezes the whole server for its duration** — `GET /` (the readiness probe target) and all file endpoints stop answering while a command runs. A legitimate 60-second command makes the sandbox appear dead to Kubernetes for 60 seconds.
2. **A command that never exits wedges the sandbox permanently and invisibly.** `sleep infinity`, a process waiting on stdin, or a crashed-but-not-exited child blocks the loop forever. The client's request timeout gives up, but the server thread stays blocked — no probe can distinguish this from a long legitimate exec, so the pod is never recycled and the claim is effectively lost.

### Reproduction

Against the example image: `POST /execute {"command": "sleep 8"}` from one client, then `GET /` from another — the health check hangs until the sleep completes. With `sleep infinity`, the sandbox never answers anything again.

### Fix that worked for us

Two small changes (verified: health answers mid-exec, runaway commands are killed server-side):

```python
process = await asyncio.to_thread(
    subprocess.run,
    args,
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
    cwd="/app",
    timeout=float(os.environ.get("SANDBOX_EXEC_TIMEOUT_SECONDS", "300")),
)
```

`asyncio.to_thread` keeps the loop free (health + file endpoints stay live during execs), and the operator-side timeout guarantees the box always comes back. `subprocess.TimeoutExpired` lands in the handler's existing `except Exception` and is reported as a failed execution, which seems like the right shape.

Happy to send this as a PR (CLA in progress on our side); filing the issue first per the contributor guide.

/kind bug

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds `clients/integrations/nemo-gym`, a Python package (`nemo-gym-k8s-agent-sandbox`) that makes Agent Sandbox a sandbox backend for [NVIDIA NeMo Gym](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym) RL training environments, alongside NeMo Gym's built-in providers (Docker, Daytona, ECS Fargate, Enroot, OpenShell, OpenSandbox, Apptainer).

NeMo Gym discovers third-party providers through its `nemo_gym.sandbox_providers` entry-point group, so installing this package next to `nemo-gym` makes `agent_sandbox` a valid provider name with no registration code and no NeMo Gym fork.

Design highlights:
- **Warm-pool claims**: sandboxes are checked out via SandboxClaim -> SandboxWarmPool, so per-rollout acquisition is claim-bind latency rather than pod start. Images route to pools through a `create.image_warmpools` mapping (claims are `warmPoolRef`-only in v1beta1).
- **TTL safety net**: NeMo Gym's `ttl_s` maps to the claim lifecycle `shutdownTime` with `Delete` policy, so the controller GCs sandboxes even if the training process dies.
- **Runtime API adaptation**: the in-sandbox runtime execs via `shlex.split` with no shell, and its file API only accepts relative paths — commands are wrapped in `sh -c` scripts (cwd/env folded in, all user input shell-quoted), and absolute-path file transfers stage through flat temp names.
- **Readiness probe**: a bound claim proves the pod is Ready, not that the runtime HTTP server (or a gateway route) is reachable, so create polls a cheap exec before handing the sandbox out.

Layout, naming, and packaging follow `clients/integrations/deepagents`. Includes 29 unit tests (fakes only, no cluster), an annotated NeMo Gym provider config, and a README documenting the spec-field mapping and limitations (no endpoint resolution / `ConnectableProvider` support yet; `entrypoint`/`user`/`resources` are template-owned).

**Note for reviewers**: the provider requires `k8s-agent-sandbox~=0.5.1` — `create_sandbox(volume_claim_templates=...)` landed in 0.5.1 — and always passes `AsyncSandboxClient(cleanup=...)` explicitly, since the client's own default flipped from `False` (0.5.0) to `True` (0.5.1).

Added a NeMo Gym integration (`clients/integrations/nemo-gym`): installing the `nemo-gym-k8s-agent-sandbox` package registers Agent Sandbox warm pools as the `agent_sandbox` sandbox provider in NVIDIA NeMo Gym.
```

title: SandboxClaim: createSandbox has no IsAlreadyExists path, so a stale-cache requeue hard-errors and the claim can never bind

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
## Summary

`SandboxClaimReconciler.createSandbox` calls `r.Create` and treats **every** error as fatal:

```go
// extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go (v0.5.0 L1238, main L1661)
if err := r.Create(ctx, sandbox); err != nil {
    err = fmt.Errorf("sandbox create error: %w", err)
    logger.Error(err, "Error creating sandbox for claim", "claimName", claim.Name)
    return nil, err
}
```

There is no `apierrors.IsAlreadyExists` branch — `IsAlreadyExists` appears **zero times** in this file, on `v0.5.0` and on `main`.

The caller reaches it from the cold path:

```go
// Cold path: no existing sandbox or warm pool candidate.
logger.V(1).Info("Cold path: no sandbox found, creating from template", ...)
return r.createSandbox(ctx, claim, template)
```

That lookup goes through the cached client. On a requeue shortly after a successful create, the cache can still be stale, so the reconciler concludes no Sandbox exists, creates a second one, and gets `AlreadyExists` — which it returns as a hard error rather than adopting the object it just made.

## Observed

Single-node cluster, five SandboxClaims created within ~90 seconds:

```
Error creating sandbox for claim ...
  error="sandbox create error: sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io \"curie-thread-6e53581a8e-d7695e\" already exists"

Failed to patch sandboxclaim status ...
  error="sandboxclaims.extensions.agents.x-k8s.io \"curie-thread-0cddbb83bd-cc4e4e\" not found"

Failed to update sandbox status ...
  error="pod \"curie-thread-0cddbb83bd-cc4e4e\" is owned by Sandbox/curie-thread-0cddbb83bd-cc4e4e
         (UID: 7a223385-...), not by sandbox \"curie-thread-0cddbb83bd-cc4e4e\""
```

The third line is the interesting one: a pod whose owner is a Sandbox of the **same name but a different UID**, i.e. the object was deleted and recreated underneath it.

## Why it is more than noise

`AlreadyExists` puts the claim into controller-runtime's exponential backoff. Our consumer gives a claim 90s to bind; claims that bind normally do so in **~19s** (pods Ready in 10–20s, node at 16% CPU). So the deadline is nowhere near the happy path — but once backoff outlasts it, the consumer tears the claim down mid-flight, which produces the orphaned pod and the UID mismatch above, and the next attempt races the leftovers again.

The user-visible result is a request that fails after 3 attempts **while the sandbox is healthy and serving** — in our case the runner came up in 5s, ran the request to completion in 36s, and the caller had already given up.

## Suggested fix

Adopt on conflict rather than failing:

```go
if err := r.Create(ctx, sandbox); err != nil {
    if apierrors.IsAlreadyExists(err) {
        existing := &v1beta1.Sandbox{}
        if getErr := r.Get(ctx, client.ObjectKeyFromObject(sandbox), existing); getErr == nil {
            if metav1.IsControlledBy(existing, claim) {
                return existing, nil          // our own object, from a stale-cache retry
            }
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("sandbox %q exists but is not controlled by claim %q",
                sandbox.Name, claim.Name)
        }
    }
    ...
}
```

The ownership check keeps the genuinely-conflicting case an error while making the self-collision idempotent, which is what a reconciler retry needs to be.

Happy to send a PR if the shape looks right.

## Environment

- controller `registry.k8s.io/agent-sandbox-controller:v0.5.0`; code inspected on `v0.5.0` and `main`
- Kubernetes v1.35 (k3s), single node
- claims created concurrently by an unrelated workload burst — three independent requests within ~7s

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds KEP-1348, the design for observing SandboxClaim startup from status
events: write-once timestamps under `status.startup`, a leader-elected
observer that records the existing Prometheus histograms off the Claim
workqueue's critical path, and lazy migration for existing Claims. The design
moves startup observability out of the authoritative reconcile path so a
failed observability PATCH can no longer turn a successful reconcile into a
retry, and makes the startup facts inspectable in status without a Prometheus
sample.

Key decisions:
- No dedicated feature gate; the fields enter v1beta1 as beta API after the
  Performance acceptance criteria are met.
- CEL transition rules enforce write-once semantics and the
  `firstReadyTime` / `firstReadyTimeUnavailable` mutual exclusion.

Docs-only change; `make toc-verify` passes.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1348

#### Release Note

```release-note
NONE
```

Overview

Added

  • Add experimental observability metrics to BatchProcessor in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log. (#7124)
  • Add the experimental WithUnsafeAttributes no-copy attribute option to go.opentelemetry.io/otel/metric/x for future performance improvements. This API is a work in progress. (#8251)
  • Add Map and MapValue functions for the new MAP attribute type in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute. (#8445)
  • Support MAP attributes in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace. (#8453)
  • Support MAP attributes in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog. (#8453)
  • Support MAP attributes in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlpmetric. (#8453)
  • Support MAP attributes in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/zipkin. (#8453)
  • Apply AttributeValueLengthLimit recursively to values contained in attribute.MAP attributes in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace. (#8454)
  • Remove duplicate keys from attribute.MAP values in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/resource using last-value-wins semantics. (#8471)
  • Remove duplicate keys by default from attribute.MAP values in instrumentation scope attributes in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log using last-value-wins semantics. (#8471)
  • Remove duplicate keys by default from attribute.MAP values in span, event, link, and instrumentation scope attributes in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace using last-value-wins semantics. (#8471)
  • Remove duplicate keys by default from attribute.MAP values in measurement and instrumentation scope attributes in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/metric using last-value-wins semantics. (#8471)
  • Extend WithAllowKeyDuplication in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log to disable duplicate-key removal in attribute.MAP values for instrumentation scope attributes. (#8471)
  • Add the go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.42.0 package. The package contains semantic conventions from the v1.42.0 version of the OpenTelemetry Semantic Conventions. See the migration documentation for information on how to upgrade from go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.41.0. (#8484)
  • Add WithoutPanicRecording as a TracerProviderOption in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/trace to disable exception event recording for panics. (#8532)
  • Add the go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.43.0 package. The package contains semantic conventions from the v1.43.0 version of the OpenTelemetry Semantic Conventions. See the migration documentation for information on how to upgrade from go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/v1.42.0. (#8628)

Changed

  • HistogramReservoir in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/metric/exemplar now uses a time-unbiased sampling algorithm for exemplars. (#8306)

(#8490)
  • Encode log bodies and attributes as go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute.Value JSON in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/stdout/stdoutlog. (#8490)
  • Improve the performance of hashing BOOLSLICE, INT64SLICE, FLOAT64SLICE, and STRINGSLICE attribute values by avoiding reflection for short slices in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/attribute. (#8511)
  • ⚠️ Breaking Change: WithEndpointURL in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlpmetric/otlpmetrichttp no longer appends the default signal path when an endpoint URL has no path, making the behavior consistent with go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploghttp and with setting the endpoint through OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT. If the URL has no path component, the root path (/) is used. Use WithEndpointURL(url.JoinPath(endpoint, "/v1/metrics")) to preserve the previous behavior. (#8538)
  • ⚠️ Breaking Change: WithEndpointURL in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracehttp no longer appends the default signal path when an endpoint URL has no path, making the behavior consistent with go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploghttp and with setting the endpoint through OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TRACES_ENDPOINT. If the URL has no path component, the root path (/) is used. Use WithEndpointURL(url.JoinPath(endpoint, "/v1/traces")) to preserve the previous behavior. (#8538)

Deprecated

  • Deprecate WithExportBufferSize in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log. The option remains available for source compatibility but no longer affects behavior; BatchProcessor no longer maintains a separate export-request buffer. (#8620)

Removed

  • ⚠️ Breaking Change: Remove Kind, Value, KeyValue, their constructors, and attribute conversion helpers from go.opentelemetry.io/otel/log. (#8490)
  • ⚠️ Breaking Change: Remove the AttributeValueLengthLimit and AttributeCountLimit fields from RecordFactory in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/log/logtest; records produced by the factory now keep attribute limits disabled so test code can append exact attributes. (#8556)

Fixed

  • Apply TLS certificates configured through environment variables to gRPC connections in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploggrpc.
  • Prevent panics in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/bridge/opentracing when OpenTracing baggage is propagated concurrently with Span.SetBaggageItem.
  • Fix an off-by-one error in FixedSizeReservoir in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/sdk/metric/exemplar that prevented the first exemplar from being sampled after the reservoir was filled. (#8309)
  • Interpret HTTP Retry-After header values as seconds instead of nanoseconds when retrying OTLP HTTP exports in go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlptrace/otlptracehttp, go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlpmetric/otlpmetrichttp, and go.opentelemetry.io/otel/exporters/otlp/otlplog/otlploghttp. (#8383)

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it

Adds `docs/performance-tuning.md` — the benchmark evidence and sizing rationale behind the high-throughput controller flags, covering burst vs. sustained traffic profiles.

Prompted by @barney-s's review comment on #1251:
> Would be useful to have a guide/readme on how to setup all these values for a high perf cluster.

#### Relationship to #1593

Since this PR was opened, #1593 added the flag documentation and a High-Throughput & Scale Tuning quick-start to `docs/configuration.md`. This PR has been restructured to complement it rather than duplicate it: `configuration.md` remains the canonical flag reference; `performance-tuning.md` adds what the reference deliberately leaves out — the A/B benchmark data, per-knob sizing rules, and trade-off analysis. The two docs cross-link and agree on sizing rules (refill rate ≥ per-pool arrival rate, warm-pool workers sized to pool count, batch size default under the expectations gate).

#### What's covered

- **Benchmark data**: GKE live A/B (75-claim burst from a 150-sandbox warm pool; worker-count sweep + per-flag configs A–I) and kops PR-level benchmarks (45/s Poisson warm-adoption latency; write-behind two-configuration A/B).
- **Warm-adoption prerequisites**: `spec.env` / `spec.volumeClaimTemplates` on a claim force a cold start and bypass the warm pool entirely (verified in `sandboxclaim_controller.go`).
- **Warm pool refill shaping**: `--sandbox-warm-pool-max-refill-rate` (~15% p50/p90 improvement, no failure mode; also paces initial fill) vs `--sandbox-warm-pool-replenish-delay` (neutral in isolation; pool-drain fragility under load — 1/75 failed claim create produced p90=205 s).
- **Write reduction**: `--disable-claim-events`, `--disable-claim-observability-annotations` (documented as removing the dedicated write; the stamped values can still persist via later full-object updates), and `--sandbox-write-behind-window` with its measured trade-off (−44% 409s, −13% burst p50, **+58% sustained p50** — omitted from the sustained profile for that reason).
- **Two benchmark-validated profiles** (sustained ✅ / burst ⚠️ with prerequisites) and an idempotent, name-aware strategic-merge patch for applying flags to a live cluster.

#### Verification

Everything in the doc was re-verified against current `main` (d9a67516) and on a live GKE cluster (gke-ai-eco-dev):
- Every flag name/default matches `cmd/agent-sandbox-controller/main.go`; both profile arg sets parse and roll out cleanly.
- 75/75 claims warm-adopted sub-second under the sustained profile; refill pacing confirmed at a rate cap of 10/s; the 20 s replenish-delay deferral observed exactly as documented; `--disable-claim-events` suppression confirmed.
- The strategic-merge patch command verified idempotent and name-targeted (the previous append-based JSON patch duplicated args on re-run and is replaced).

labels.name: size/L

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`commands.run()` sends `POST /execute`, which runs a shell command inside the
sandbox. Both Python connectors retried that request on 500/502/503/504, so a
command whose response failed after the runtime had already run it was executed
again — six attempts in total. The caller saw a single `SandboxRequestError`
with no indication that the command had run more than once.

A retryable status code means the connection succeeded and the request body
reached the server, so the work it describes may already be done. This change
limits transport-level replay to `GET`, `PUT` and `DELETE`: the sync connector
drops `POST` from the urllib3 `Retry(allowed_methods=...)`, and the async
connector checks the method alongside the status code.

Concretely, for a `POST`:

| Failure mode | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Server answers 5xx | replayed | not replayed |
| Body sent, no response (read error, sync connector) | replayed | not replayed |
| Never connected (dial error) | unchanged | unchanged |

The read-error row changes for the same reason as the 5xx row: the body reached
the server, so the command may already be running. Dial-time failures are
untouched — urllib3's `allowed_methods` does not gate connect-error retries, and
the async connector never retried transport errors to begin with.

This matches how the rest of the project draws the line. `Run()` in the Go SDK
defaults to a single attempt, and the router retries dial-class failures only
because replaying a body that may already have been sent could duplicate side
effects.

Testing: two regression tests were added, both failing before this change and
passing after — `test_connector.py::TestSandboxConnectorStrategySelection::test_post_requests_are_not_retried`
and `test_async_sandboxclient.py::TestAsyncConnector::test_post_requests_are_not_retried_on_server_error`.
`make test-unit` passes. The behaviour was also verified end to end against a
stub runtime that performs a side effect and then answers 503: it records the
command executed 6 times on `main` and once with this change, for both the sync
and async connectors.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1352

#### Release Note

```release-note
Fixed the Python SDK re-executing sandbox commands after a transient server error.
```

title: Python SDK re-executes sandbox commands after a transient 5xx

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### What happened?

`commands.run()` sends `POST /execute`, which runs a shell command inside the
sandbox. Both Python connectors retry that request on 500/502/503/504, so a
command whose response failed *after* the runtime already ran it is executed
again — six attempts in total.

The retry policy lives in the transport layer, which only sees the HTTP method
and the status code, never the endpoint:

- `k8s_agent_sandbox/connector.py` lists `POST` in the urllib3
  `Retry(allowed_methods=...)` mounted on the session.
- `k8s_agent_sandbox/async_connector.py` retries on the status code alone,
  without looking at the method.

Retrying here is different from retrying a request that never arrived. A status
code means the connection succeeded and the body reached the server, so the
command has most likely already run. Re-sending it runs the command a second
time.

I expected the SDK to surface the error after a single execution, which is what
the rest of the project does:

- The Go SDK defaults `Run()` to one attempt and documents why command
  execution must not be replayed (`clients/go/sandbox/commands.go`,
  `clients/go/README.md`).
- The router retries dial-class failures only, because "failures after the
  request body may have been sent ... bubble up immediately because replaying a
  partially-sent body could duplicate side effects"
  (`sandbox-router/proxy/retry.go`, `sandbox-router/README.md`).

Nothing on the server side makes the replay safe: `/execute` runs the command
and returns, with no request de-duplication.

The practical trigger does not require an unhealthy cluster. A command that
outlives the router's `--proxy-timeout` (default 180s) gets a 504 while the
process keeps running in the pod, and the SDK then starts the command again.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

No cluster required. This stub runtime performs a real side effect and only
then answers 503, mirroring a runtime that finished the command but failed the
response. It counts side effects rather than requests:

```python
import json, threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer
from k8s_agent_sandbox.connector import SandboxConnector
from k8s_agent_sandbox.exceptions import SandboxRequestError
from k8s_agent_sandbox.models import SandboxDirectConnectionConfig

executions = []

class FakeRuntime(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
    def do_POST(self):
        body = self.rfile.read(int(self.headers.get("Content-Length") or 0))
        executions.append(json.loads(body)["command"])   # the side effect
        self.send_response(503)
        self.send_header("Content-Length", "0")
        self.end_headers()

    def log_message(self, *_):
        pass

server = HTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), FakeRuntime)
threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True).start()

connector = SandboxConnector(
    sandbox_id="repro", namespace="default",
    connection_config=SandboxDirectConnectionConfig(
        api_url=f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}"),
    k8s_helper=None,
)
try:
    connector.send_request("POST", "execute", json={"command": "echo x >> /app/log.txt"})
except SandboxRequestError as exc:
    print("caller saw:", exc)
print("commands executed:", len(executions))
```

Output on current `main`:

```
caller saw: Failed to communicate with the sandbox at http://127.0.0.1:.../execute.
commands executed: 6
```

Expected: `commands executed: 1`.

The async connector behaves the same way; substituting `AsyncSandboxConnector`
also records 6 executions, with `Retryable status 503 ... attempt 1/6 ... 5/6`
in the logs.

The caller sees a single `SandboxRequestError` in both cases, with no
indication that the command already ran six times. The retries also add about
15s of latency to a failure the SDK cannot recover from.

### Version

Current `main` (`108be73`). Present since `749a1ce5` (sync connector) and
`e272eee8` (async connector).

### Anything else we need to know?

I have a fix and regression tests ready and will open a pull request shortly.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

A `get_sandbox_status` tool for the Agent Sandbox MCP server (clients/integrations/mcp-server).
The tool takes a sandbox claim name + namespace and returns the sandbox's readiness, 
e.g.:
```
json
{ "status": "SandboxReady", "ready": true, "message": "..." }
```
status is one of SandboxReady / SandboxNotReady / SandboxNotFound.

It is a thin wrapper over the existing Python SDK method `AsyncSandbox.status()`, which already reads the Sandbox's Kubernetes Ready condition. No SDK or runtime changes are required. Like the other tools, it routes through the existing `get_sandbox()` helper, so it inherits the per-session ownership check unchanged and fails closed.

### Why is this needed?

The MCP server exposes `create_sandbox`, `delete_sandbox`, `execute_command`, `upload_file`, `download_file`, etc. but has no way to check whether a sandbox is `Ready`. An agent driving the server currently has to blindly call `execute_command` and interpret a connection error, instead of confirming readiness after creation, resume, or warm-pool adoption.

Follows the same cross-surface-parity motivation as #1329 (list_files/file_exists).

title: Observe SandboxClaim startup from status events

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Move SandboxClaim startup timing data from metadata annotations into write-once fields under status.startup. Add admissionObservedTime, controllerObservedTime, and firstReadyTime as metav1.MicroTime fields in v1beta1, the served storage version. Also add a true-only firstReadyTimeUnavailable marker for Claims where legacy evidence proves that First Ready occurred but no trustworthy timestamp can be recovered. The deprecated v1alpha1 API does not gain the fields.

The webhook continues to write the admission timestamp annotation during CREATE. The SandboxClaim controller remains the only component that writes `status.startup`: it initializes `controllerObservedTime` during startup-status initialization and sets `firstReadyTime` when it first computes `Ready=True`. Both fields may be persisted in a single status PATCH.

A separate leader-elected controller, `SandboxClaimMetricsObserver`, attaches to the shared SandboxClaim informer and enqueues only Update events where `firstReadyTime` changes from nil to non-nil. It rejects Create events, including initial Add delivery after restart or leader handoff. The controller uses its own workqueue and the shared manager cache, performs no writes to the API server, and records the existing Prometheus histograms.

Metric delivery remains best-effort and is not exposed through the API. A leader failure may lose queued work. Deployments with multiple controller replicas must keep leader election enabled to prevent duplicate observations.

CEL transition rules enforce timestamp immutability, prevent field removal, and keep `firstReadyTime` mutually exclusive with `firstReadyTimeUnavailable`.

New Claims stop receiving the controller-observation and First Ready annotations, and the controller stops persisting trace context on Claims. The webhook admission annotation remains as the handoff. The controller may read existing annotations during migration but does not delete them.

The fields enter v1beta1 as API compatibility commitments without a dedicated feature gate. A feature gate could stop future controller writes but cannot remove the published schema or existing status data. The supported downgrade rolls back only the controller and retains the new CRD schema.

### Why is this needed?

Startup observability currently runs inside the main SandboxClaim Reconcile loop. A Claim that reaches Ready may receive up to two extra metadata PATCHes:

1. The first active reconcile stores the controller observation time and optional trace context.
2. After the Ready status write, another PATCH stores the guard annotation used to prevent duplicate histogram observations.

The second PATCH runs after the Ready status write. If it fails, Reconcile returns an error even though the status update succeeded. A controller crash between the status write and the guard PATCH can also cause the sample to be recorded again after restart.

At a scale of 36,000 Claims in a single namespace, with every Claim reaching Ready, the two extra metadata PATCHes per Claim yield an arithmetic upper bound of 72,000 additional metadata writes. We'll include A/B benchmarks in the KEP to measure actual API server impact.

The SandboxClaim controller can persist startup timestamps with the existing status PATCH. The separate observer moves metric processing off the SandboxClaim controller's worker pool. The proposal removes up to two observability-related metadata PATCHes per Ready Claim while preserving existing histogram names, labels, buckets, and millisecond precision. Any impact on Ready latency will be evaluated in the KEP's A/B benchmarks.


**KEP:** In progress. A draft PR will be linked when it is ready for review.

body:
## What this PR does / why we need it

Part 3 of KEP-539.2 migrates the Go and Python client SDKs onto the `sandboxd` daemon (merged in Part 2, #1257): REST filesystem on `:8080` (`GET/PUT/DELETE /v1/files/{path}`, `/v1/health`, `/v1/metadata`) and the gRPC `ProcessService` on `:9090`, replacing the legacy `python-runtime` HTTP API (`/upload`, `/download`, `/list`, `/exists`, `/execute` on `:8888`).

Runtime selection is **explicit** — no probing. Legacy remains the default; nothing changes for existing users until they opt in.

## Transport: pod port-forward (0.0.0.0 bind)

`sandboxd` now binds `0.0.0.0` by default (new `--listen-host` flag; `--listen-host=127.0.0.1` still available for local dev), so it is reachable on the pod network like any other in-pod service — via a Kubernetes Service or the sandbox-router. This also fixes the kubelet `httpGet /v1/health` readiness probe and gVisor reachability.

The SDKs connect via a **pod port-forward** to the sandbox pod (both `:8080` and `:9090`); filesystem calls go over REST, `Run` over gRPC. The `ConnectionStrategy` seam is left in place so router/Service can become the default later without SDK API changes. Making the **router the default** is a follow-up: `sandbox-router` is HTTP/1.1-only and needs h2c/gRPC passthrough to proxy the `ProcessService`.

## Changes

**Daemon (`packages/sandboxd/cmd/sandboxd/main.go`)**
- `--listen-host` flag, default `0.0.0.0` (was hardcoded loopback). Containment is reframed as pod isolation + NetworkPolicy rather than loopback binding.

**Go SDK (`clients/go/sandbox/`)**
- `Options.Runtime` (`RuntimeLegacyPython` default / `RuntimeSandboxd`) + `SandboxdRESTPort`/`SandboxdGRPCPort`; validation rejects `RuntimeSandboxd` + `GatewayName`.
- `podtunnel.go`: SPDY port-forward to the sandbox pod forwarding both ports, publishing the REST base URL and gRPC target.
- Dual-path `Files` (`Write` PUT / `Read` / `List` / `Exists` HEAD) plus new `Delete(path, recursive)`; runtime-neutral `FileEntry` that parses both wire formats; `APIError` decoding; lazy gRPC `ProcessService.Execute` for `Run` (wrapped in `/bin/sh -c`). Write rejects `..` path segments client-side as defense in depth.

**Python SDK (`clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/`)**
- `SandboxdPodTunnelConnectionConfig` + `SandboxdPodTunnelStrategy` (kubectl port-forward to the pod, exposing REST + gRPC).
- Dual-path filesystem incl. `delete()`; `FileEntry` parses both formats; `run()` over gRPC (lazy stubs). Async client raises a clear `NotImplementedError` for sandboxd (out of scope; use the sync client).
- Codegen: `buf.gen.python.yaml` + `generate.go` wiring; stubs vendored under `_proto/` and imported through a `_process_stubs` shim. New `grpc` extra in `pyproject.toml`.

**Template / e2e / docs**
- `examples/sandboxd-sandbox/sandbox-template.yaml` (sidecar model; `httpGet /v1/health` readiness probe, enabled by the `0.0.0.0` bind).
- `test/e2e/extensions/sandboxd_test.go` — boots sandboxd and exercises REST (health + PUT/GET) and gRPC (`Execute`) via pod port-forward.
- USER_GUIDE "SDK access" + "Security model" sections; `generate-go-docs` strips brittle `#L<line>` anchors from generated source links.

## Testing

- **Go:** `go build ./...`, `go vet`, `golangci-lint`, and unit tests under `clients/go/sandbox/` (httptest REST + bufconn gRPC).
- **Python:** unit tests in `k8s_agent_sandbox/test/unit/test_sandboxd.py` (REST + model + config); requires `pip install -e .[test,grpc]` and a `buf generate --template buf.gen.python.yaml` pass to vendor the stubs.
- **e2e:** `IMAGE_PREFIX=<registry>/ IMAGE_TAG=<tag> go test ./test/e2e/extensions/ -run TestRunSandboxdSandbox`.

## Breaking changes

`FileEntry` changes shape (KEP-sanctioned, pre-1.0): 
- Go: `ModTime float64` → `time.Time` + new `Mode`
- Python: `mod_time` → `modified: datetime` + `mode`

Callers reading these fields must update.

## Not in scope (follow-ups)

Router/Gateway gRPC passthrough (router h2c) so the router can be the default transport, async-Python sandboxd support, and auto-detection of runtime.

## Related

KEP: #747 · Part 1 (spec): #956, #1116 · Part 2 (daemon): #1257

## Release Note
```release-note
Go and Python SDKs can now target the sandboxd runtime (REST filesystem + gRPC ProcessService) via pod port-forward, selected explicitly (Go: Runtime: RuntimeSandboxd; Python: SandboxdPodTunnelConnectionConfig). sandboxd binds 0.0.0.0 by default (configurable via --listen-host).

title: Add controller-managed, time-bounded disruption protection for Sandbox pods

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add an opt-in field to the Sandbox API that instructs the controller to create and manage a dedicated K8s PodDisruptionBudget for the Sandbox pod.

Example API:

```yaml
  apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
  kind: Sandbox
  metadata:
    name: tool-sandbox
  spec:
    disruptionProtection:
      duration: 4h
```
When disruption protection is requested, the controller would:

  - Create a policy/v1 PDB selecting only the corresponding Sandbox pod.
  - Use integer minAvailable: 1, which is suitable for singleton Sandboxes.
  - Set an owner reference to the Sandbox.
  - Start the duration when protection is established.
  - Store the calculated expiration time in Sandbox status.
  - Ensure reconciliation and controller restarts do not reset the timer.
  - Remove the PDB when protection expires or the Sandbox is deleted.
  - Report whether protection is active, expired, or could not be established.

  Example status:

```yaml
  status:
    disruptionProtection:
      state: Active
      protectedUntil: "2026-08-07T12:00:00Z"
```

Mitigating blocked cluster maintenance:

 To limit this risk, we could make this feature - 
- Opt-in
- Time-bounded
- Subject to a controller-configured maximum duration
- Automatically removed when the duration expires


### Why is this needed?

Context on why this feature: I am a contributor to OpenShell (https://github.com/NVIDIA/OpenShell), a sandbox runtime for running AI agents in secure, sandboxed environments. OpenShell’s k8s compute driver uses Agent Sandbox as its backend for provisioning and managing Sandbox workloads.

While evaluating workload persistence and recovery in OpenShell, we found that persistent volumes can preserve filesystem data, but cannot preserve running processes and memory, in-flight tool executions, interactive sessions from long running jobs etc

Our preferred architecture keeps the agent harness and durable agent state outside the Sandbox, using the Sandbox primarily for isolated tool execution. Even with this separation, an avoidable voluntary disruption can terminate active tool execution. Controller-managed, time-bounded disruption protection would improve reliability during these active execution windows without presenting the Sandbox as permanently available.

 ### Limitations of the current manual approach:
Users can create a PDB manually, as demonstrated by PR #85 (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/85). This requires every client or platform integration to:
- Add and coordinate selector labels.
- Create a separate PDB.
- Choose a singleton-compatible PDB configuration.
- Track the protection period.
- Delete stale PDBs.
- Handle Sandbox deletion and recreation.
- Determine whether protection was successfully established.

Controller ownership would provide consistent selectors, lifecycle management, expiration, cleanup, and status reporting through a single declarative Sandbox API.

title: Proposal: Reduce Sandbox Resume Latency by Reusing Pre-Warmed Worker Pods

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/awaiting-more-evidence
labels.description: Lowest priority. Possibly useful, but not yet enough support to actually get it done.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Explore an optional runtime backend that keeps a logical Sandbox independent of a specific worker Pod:

~~~text
Sandbox identity -> Binding / Lease -> warm Worker Pod -> isolated runtime slot
~~~

- **Suspend:** persist or checkpoint required state, then release the runtime slot to the pool.
- **Resume:** bind the Sandbox to a compatible warm slot, restore state, and update routing.
- Create a Worker Pod only when no compatible warm slot is available.

This would complement the existing 1:1 Sandbox-to-Pod model and requires strong per-slot isolation, such as a nested container sandbox or microVM, plus reliable cleanup before reuse.

Unlike SandboxWarmPool, which pre-creates complete Sandbox/Pod instances, this model reuses generic Worker Pod slots across suspend/resume. Compared with #824, this proposal is narrowly focused on releasing and restoring suspended Sandboxes.

Key questions are the API/runtime-backend shape, restore fidelity (filesystem only or process/memory too), isolation and cleanup guarantees, and how storage, identity, and routing follow a Sandbox between workers.

### Why is this needed?

The official Kubernetes blog [Running Agents on Kubernetes with Agent Sandbox](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/03/20/running-agents-on-kubernetes-with-agent-sandbox/) says mostly idle agents "require a lifecycle that supports mechanisms like suspension and rapid resumption." It also notes that starting a new Pod adds about a second of overhead and breaks interaction continuity.

The issue is not the 1:1 cardinality alone, but that the current lifecycle makes Pod creation part of every resume. A warm worker-slot backend could remove that dependency while preserving a stable logical Sandbox identity.

#### Current implementation

The community controller supports only [**Running** and **Suspended**](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/76ec022fb0a4e96b5c571ef11edf6cb8a1fce651/api/v1beta1/sandbox_types.go#L156-L163). Suspending [deletes the owned Pod](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/76ec022fb0a4e96b5c571ef11edf6cb8a1fce651/controllers/sandbox_controller.go#L1012-L1042); returning to **Running** [creates a Pod from the template](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/76ec022fb0a4e96b5c571ef11edf6cb8a1fce651/controllers/sandbox_controller.go#L1186-L1216). Resume therefore remains coupled to Pod startup.

The GKE-specific snapshot extension can preserve memory and root filesystem state, but it still [terminates the old Pod](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/76ec022fb0a4e96b5c571ef11edf6cb8a1fce651/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/gke_extensions/snapshots/sandbox_with_snapshot_support.py#L197-L245) and [restores into a newly created Pod](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/76ec022fb0a4e96b5c571ef11edf6cb8a1fce651/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/gke_extensions/snapshots/sandbox_with_snapshot_support.py#L261-L287). There is currently no generic in-place freeze/resume path that avoids Pod recreation.

### Related issues and PRs

- #824 — Managed Sandbox prototype using pool Pods, a pod-side agent, and multiple sandbox slots per Pod.
- #127 — Strict 1:1 mapping between a Sandbox and its backing Pod in the current API.
- #694 — Suspend/resume API and pluggable snapshot provider discussion.
- #1237 — In-sandbox guest agent for freeze, snapshot, and resume lifecycle hooks.
- #688 — Preserving sticky scheduling attributes across suspend/resume.
- #952 — Defining when a restored Sandbox is ready during background restore.
- #34 — Existing SandboxWarmPool design, which pre-creates complete Sandbox/Pod instances.
- #747 — Standardized portable runtime interfaces for sandbox capabilities.

labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Generate the controller Prometheus metrics reference from `internal/metrics/` instead of
maintaining it by hand, following the pattern already used for the API and SDK references.

- A `make generate-metrics-docs` target writing `docs/metrics.md`, added to the list in
  `dev/tools/fix-api-docs`.
- `metrics.md` added to the `../docs` mount whitelist in `site/hugo.yaml`, plus a thin page
  including it, the way `site/content/docs/api/_index.md` surfaces `docs/api.md`.
- A CI job asserting the output is current, mirroring the TOC check in
  `.github/workflows/check.yml` (`make <target> && git diff --exit-code`).

Generated columns are metric name, type, help, and label keys. Every metric is a package-level
var with literal `Name`, `Help`, and label-key slices, so extraction works by parsing the AST
or by importing the package and calling `Describe()`. `promlinter` already does the former and
is worth evaluating first.

Label *values* and emission semantics stay hand-written, since they live in branching logic
rather than the definitions. Open questions are whether to also cover the sandbox-router's
separate registry, and whether the table extends the existing metrics page or gets its own.

### Nice to have

Version the docsite so readers can select the docs for the release they are running.

The site currently publishes a single set tracking `main`, so a generated metrics table would
describe unreleased labels. `created_by` illustrates the gap, having merged on July 10 and
first shipped in v0.5.2, meaning anyone still on v0.5.1 would read about a label their build
does not emit.

Most of the scaffolding is already in place. `site/layouts/partials/navbar-version-selector.html`
exists and reads `params.version_menu` and `params.versions`, and `params.versions` is sitting
commented out in `site/hugo.yaml`. The remaining work is deciding what to build the older docs
from, since there are no `release-*` branches today, and picking a URL scheme. Happy to split
this out if it is better tracked separately.

### Why is this needed?


The hand-maintained version drifts faster than review can keep up with. PR #901 shows this
within its own review cycle. `created_by` was added in #1039 after the PR was last updated, so
its table is already missing a label. `warmpool_name` was added to the claim latency histograms
in #1050 and removed in #1073, so a correct review request from July 6 became wrong on July 21
and acting on it would now introduce an error. The PR has been open since May 31 and is stale.

The CI check matters as much as the generator. None of the three existing generated docs is
drift-checked today, so generation alone would leave the same rot with extra steps.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The MCP server ships a Dockerfile that serves streamable HTTP on `0.0.0.0:8000`, so it is
deployed as a long-running network service — but it exposes no probe endpoints. A Deployment
has no way to tell a wedged replica from a healthy one, or to keep traffic off one that cannot
reach the Kubernetes API.

Adds the two-endpoint split `sandbox-router` already uses (`sandbox-router/server/server.go:41`):

| Endpoint | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `GET /healthz` | **Liveness.** 200 once the ASGI app routes the request. Never contacts the Kubernetes API. |
| `GET /readyz` | **Readiness.** Lists SandboxClaims in a configurable `probe_namespace`. `503` while starting or when the API is unreachable. |

Keeping liveness independent of the Kubernetes API is the deliberate part: wiring it to an
external dependency would turn a transient control-plane blip into a rolling restart of every
replica, which is worse than briefly serving no traffic. A test asserts `/healthz` makes no
Kubernetes call.

`/readyz` returns a generic reason string rather than the underlying exception, since the
endpoint is unauthenticated.

Two implementation notes for reviewers:

* **`/readyz` calls the public `list_sandbox_claims`, not `_ensure_initialized`.** The latter only
  loads credentials and builds API objects without contacting the apiserver, so it would report
  ready while the cluster was unreachable. It is also private, and nothing else in the repo
  depends on SDK internals.
* **The client is stashed on the `FastMCP` server object.** The lifespan's yielded mapping reaches
  tools via `ctx.lifespan_context` but is not published on the ASGI app, so routes read it as
  `request.app.state.fastmcp_server`.

`httpx` is now declared in the `test` extra — the probe tests drive the ASGI app with it, and it
was previously only available transitively through `fastmcp`.

#### Testing

Six new tests: `/healthz` 200, `/healthz` makes no Kubernetes call, `/readyz` ready,
`/readyz` 503 when the API fails (asserting the exception text is not leaked), `/readyz`
reports `starting` before the lifespan runs, and the configured namespace is honoured.
Suite 19 → 25. `dev/tools/test-unit` green across all suites locally.

Suggested probe config is documented in the README; because `/readyz` makes a real API call,
it recommends a modest `periodSeconds` rather than aggressive polling.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Follow-up hardening for the MCP server added in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/1141

#### Release Note
```release-note
Added `/healthz` and `/readyz` endpoints to the Agent Sandbox MCP server for Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes.
```

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
The Sandbox controller could create an additional Pod when the pod-name annotation was stale or missing even though a Pod controlled by the same Sandbox UID still existed.

This PR treats the tracking label as a candidate index and the controller owner-reference UID as the authoritative Sandbox-to-Pod mapping. It recovers a unique owned Pod instead of adopting or creating another Pod, and waits for an owned terminating Pod rather than overlapping it.

If multiple Pods are controlled by the same Sandbox UID, reconciliation now fails closed: it does not select, create, or delete a Pod; it does not create or modify the routing Service; and it reports Ready=False with reason MultiplePods plus a Warning Event. This preserves stateful Pods for operator inspection and avoids hot-loop retries while the conflict remains unchanged.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes #1332
Follow-up to #127.
Related to #1297.

#### Release Note

```release-note
Fixed Sandbox reconciliation to avoid creating an additional Pod when the pod-name annotation is stale or an owned Pod is terminating. Multiple owned Pods now fail closed and report Ready=False with reason MultiplePods.
```

title: Dynamic side-loading of execution daemons (execd) for arbitrary container images

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

# Dynamic side-loading of execution daemons (`execd`) for arbitrary container images
## Problem Statement
Currently, `agent-sandbox` users cannot expose a standardized execution interface (such as an HTTP/WebSocket execution daemon, `execd`, SSH, or code interpreter service) inside a `Sandbox` without first rebuilding their container images to bake in those dependencies (see [Python Runtime](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/examples/python-runtime-sandbox) reference implementation).  [KEP 539.2-runtime-standardization](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/docs/keps/539.2-runtime-standardization/README.md) is an important step in the right direction but still requires that images be built with the common proto.

While custom base images work well for static development environments, they become a major bottleneck in workflows that require **Bring-Your-Own-Image (BYOI)** at scale. In use cases such as **Reinforcement Learning (RL)**, automated agent benchmarking, and multi-environment evaluation pipelines, `agent-sandbox` may need to orchestrate hundreds of arbitrary, off-the-shelf container images. Rebuilding, publishing, and maintaining custom variants of every target image just to inject an execution interface is inefficient, operationally brittle, and limits platform flexibility.
## Proposed Solution
We should support **runtime side-loading of self-contained execution daemons** (e.g., a statically compiled Go daemon like `execd`) directly into arbitrary container images at Pod creation time. 
Instead of coupling the execution engine to the workload's root filesystem, the controller or client would inject:
1. A shared volume (`emptyDir`) mounted into the sandbox container.
2. An `initContainer` that copies statically compiled execution binaries and a POSIX shell bootstrap script into the shared volume.
3. An entrypoint wrapper on the target container that starts the execution daemon in the background before launching the user's original container entrypoint.

## Key Considerations
- Static Binary Compilation: Any side-loaded daemon (execd) must be compiled statically (e.g., CGO_ENABLED=0 for Go, zero glibc dependencies) so it runs reliably across Alpine (musl), Ubuntu/Debian (glibc), or minimal scratch containers.
- Warm Pool Compatibility (SandboxWarmPool): Side-loading via initContainer is natively compatible with warm pooling. When a warm pod is created from a SandboxTemplate, the execution daemon initializes immediately and sits warm in the background until adopted by a SandboxClaim.
- Service Exposure: When spec.service is enabled, the controller should automatically expose the execution agent port (e.g., 44772) on the generated headless Service so clients can access the execution API via cluster DNS or port-forwarding.


### Why is this needed?

- True BYOI: Run any public or private OCI image as an agent sandbox immediately without custom Dockerfiles or image rebuilding.
- High-Throughput RL / Eval Ready: Scale across hundreds of distinct evaluation images with zero image-build overhead.
- Clean Layering: Decouples the user's workload environment from the execution interface daemon.
