body:
This commit introduces a new example demonstrating how to run the [nono](https://github.com/nolabs-ai/nono) agent security runtime -  inside an Agent Sandbox.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The example mocks a payments incident workflow using a real, disposable Grafana Loki service and LogCLI. It demonstrates:

- filesystem isolation, including a permitted `/workspace` write and denied reads of mounted secret and audit state;
- scoped agent egress, with non-allowed hosts and API paths denied;
- credential brokering, where the supervisor retains source credentials and the agent or tool receives only a session-scoped phantom;
- a LogCLI child sandbox with a pinned executable and one exact incident query;
- command policy denying modified query arguments and Loki management commands before execution;
- L7 policy allowing only Loki's query-range endpoint, independently denying an argv-approved labels request;
- ephemeral private CA, ensuring brokered credentials are not forwarded over plaintext
- a tamper-evident audit trail covering network and command-policy decisions, with event-chain, Merkle root, ledger, and DSSE signature verification;
- portable audit export for later offline verification.

The runtime image checksum-verifies LogCLI for both amd64 and arm64. The repository includes a `Sandbox`, reusable `SandboxTemplate`, disposable Loki manifests, audit storage and verifier resources, and a kind smoke-test script.

This gives kubernetes users a runnable defense-in-depth example, where agent-sandbox manages the pod boundary and lifecycle. Inside the pod, nono constrains the agent process and each tool it invokes. 

The smoke test uses the default kind runtime and requires Landlock from the kernel backing the container runtime. An opt-in Kustomize variant selects the `kata-qemu` RuntimeClass when the Kata guest supports Landlock. gVisor remains blocked for filesystem enforcement, but we are working with the gvisor community to integrate ([google/gvisor#13439](https://github.com/google/gvisor/issues/13439)); until then nono fails closed rather than silently running without that boundary.

Tested with:

```bash
KIND_CLUSTER_NAME=agent-sandbox ./run-test-kind.sh
```

The test builds and loads the image, starts and seeds Loki, asserts every expected allow and deny decision, finalizes the audit session, verifies the pinned signing identity, and exports the signed audit bundle.

This work was socialized in `#sig-apps` first  where an example was welcomed as the initial integration step:

https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C09QC8C676E/p1785173790581889?thread_ts=1785170620.536329&cid=C09QC8C676E

title: Sandbox controller can create an additional Pod when the pod-name annotation is stale

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
## What happened?

The Sandbox controller does not fully enforce the invariant that a Sandbox must have at most one backing Pod.

At commit `aceb76308b992579f282eaea70409cd970d2b456`, `reconcilePod` lists Pods carrying the Sandbox tracking label, but the list is only used to log when multiple Pods are found. It is not used to recover the canonical Pod or prevent another Pod from being created.

A deterministic recovery state is:

```text
Sandbox: demo
UID: sandbox-uid
agents.x-k8s.io/pod-name: warm-pod-missing

warm-pod-missing:
  no longer exists

warm-pod-survivor:
  agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash: <hash-of-demo>
  controller ownerReference UID: sandbox-uid
```

During reconciliation, the controller:

1. Fails to get `warm-pod-missing`.
2. Clears the stale `pod-name` annotation.
3. Ignores `warm-pod-survivor`, even though it is already controlled by the current Sandbox UID.
4. Creates a new Pod named `demo`.

The result is two Pods controlled by the same Sandbox UID. A Service using the Sandbox tracking-label selector may also select both Pods.

The expected behavior is:

- The controller ownerReference UID is the authoritative mapping.
- If exactly one owned Pod exists, reconcile that Pod and repair the stale compatibility annotation.
- If multiple owned Pods exist, fail closed:
  - do not create another Pod;
  - do not automatically delete a stateful Pod;
  - do not create or modify the routing Service;
  - report `Ready=False` with a stable reason such as `MultiplePods`;
  - emit a Warning Event so the conflict is diagnosable.

## How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

This can be reproduced deterministically with the controller fake client; no timing race or live cluster is required.

1. Create a Sandbox with UID `sandbox-uid` and set `agents.x-k8s.io/pod-name=warm-pod-missing`.
2. Do not create `warm-pod-missing`.
3. Create `warm-pod-survivor` with:
   - the Sandbox name-hash tracking label;
   - a controller ownerReference whose UID is `sandbox-uid`.
4. Run `SandboxReconciler.reconcilePod`.
5. Observe that the existing implementation creates a new Pod using the Sandbox name while `warm-pod-survivor` still exists.

Related deterministic cases:

- A stale annotation points to an unowned adoptable Pod while another Pod is already owned by the Sandbox. The stale target can currently be adopted, creating a second owned Pod.
- Two owned Pods only produce a log message and reconciliation can continue creating another Pod.
- A uniquely owned terminating Pod can be ignored when the annotation is absent, allowing an overlapping Pod to be created.

## Version

`aceb76308b992579f282eaea70409cd970d2b456` the current main

## Anything else we need to know?

This is a follow-up to #127.

#127 was closed with "Fixed with warmpool of sandboxes." The sandbox-based warm-pool architecture removed the normal path where a Sandbox adopted a Pod with a different name, but the controller still does not enforce the original `<=1 owned Pod` invariant in compatibility and recovery states.

The current roadmap still lists "Strict Sandbox-to-Pod Mapping" as in progress.

This should also be compatible with #1297, which proposes removing the `agents.x-k8s.io/pod-name` annotation. The ownership invariant should be based on controller ownerReference UID, not on that annotation.

### Scope and non-goals

This issue is limited to the controller's compatibility and recovery behavior.

- It does not change the normal path where `Sandbox.Name == Pod.Name`.
- It does not propose keeping the `pod-name` annotation permanently.
- It does not automatically delete either stateful Pod when ownership is ambiguous.
- It does not include the sandbox-router cache fencing work, which should be investigated separately if it remains relevant.
- It does not treat the tracking label as proof of ownership; the controller ownerReference UID remains authoritative.

Although #1297 proposes removing the annotation, it is still read and written by the current controller, and the stale-annotation recovery path still exists on main. Until that behavior is removed together with an upgrade/migration strategy, recovery should not violate the Sandbox singleton invariant.

I have deterministic regression tests and a local implementation available. Before opening the PR, I would like to confirm:

1. Is fail-closed behavior preferred when multiple owned Pods are found?
2. Should the controller avoid automatically deleting either stateful Pod?
3. Is `Ready=False`, reason `MultiplePods`, plus a Warning Event the expected diagnostic behavior?

title: feat(mcp): add list_files and file_exists tools

labels.name: lgtm

labels.name: approved

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The MCP server exposes `upload_file` and `download_file`, but there is no way to
list a directory or test whether a path exists. An agent can write a file and
read it back, yet cannot discover what is in a directory, and can only probe for
a path by attempting a read and interpreting the failure.

Both operations already exist on the Python SDK's filesystem interface —
`AsyncFilesystem.list()` and `.exists()` in
`clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/files/async_filesystem.py`
— and both are already exposed by the Go SDK (`Sandbox.List`, `Sandbox.Exists`).
So this is a **cross-SDK parity gap** rather than new functionality: the
capability is present and simply unexposed over MCP.

This PR adds two thin tools over those calls, following `download_file.py` line
for line:

* **`list_files`** — returns each entry's `name`, `size`, `type`
  (`file`/`directory`) and `mod_time` (POSIX timestamp), mapped from the SDK's
  `FileEntry`. An empty directory returns an empty list, not an error.
* **`file_exists`** — returns a boolean. A missing path is a successful
  `exists: false` answer rather than a failure, which is a more useful contract
  for an LLM caller than an exception.

Notes for reviewers:

* **Session isolation is preserved and now asserted.** Both tools go through the
  existing `get_sandbox()` helper, so they inherit the per-session ownership
  check unchanged — no new authorization path. Each tool's
  `test_session_id_not_found` additionally asserts the sandbox is **never**
  touched when that check rejects, so the tools provably fail closed.
* Timeouts reuse `TOOL_DEFAULT_TIMEOUT` / `TOOL_MAX_TIMEOUT`, so bounds and
  validation match the other file tools.
* Purely additive: no existing tool, schema, or behaviour is modified.
* `README.md` documents both tools in the established per-tool format.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Follow-up to the MCP server added in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/1141

#### Release Note
```release-note
Added `list_files` and `file_exists` tools to the Agent Sandbox MCP server, bringing its filesystem tool surface in line with the Go SDK.
```

title: SandboxWarmPool: reliable rollout outcome for SandboxTemplate updates (updatedReadyReplicas + progress deadline)

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

body:
### What would you like to be added?

A reliable **rollout outcome** for `SandboxTemplate` updates on a `SandboxWarmPool`, so deployment automation can distinguish a *failed* rollout from one still *progressing*. Proposed shape:

- `status.updatedReadyReplicas` — count of Ready pool sandboxes built from the **current** template hash (analogous to Deployment's `updatedReplicas`).
- A **progress deadline**: when current-hash sandboxes cannot reach Ready within the deadline, set `Progressing=False, reason=ProgressDeadlineExceeded` (a "TemplateRolloutFailed" outcome). Otherwise `Progressing=True` while the rollout converges.

### Why is this needed?

From @mterwill on #188:
> A SandboxTemplate update has no reliable rollout outcome. If the new template cannot produce ready Sandboxes, deployment automation cannot distinguish a failed rollout from one still progressing, allowing a bad template to be considered successfully deployed.

The gap is structural in today's status:
- `status.readyReplicas` counts Ready sandboxes on **any** template hash (`extensions/controllers/sandboxwarmpool_controller.go`), so it can't answer "is the *current* template producing Ready sandboxes?"
- The default `OnReplenish` update strategy does not recreate existing sandboxes on a template change — old-template sandboxes stay Ready. So after applying a **broken** template, `readyReplicas == desiredReplicas` indefinitely and the pool looks healthy. A GitOps controller reads "success" and blesses the bad template — exactly the failure above.

Without a current-hash Ready count + a deadline, no condition can express rollout health.

### Design questions (needs discussion before implementation)

1. **Templates mutate in place** (same name, changed content — see #1078), so the pool's `spec`/`generation` does not change on a template-content edit. Rollout detection must therefore key on the **observed template hash**, not `observedGeneration`. Where do we store the rollout-start clock — a new `status.observedTemplateHash` + timestamp, or derive from the `Progressing` condition's `lastTransitionTime`?
2. **Strategy-dependent semantics.** Under `Recreate`, stale sandboxes are deleted so `updatedReadyReplicas` should climb and a stuck rollout is clear. Under `OnReplenish`, replacement is lazy, so `updatedReadyReplicas` can legitimately stay low for a long time — does "rollout failed" even apply there, or only under `Recreate`?
3. **Deadline surface:** add a `spec.progressDeadlineSeconds` (API, Deployment-like) or a controller flag / constant?

Filing per the pattern of #1281 — additive API change, deserves its own design discussion.

### Related

- #188 — parent; the `conditions` field + `Available`/`Progressing` conditions land there and in the Progressing follow-up
- #1078 — Recreate strategy stale-pod handling (same hash/staleness code this builds on)
- #1266 — pool-level `WarmPoolNotProgressing` event
- #1281 — object-level pod-status signals; composes with the per-sandbox readiness view

/kind feature
/kind api-change

title: SandboxWarmPool: add a durable Progressing condition to status

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

body:
### What would you like to be added?

A durable `Progressing` condition on `SandboxWarmPool.status`, promoting the controller's existing "not progressing" signal from an ephemeral Event into a first-class status condition.

Concretely:
- `Progressing=False, reason=WarmPoolNotProgressing` when the pool is holding unschedulable sandboxes past the readiness grace period (the case surfaced today via the `WarmPoolNotProgressing` event, #1266).
- `Progressing=False, reason=SandboxTemplateError` when the referenced `SandboxTemplate` cannot be resolved/hashed.
- `Progressing=True, reason=WarmPoolProgressing` otherwise.

### Why is this needed?

Today the not-progressing signal is computed in `setNotProgressing` (`extensions/controllers/sandboxwarmpool_controller.go`) but only exists as (a) a Kubernetes **Event** and (b) an **in-memory map** used to emit that event once. Both are ephemeral: the signal is lost on controller restart, is not queryable, and cannot be waited on. A pool that has settled at "can't make progress" (e.g. unschedulable under capacity pressure, #1215) shows nothing durable in its status.

A status condition makes the pool self-describing: `kubectl get sandboxwarmpool -o yaml` and automation can see *why* a pool isn't converging, and GitOps can gate on it. This is the pool-level companion to the object-level pod-status signal proposed in #1281.

### Design notes

- Builds on the `status.conditions` field added for the `Available` condition in #188 (must land after that).
- Reuse the existing unschedulable/grace-period computation and the `reasonWarmPoolNotProgressing` / `reasonWarmPoolProgressing` reasons already defined for the events, so the event and the condition never disagree.
- Set `observedGeneration` on the condition.

### Related

- #188 — parent (SandboxWarmPool status: Ready/Available/Conditions); the `Available` condition + `conditions` field land there
- #1266 — added the `WarmPoolNotProgressing` event this promotes to a condition
- #1281 — object-level (`Sandbox.status`) counterpart; the two compose
- #1274 — configurable readiness grace / re-check interval, composes with this signal

title: chore: raise minimum Python to 3.11 ahead of 3.10 EOL

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: size/S
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 10-29 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Raises the minimum supported Python from 3.10 to 3.11 across every Python package in the repo, and drops 3.10 from CI.

Python 3.10 reaches end of life on **2026-10-31** and stops receiving security patches. After that date, continuing to advertise `requires-python = ">=3.10"` means publishing wheels that claim support for an unsupported runtime.

This change was carved out of #565 at reviewer request. That PR needs 3.11 for the `datetime.UTC` alias, and reviewers asked that dropping 3.10 be an explicit, standalone change rather than an implicit side effect of a metrics PR. Landing this first unblocks #565 and keeps the version-support decision reviewable on its own terms.

**Packages** (`requires-python` `>=3.10` → `>=3.11`):
- `clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client`
- `clients/integrations/deepagents`
- `clients/integrations/mcp-server`
- `examples/agent-sandbox-rl`

**Workflows:**
- `pypi-publish.yml` — test matrix `3.10` → `3.11`, build job pin `3.10` → `3.11`
- `release.yml` — draft-release tooling pin `3.10` → `3.11`

**Docs and review config** that stated the old floor: `AGENTS.md`, `examples/agent-sandbox-rl/README.md`, `.coderabbit.yaml`, `.github/copilot-instructions.md`.

Also bumps `python:3.10-slim` → `python:3.11-slim` in the client's `python-counter-template.yaml`, which otherwise ships an EOL runtime image. Happy to drop that hunk if reviewers would rather keep this strictly to packaging metadata.

The `3.13` leg of the test matrix is unchanged, so the client is still exercised at both ends of the supported range.

#### Testing

None of the changed files are exercised by PR CI — `pypi-publish.yml` triggers on tag push, `release.yml` on schedule/dispatch, and neither `ci.yml` nor `check.yml` runs Python at all. The three integration/example packages have no CI whatsoever. So everything below was run locally against a real **Python 3.11.15** interpreter (`python:3.11-slim`), which is the version this PR newly makes the floor.

| Package | Tests on 3.11.15 |
| :--- | :--- |
| `agentic-sandbox-client` | 405 passed |
| `agent-sandbox-rl` | 307 passed |
| `deepagents` | 32 passed |
| `mcp-server` | 19 passed |

763 tests, all passing.

Also verified the release-job path and the breaking-change behaviour:

- `python -m build` + `twine check` on 3.11 — both artifacts PASSED, wheel metadata carries `Requires-Python: >=3.11`.
- Installing the resulting wheel on Python 3.10.20 is correctly refused:
  ```
  ERROR: Package 'k8s-agent-sandbox' requires a different Python: 3.10.20 not in '>=3.11'
  ```

Worth flagging for reviewers: 3.11 itself reaches EOL in October 2027, so this buys roughly 14 months. Going straight to 3.12 is a reasonable counter-proposal — 3.11 was chosen here to match what #565 already assumes and to keep the compatibility risk minimal.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/565#discussion_r3524308420 (request to split this out into a separate, explicit change)
Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/565#discussion_r3102056107 (original 3.10 compatibility question and EOL rationale)

#### Release Note

```release-note
ACTION REQUIRED: The minimum supported Python version is now 3.11 (previously 3.10) for `k8s-agent-sandbox` and the `deepagents` and `mcp-server` integration packages. Python 3.10 reaches end of life on 2026-10-31. Users still on Python 3.11 or newer are unaffected; users on Python 3.10 must upgrade before taking this release, as `pip` will refuse to install newer versions of these packages on Python 3.10.
```

* **Chores**

  * Updated sandbox environments to use Python 3.11.
* **Documentation**
  * Updated setup guidance and prerequisites to reflect the Python 3.11 requirement.
* **Release Engineering**
  * Updated publishing and release processes to build and test with Python 3.11.

Follows the existing warm-pool flag family (`-concurrent-workers`, `-max-batch-size`).

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
<!--
To automatically close the linked issue(s) when this PR is merged,
add the word "Fixes" before the issue number or link.

Examples:
Fixes #<issue number>
Ref <issue link> (issue in a different repository)
-->

**Note:** A sandbox's time-to-Ready is dominated by image pull for typical agent workloads — multi-GB images (SWE-bench-class, ~1.3 GB compressed and up) can take minutes to pull cold, so a fixed 5m grace sits uncomfortably close to normal startup time: a sandbox mid-pull past the deadline gets replaced by a new sandbox that begins the same pull. The measurements below deliberately exclude that effect (images were node-preloaded, ~1 s pulls) and show the grace period matters even then:

The grace period has to exceed a pool's expected fill horizon — and that's a property of the workload and cluster, not of the controller. Two measured failure modes when it doesn't (200K-sandbox scale test: 500 warmpoolpools × 400 replicas on 850 nodes, controller at 400-500 sandbox workers / 50 warm-pool workers / qps 1000):

1. Performance, even with zero reaping. One-constant controlled diff, otherwise identical builds and workload: 5m grace = 52.2 min to all-Ready; 60m grace = 17.6-18.8 min. Same exact result, zero replacements in both — the 3× comes from the self-scheduled post-grace evaluations: with deadlines landing inside a long fill, some sandbox's deadline is always seconds away, so pools requeue and re-scan near-continuously for the whole fill. (The existing requeue jitter spreads the spikes but can't remove the rescans while deadlines keep landing mid-fill.)
2. Correctness risk under status lag. On a saturated control plane, readiness-status writes can lag minutes behind pods actually being Ready; a grace shorter than that lag replaces healthy, Running sandboxes, feeding delete/create churn into exactly the conditions #1215/#1266 addressed.

New regression test (`TestReconcilePool_ConfigurableReadinessGracePeriod`) covers both directions: a longer configured grace holds a sandbox the default would replace (and the post-grace requeue targets the configured deadline), and a shorter one replaces a sandbox the default would hold. All existing tests construct the reconciler without the field, so they exercise the defaulting path unchanged.

title: SandboxClaim Ready condition uses the backing Sandbox observedGeneration

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What happened?

After updating the spec of a Ready SandboxClaim, its Ready condition can keep an observedGeneration that does not match the Claim:
```
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxClaim
metadata:
  generation: 4
  ...
status:
  conditions:
  - message: Pod is Ready
    observedGeneration: 2 <------- this is different from metadata.generation
    reason: DependenciesReady
    status: "True"
    type: Ready
```

The backing Sandbox is generation 2, so the Claim condition appears to be reporting the Sandbox generation instead.

This makes the Claim condition look stale to clients that compare its observedGeneration with the Claim's metadata.generation, even after reconciliation has completed.

The likely cause is that computeReadyCondition forwards the entire Ready condition from the backing Sandbox:
```
for _, condition := range sandbox.Status.Conditions {
    if condition.Type == string(v1beta1.SandboxConditionReady) {
        return condition
    }
}
```
This also forwards the Sandbox's ObservedGeneration into the Claim status.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Create a SandboxClaim backed by a ready SandboxWarmPool.

2. Wait for the Claim to become Ready.

3. Update a Claim-only field such as spec.lifecycle.shutdownTime.

4. Compare the Claim's metadata.generation with its Ready condition's observedGeneration. 

The Claim generation advances, while the condition continues to report the backing Sandbox generation.

### Version

main at 79f3175

### Anything else we need to know?

Reproduced with kind v0.32.0 and Kubernetes v1.36.1.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Creating a previously missing `SandboxTemplate` now immediately enqueues affected `SandboxClaim` resources instead of making them wait for the one-minute fallback requeue.

The claim controller watches `SandboxTemplate` create events only and uses the existing field indexes to map each template through its referencing `SandboxWarmPool` resources to the relevant claims. 1. **Deep Container Spec Merging for CoW (Required)**:
   - In `Resources._template_manifest()`, previously a shallow `pod_spec.update(extra)` would overwrite `containers[0]`, clobbering task-specific dynamic container images and sibling fields (like `resources.requests`) when injecting custom `env` or `volumeMounts` (e.g. CoW RAM redirection / `PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE`).
   - Implements recursive `_deep_merge` for nested container mappings while preserving the original task image and existing specs.

2. **Safe Stream Handling in `run_pod_exec`**:
   - When executing commands with `kubernetes.stream` that yield no stdout/stderr or during abrupt WebSocket closures, `stream()` can return `None` or unparsed `bytes`.
   - Adds defensive handling in `handles.py` to ensure `run_pod_exec` always returns a valid string (`str`), eliminating unhandled `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute ...` crashes.

3. **Concurrent Batch Fleet Teardown & Safe Replica Accounting**:
   - Adds `unwarm_images()` to batch pool and template deletions across clusters.
   - Fixes warm replica pop accounting in `_unwarm_entry` to prevent replica decrement leaks when images are not warmed.

---

### Which issue(s) this PR fixes
Fixes container image clobbering under `extra_pod_spec`, NoneType exec stream crashes, and optimizes fleet cleanup.

title: sandboxclaim: cap the Create→AlreadyExists cache-lag requeue to avoid unbounded flat-rate churn on a persistently lagging informer

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### Summary

The `errSandboxAlreadyExists` cache-lag path added in #1072 converts a cold-start `Create` that returns `AlreadyExists` into a bounded `RequeueAfter` with a **nil** error, so the benign informer-cache-lag race does not ride the exponential failure rate limiter or wipe `SandboxStatus.Name` (#1042). Because the nil return resets the workqueue failure counter on every pass, a *persistently* lagging informer re-issues `Create` at a flat rate with no upper bound. It is not a CPU hot loop (the delay parks the item), but it is unbounded flat-rate write churn against the API server in a degraded-informer state. Found during review of #1072; the mitigation shipped there is a delay bump, this issue tracks the real cap.

### Details

`Reconcile` handles the sentinel by requeueing at a flat `cacheLagRequeueDelay` with a nil error ([sandboxclaim_controller.go#L375-L381](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/5f3fe4495add3ccfbf4a4d5f7307cb400f8df8e4/extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go#L375-L381)):

```go
if errors.Is(reconcileErr, errSandboxAlreadyExists) {
    logger.V(4).Info("Sandbox already exists; requeueing to let cache converge", ...)
    requeueDelay := cacheLagRequeueDelay
    if result.RequeueAfter > 0 && result.RequeueAfter < requeueDelay {
        requeueDelay = result.RequeueAfter
    }
    return ctrl.Result{RequeueAfter: requeueDelay}, nil
}
```

In the normal case the `Owns(&Sandbox{})` watch (or one bounded requeue) converges in a single extra pass. But if `AlreadyExists` persists — a wedged/desynced informer that never delivers a sandbox that provably exists on the server — the reconcile repeats indefinitely:

```
cached Get -> NotFound -> Create -> AlreadyExists -> RequeueAfter(delay), nil
      ^                                                        |
      +------------------------ delay ------------------------ +
```

The nil return keeps resetting the failure counter, so there is no backoff growth and no ceiling: the controller re-issues `Create` (a real API-server write) at the flat delay for that claim forever, and hits every affected claim at once if the informer is wedged pool-wide.

Two hard constraints shape the fix:

- **`AlreadyExists` must never surface as a reconcile error.** That is the entire purpose of the sentinel — no error-level logs, no `ReconcilerError` on the claim, no failure metric. So "fall back to the error path" (letting the workqueue's exponential backoff engage) is not acceptable.
- **No direct API-server reads (`APIReader`) on this path.** Informers exist to keep the hot path off the API server; adding uncached reads at warm-pool scale erodes that.

### Suggested fix

Cap the flat-rate churn with an in-memory, per-claim consecutive-attempt counter, growing the requeue delay geometrically and capping it (`cacheLagRequeueDelay` → a few seconds), while staying on the benign nil-error path throughout:

1. Add a `map[types.NamespacedName]int` + mutex on the reconciler, mirroring the warm pool controller's `notProgressing` tracking ([sandboxwarmpool_controller.go#L115-L118](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/5f3fe4495add3ccfbf4a4d5f7307cb400f8df8e4/extensions/controllers/sandboxwarmpool_controller.go#L115-L118)). No API reads or writes.
2. On each consecutive `errSandboxAlreadyExists` pass, increment and derive a delay of `cacheLagRequeueDelay << (attempts-1)` capped at a max (~5s). Attempt 1 (the common single-pass lag) keeps the current fast delay, so there is no happy-path regression.
3. Clear the counter (e.g. via `defer`, and on the NotFound cleanup at [sandboxclaim_controller.go#L204](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/5f3fe4495add3ccfbf4a4d5f7307cb400f8df8e4/extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go#L204)) as soon as the claim reconciles to anything other than the race, so a later race starts fresh.

Net effect: the common case is unchanged, a persistently lagging informer decays to one benign requeue every ~5s instead of a flat rate, and the race is still never surfaced as an error.

### Interim mitigation

#1072 raises `cacheLagRequeueDelay` from 50ms to 200ms to cut the flat-rate churn ~4x, with a `TODO` pointing at this issue.

### Related

- #1072 — introduced the `errSandboxAlreadyExists` sentinel + bounded requeue (mitigation lands here)
- #1108 — established the sentinel + bounded-requeue pattern for adoption cache lag
- #1042 — the original AlreadyExists / status-wipe bug

/kind bug

title: [Performance] Reconcile SandboxClaims immediately when a missing SandboxTemplate is created

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What happened?

When a SandboxClaim references a WarmPool whose SandboxTemplate is temporarily
missing, the claim is requeued after one minute.

If the missing SandboxTemplate is created shortly afterwards, the claim is not immediately reconciled because SandboxClaimReconciler does not watch SandboxTemplate events.

As a result, the claim may wait for up to one minute before provisioning starts.

### Expected behavior

Creating a previously missing SandboxTemplate should immediately enqueue affected SandboxClaims.

### Proposed solution

 - Index SandboxWarmPools by `spec.templateRef.name`.
 - Watch SandboxTemplate create events only.
 - Map a newly created template to referencing WarmPools, then map those pools
    to SandboxClaims.
 - Keep the existing one-minute `RequeueAfter` as a fallback.
 - Do not enqueue claims on SandboxTemplate updates; update/version consistency
    remains handled by the WarmPool rollout behavior and #764.

### Additional context

The current code contains TODOs describing this latency regression:

- extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go:347
- extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go:2179

### Relationship to #764

This issue is related to #764 but addresses a different lifecycle point.

- #764 and #1078 handle template-version correctness when an existing SandboxTemplate is updated.
- This issue only handles creation of a previously missing SandboxTemplate.

The proposed watch intentionally does not enqueue claims on template update
  events, so it does not change Recreate or OnReplenish adoption semantics.

I would be happy to implement this if maintainers agree with the approach.

title: fix(sandboxclaim): default Delete+TTL=0 lifecycle for warm pool claims

body:
## Summary

- When a `SandboxClaim` references a `WarmPool` but omits `spec.lifecycle`, `checkExpiration()` short-circuits at the nil check and returns `(false, 0)` — the expiration reconciler never runs, so the claim, sandbox, pod, and VM persist **indefinitely**
- This leaks VPC IPs, auto-refreshes SA tokens, and holds cloud IMDS access with no expiration path
- Inject an in-memory default `Lifecycle{ShutdownPolicy: Delete, TTLSecondsAfterFinished: 0}` for warm-pool-sourced claims that omit it — the default is deterministic and reconcile-local (not persisted to the API server)
- Non-warm-pool claims retain the existing behavior (immortal when Lifecycle is nil)
- Explicit Lifecycle settings (e.g. `Retain` for debugging) are never overridden

## Details

The root cause is in `checkExpiration` ([sandboxclaim_controller.go:427](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go#L427)):

```go
if claim.Spec.Lifecycle == nil {
    return false, 0  // claim never expires
}
```

This is correct for bare `Sandbox` objects (GitOps safety — see #201), but warm pool claims are ephemeral by definition and should not accumulate indefinitely. The fix adds a warm pool check before the early return:

```go
if claim.Spec.Lifecycle == nil {
    if claim.Spec.WarmPoolRef.Name == "" {
        return false, 0  // non-warm-pool: preserve existing behavior
    }
    // Inject default: Delete + TTL=0
    ttl := int32(0)
    claim.Spec.Lifecycle = &extensionsv1beta1.Lifecycle{
        ShutdownPolicy:          extensionsv1beta1.ShutdownPolicyDelete,
        TTLSecondsAfterFinished: &ttl,
    }
}
```

### Follow-up (not in this PR)

A configurable default reaper TTL for explicit `Retain` claims could prevent stale object accumulation for debugging scenarios. See #1306 comment for the full security analysis.

Fixes #1306

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./...` passes
- [x] `go vet ./...` passes
- [x] New unit tests (4 cases):
  - Warm pool claim, nil lifecycle, finished → claim deleted ✅
  - Warm pool claim, nil lifecycle, not finished → claim stays active ✅
  - Warm pool claim, explicit Retain → respected, no override ✅
  - Non-warm-pool claim, nil lifecycle → immortal (old behavior) ✅
- [x] All existing controller tests pass unchanged

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->
## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Warm-pool SandboxClaims without an explicit lifecycle now automatically delete after their workload finishes.
  * Claims remain active before completion and continue honoring explicit retention settings.
  * SandboxClaims not associated with a warm pool retain their existing behavior.

* **Documentation**
  * Clarified lifecycle defaults and how explicit settings override them.

Adds longevity/soak testing mode to `TestRuntimeClassBurstRecovery` with adaptive
batch sizing, and applies `ShutdownPolicy: Delete` + `TTL=0` to all claim creation
sites to prevent zombie claim/sandbox/pod accumulation.

Validated across three runtimes: runc (pool-40), gVisor (pool-40), kata-clh (pool-20)
on a 4-worker GCP cluster (4×n2-standard-8, 28 vCPU).

### Commits

- **`28ea016` — baseline functions, adaptive batch cap, longevity mode**
  Extract reusable `baselineColdStart`, `baselineWarmClaim`, `baselinePoolFill`.
  Add `SANDBOX_LONGEVITY` env var for time-bounded soak runs with adaptive batch
  sizing that self-tunes to the controller's refill rate.

  Heuristic initial batch sizing, static inter-batch delay, ±1 adaptive thresholds
  with wide steady zone. Scoped controller log capture (`DumpControllerLogsSince`).
  Summary CSV emitted every 10 batches. Workload override and minimum pool size (20).

  `MinReadyReplicasPredicate` + `WaitForWarmPoolMinReady` (watch-based, no polling).
  Longevity waits for 2×batchSize ready instead of full pool fill. Fix workload
  CrashLoopBackOff: derive duration from cold start calibration (`max(10, coldStart×5)`).

- **`bce0322` — ShutdownPolicy Delete for all claims, configurable TTL, 0.3 coefficient**
  Shared `claimLifecycle` var with `ShutdownPolicy: Delete` + `TTL=0` (configurable
  via `SANDBOX_TTL`). Applied to all 5 claim sites (lifecycle, burst, baseline,
  benchmarks). Batch coefficient 0.5→0.3 for 3× refill margin. See #1306 for the

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Removes the `v1alpha1` API version from both API groups (`agents.x-k8s.io` and `extensions.agents.x-k8s.io`), along with the conversion webhook infrastructure that existed solely to serve it. `v1beta1` becomes the only served version for all four CRDs: `Sandbox`, `SandboxClaim`, `SandboxTemplate`, and `SandboxWarmPool`.

**Motivation.** Serving `v1alpha1` costs real CPU even when nobody requests it — the apiserver invokes the conversion webhook to build informer caches regardless of client demand (ref #1234). Beyond that, every `v1beta1` change required a matching lossless conversion, and the self-signed cert machinery, webhook Service, and eight controller flags all existed only to keep `/convert` reachable.

**Targeting `feature/drop-v1alpha1`, not `main`**, per #1265.

#### Epic: Drop deprecated v1alpha1 API support

This PR serves as the **Epic Tracker** for dropping `v1alpha1` support ahead of the v1.0.0 release (Issue #1265). 

To ensure clean, reviewable diffs and independent validation, the changes have been split into **4 focused PRs** targeting `feature/drop-v1alpha1`:

- [x] **PR 1**: `api: drop v1alpha1 spoke packages and regenerate clients` (#1393)
- [x] **PR 2**: `controller, olm: remove conversion webhook infrastructure` (blocked on PR 1) (#1404)
- [x] **PR 3**: `test-migration: remove v1alpha1 to v1beta1 upgrade harness` (#1414)
- [x] **PR 4**: `docs, examples: v1alpha1 removal` (#1427)

---

#### Preserved Discussion & Context
* All previous review threads and architectural Q&A (including OLM lifecycle and upgrade validation) remain recorded here for history.

*(This branch is frozen as discussion substrate; please review the individual child PRs above).*

##### Deliberately unchanged

- Version-agnostic owner-ref checks in `sandboxclaim_controller.go`, `internal/metrics/sandbox_collector.go`, and `sandbox-router/cache/cache.go`, plus their tests — they match on API group rather than version and still guard against legacy owner refs (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1265#issuecomment-5064823338).
- `examples/agent-sandbox-rl/tests/test_preflight.py` — `test_crd_wrong_version` uses v1alpha1 as its negative case, which is exactly the realistic stale-cluster scenario the preflight check guards against.
- `site/content/docs/use-cases/anthropic-managed-agents/_index.md` — the GKE Agent Sandbox add-on doesn't serve v1beta1 yet.
- Historical or external-system references in `dev/load-test/test-recipes/README-rapid-burst.md` (a GKE Cluster Autoscaler caching note) and `examples/agent-sandbox-rl/examples/rl_integration.md`.

##### Validation

`make all`, `make test-e2e`, and `./dev/ci/presubmits/test-autogen-up-to-date` all pass. On kind:

- **Fresh install** — CRDs report only `v1beta1`, no webhook Service or cert Secret is created, a v1beta1 Sandbox reconciles to Ready, and all four v1alpha1 kinds are rejected at discovery.
- **Upgrade from v0.5.2** — succeeds when `storedVersions` is pruned to `["v1beta1"]`; correctly rejected by the apiserver when `v1alpha1` remains. All four controllers exercised with the trimmed RBAC, no `Forbidden` errors.
- **GKE** — the latebind storage example ran end-to-end on GKE v1.36.0-gke.3302001 (Filestore CSI + gVisor node pool) against the OSS controller.
- **Helm upgrade path** — verified on kind: install v0.5.2 → prune storedVersions → apply v1beta1-only CRDs → helm upgrade. Helm prunes the webhook Service, Role, and RoleBinding; the runtime-created cert Secret survives (no owner reference, never a chart template) and needs manual deletion. 
-**Upgrade — OLM path (kind + OLM)** — `operator-sdk run bundle` v0.5.2 → `run bundle-upgrade`
  to the new bundle. Verified:
  - the webhook Service carries an `ownerReference` to the CSV
  - upgrading before pruning `storedVersions` is rejected by the apiserver with the error above
  - after pruning, the Service, Role, and RoleBinding are all garbage-collected on CSV replacement
  - the cert Secret is **not** garbage-collected — no owner reference, so OLM has no ownership link

body:
## Problem

The `ShutdownPolicy` on `SandboxClaim.spec.lifecycle` defaults to `Retain` (`+kubebuilder:default=Retain`). This default was chosen to protect GitOps workflows (#201): if a bare `Sandbox` were deleted on expiry, ArgoCD/Flux would see it disappear and immediately recreate it, causing an infinite create-delete loop. `Retain` breaks that cycle — the object stays, GitOps sees it as "present", and the underlying pods/services are cleaned up.

However, **SandboxClaims sourced from a WarmPool are ephemeral by definition** — they are dynamically provisioned, never declared in GitOps manifests, and have no state worth preserving after the workload finishes. The GitOps rationale from #201 does not apply.

Under sustained load (longevity/soak tests, production warm pools), `Retain` causes unbounded accumulation of stale SandboxClaim and Sandbox objects. This affects **every runtime equally** — runc, gVisor, and kata all leak at the same rate. A warm pool churning hundreds of claims per hour leaves hundreds of dead objects that must be GC'd manually or by a separate controller.

## Proposal

Add an optional `claimDefaults` field to SandboxWarmPoolSpec that lets pool operators define default Lifecycle settings applied to claims at adoption time. Claims with an explicit **Lifecycle** are not overridden.

Important: `TTLSecondsAfterFinished` alone is insufficient. It only fires after the Sandbox reaches a terminal state. For long-running workloads with `RestartPolicy: Always` (the default for agents, notebooks, dev environments), the container restarts indefinitely — the Sandbox never **"finishes"** and TTL never fires. VMs accumulate _exactly_ as with Retain.

The claimDefaults mechanism must support time-bounded shutdown to cover both workload patterns:

- Batch/job workloads (RestartPolicy: Never): ShutdownPolicy: Delete + TTLSecondsAfterFinished: 5 - delete akmost immediately when done
- Long-running workloads (RestartPolicy: Always): ShutdownPolicy: Delete + ShutdownTime or a duration-based equivalent (e.g., maxLifetime: 30m → computed ShutdownTime at adoption time) — hard deadline regardless of pod state

Example:

```
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxWarmPool
spec:
  claimDefaults:
    lifecycle:
      shutdownPolicy: Delete
      maxLifetime: 30m        # translated to ShutdownTime at adoption
```

Users who need Retain for warm pool claims can still set it explicitly on the claim.

See PR #1420 (KEP-1306) for the full design.

## Evidence

From longevity testing across three runtimes (runc pool-40, gVisor pool-40, kata-clh pool-20) on a 4-worker cluster:

- Without `ShutdownPolicy: Delete` — hundreds of stale claim objects accumulate, namespace cleanup takes minutes, and deferred cleanup storms compete with the controller's reconcile loop
- With `ShutdownPolicy: Delete` + `TTL=5` — claims auto-delete almost immediately after workload completion, namespace cleanup drops to seconds, and the controller stays focused on pool refill

| Metric | runc | gVisor | kata-clh |
|--------|------|--------|----------|
| Total claims (2min run) | 839 | 818 | 108 |
| Namespace cleanup | 65s | 68s | 16s |

Even with Delete+TTL=5, cleanup takes over a minute for high-throughput runtimes. Without it, the object count grows without bound.

## References

- #201 — original discussion of Retain rationale (GitOps safety)
- #222 — PR that introduced ShutdownPolicy with Retain as default
- #21 — original TTL feature request and implementation

title: Performance: remove `agents.x-k8s.io/pod-name` annotation

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
Related to work on [performance](https://storage.googleapis.com/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1276/presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp-kindnet/2081205271614459904/artifacts/stress-test/report/index.html), we found that the `pod-name` annotation on sandbox objects is relatively expensive because we can’t combine it into the status update.

The annotation was introduced in commit dca369b to support adopting bare Pods from a warm pool, where the pre-existing Pod's name differed from the newly created Sandbox CR's name.

A later refactor (b2f04f1) changed the warm pool to create full Sandbox CRs instead of bare Pods. Because of this, the Pod name now always matches the Sandbox name.

We can consider removing the `pod-name` annotation, and removing the support to adopt a Pod with a different name (warmpool creates sandboxes directly now, so this adoption logic isn't necessary anymore). This means new sandbox's name and its pod name will always be identical. Removing the `pod-name` annotation will improve performance by eliminating redundant write operations (patches) and subsequent reconciliation loops.

We will need to update the controller, the Go/Python SDKs, and associated tests. External clients that read this annotation will safely fall back to the Sandbox name, but should eventually be updated.

title: feat: implement Auto-Suspension and Traffic-Triggered Resume

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: needs-rebase
labels.description: Indicates a PR cannot be merged because it has merge conflicts with HEAD.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

body:
# feat: implement Auto-Suspension and Traffic-Triggered Resume (KEP-0968)

## What this PR does / why we need it

This PR implements the **Auto-Suspension and Traffic-Triggered Resume** lifecycle feature proposed in **[KEP-0968](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/972/changes)**.

Long-running interactive AI Agent Runtimes, notebooks, and dev environments often sit idle between user prompts or reasoning steps, continuously consuming CPU and GPU resources. This implementation solves idle compute waste by:
1. **Declarative Auto-Suspension**: Automatically transitioning `.spec.operatingMode` to `Suspended` (deleting the underlying Pod while preserving PersistentVolumeClaims and workspace files 100% intact) after a configurable `.spec.autoSuspension.inactivityTimeoutSeconds` expires.
2. **Transparent Traffic-Triggered Resume**: Integrating with **Envoy Gateway** via a lightweight gRPC `ExternalProcessor` (`ext_proc`) filter (`sandbox-router`) that intercepts incoming L7 HTTP traffic (`X-Sandbox-ID`), dynamically thaws suspended Sandboxes back to `Running`, and proxies the initial request without connection drops.

---

## Architectural & Design Highlights

### 1. Security & Access Control (`:8090` REST API)
* **Secure by Default**: Because `--enable-auto-suspend-and-resume=false` is the default on `agent-sandbox-controller`, the `:8090` HTTP server is disabled out-of-the-box and presents zero attack surface.
* **Out-of-the-Box NetworkPolicy Isolation**: Both `k8s/auto-suspension.yaml` and our Helm chart (`helm/templates/networkpolicy-suspension.yaml`) automatically include a Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` (`allow-sandbox-router-to-controller-suspension-api`) that restricts ingress to port `8090` exclusively to `sandbox-router` pods.

### 2. Modular Deployment & Helm Integration
* **`k8s/auto-suspension.yaml` Overlay**: Pure networking overlay deploying `Deployment/sandbox-router`, `Service/sandbox-router`, `Gateway/sandbox-gateway`, `HTTPRoute/sandbox-route`, `EnvoyExtensionPolicy/sandbox-ext-proc-policy`, `Service/agent-sandbox-controller`, and `NetworkPolicy/allow-sandbox-router-to-controller-suspension-api`.
* **Release & Kind Tooling**:
  * Added `--auto-suspension` opt-in flag to `dev/tools/deploy-to-kube` and `Makefile` (`AUTO_SUSPENSION=true make deploy-kind`).
  * Bundled independent release asset `release_assets/auto-suspension.yaml` in `dev/tools/release`.
  
### 3. Control Plane: Controller & Idleness Garbage Collection (`controllers/`)
* **Core `SandboxReconciler` Auto-Suspension**: Integrated directly into the main `SandboxReconciler` (`controllers/sandbox_controller.go`), monitoring Sandboxes configured with `.spec.autoSuspension.inactivityTimeoutSeconds` (`AutoSuspensionPolicy`). When `time.Since(status.lastActivityTime) >= inactivityTimeoutSeconds`, the reconciler automatically handles suspending the Sandbox and terminating the underlying Pod.
* **Lightweight REST API (`controllers/suspension_server.go` on `:8090`)**:
  * `POST /v1/sandboxes/resume`: Idempotent resume endpoint invoked by `sandbox-router` on cache misses. Updates `status.lastActivityTime = Now()` **before** patching `.spec.operatingMode = Running` to prevent instant re-suspension race conditions. 
  * `POST /v1/sandboxes/activity`: Batched HTTP handler (`SuspensionServer`) that updates `status.lastActivityTime` for active Sandboxes.
* **Admin Guardrail (`--enable-auto-suspend-and-resume=false` Default)**: The controller reconciler flag `--enable-auto-suspend-and-resume` defaults to `false` (`controller.enableAutoSuspendAndResume: false` in Helm). This ensures that no Sandbox is auto-suspended unless an administrator explicitly opts in, confirming that the data-plane router (`auto-suspension.yaml`) is installed to resume workloads.

### 4. Data Plane: `sandbox-router` & Envoy Gateway `ext_proc` (`sandbox-router/`)
* **gRPC `ext_proc` Server (`:9002`) & L7 Proxy (`:8080`)**: Implements Envoy Gateway `ExternalProcessorServer` and upstream reverse proxy. Runs with full Kubernetes security defaults (`runAsNonRoot: true`, user `65532`, dropped capabilities `ALL`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, read-only root filesystem, and `RuntimeDefault` seccomp profile).
* **Contract Header Integration**:
  * Evaluates `X-Sandbox-ID`, `X-Sandbox-Namespace`, and `X-Sandbox-Port` (default `8888`), or parses hostname format `<id>.<namespace>.sandbox.local` from the `Host` header.
  * Injects `x-sandbox-pod-ip`, `x-sandbox-id`, and `x-sandbox-gateway-processed` for Envoy Gateway routing (`HTTPRoute/sandbox-route`).
* **Dynamic TCP Readiness Check & Thundering Herd Protection**:
  * Uses Go `singleflight.Group` to deduplicate concurrent `/v1/sandboxes/resume` calls for the same suspended Pod.
  * Dynamically parses `X-Sandbox-Port` and dials that exact target container TCP port (`net.DialTimeout`) during cold-start resume before unpausing Envoy's request stream.
* **Configurable Resume Timeout (`--default-resume-timeout`)**:
  * Default resume timeout raised to `60s` (`--default-resume-timeout=60s`), configurable on the `sandbox-router` deployment to accommodate VM boot and initialization latency on VM-isolated clusters.

---

## Documentation & Runnable Examples

* **Comprehensive User & Operator Guide (`docs/auto_suspension.md`)**: Full documentation with Mermaid sequence/architecture diagrams, Setup instructions, security & NetworkPolicy isolation rules, and latency/cost trade-off tables.
* **Runnable OpenClaw Example (`examples/openclaw-gvisor-sandbox/`)**: Added `openclaw-sandbox-auto-suspension.yaml` and documented end-to-end auto-suspension and traffic-triggered resume testing in `README.md`.
* **Runnable GKE Kata Container Example (`examples/kata-gke-sandbox/`)**: Added `sandbox-kata-auto-suspension.yaml` and documented end-to-end auto-suspension and traffic-triggered resume testing in `README.md`.

---

## Verification & Testing

All unit test suites pass (`go test -v ./controllers/... ./sandbox-router/proxy/...`).

body:
Follow-up from #1274 (controller flags, implemented in #1290) and @esposem's review comment there (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/1290#issuecomment-5092078218).

The flags set one global value per controller deployment. For mixed fleets — a heavy Kata/gVisor pool that legitimately needs 10m next to fast runc pools where 5m is right — a per-WarmPool `spec` field is the better shape: no controller redeploy to tune a single pool, and each pool gets a value matching its runtime profile. #1274 deferred this because it's an API change deserving its own discussion.

### Proposed shape (open to discussion)

- `spec.readinessGracePeriod` (and possibly `spec.unschedulableRecheckInterval`) on SandboxWarmPool, `metav1.Duration`
- Precedence: pool field > controller flag > built-in default (5m/1m)
- Validation: must be > 0 if set; CEL or webhook TBD

### Open questions

- Should the recheck interval also be per-pool, or is that knob operator-level enough to stay flag-only?
- Interaction with #1292 (centralized config): the flag layer may eventually live there; the pool-field precedence should be defined against "controller-level config" generically rather than flags specifically.

/kind feature
/kind api-change

title: New CRD/Configmap to handle all controller knobs

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/awaiting-more-evidence
labels.description: Lowest priority. Possibly useful, but not yet enough support to actually get it done.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

The controller is gradually taking more and more flags, and as some of them are tunable, a complete reinstall/redeploy of the controller when it's deployed via `kubectl apply`/operator bundle seems an overkill.

What about adding a CRD `AgentSandboxConfig` encapsulating all the flags that can be tuned? Or simply a configmap would work too.

ConfigMap is simpler when:
  - We don't need schema validation, status reporting, or typed clients
  - We're fine with string-based key/value pairs

  CRD is better when:
  - We want `kubectl edit agentsandboxconfig` default with tab-completion, validation, and defaulting built into the API server
  - We want the controller to report back "here's what I'm actually using" via status.effectiveConfig
  - We want RestartRequired condition so operators know when a restart is needed
  - We want typed Go clients, listers, informers 
  - We're in an OLM-managed environment where values.yaml isn't easily editable

Note this will cover only the tunable flags.

### Why is this needed?

To make the controller deployment tunable and have all the flags in a single place, without the need of reinstalling or redeploying it.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds a `PodScheduled` condition to `Sandbox.status.conditions` that mirrors the backing pod's scheduling state, so controllers, SDKs, and humans running `kubectl get sandbox -o yaml` can tell **why** a sandbox is not Ready (`Unschedulable`, `SchedulingGated`, ...) without pod access or pod RBAC.

Mirroring rules:

- The pod condition's `status`, `reason`, and `message` are copied through verbatim, so current and future scheduler reasons surface without controller changes. The only mapping: the scheduler sets an empty reason on `PodScheduled=True`, and `metav1.Condition` requires a non-empty one, so empty maps to a `PodScheduled` reason constant.
- Pod exists but hasn't reported a `PodScheduled` condition yet → `Unknown` / `PodSchedulingUnknown`.
- No backing pod (suspended / expired / not yet created) → the condition is **removed**, following the existing `Finished` condition lifecycle, rather than reporting a misleading `False` on a deliberately suspended sandbox.

No CRD schema change (the conditions array already exists), no RBAC change; codegen produces no diff. `Ready` semantics are untouched — consumers match on `Ready` reasons, so this is a separate condition rather than new `Ready` reasons.

Deferred to follow-ups (per the design comment on the issue): container-level signals (image pull, waiting reasons), and switching the warm-pool unschedulable-hold to consume this condition instead of reading pods.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1281

#### Release Note

```release-note
Sandbox status now includes a `PodScheduled` condition mirroring the backing pod's scheduling state (e.g. reason `Unschedulable` or `SchedulingGated`), so consumers can see why a sandbox is not scheduled without reading the pod.
```

body:
## Summary

- Makes the SandboxWarmPool stuck-sandbox readiness grace period and the unschedulable-hold re-check interval configurable via controller flags, per the scope suggested in #1274:
  - `--sandbox-warm-pool-readiness-grace-period` (default `5m`, today's behavior)
  - `--sandbox-warm-pool-unschedulable-recheck-interval` (default `1m`, today's behavior)
- The former constants become exported defaults (`DefaultWarmPoolReadinessGracePeriod`, `DefaultUnschedulableRecheckInterval`) shared by the flag defaults and the reconciler's zero-value fallback, so the CLI default and the in-package fallback cannot drift. Bare reconciler literals (tests) keep current behavior.
- Flag values `<= 0` are rejected at startup — an explicit `=0` fails loudly rather than silently meaning the default.
- The `WarmPoolNotProgressing` event message now reports the configured grace period instead of the compile-time constant.
- Docs (`docs/configuration.md`) and Helm chart (`values.yaml`, `_controller-args.tpl`, `README.md`) updated; the new chart values are `hasKey`-guarded so unset values keep binary defaults.
- No API change — the per-pool `spec` knob mentioned in the issue is deliberately left to its own discussion.

## Motivation

- Images with heavy initialization can legitimately take longer than the fixed 5m grace to become Ready; previously they were delete-and-replaced in a loop even though they would have become Ready.
- Autopilot / node-auto-provisioning clusters can hold pods Pending well past 5m; post-#1266 those pods are held rather than churned, but the grace deadline and re-check cadence should match the cluster's provisioning latency profile.

## Test plan

- New two-phase fake-clock test `TestReconcilePool_ConfigurableGraceAndRecheck`:
  - Phase 1: a 6-minute-old not-Ready sandbox with a configured 10m grace (past the 5m default) is held as still-warming — not deleted, no replacement — with the requeue armed for the remaining configured grace.
  - Phase 2: past the configured grace with an Unschedulable pod, the sandbox enters the unschedulable hold and the requeue uses the configured 30s interval; exactly one `WarmPoolNotProgressing` event.
- Existing tests updated only for the constant rename (no assertion changes), demonstrating defaults preserve current behavior.
- Verified: `make build`, `go vet`, `go test ./controllers/... ./extensions/... ./internal/...` all green; `helm template` renders both flags when set and omits them when unset; the built binary rejects `--sandbox-warm-pool-readiness-grace-period=0` at startup and `--help` shows correct defaults.

Fixes #1274

* `warmpool-overcreate` — creates `--wp-pools` (20) x `--wp-replicas` (25)
  SandboxWarmPools in one burst and watches every pool-owned Sandbox.
  Asserts:
  * exactly pools x replicas **distinct sandbox creates** (distinct UIDs on
    the watch = POST-equivalent count), with legitimate replacements — a
    create observed only *after* a member's delete — counted and reported
    separately, tolerated up to `--wp-replacement-tolerance` (2);
  * the **concurrent live population never exceeds the target** (per pool,
    peak <= replicas at all times);
  * reports time-to-all-pools-Ready; cleans up pools/template and waits for
    the drain.
* `warmpool-unschedulable` — one pool of `--wp-unsched-replicas` (3) whose
  template requests `--wp-unsched-cpu` (1000) CPUs, robustly unschedulable
  on any machine shape sold today; quiet `--wp-unsched-watch` (8m) window
  covering the 5-minute readiness grace plus the jittered post-grace
  requeue (worst case ~7m35s). Asserts:
  * **zero delete/recreate churn** — member UIDs exactly stable;
  * **exactly one** `WarmPoolNotProgressing` Warning event for the pool,
    no duplicates (deduplication-aware: a count-bumped event object also
    fails exactly-once).

Verdicts land in `summary.json` (`warmPoolOvercreate` /
`warmPoolUnschedulable` per-phase reports) and in the printed report; both
phases PASS on current main and FAIL loudly on pre-fix controllers.

**Scenario wrapper** (`test/benchmarks/scenarios/benchmarks-kops-gcp-warmpool/`
+ `dev/ci/presubmits/benchmarks-kops-gcp-warmpool`, mirroring the
benchmarks-kops-gcp-claims structure): 12 worker nodes, the two phases, and
the adversarial `--sandbox-warm-pool-concurrent-workers=1000` controller
setting the over-creation reproduced under. The overcreate template uses
the stress tool's standard small image — a review question ("once pulled,
the image sits on the nodes — any need for a big one?") prompted a
head-to-head measurement showing the small image trips the pre-fix asserts
*harder* (6.1x vs 3.1x, table below), so the multi-GB default was dropped
and `--wp-image` kept as the escape hatch. The scenario README documents
the kOps config and steps, the expected PASS/FAIL shapes, and the
~35-45 min / one-12-node-cluster cost — it is optional/manual because it
needs a real GCP cluster.

**Harness plumbing**: `Tracker.AddObserver` (phases can observe watch events
for objects the harness did not create — here: controller-owned Sandboxes
and pool Events), phase registration/validation/capacity-check/report
wiring in `main.go`, and a shared `waitOwnedSandboxesDrained` helper
(extracted from the claims-warm cleanup).

## Why

The invariants these phases encode were only provable by ad-hoc live runs
during the issue-1215 / PR-1266 work. Encoding them as a permanent scenario
gives warm-pool reconciler changes (expectations tracker, create/delete
gating, readiness-grace/unschedulable handling) a repeatable, whole-system
regression gate with a documented runbook, instead of a one-off script in a
GCS bucket.

## Validation

* `go build ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt`, `dev/tools/lint-go` (0 issues).
* `go test -race ./test/stress/` — new unit tests cover the watch
  accounting (replacement vs over-create attribution, per-pool and global
  peaks, namespace/owner filtering), the dedup-aware event counting, the
  unschedulable template shape, phase flag validation, and report
  attachment.
* Live two-direction run on a kOps GCP cluster (one tuned cluster, both
  controllers deployed back to back):

| Leg | Controller | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PASS | fixed (current main, af8a790) | **rc=0.** overcreate: 500/500 distinct creates, 0 replacements, 0 over-creates, per-pool peak 25/25, all pools Ready in 18.1s. unschedulable: 3 creates / 0 deletes over the 480s window, UIDs stable, exactly one `WarmPoolNotProgressing` Warning at +365s (inside the 5m-7m35s jitter window). |
| FAIL, small image (the scenario default) | pre-fix (95380d9, before the expectations gate) | **rc=1 in phase 1:** 3,070 distinct creates for the 500 target (**6.1x**), 1,312 over-creates, 1,258 replacements (tolerance 2), worst pool peak 117 vs 25, global peak 1,796 vs 500, 2,570 deletes during the fill; failing leg wall ~7 min. |
| FAIL, multi-GB image (supplementary, via `--wp-image`) | pre-fix (95380d9) | **rc=1 in phase 1:** 1,535 distinct creates (3.1x), all 20 pools exceeded their population caps (worst peak 75 vs 25), replacement tolerance blown (534 vs 2). |

  The small-image leg is why the scenario default changed during review
  (see the wrapper paragraph above): fast readiness transitions drive more
  status-update reconciles/sec against the stale cache, and the quick
  create->Ready->excess-delete cycle adds delete churn a slow pull never
  reaches. PASS-direction evidence with the same small image: the fixed
  controller produced exactly-600-for-600 in the single-pool gate-cost
  run. Optional follow-up validation (not blocking): a 20x25 small-image
  PASS leg can ride along a future cluster run as belt-and-braces.

  Verbatim abort from the small-image FAIL leg (the scenario default; the
  per-pool forensics the phase reports):

  aborting after error: warmpool-overcreate#1 phase: [warmpool-overcreate#1] warm pool
  invariants violated: 1312 sandbox creates beyond target without a preceding delete

body:
A client-go rate limiter hurts in two ways with opposite statistical
signatures, and the report only caught one of them. Queueing (demand
above QPS, open-loop callers) builds a backlog with a growing tail -
the existing >100ms finding fires. Pacing (demand at QPS, closed-loop
callers) meters every request by up to one token interval: waits are
uniform on [0, 1/QPS], the mean is half the interval, and no request
ever exceeds it - so tail- and threshold-based checks read a fully
engaged limiter as healthy.

The uniform shape also makes the mean a limit estimator: implied
per-instance QPS ~= 1/(2 x mean wait). New 'Limiter Regime by
Component' table on the Rate Limiting page shows per phase/component:
instances, req/s per instance, mean wait, implied QPS limit, and a
verdict badge (queueing / pacing / metered / ok); a new index finding
fires on pacing during throughput phases.

title: WIP: controller: strip managedFields from created Pods

labels.name: do-not-merge/work-in-progress
labels.description: Indicates that a PR should not merge because it is a work in progress.

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

labels.name: lifecycle/stale
labels.description: Denotes an issue or PR has remained open with no activity and has become stale.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it

**Experiment**: opt sandbox Pods out of API-server managedFields tracking, by issuing one merge patch with the documented reset sentinel (`metadata.managedFields: [{}]`) right after Pod creation.

**Why**: profiling the mif600 stress phase (run `2080880843894558720`, 40 nodes, 214 claims/s) shows **field tracking at 14.6% of kube-apiserver CPU** (`FieldManager.Update` 9.1% cumulative — ~2.1 of 14.7 cores), and Pods are the dominant payer: every scheduler binding, kubelet status PATCH, and teardown write converts the full object to structured-merge-diff typed form twice and diffs it.

**Mechanism** (verified in apimachinery v0.34 source):
- `skipNonAppliedManager` short-circuits the entire smd chain for plain (non-apply) writes when the live object has no managedFields — this is an existing, deliberate fast path.
- Objects are always born tracked (`DefaultTrackOnCreateProbability=1`, and the reset sentinel is ignored on create), so the strip must be a follow-up write: one extra patch buys the fast path for the Pod's remaining ~6–10 writes.
- **Status writes cannot re-seed tracking**: the subresource path reads managedFields from the live object only (`fieldmanager.go:83-87`), and re-seeding would require the chain the skip manager returns above. The only way back to tracking is a server-side apply against the Pod — nothing in the sandbox lifecycle does that, and if an external client ever does, tracking resumes benignly (`before-first-apply`).

**Why it matters beyond apiserver headroom**: cheaper `pods/status` PATCHes feed directly into kubelet's *serialized* status-sync loop — the measured end-to-end bottleneck (bound→kubelet-first-status 818ms p50 at mif600). Reducing per-PATCH server cost speeds the exact lane that caps claim throughput.

**Trade-off, stated plainly**: stripped Pods lose SSA conflict-detection semantics (a later `kubectl apply`/SSA force-takes-over as `before-first-apply`). Sandbox Pods are controller-owned and ephemeral; per team discussion this ships unflagged as an experiment. Sandboxes themselves stay tracked for now (Pods first).

**What to read in the presubmit**: apiserver CPU and managedFields share in the mif600 pprof, `PATCH pods/status` server-side latency, kubelet-observed PATCH latency, mif600 claims/s, and the watch stream (stripped pods must show no managedFields entries after creation — a built-in correctness check).

```release-note
Sandbox Pods are created with API-server managedFields tracking disabled, reducing apiserver CPU per pod write. Server-side apply against sandbox Pods resumes tracking with before-first-apply semantics.
```

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Newly created Sandbox Pods no longer retain managed field tracking immediately after creation.
  * Reconciliation avoids repeating the cleanup when the Pod already exists.

title: Surface backing-pod status aspects (Unschedulable, etc.) in Sandbox status

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Surface relevant backing-pod status aspects in `Sandbox.status` — starting with scheduling state (`PodScheduled=False` / reason `Unschedulable`), and considering other consumer-relevant signals (e.g. image-pull progress, container waiting reasons).

### Why is this needed?

Follow-up from the PR #1266 review ([thread](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/1266#discussion_r3645870361), request by @barney-s): today, controllers and clients that need to know *why* a sandbox is not Ready must look up the backing Pod. Inside the manager this is a cache read (pods are informer-cached via the sandbox controller's `Owns`), but:

- **Cross-controller contract:** the warm-pool controller's unschedulable-hold logic reads pod conditions directly — surfacing this in Sandbox status would make the Sandbox API self-describing and decouple consumers from pod internals.
- **External consumers** (SDKs, gateways, humans running `kubectl get sandbox`) currently can't distinguish "unschedulable" from "slow image pull" from "crashlooping" without pod access and RBAC for it.
- The `WarmPoolNotProgressing` event added in #1266 covers the pool-level signal; a per-sandbox status field would cover the object-level one.

Related: #1274 (configurable readiness grace / re-check interval — the two knobs would compose with this signal).

Note: this is an additive API change (new status field/condition) and deserves its own design discussion — filing per reviewer request to track it.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it

Adds `GenerationChangedPredicate` to the Sandbox controller's `For()` watch, so status-only Sandbox updates — which are overwhelmingly the controller's *own* status writes echoed back through the informer — no longer re-enqueue a reconcile that reads an unchanged spec and writes nothing (`updateStatus` already no-ops on `DeepEqual`).

**Measured on current main** (run `2080848067543699456`): 592 sandbox reconciles/s against 156 sandbox lifecycles/s, with exactly 2 status writes per lifecycle — i.e. the echo is roughly **half of all reconcile executions**. This is also the amplifier that made raising worker counts counterproductive in the #1259 200-worker experiment (5× request volume, throughput halved): more workers processing echo reconciles against a loaded apiserver is pure waste. The predicate removes the amplifier rather than tuning around it.

Correctness analysis (also in the code comment):
- Creates, deletes, and child Pod/Service events (via `Owns`) are unaffected — only Sandbox UPDATE events are filtered.
- Pod metadata propagation reads `spec.podTemplate.metadata`, and warm-pool adoption mutates `spec.podTemplate` — both bump `metadata.generation` and still reconcile.
- The only filtered edits are the Sandbox's own top-level labels/annotations, which the reconciler doesn't act on.

Cherry-picked from #1122 (`0f969efb`), with the reconcile-echo numbers re-measured against current main (the original ~44-reconciles/lifecycle figure predates other churn fixes that have since landed). Includes the test from the original commit.

Note: this was audited alongside the other #1122 controller optimizations; two of them (stable Ready message, pod-name annotation skip) were *dropped* after measurement showed their churn no longer reproduces on current main — see the analysis on run `2080848067543699456`: all 22,776 throughput sandboxes show exactly 2 status writes with a single message sequence. The fast-path child deletion commit remains a candidate for a separate PR.

```release-note
The Sandbox controller no longer re-reconciles on status-only Sandbox updates, roughly halving reconcile volume under churn.
```

body:
Replaces standard `reflect.DeepEqual` with `apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual` for comparing Kubernetes API objects in `controllers/sandbox_controller.go`.

Using `reflect.DeepEqual` on Kubernetes API objects is risky because:
1. It can fail on `metav1.Time` fields (e.g. in status conditions) if internal timezone location pointers differ, even if they represent the exact same time.
2. It treats `nil` and empty slices/maps as different.

Using `apiequality.Semantic.DeepEqual` is the standard and safer practice in Kubernetes controllers.
