body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds a `--namespace` flag to restrict the controller to watching and reconciling resources in one or more namespaces. The flag takes precedence over the `WATCH_NAMESPACE` environment variable and accepts comma-separated namespaces, following the Operator SDK convention. This enables operators in multi-tenant clusters to scope the controller cache and reconciliation activity instead of running cluster-wide.

When namespaced mode is enabled, the controller:

- Configures `cache.Options.DefaultNamespaces` for the selected namespaces.
- Requires `--enable-webhook=false` and skips the webhook server, certificate generation, and CRD `caBundle` patching.
- Resolves leader election in the controller Pod namespace in-cluster, or requires `--leader-election-namespace` when running out-of-cluster.
- Validates namespace and webhook configuration before starting the manager.

The Helm chart exposes this through `controller.watchNamespace`, injects the namespace, webhook, and leader-election arguments, and does not render ClusterRoles, ClusterRoleBindings, or the webhook Service in namespaced mode. The installation notes explain that advanced users must provide workload and leader-election Roles and RoleBindings for the selected namespaces.

Conversion webhooks remain a cluster-scoped responsibility. Before disabling them, migrate stored v1alpha1 objects to v1beta1 or keep a cluster-scoped conversion webhook available; otherwise API requests requiring conversion will fail.

The change includes unit tests, an end-to-end namespaced-mode test, Helm documentation, and controller configuration documentation.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #484

Supersedes #924.

#### Release Note

```release-note
Add `--namespace` to enable namespace-scoped controller deployments. Namespaced mode requires `--enable-webhook=false` and operator-provided workload and leader-election RBAC. Migrate stored v1alpha1 objects to v1beta1 or keep a cluster-scoped conversion webhook available, otherwise API requests requiring conversion will fail.
```

Nothing on the GitHub PR itself changes — kubernetes prow has no per-job PR-comment mechanism — but this removes all of the artifact-browser digging.

body:
Stacked on #1194 (first two commits) and #1202 (next two); **review the last commit only**. Stacking all of it means this PR's presubmit runs the full tuned configuration and its report demonstrates the new finding on real data.

The tuning sequence so far took throughput-mif200 from 4.4 → 8.5 → **15.6 ready/s** (mean launch latency 31s → 9.3s → 7.8s). But the latest run's report was silent: `run_podsandbox` dropped to 3.4s, under the CRI finding's 5s threshold, and nothing else tripped — no warning about what limits us now.

What limits us now, from run 2078062675492868096: the node-local pod-start pipeline. `kubelet_pod_start_sli` (kubelet's own pod-startup time, excluding image pulls and scheduling) averages **7.1s at mif200 vs a 1.5s uncontended probe baseline** — 3.4s inside the CRI `run_podsandbox` call and 3.7s queued around it in kubelet pod workers — while every control-plane stage is healthy (apiserver 4ms, scheduler 4ms, controller ack ~0, Cilium limiter/processing/client-throttle all near zero).

This commit adds:
- A **Kubelet Pod Start Pipeline** table on the CRI page: per phase, average pod start (SLI) split into `run_podsandbox` vs kubelet-worker time. On the pre-tuning run it cleanly shows the old story too (30.1s start, 28.9s of it in the sandbox call); on the new run it shows the even CRI/worker split.
- A finding — **Kubelet Pod-Start Pipeline Congested** — that fires when a throughput phase's average pod start exceeds 3× the probe baseline (and 3s absolute); critical above 10s. Baselining against the probe phase avoids a magic constant that goes stale as we keep tuning.

With this, the report for the tuned configuration says: `Kubelet Pod-Start Pipeline Congested (7.1s avg)` — and, from the #1202 page, `Client-side API Throttling in kube-controller-manager (0.19s avg wait)`, which is the next layer already becoming visible at 15.6 pods/s. Digging into the kubelet/containerd side will need node-level data (containerd metrics or the bpftrace profiler from #1122).

title: [bug] SandboxClient cannot be used for multi-cluster consumers — K8sHelper clobbers global kube config

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### What happened?

SandboxClient cannot be used for multi-cluster consumers. Any process that constructs more than one SandboxClient targeting different clusters ends up with all clients routing to the same cluster — whichever kubeconfig context was current-context when the last `SandboxClient()` was constructed.

Observed in a live 3-cluster GKE Standard fleet:
  - 100% success on the last-primed cluster
  - 100% SandboxWarmPoolNotFoundError on the other two — because the SDK was querying the last-primed cluster for warmpools that only live on the resolver-picked cluster

No warning or error surfaces in-process; the misroute manifests as a data-shaped error (`SandboxWarmPoolNotFoundError`, `SandboxNotFoundError`), so diagnosis needs a stress-test run and a per-cluster success-vs-failure pattern to spot.

Impact: any consumer that talks to more than one cluster in one process — fleet drivers, cross-cluster aggregators, load-balancing SDK wrappers...


### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Prereqs: two GKE clusters `cluster-a` and `cluster-b` with `SandboxWarmPool` `warmpool-a` on `cluster-a` and `warmpool-b `on cluster-b. Both contexts primed via `gcloud container clusters get-credentials`.

```
  from kubernetes import config
  from k8s_agent_sandbox import SandboxClient

  # Load context for cluster A, build a client for it.
  config.load_kube_config(context="gke_proj_us-central1-a_cluster-a")
  client_a = SandboxClient()

  # Load context for cluster B, build a client for it.
  config.load_kube_config(context="gke_proj_us-central1-a_cluster-b")
  client_b = SandboxClient()

  # Expected: client_a hits cluster-a, client_b hits cluster-b.
  # Actual:   BOTH hit cluster-b (the last-primed context), because K8sHelper's
  #           __init__ calls load_kube_config() with no args on every
  #           SandboxClient construction and resets the global default to
  #           whatever `current-context` in ~/.kube/config says at that moment.
  client_a.create_sandbox(warmpool="warmpool-a", namespace="ns")
  # → SandboxWarmPoolNotFoundError: "warmpool-a" not found  (looked on cluster-b)
```
  Repros deterministically. Order of construction is irrelevant — whichever context was set most recently before the SECOND `SandboxClient()` construction wins for both clients.

### Version

v0.5.1

### Anything else we need to know?

Root cause — [clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/k8s_helper.py:38-44](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/k8s_helper.py#L38-L44):

Two things compound:
1. `config.load_kube_config()` (no arg) resets the process-wide default Configuration to whatever current-context in `~/.kube/config` says. Runs on every `SandboxClient()` construction -> silently overwrites whatever the caller had loaded.
2. `CustomObjectsApi()` / `CoreV1Api()` constructed with no explicit configuration -> they capture that global default. All operations route via it. 

Same shape in [async_k8s_helper.py](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/async_k8s_helper.py).

Proposed fix: accept an explicit api_client in SandboxClient and thread it through `K8sHelper`:

```
  class K8sHelper:
      def __init__(self, api_client: kubernetes.client.ApiClient | None = None):
          if api_client is not None:
              self._api_client = api_client
          else:
              try:
                  config.load_incluster_config()
              except config.ConfigException:
                  config.load_kube_config()
              self._api_client = client.ApiClient()   # captures the just-loaded default
          self.custom_objects_api = client.CustomObjectsApi(self._api_client)
          self.core_v1_api = client.CoreV1Api(self._api_client)


  class SandboxClient:
      def __init__(self, ..., api_client: kubernetes.client.ApiClient | None = None):
          ...
          self.k8s_helper = K8sHelper(api_client=api_client)
```
  Gives callers this pattern:
```
  from kubernetes import client as k8s, config
  cfg = k8s.Configuration()
  config.load_kube_config(context="cluster-a", client_configuration=cfg)
  client_a = SandboxClient(api_client=k8s.ApiClient(configuration=cfg))
```

No global state; multiple concurrent SandboxClients coexist cleanly. Backward compatible (zero-arg constructor path unchanged).

Current workaround (fragile, not the fix) — external code rebinds internal APIs after construction:

```
  sandbox_client = SandboxClient()
  api_client = k8s.ApiClient(configuration=cfg)
  sandbox_client.k8s_helper.custom_objects_api = k8s.CustomObjectsApi(api_client)
  sandbox_client.k8s_helper.core_v1_api = k8s.CoreV1Api(api_client)
```

title: Rebalance test pyramid: migrate redundant E2E assertions to unit tests

labels.name: help wanted

body:
Output of a full test-pyramid analysis of the repo (generated with the `test-pyramid` agent skill proposed in #1199). Goal: anything unit-testable should be a unit test; E2E reserved for what genuinely needs a real cluster. Every recommendation below was verified by locating the exact reconciler seam and confirming the cited unit twin exists.

## Pyramid snapshot

| Layer | Now | After |
|---|---|---|
| Unit test functions (Go) | 380 | ~385 (5 new) |
| Unit test functions (Python, `clients/python/**/test/unit/`) | 364 | 364 |
| Go E2E test functions | 30 | 22 (−8 deleted, ~8 thinned) |
| Python SDK E2E | 5 | 5 (1 thinned) |

(Correction 2026-07-16: the initial snapshot omitted the 364 Python unit tests due to a wrong inventory glob — caught in review of #1199. True unit:E2E ratio is ~21:1, not ~11:1. Recommendations unaffected: coverage verification always used the real `test/unit/` files.)

Context: TestGrid shows the e2e job's red runs are overwhelmingly infra failures, so every E2E test removed shrinks flake exposure without losing logic coverage.

## Delete / fully migrate (8 E2E tests — all assertions have verified unit twins)

| E2E test | Unit twin |
|---|---|
| `test/e2e/extensions/warmpool_rollout_test.go` `TestWarmPoolRolloutSwitchTemplate` | `sandboxwarmpool_controller_test.go` `TestReconcilePool_TemplateRefUpdate_SameSpec` |
| `TestWarmPoolRolloutMetadataUpdate` (5s-sleep negative, flake-prone) | `TestReconcilePool_TemplateUpdateRecreate` label/annotation-drift cases |
| `TestWarmPoolRolloutMultiTemplateIsolation` | `TestFindWarmPoolsForTemplate` + new two-pool case (below) |
| `test/e2e/extensions/shutdown_policy_test.go` `TestSandboxClaimTTLAfterFinished` | `TestSandboxClaimCleanupPolicy`, `TestSandboxClaimTTLAfterFinishedCleanupPolicy` |
| `TestSandboxClaimExpiryUsesEarlierOfShutdownTimeAndTTL` (wall-clock `require.Never`, flake-prone) | `internal/lifecycle/expiry_test.go` `TestTimeLeft` earlier-of cases |
| `TestSandboxClaimFinishedWithoutTTLIsRetained` | `TestTimeLeft` "no expiry" + new cleanup-policy case (below) |
| `TestSandboxClaimTTLZeroRetainPreservesFinishedConditionDuringCleanup` | `TestSandboxClaimCleanupPolicy` / `...TTLAfterFinishedCleanupPolicy` / `...RequiresPersistedExpiredStatus` |
| `test/e2e/extensions/sandboxclaim_metric_test.go` `TestSandboxClaimObservabilityAnnotation` (never scrapes metrics) | new `TestInitializeAnnotations` (below — genuine unit gap) |

## Thin (keep physics core, drop assertions already unit-covered)

- `basic_test.go:TestSimpleSandbox` — keep golden-path smoke; drop owner-ref/label/FQDN predicates (covered by `TestReconcile`).
- `mode_test.go:TestSandboxOperatingMode` — keep real pod-termination ordering; drop condition tuples/service retention.
- `shutdown_test.go:TestSandboxShutdownTime` — keep not-before-deadline + physical deletion; drop status/decision predicates.
- `shutdown_test.go:TestSandboxRetainedExpiryPreservesFinishedCondition` — near-duplicate of unit `TestSandboxShutdownExpiryUsesTwoPassAndPreservesFinishedCondition`; reduce to real-exit-0→`Finished=PodSucceeded` or fold into the test above.
- `volumeclaimtemplate_test.go` — keep real provision/bind/mount (add `Phase==Bound`); drop PVC field predicates.
- `extensions/warmpool_rollout_test.go:TestWarmPoolRollout` — keep one Recreate rollout end-to-end; drop sleep-based onreplenish/default negatives (`TestReconcilePool_TemplateUpdateRollout` covers the matrix).
- `extensions/warmpool_sandbox_watcher_test.go:TestWarmPoolSandboxWatcher` — keep pod-adoption + deletion→not-Ready physics; drop owner-ref/status asserts.
- `extensions/sandboxclaim_vct_test.go` — collapse 8 policy-matrix subtests to 1-2 (cold chain + warm adoption); the matrix is covered by `TestCreateSandboxClaimVolumeClaimTemplatesSuccess`/`...Errors`.
- Python SDK `test_python_sdk_volume_claim_templates` — keep PVC-exists + `df -h`; drop spec/field asserts (covered in `test_sandboxclient.py` + controller tests). Note overlap with the Go VCT E2E — one of the two is redundant.
- `shutdown_policy_test.go:TestSandboxClaimTTLDeleteForegroundAfterFinished` — fold into `TestSandboxClaimDeleteForeground` or keep as sole TTL-cascade physics test.

## New unit tests required (5)

1. `TestInitializeAnnotations` (claim controller): assert `ObservabilityAnnotation` is actually WRITTEN with RFC3339Nano format and not overwritten — today unit tests only seed it as input.
2. Two-pool/two-template `reconcilePool` fake-client case asserting cross-pool non-interference.
3. Running→Suspended two-pass `Reconcile` case in `controllers/sandbox_controller_test.go` (gen-2 conditions + service retained).
4. `TestSandboxClaimCleanupPolicy` case: Delete policy + no expiry fields → nothing deleted.
5. Optional: direct pure-function table test for `mergeVolumeClaimTemplates`/`validateVolumeClaimTemplates`; interceptor-client assert that DeleteForeground passes `PropagationPolicy=Foreground`.

## Keep-E2E (confirmed, no action)

Chrome startup/benchmark, parallelism (×3), warmpool parallel-claim benchmark, python-runtime (×3), density, `TestWarmPoolPodNameAnnotationBeforeReady` (cross-controller watch-ordering), `TestSandboxClaimDeleteForeground` (real foreground GC), Python SDK routing modes (×4), migration + stress harnesses. Also: `test/e2e/framework/{client,watchset}_test.go` are already cluster-free unit tests — add `./test/e2e/framework/...` to the no-cluster unit CI lane.

## Suggested order (CI time + flake surface per effort)

1. Delete `TestWarmPoolRolloutSwitchTemplate` + `TestWarmPoolRolloutMetadataUpdate` (zero new code).
2. Delete the 4 shutdown-policy logic tests + add cleanup-policy unit case.
3. Migrate `TestSandboxClaimObservabilityAnnotation` (closes a real unit gap).
4. Collapse the VCT matrix 8→1-2 subtests.
5. Run `test/e2e/framework` in the unit lane.

/kind cleanup

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds `.agents/skills/test-pyramid/SKILL.md` — an agent skill that analyzes the repo's unit and E2E test suites and produces an evidence-backed rebalancing report toward a test pyramid: anything unit-testable should be a unit test; E2E should be reserved for what genuinely needs a real cluster (scheduling, real traffic/routing, kubelet behavior, GC/foreground-deletion semantics, cross-controller watch ordering, upgrade/migration).

The skill's core discipline is the **seam rule**: a suggestion to demote an E2E assertion to unit level is only valid if the analysis names the exact function (file:line) that computes the asserted value, confirms it is callable with the repo's existing fake-client house style (e.g. `extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller_test.go`), and greps for an existing unit twin first. Assertions are classified per-assertion (cluster-physics vs. logic), so mixed E2E tests get *thinned* rather than deleted. The report includes a pyramid snapshot (before/after test-function counts), an E2E→unit table, rare unit→E2E promotions, redundant-coverage listings, and quick wins ranked by CI time + flake surface removed (cross-referencing `dev/tools/flake-report` output / open `kind/flake` issues where available).

Validated by a full run against main: it correctly kept physics-dominated tests (parallelism, python-runtime, density, foreground-GC, watch-ordering) as E2E, identified E2E tests whose assertions have exact existing unit twins (e.g. `TestWarmPoolRolloutSwitchTemplate` vs `sandboxwarmpool_controller_test.go`'s `TestReconcilePool_TemplateRefUpdate_SameSpec`), and surfaced genuine unit gaps (e.g. no unit test asserts the observability annotation is actually written with RFC3339Nano format — only seeded as input).

Follows the existing `.agents/skills/` conventions (`bump-go-version`, `dev-rules`, `k8s-api-conventions`, `triage-issues`): frontmatter with name + trigger description, imperative phased instructions, repo-specific file references.

title: Agent Sandbox Gateway KEP with POC

labels.name: size/XXL

body:
## Description

This PR implements **KEP-1174: Agent Sandbox Gateway (Request-Buffering Auto-Resume)**, establishing a standards-compliant, zero-loss request-buffering auto-resume architecture using standard Kubernetes Gateway API (`gateway.networking.k8s.io`) and Gateway API Inference Extension (`inference.networking.k8s.io` `InferencePool`).

### Key Changes in the example POC
- **gRPC External Processor (`ext_proc`) Engine**: Extends `sandbox-router` (`cmd/sandbox-router/`) to act as a protocol-compliant Envoy `ext_proc` gRPC service on port `:50051`, handling all stream phases (`RequestHeaders`, `RequestBody`, `ResponseHeaders`, `ResponseBody`, `Trailers`).
- **Router-Less Direct Pod IP Forwarding**: Returns `x-gateway-destination-endpoint` ext_proc response metadata, allowing Envoy Ingress Gateway to stream request payloads directly to target Sandbox Pod IPs (`10.244.x.y:port`) without intermediate proxy hops.
- **Authenticated Thaw Signaling**: Integrates out-of-band signaling (`POST /v1/sandboxes/resume` on port `:8090`) carrying projected ServiceAccount JWT tokens to `sandbox-suspension-manager`.
- **Zero-Latency Informer Cache & Singleflight**: Incorporates real-time `Sandbox.status` Informer watching and `singleflight.Group` request deduplication to collapse concurrent thundering-herd cold-start requests.
- **Reference Manifests & Examples**: Provides multi-tenant sample manifests (`tenant-a`, `tenant-b`) and Envoy Gateway configuration in `examples/auto-resume-sandbox/`.
- **KEP Documentation Audit**: Updated [docs/keps/1174-agent-sandbox-gateway/README.md](docs/keps/1174-agent-sandbox-gateway/README.md) metadata key references and synchronized Markdown TOC (`make toc-verify`).

### Testing & Validation
- **Local Kind Cluster Testing**: Deployed Envoy Gateway + GAIE via `make deploy-envoy-epp` and verified cold-start thaw auto-resume and sub-millisecond warm request forwarding.
- **Linter & Build Checks**: Ran `make all` (`fix-go-generate`, `build`, `lint-go`, `lint-api`, `toc-verify`).

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds migration-test coverage for the upgrade regression fixed in #1191: SandboxClaims failing to warm-adopt sandboxes whose owner references were written by a pre-v1beta1 (v0.4.x) pool controller. Requested by reviewers on #1191 (SHRUTI6991, janetkuo) — kept as a separate PR so the fix could merge independently.

What the test does in `dev/tools/test-migration.py`:

1. **Pre-upgrade:** adds a v1alpha1 `SandboxWarmPool` (`upgrade-pool-adopt`, replicas 1) and waits for the *real v0.4.x controller* to create its warm sandbox — so the sandbox's owner reference is authentically stamped `extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1`, not synthesized. Captures the sandbox name and asserts the owner-ref apiVersion.
2. **Post-upgrade precondition:** asserts the sandbox survived migration with its owner reference still v1alpha1 (storage migration does not rewrite owner refs). If a future migration ever starts rewriting them, this assert flags that the test no longer exercises the legacy path.
3. **The regression check:** creates a fresh v1beta1 `SandboxClaim` against the pool and asserts it binds to the *pre-upgrade* sandbox. Distinct failure messages separate the #1190 failure mode (cold-started a sandbox named after the claim — legacy owner refs not matched) from the sandbox being skipped/replaced, with controller-log diagnostics dumped on failure.

**Verification:** ran `dev/ci/periodics/test-migration` end-to-end (kind, v0.4.6 → local build, `--test-rollback`) on a build containing the #1191 fix: both the kubectl and helm methods passed, with the new claim adopting the pre-upgrade sandbox in each run (`upgrade-pool-adopt-d5tbj` / `upgrade-pool-adopt-xmgk5`); all existing migration and rollback validations unaffected. On a pre-fix build the new check fails with the cold-start message, matching the behavior originally reported.

body:
Stacked on #1187 (first two commits are that PR; review the last commit here).

#1187's presubmit run gave us the first cilium-agent metrics, and they close the case on the launch-throughput ceiling: it is cilium-agent's own API rate limiter, not the datapath.

- `PUT /v1/endpoint` (the synchronous endpoint-create the CNI plugin issues during every pod sandbox creation) averaged 28.7s at throughput-mif200 — matching CRI `run_podsandbox` (28.9s) almost exactly.
- Of that, the `endpoint-create` API limiter accounted for a 20.8s mean wait (60s max), against 1.6s mean processing once admitted, and ~80ms of actual endpoint regeneration (BPF) work.
- The limiter defaults to 0.5/s (burst 4, 4 parallel) with auto-adjust anchored to a 2s estimated processing duration. Under churn, queueing pushes mean processing toward the anchor, so the adjusted limit converges to ~1.5–2.6 creates/s per node — precisely the ~2 sandboxes/s/node ceiling every stress run has hit. In-flight averaged <2 against a parallel capacity of 30+: the agent throttles itself while nearly idle.

This PR patches `cilium-config` after cluster validation to `endpoint-create=rate-limit:100/s,rate-burst:100,parallel-requests:32,auto-adjust:false` and restarts the cilium DaemonSet, so the stress test measures what the CNI can actually do. The report's new Cilium page distinguishes limiter wait from processing time, so if the bottleneck moves into endpoint processing itself (or somewhere else entirely), the next run's report will say so explicitly.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds opt-in failed-pod recreation for `Sandbox` via `spec.podFailurePolicy`.

When `podFailurePolicy` is set to `Recreate`, the controller deletes a controller-owned backing `Pod` that has entered `phase=Failed`, clears the sandbox pod-name annotation, and relies on the existing missing-pod create path to provision a fresh `Pod`. This preserves `Sandbox` identity and `Sandbox`-owned `PVC`s while allowing workloads that fail with `restartPolicy: Never` to recover automatically.

The controller only recreates `Pod`s that belong to the `Sandbox`, refuses to delete foreign-owned `Pods`, tolerates delete
races where the `Pod` is already gone, and avoids patching metadata onto a `Pod` that is about to be deleted. If an unowned
but adoptable failed `Pod` needs to be recreated, the controller first persists ownership and then deletes it.

The PR also updates the KEP, lifecycle/API docs, and test coverage for the recreate flow, including replacement of the
failed `Pod` and persistence of `PVC`-backed data across recreation.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #729

#### Release Note

Add opt-in `Sandbox.spec.podFailurePolicy=Recreate` support so the controller deletes controller-owned failed Pods and
recreates them while preserving Sandbox identity and Sandbox-owned PVCs.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`isAdoptable` in the SandboxClaim controller rejects any warm-pool candidate whose controller owner reference `apiVersion` is not exactly `extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1`. Owner references keep the apiVersion that was current when they were written — CRD storage migration never rewrites them — so warm Sandboxes created by a v0.4.x (v1alpha1) pool controller still carry `extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1` after an in-place upgrade to v0.5.x. Every candidate then fails with `sandbox ... is not managed by warm pool`, and each new SandboxClaim logs `Failed to adopt any sandbox after checking all candidates` and silently cold-starts (~5-8s) instead of warm-adopting (sub-second). This blocks in-place v0.4.x → v0.5.x fleet migrations with long-lived warm pools, as reported by Vertex AI Agent Engine.

This PR fixes both occurrences of the strict-version match (a repo-wide sweep for `.APIVersion ==`/`!=` comparisons shows these are the only two):

1. **Adoption path** (`extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go`): the controller reference is parsed with `schema.ParseGroupVersion` and matched on **group + kind** only. References from other groups (e.g. a `SandboxWarmPool` kind in a foreign group) are still rejected.
2. **Metrics collector** (`internal/metrics/sandbox_collector.go`, found in review): the `owned_by` label used the same exact-`v1beta1` string comparison, so legacy v1alpha1-owned sandboxes were reported as `owned_by="None"` after an upgrade, breaking fleet observability. The collector now matches on group only, so they correctly report `SandboxWarmPool`/`SandboxClaim`.

**Verification** (kind cluster, controller built at unfixed `e2a18b5` vs. this branch):
1. Created a v1beta1 SandboxTemplate + SandboxWarmPool (replicas 3), waited for all warm Sandboxes Ready, then patched each warm Sandbox's `ownerReferences[0].apiVersion` to `extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1` to recreate the post-upgrade state.
2. Unfixed controller: a new claim logged `Failed to adopt any sandbox after checking all candidates` → `creating sandbox from template`; all 3 warm Sandboxes untouched (reproduces the report exactly).
3. This branch, same cluster/objects: the next claim logged `Attempting sandbox adoption` → `Successfully adopted sandbox from warm pool` for a v1alpha1-ownerRef Sandbox, and the pool refilled.

**Regression tests** (each verified to fail against the unfixed code and pass with the fix):
- `TestIsAdoptable_RejectsUnowned` extension: a v1alpha1-ownerRef warm Sandbox is adoptable, and a same-kind reference from a foreign group (`apps/v1`) is still rejected, so the check does not become group-blind.
- `TestSandboxCollector` new case `legacy v1alpha1-owned warmpool sandbox`: asserts `owned_by:SandboxWarmPool` for a v1alpha1-ownerRef sandbox.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1190

#### Release Note

```release-note
Fixed two places where owner references written by pre-v1beta1 (v0.4.x) controllers were not recognized after an in-place upgrade: SandboxClaims failed to warm-adopt Ready sandboxes from pre-upgrade SandboxWarmPools and silently cold-started, and the agent_sandboxes metric reported owned_by="None" for pre-upgrade sandboxes. Owner references are now matched by group and kind instead of the exact apiVersion.
```

title: SandboxClaims fail to warm-adopt from SandboxWarmPools created before the v1beta1 upgrade

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

body:
**What happened:**

On a cluster upgraded in place from a v0.4.x (v1alpha1) controller to v0.5.x/main, a new SandboxClaim referencing an existing, healthy SandboxWarmPool never warm-adopts any of the pool's Ready sandboxes. The reconciler logs `Failed to adopt any sandbox after checking all candidates` and silently falls through to the cold-start path (`creating sandbox from template`). Claims still become Ready, so the regression is invisible to health checks — it only shows up as ~5-8s cold-start latency instead of sub-second adoption.

**Root cause:**

`isAdoptable` in `extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go` requires the candidate's controller owner reference to match `extensionsv1beta1.GroupVersion.String()` exactly (`extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1`). Owner references preserve the apiVersion that was current when they were written and are not rewritten by CRD storage migration, so warm Sandboxes created by a v0.4.x pool controller still carry `extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1` after the upgrade and every candidate is rejected with `sandbox ... is not managed by warm pool`.

**How to reproduce (verified on kind at main HEAD e2a18b5):**

1. Create a v1beta1 SandboxTemplate + SandboxWarmPool (replicas: 3); wait for warm sandboxes to be Ready.
2. Simulate v0.4.x-origin sandboxes: `kubectl patch sandbox <name> --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/metadata/ownerReferences/0/apiVersion","value":"extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1"}]'` for each warm sandbox.
3. Create a SandboxClaim referencing the pool.
4. Observe: `Failed to adopt any sandbox after checking all candidates` + cold start; warm sandboxes untouched. Patching a single sandbox's ownerRef back to v1beta1 makes exactly that sandbox adoptable.

**Why existing tests miss it:** the e2e warm-pool benchmark and the adoption unit tests create pool + claim in the same run, so owner references are always stamped v1beta1; the cross-version case is only reachable via an in-place v0.4.x → v0.5.x upgrade.

**Impact:** blocker for in-place v0.4.x → v0.5.x fleet migrations with long-lived warm pools (reported by Vertex AI Agent Engine against their GKE eval cluster; every claim on every upgraded tenant cluster would silently cold-start).

**Fix:** match the owner reference on group + kind instead of the full apiVersion.

/kind bug

body:
## What

Add an optional `ttlSecondsAfterCreated` field to both `SandboxWarmPool` and `SandboxClaim`, the upstream equivalents of `OSGymWorkspacePool` and `OSGymSandboxClaim`.

## Semantics

- Setting `ttlSecondsAfterCreated` opts the resource into server-side reaping.
- The controller deletes the resource once the configured number of seconds has elapsed since `metadata.creationTimestamp`.
- Leaving the field absent or nil means the resource lives forever and is never automatically reaped based on age.
- The behavior applies to both pool and claim resources.

## Implementation

- Adds the field to `v1alpha1` and `v1beta1` API types with a minimum value of zero.
- Preserves the field across version conversion and generated CRDs/deep-copy code.
- Requeues controllers for the remaining TTL and deletes expired resources.
- Adds lifecycle, controller, and conversion tests.

## Validation

- `go test ./internal/lifecycle ./extensions/api/v1alpha1 ./extensions/controllers`
- `make lint-go lint-api`
- `make test-unit` ran all 973 Go tests successfully; the wrapper then could not start its Python tests because this environment lacks the system `python3-venv` package.

Analysis of the first post-#1183 stress run ([artifacts](https://gcsweb.k8s.io/gcs/kubernetes-ci-logs/pr-logs/pull/kubernetes-sigs_agent-sandbox/1183/presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp/2077449092094496768/artifacts/stress-test/)) shows the capacity fix landed but throughput is unchanged: launch rate is still ~4.4 ready/s at mif200 and *drops* as concurrency rises.

We suspect the CNI ADD path — Cilium endpoint creation + BPF regeneration — as the prime suspect, and we currently have zero visibility into it: `promscrape.go` already targets cilium-agent on :9090 (merged in #1176), but the kOps cluster never enabled the endpoint, so every scrape fails with connection refused.

This enables `cluster.spec.networking.cilium.enablePrometheusMetrics=true` (agent port defaults to 9090, matching the scraper).

We then add a page to our report that shows the information, and indeed it shows we are client-side rate-limited on PUT on /v1/endpoints, and this accounts for most of the time for pod launch (as much as 20 seconds!).  The client-side rate limiting appears to be Cilium's own rate limiting, not kubernetes rate limiting; a fix to raise the rate limit will follow in a separate PR.

title: gate webhook implementation

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
### Summary
This change introduces an `--enable-webhook` flag (default: `true`) to allow operators to explicitly enable or disable the controller-runtime webhook server and webhook registrations independently of certificate management (`--manage-webhook-certs`).

### Problem
Previously, `--manage-webhook-certs` controlled both **how** certificates were managed AND implicitly assumed that the webhook server should always run:
1. When `--manage-webhook-certs=false`, the controller unconditionally checked for `tls.crt`/`tls.key` in `--webhook-cert-dir` on startup and exited with status `1` if they were missing.
2. Even when CRDs did not require webhook conversion (`conversion: strategy: None`) or validating/mutating webhooks, the `WebhookServer` was always initialized and passed to `ctrl.NewManager()`, and all `NewWebhookManagedBy()` calls registered the `/convert` endpoint because the Go types implement `conversion.Hub`.
3. This made it impossible to run the controller cleanly with webhook conversion disabled without either granting unnecessary secret-creation RBAC permissions to the controller or mounting dummy TLS certificate volumes.

### Solution
- **`--enable-webhook` flag (`bool`, default `true`)**: Gates the entire webhook subsystem.
  - When `--enable-webhook=false`:
    - Skips `generateWebhookCerts()` and `patchCRDs()` completely.
    - Skips the `os.Stat` pre-check for `tls.crt` and `tls.key` on disk.
    - Omits configuring `ctrl.Options.WebhookServer` when creating the manager (`ctrl.NewManager()`).
    - Skips calling `ctrl.NewWebhookManagedBy(...).Complete()` for `Sandbox`, `SandboxClaim`, `SandboxTemplate`, and `SandboxWarmPool`.
- **Operator Guidance Warning**: Added a startup log warning when `--enable-webhook=false` is combined with `--manage-webhook-certs=true` (`setupLog.Info("--manage-webhook-certs has no effect when --enable-webhook=false")`) to prevent operator confusion regarding flag precedence.

### Impact
- **Non-breaking**: Defaults remain `--enable-webhook=true` and `--manage-webhook-certs=true`, preserving existing behavior for standard deployments and local development.
- **Improved Operator Experience**: Deployments that do not use webhooks (e.g., GKE Addon / distro deployments using `v1beta1` with `conversion: strategy: None`) can set `--enable-webhook=false` to run with zero webhook certificate footprint and reduced RBAC requirements.

* **Bug Fixes**

  * Prevented unnecessary webhook configuration and certificate processing when disabled.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds a new example under `examples/containarium-ssh-sandbox` that runs
[Containarium](https://github.com/FootprintAI/Containarium)'s `agent-box`
runtime as a `Sandbox` workload, giving an AI agent an **SSH-reachable,
MCP-native** environment in which the agent holds only an SSH key — never a
kube-apiserver token or any cluster-scoped credential.

The example demonstrates an access pattern layered on top of the `Sandbox`
CRD that complements the existing `mcp-server-sandbox` example. Where
`mcp-server-sandbox` uses `kubectl exec` as its MCP transport (spending a
cluster-scoped credential on every agent call), here the box runs a dropbear
SSH server pinned by a forced command straight into the in-container MCP
server, so the agent's ongoing credential is a single SSH key that can do
nothing cluster-scoped even if it leaks.

What's included:

- **`agent-box` as a `Sandbox` workload** — `automountServiceAccountToken:
  false`, a persistent workspace via `volumeClaimTemplates`, a headless
  `service`, and a rootless container (`runAsNonRoot`, `drop: [ALL]`,
  `RuntimeDefault` seccomp).
- **A username-routed SSH gateway** (sshpiper): `ssh box-a@<gateway>` and
  `ssh box-b@<gateway>` reach different boxes over the same endpoint and the
  same key, with a two-hop key chain (agent key at the gateway, a separate
  upstream key the box authorizes). Raw manifests, no templating.
- **A local `kubectl port-forward` smoke test** for a single box, documented
  explicitly as a convenience rather than the access model.
- **`run-test-kind.sh`** exercises both paths on kind and verifies each with
  a real MCP `initialize` handshake (and, for the gateway, a
  `shell_exec(hostname)` round-trip proving the username routed to the
  right box).

Everything is pinned to a published Containarium release (`v0.52.1`) — both
the container images and the sshpiper `Pipe` CRD, which is fetched from that
release tag at apply time (not vendored into the repo) — so the example is

labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
Spoiler alert: #1122 ended up with kube-apiserver CPU being a bottleneck, so I think it's interesting to track the CPU profile as we go along our journey here.


- **stress-test: capture apiserver CPU profiles during throughput levels**
  Extracted from #1122: fetch /debug/pprof/profile from the kube-apiserver
  during each throughput level (20s window starting 5s in, to skip the
  slot-fill burst) and write it to pprof-apiserver-<phase>.pprof. The
  apiserver is the dominant control-plane CPU consumer under churn, and
  its CPU pressure inflates every client's observed API latency.
  
  The files are standard pprof format (gzip-compressed profile.proto);
  analyze with go tool pprof, or with the report's flamegraph page.
  
  Enabled by default; disable with --profile-apiserver=false. Capture
  failures are logged, never fatal.
  

- **stress-report: render CPU profile flame graphs client-side**
  Add a CPU Profiles page to the stress report that renders flame graphs
  from the pprof files captured during throughput levels. In keeping with
  the report's client-side architecture, the pprof file (gzip-compressed
  profile.proto) is fetched and decoded entirely in the browser: a small
  protobuf wire-format parser in flamegraph.js builds the call tree, and
  d3-flame-graph (CDN) renders it with zoom and search. No server-side
  conversion, and the raw .pprof files sit next to the report for offline
  go tool pprof analysis.
  
  download_results.py now derives pprof filenames from summary.json
  phases (handling both the current and older phases schemas) and saves
  older .pb captures under the canonical .pprof name; the gzip extension
  restore is now limited to .jsonl artifacts since pprof files are
  gzip-compressed by definition.

The stress-test presubmit has been running a configuration that exceeds cluster capacity: fill=150 plus throughput-mif200 needs up to 350 concurrent pods, but the 3-node cluster only has ~320 spare pod slots (3 nodes × 110 max-pods, minus ~10 pre-existing pods). title: Add a capacity-cliff load-test recipe for SandboxWarmPool

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?


A ClusterLoader2 load-testing recipe similar to #1100 to finds the point at which the SandboxWarmPool controller can no longer keep a pool converged, i.e. where "performance falls off a cliff."

It would include two scenarios, each targeting a different hot path in the warm-pool controller:

- Single large pool convergence: Deploy a `SandboxTemplate` and a single `SandboxWarmPool`, then ramp the pool's `spec.replicas` upward in discrete steps (e.g. 1k→2k→…), snapshotting diagnostics at each step. The cliff is the first step whose pool fails to reach readyReplicas == spec.replicas within the convergence timeout.
- Many small pools convergence: Deploy one `SandboxTemplate` referenced by many `SandboxWarmPools` (1-to-N) with `updateStrategy: Recreate`, then ramp the pool count. Then mutate the shared template to trigger the `SandboxTemplate`→`SandboxWarmPool` watch fan-out. The cliff is where the controller can no longer re-reconcile all N pools after a template change.

### Why is this needed?

As a follow-up to [#1137](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/1137#issuecomment-4973474095), we need a load test to verify the warm-pool controller's performance after the fix and to serve as a reusable benchmark for future optimizations.

labels.name: size/M

labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
## Summary
- Replace `time.After` in `retryTransport.RoundTrip` with a single `time.NewTimer` reused across all retry iterations via `Stop` + non-blocking drain + `Reset`.
- `time.After` allocates a new timer per iteration that is not GC'd until it fires; in a retry loop this causes unnecessary timer allocations.
- The drain must be non-blocking (`select` with `default`) because the prior `select` may have already consumed the timer value — a blocking read would deadlock on the second retry iteration.

ref: https://pkg.go.dev/time#Timer

## Changes
- `sandbox-router/proxy/retry.go`: refactor `RoundTrip` to reuse a single timer.
- `sandbox-router/proxy/retry_test.go`: add two regression tests:
  - `TestRetryTransport_TimerReuseAcrossManyRetries`: 20 retries with 1ms delay, guarded by a 10s timeout so a drain regression fails rather than hangs.
  - `TestRetryTransport_TimerDrainToleratesAlreadyConsumedChannel`: targets the exact bug scenario where the timer fires, `select` consumes `timer.C`, and the next iteration's `Stop` returns false.

  * Added coverage for many rapid retries to ensure requests complete without timing deadlocks.
  * Added coverage to ensure retry waiting remains safe even when the wait mechanism fires/has already been consumed.

title: Add a new `sandbox-gateway` to Agent Sandbox

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/awaiting-more-evidence
labels.description: Lowest priority. Possibly useful, but not yet enough support to actually get it done.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

**`sandbox-gateway`** component for the opt-in auto-suspend and auto-resume feature.

### Why is this needed?

We need to extend `sandbox-router` because its legacy prototype architecture cannot scale to production multi-tenant Kubernetes environments due to fundamental design limitations:
1. **User-Space Memory & Bandwidth Bottlenecks**: `sandbox-router` proxies full request payload bodies through its Python user-space process. Accumulating large payload requests in memory during container cold-starts risks Out-of-Memory (OOM) proxy crashes and severely bottlenecks data streaming throughput.
2. **Lack of Gateway API Standardization**: It relies on custom proxy routing rather than hooking natively into standard Kubernetes Gateway API primitives (`gateway.networking.k8s.io`) and production edge load balancers (Envoy Gateway, GKE Gateway).
3. **No Automatic Auto-Resume Signaling**: The legacy router cannot intercept traffic targeting suspended sandboxes to trigger dynamic container wakeups or hold connection streams during cold starts.
4. **Lack of Cold-Start Buffering & Protection**: It cannot pause incoming TCP connections at the kernel socket layer during 5–10 second container boot windows, nor does it provide context-aware rate limiting to protect cluster worker nodes from thundering-herd scheduling storms.

This is needed to comply with the on-going auto suspend and resume design: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/972/changes

body:
Add `IdleLifecyclePolicy` to `SandboxSpec` enabling two-phase TTL-based lifecycle management: Running sandboxes auto-suspend after an idle timeout, and suspended sandboxes are deleted after a retention period.

The controller tracks activity via `status.lastActivityTime` (updated by the router/SDK) and enforces the configured TTLs with configurable expiration policies (Suspend/Delete for active, Delete/Retain for suspended).

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Long-lived sandboxes (browser IDEs, notebooks, agent workspaces) waste resources when idle but are expensive to rebuild. This PR adds `spec.idleLifecycle` with a two-phase TTL model:

- `activeTTLSeconds` — how long a Running sandbox can remain without activity before the `activeExpirationPolicy` applies (Suspend or Delete)
- `suspendedTTLSeconds` — how long a Suspended sandbox remains before the `suspendedExpirationPolicy` applies (Delete or Retain)
- `status.lastActivityTime` — tracks last activity, updated by the router/SDK, used by the controller to enforce idle TTLs

The controller handles the full lifecycle: auto-suspend on idle, proper resume with TTL reset, and cleanup of the Suspended condition on resume.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #849

Relates to #968, #694, #103

#### Release Note

```release-note
Added idle lifecycle policy (`spec.idleLifecycle`) to Sandbox, enabling automatic suspend after idle timeout and automatic deletion after a configurable retention period.
```

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This is a follow-up to #1115. That PR fixed the Go SDK-side dot-path encoding, but review feedback on #1115 showed the encoded path did not survive the Python sandbox-router hop in the actual reported topology.

Preserve the original raw path and query string when the Python sandbox-router proxies HTTP and WebSocket traffic to a sandbox backend.

The router previously rebuilt backend URLs from the decoded Starlette URL object. That decoded percent-encoded dot segments such as `%2E` and `%2E%2E` before forwarding, so a Go SDK request that intentionally encoded `.` or `..` could still reach the backend as `/list/.` or `/list/..` through the router topology.

This change uses the ASGI scope's `raw_path` and `query_string` values when constructing the backend URL, with a fallback to the existing URL object when raw scope values are unavailable. It also adds regression coverage for escaped dot and dotdot path segments.

Validation:
- Temporarily restored the old `url.replace(...)` target URL construction and confirmed the new regression tests fail because `%2E` and `%2E%2E` are decoded before forwarding.
- Restored the fix and confirmed the same regression tests pass:
  `bin/python-venv-sandbox-router/bin/python -m pytest clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/sandbox-router/test_sandbox_router.py -k "preserves_raw_escaped"`
- `bin/python-venv-sandbox-router/bin/python -m py_compile clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/sandbox-router/sandbox_router.py clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/sandbox-router/test_sandbox_router.py`
- `git diff --check`

title: Proposal: KubeVirt VirtualMachine runtime backend

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

body:
## Summary

Add `runtimeBackend: VirtualMachine` to Sandbox (and SandboxTemplate) so the controller can provision sandboxes as KubeVirt VirtualMachines instead of Pods. This enables full-OS sandboxes with kernel-level isolation, persistent root disks, and workloads that need systemd, custom kernels, or nested containers (rootless podman, for example).

I have a working POC on a fork branch ([`shanemcd/agent-sandbox:kubevirt-backend`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/compare/main...shanemcd:agent-sandbox:kubevirt-backend)) with unit tests. Happy to open a PR once the design direction is agreed on.

## Motivation

Pod sandboxes are a great default, but some agent workloads benefit from a VM boundary:

- **Stronger isolation.** A VM gives a full kernel boundary rather than shared-kernel namespaces.
- **Full OS environments.** Agents that need systemd services, custom networking, or rootless podman cannot run in a standard Pod.
- **Persistent root disk with in-place upgrades.** A containerDisk can be swapped and the VMI restarted without losing PVC data, which is useful for long-lived agent workspaces.

KubeVirt is already a CNCF project and widely deployed alongside Kubernetes. The goal is to let users opt into VMs without changing the Sandbox API shape they already use.

## Design

### API: how the VM spec maps into Sandbox and SandboxTemplate

A single new field on `SandboxBlueprint` (shared by Sandbox and SandboxTemplate):

```go
type RuntimeBackend string

const (
    RuntimeBackendPod            RuntimeBackend = "Pod"
    RuntimeBackendVirtualMachine RuntimeBackend = "VirtualMachine"
)

type SandboxBlueprint struct {
    // ... existing fields ...

    // runtimeBackend selects the compute backend.
    // "Pod" (default) creates a Kubernetes Pod.
    // "VirtualMachine" creates a KubeVirt VirtualMachine.
    // +kubebuilder:default=Pod
    // +optional
    RuntimeBackend RuntimeBackend `json:"runtimeBackend,omitempty"`
}
```

The existing `podTemplate` fields are reinterpreted for the VM backend rather than duplicated into a new API surface:

| `podTemplate` field | Pod backend | VirtualMachine backend |
|---|---|---|
| `containers[0].image` | Container image | KubeVirt containerDisk source (OCI image with qcow2 at `/disk/`) |
| `containers[0].env` | Container env vars | Serialized into a metadata Secret as `KEY=VALUE` lines |
| `containers[0].volumeMounts` | Standard mounts | Determines which PVCs/Secrets attach as virtio disks |
| `volumes[].secret` | Pod Secret volume | KubeVirt Secret virtio disk |
| `volumeClaimTemplates` | StatefulSet-style PVCs | Same PVCs, attached as virtio disks |
| `operatingMode` | Pod start/stop | VM `spec.running: true/false` |

A user's Sandbox CR looks like this:

```yaml
apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
metadata:
  name: my-vm
spec:
  runtimeBackend: VirtualMachine
  volumeClaimTemplates:
  - metadata:
      name: workspace
    spec:
      accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
      resources:
        requests:
          storage: 10Gi
  podTemplate:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: sandbox
        image: quay.io/containerdisks/fedora:latest
        env:
        - name: GREETING
          value: hello
        volumeMounts:
        - name: workspace
          mountPath: /workspace
```

SandboxTemplate works identically since it inherits `SandboxBlueprint`.

### Controller: how VM management integrates

The VM backend lives alongside the Pod backend in the existing `SandboxReconciler`, branching on `spec.runtimeBackend` during child resource reconciliation:

```
reconcileChildResources()
├── reconcilePVCs()            # shared: both backends
├── if VirtualMachine:
│   └── reconcileVirtualMachine()
│       ├── createSandboxMetaSecret()   # env + volumes.json
│       ├── createVirtualMachine()      # unstructured KubeVirt VM
│       ├── syncVMContainerDiskImage()  # in-place image update
│       └── updateStatusFromVMI()       # VMI phase → Sandbox conditions
├── else (Pod):
│   └── reconcilePod()         # unchanged
├── reconcileService()         # shared: both backends
└── computeConditions()        # Pod only; VM sets its own
```

Key implementation details:

1. **No kubevirt.io Go dependency.** The controller uses `unstructured.Unstructured` with typed local structs that convert via `runtime.DefaultUnstructuredConverter`. This avoids pulling in the large kubevirt.io module tree.

2. **Guest metadata contract.** Instead of cloud-init, the controller creates a Secret (`<sandbox>-meta`) with two keys:
   - `env`: all container env vars as `KEY=VALUE` lines (systemd EnvironmentFile-compatible)
   - `volumes.json`: a JSON array describing each attached disk (name, virtio serial, mount path, source type, claim/secret name)
   
   This Secret is attached as a virtio disk with the fixed serial `sandboxmeta`. The guest is responsible for reading these and mounting disks accordingly. This keeps the controller guest-OS-agnostic without assuming cloud-init or any specific distro tooling.

3. **Volume mapping.** `volumeClaimTemplates` with matching `volumeMounts` on the first container become virtio PVC disks. `volumes[].secret` entries with matching mounts become virtio Secret disks. Both are described in `volumes.json` so the guest can discover them by serial at `/dev/disk/by-id/virtio-<serial>`.

4. **Lifecycle.** `operatingMode: Suspended` patches the VM to `spec.running: false`. Resuming patches it back to `true`. The controller watches VMI status and maps its phase to the Sandbox `Ready` condition (`Running` = Ready, `Succeeded`/`Failed` = Finished).

5. **In-place containerDisk sync.** When the Sandbox `containers[0].image` changes, the controller patches the VM's containerDisk volume to match. It does not auto-restart the VMI, allowing operators to reboot at their convenience while preserving PVC data.

6. **Opt-in RBAC.** KubeVirt permissions (`kubevirt.io` VirtualMachine/VMI CRUD) live in a separate ClusterRole (`agent-sandbox-controller-kubevirt`) so Pod-only installs carry no extra RBAC. Enablement is a one-line `kubectl apply` or Helm `--set controller.kubevirt=true`.

### What I'd like feedback on

1. **Reusing `podTemplate` vs. a new VM-specific section.** The POC reuses `podTemplate` fields to keep the API surface small and make it easy to switch backends. The trade-off is that some Pod-specific fields are not applicable in VM mode. An alternative would be a dedicated `vmTemplate` section, but that duplicates a lot of shared structure.

2. **Guest metadata via Secret+serial vs. cloud-init.** The POC avoids cloud-init to stay guest-OS-agnostic. The trade-off is that the guest needs its own bootstrap logic to consume `volumes.json`. Is there a preferred approach?

3. **Scope for a first PR.** I can structure this as one PR or split it (API types, controller, RBAC/Helm, tests). What would reviewers prefer?

/kind feature
/kind api-change

title: feat: Prometheus metrics for Sandbox suspend, resume, Finished, and expiry lifecycle

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Prometheus metrics (and optional inventory labels) for the existing Sandbox **suspend / resume**, **Finished**, and **expiry / deletion** lifecycle paths.

Optional inventory label extensions on `agent_sandboxes` (and claim gauge if present):
- `suspended` ∈ {`true`,`false`}
- optionally `finished` / `finished_reason` ∈ {`none`,`PodSucceeded`,`PodFailed`}

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `agent_sandbox_suspend_total` | Counter | `namespace`, `sandbox_template`, `owned_by`, `result` ∈ {`requested`,`pod_terminated`,`error`} | Suspend path progress |
| `agent_sandbox_suspend_latency_ms` | Histogram | `namespace`, `sandbox_template`, `owned_by` | Suspend requested → `Suspended=True` (`PodTerminated`) |
| `agent_sandbox_resume_total` | Counter | `namespace`, `sandbox_template`, `owned_by`, `result` ∈ {`requested`,`ready`,`error`} | Resume path progress |
| `agent_sandbox_resume_latency_ms` | Histogram | `namespace`, `sandbox_template`, `owned_by` | Resume requested → Ready again |
| `agent_sandbox_finished_total` | Counter | `namespace`, `sandbox_template`, `owned_by`, `reason` ∈ {`PodSucceeded`,`PodFailed`} | `Finished` condition becomes True |
| `agent_sandbox_expired_total` | Counter | `namespace`, `sandbox_template`, `owned_by`, `shutdown_policy` | Sandbox marked expired / child teardown starts |
| `agent_sandbox_deletion_latency_ms` | Histogram | `namespace`, `kind` ∈ {`Sandbox`,`SandboxClaim`}, `shutdown_policy` | Expiry/deletionTimestamp → cleaned up |

Related: [#1113](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1113), [#1114](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/1114), [#759](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/759), [#103](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/103), [#694](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/694).

### Why is this needed?

Basic suspend/resume is implemented via `spec.operatingMode: Running|Suspended` (delete Pod on suspend; recreate on resume; `Suspended` condition). Sandbox also has `Finished` and expiry (`SandboxExpired`) paths. **None of this is exported as Prometheus metrics.** `agent_sandboxes` has no `suspended` / `finished` labels.

Open work around [#1113](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1113) / [#1114](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/1114) only prevents creation-latency histograms from being re-recorded on resume — it does not add resume/suspend telemetry. Resume timing must not reuse creation/startup histograms.

Auto suspend-on-idle remains roadmap-planned; snapshot/soft-pause is separate. This issue covers metering the **existing** PVC-based suspend/resume and related terminal lifecycle first.

Alternatives (insufficient alone): only Kubernetes Events; waiting for soft-pause / snapshot APIs before any suspend metrics.

title: Proposal: Add E2B-compatible HTTP API gateway for seamless SDK migration

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/awaiting-more-evidence
labels.description: Lowest priority. Possibly useful, but not yet enough support to actually get it done.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

An **E2B-compatible HTTP API gateway** that translates the standard E2B REST API (`/api/v1/sandboxes`, `/api/v1/templates`, etc.) into `agent-sandbox` CRD operations, enabling zero-code migration for users of the official [E2B Python/JS SDKs](https://e2b.dev/docs), CLI, and downstream AI Agent frameworks (LangChain, AutoGPT, OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, etc.).

#### Proposed Architecture

```
 E2B SDK (Python/JS)  /  E2B CLI
         │
         │  HTTPS (E2B protocol)
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  E2B API Gateway (this proposal)    │
│  ┌───────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ Route Handler                 │  │
│  │  POST /api/v1/sandboxes       │──┼──▶ Create SandboxClaim / Sandbox CR
│  │  GET  /api/v1/sandboxes       │──┼──▶ List Sandboxes
│  │  GET  /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}  │──┼──▶ Get Sandbox
│  │  POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/pauses  │──┼──▶ Set operatingMode: Paused
│  │  POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/resumes │──┼──▶ Set operatingMode: Running
│  │  DELETE /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}│──┼──▶ Delete Sandbox CR
│  │  POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/code    │──┼──▶ exec into Pod (runtime interface)
│  │  POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/files  │──┼──▶ exec cp / filesystem ops
│  │  GET  /api/v1/templates       │──┼──▶ List SandboxTemplates
│  └───────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                     │
│  Auth: API Key validation           │
│  Metrics: Prometheus + OTel         │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
         │
         │  K8s API
         ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  agent-sandbox controller           │
│  (existing CRDs: Sandbox,           │
│   SandboxTemplate, SandboxWarmPool, │
│   SandboxClaim)                     │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

#### API Endpoint Mapping

| E2B API | Method | agent-sandbox Operation |
|---------|--------|------------------------|
| `POST /api/v1/sandboxes` | Create sandbox | Create `SandboxClaim` referencing a `SandboxTemplate`, wait for Pod Ready |
| `GET /api/v1/sandboxes` | List sandboxes | List `Sandbox` CRs in namespace |
| `GET /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}` | Get sandbox | Get `Sandbox` CR + Pod status |
| `DELETE /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}` | Kill sandbox | Delete `Sandbox` CR (cascading pod deletion) |
| `POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/pauses` | Pause sandbox | Patch `Sandbox.spec.operatingMode: Paused` |
| `POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/resumes` | Resume sandbox | Patch `Sandbox.spec.operatingMode: Running` |
| `POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/code` | Execute code | Exec into Pod → runtime sidecar (see KEP-539.2) |
| `POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/commands` | Run command | Exec into Pod → runtime sidecar |
| `POST /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/files/write` | Write file | Exec cp or runtime sidecar filesystem API |
| `GET /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}/files/read` | Read file | Exec cat or runtime sidecar filesystem API |
| `GET /api/v1/templates` | List templates | List `SandboxTemplate` CRs |

#### Implementation Suggestions

1. **Separate binary or sidecar deployment** — a new `cmd/e2b-gateway` or deploy as a sidecar to the controller pod. The gateway is stateless and horizontally scalable.

2. **Resource mapping**:
   - E2B Sandbox ↔ `Sandbox` CR (with `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-id` annotation mapping to E2B sandbox ID format)
   - E2B Template ↔ `SandboxTemplate` CR
   - E2B Warm Pool ↔ `SandboxWarmPool` CR (transparent — SDK `create()` auto-uses warm pool when available)
   - E2B API Key ↔ K8s `Secret` or configurable header token

3. **Integration with KEP-539.2 runtime interface** — the gateway delegates code execution and file operations to the standardized in-pod runtime (REST sidecar `execd` or gRPC sidecar `envd`), keeping the control-plane (CRD lifecycle) and data-plane (code execution) cleanly separated.

4. **Sandbox ID format** — generate E2B-compatible sandbox IDs (e.g., `abc123def456`) and store as annotation on the `Sandbox` CR, so `GET /api/v1/sandboxes/{id}` can look up by annotation index.

#### Example Usage (zero code change for E2B users)

```python
import os
# Point E2B SDK at self-hosted agent-sandbox
os.environ["E2B_API_URL"] = "https://sandbox.example.com"
os.environ["E2B_API_KEY"] = "my-api-key"

from e2b_code_interpreter import Sandbox

# Standard E2B code — no modifications needed
sbx = Sandbox.create(template="code-interpreter")
result = sbx.run_code("print('Hello from agent-sandbox!')")
print(result.text)
sbx.kill()
```


### Why is this needed?

**The problem:** E2B has become the de-facto standard API for AI agent sandboxing. Major frameworks (LangChain, AutoGPT, OpenAI Agents SDK, CrewAI, Dify) integrate with the E2B SDK. However, E2B is a SaaS-only product — teams with compliance, data sovereignty, or latency requirements cannot self-host it.

`agent-sandbox` already provides the core infrastructure (CRD-based lifecycle, warm pools, templates) that is functionally equivalent or superior to E2B. However, the lack of an E2B-compatible API layer means:

1. **No SDK compatibility** — Users must rewrite their AI Agent code to use the `agent-sandbox` Go/Python clients instead of the ubiquitous E2B SDK.
2. **Framework lockout** — LangChain, AutoGPT, CrewAI, Dify, and other frameworks that have native E2B integration cannot use `agent-sandbox` as a backend without custom adapters.
3. **Migration friction** — Teams currently using E2B SaaS who want to self-host must fork and modify their entire codebase to switch clients.

**This proposal is complementary to existing work:**
- [#235](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/235) asks about E2B API support — this provides a concrete implementation plan.
- [KEP-539.2](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/tree/main/docs/keps/539.2-runtime-standardization) standardizes the **in-sandbox runtime interface** (code execution, filesystem). This proposal covers the **external control-plane API** — the two layers are orthogonal and both needed.
- [#539](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/539) proposes a gRPC contract for SDK interoperability. The E2B gateway can serve as a REST transport that delegates to the gRPC runtime defined there.

**Precedent:** [openkruise/agents](https://github.com/openkruise/agents) already supports the E2B API ([referenced in #235](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/235#issuecomment-...)), demonstrating community demand for this capability in the K8s-native sandbox space.

**Impact:** An E2B-compatible gateway would make `agent-sandbox` a drop-in self-hosted replacement for E2B, unlocking adoption from the entire E2B ecosystem without requiring any code changes from users.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR formally implements the `Suspended` persistent condition for `Sandbox` resources to accurately track the suspension state and lifecycle. 

*Note: These changes are based out of PR #893.*


**Current behavior:**
`computeSuspendedCondition` returns `nil` whenever `spec.operatingMode == Running`, so the controller only sets/updates the `Suspended` condition while the Sandbox is suspended. As a result:
  - A newly created (running) Sandbox has **no** `Suspended` condition at all.
  - After a suspend → resume, the condition is left **stale at `True`** — it never transitions
    to `False`, so its `lastTransitionTime` never records when the Sandbox resumed.
  - Wait command `kubectl wait --for=condition=Suspended=False` can’t work, because the
    condition is not maintained as a proper `False` state.

This contradicts the Kubernetes convention that conditions are persistent once initialized and transition their `status` (rather than appearing/disappearing), and that`lastTransitionTime` is preserved as history.

**Applied behavior:**

The `Suspended` condition is now persistent once initialized, properly transitioning its status (`True` or `False`) instead of appearing and disappearing. This preserves the `lastTransitionTime` history and enables standard `kubectl wait` commands.

**States and their meaning:**

*   **Status `False` (Reason: `NotSuspended`)**: The Sandbox is active. This state is set immediately upon creation or when resumption is requested (`Spec.OperatingMode = Running`), even before the underlying Pod is actually provisioned.
*   **Status `False` (Reason: `PodTerminating`)**: The Sandbox is in a transient suspension phase where the underlying Pod is currently terminating.
*   **Status `True` (Reason: `PodTerminated`)**: The Sandbox is fully suspended, and the underlying Pod has been successfully terminated.


**Key changes:**
* **API Update (`sandbox_types.go`)**: Added `SandboxConditionSuspended` and specific suspension reasons (`PodTerminated`, `PodTerminating`, `NotSuspended`).
* **Controller Logic (`sandbox_controller.go`)**: Updated `computeSuspendedCondition` to properly construct and populate `metav1.Condition` objects for the `Suspended` type. The condition evaluates to `True` when fully suspended (Pod is terminated) and `False` when active or during a transient suspension phase (e.g., `PodTerminating`).
* **Documentation (`keps/119-sandbox-suspended-state`)**: Updated the condition hierarchy documentation to explicitly define the `Suspended` status values and reasons, reflecting the new standard Kubernetes condition mechanics.

**Testing**: 

- Updated the `sandbox_controller_test.go` and all E2E test suites (`basic_test.go`, `shutdown_test.go`, `volumeclaimtemplate_test.go`) to assert the presence and accuracy of the new `Suspended` condition under various scenarios.
- Added new e2e tests in `mode_test.go` - `TestSandboxSuspendResumeCycleWithOperatingMode`, `TestSandboxSuspensionWithTerminatingPod`, `TestSandboxPodDeletionKeepsSuspendedFalse`

```
$ kubectl wait --for=condition=Suspended=False sandbox/sandbox-claim-8ed4a267 -n sandbox-test
sandbox.agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-claim-8ed4a267 condition met
```
This enables `kubectl wait --for=condition=Suspended=False` and preserves the suspend/resume transition history via `lastTransitionTime`.


**Note:** When resume is requested (`Spec.OperatingMode = Running`), the `Suspended` condition status transitions to `False` (`Running`) immediately, even before the underlying Pod is actually provisioned or created (`pod == nil`).

 #### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
 Fixes #873

#### Release Note
```release-note
Implemented the `Suspended` condition for `Sandbox` objects to track suspension lifecycle states (NotSuspended, PodTerminating, PodTerminated). Note that the legacy `PodNotTerminated` reason is deprecated in favor of `PodTerminating`. Additionally, the `Suspended` condition is now always present on the resource after initial reconciliation; clients should evaluate its boolean `status` value rather than checking for its presence.
```

body:
Intent:
* Add more tests with this framework. 
* Have different cluster config size which can be selected based on the test

Split the monolithic benchmarks-kops-gcp/run script into independent phase scripts so a cluster can be created once, have one or more tests run against it selectively, and be torn down separately:

- create-cluster: apply a standard kOps config (configs/*.yaml) as-is with `kops create -f`, stamp the resolved GCP project via `kops set`, provision, and deploy the controller.
- run-tests: run one or more tests (benchmarks, stress) against an existing cluster; re-runnable, with stress passthrough flags.
- teardown: delete the cluster, optionally the state bucket, and release Boskos resources.
- lib.sh: shared helpers (tool install, project/image/state-store setup, per-cluster state under .build/clusters/<name>).

Cluster shape is selected via named standard kOps config files (default, small, large); KOPS_STATE_STORE is exported so kOps derives configBase, and spec.project is stamped at create time to keep Boskos working. The existing `run` entrypoint is retained as a backward-compatible all-in-one wrapper.

title: Prometheus metrics for Sandbox stage latencies and child-resource reconcile errors

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Prometheus metrics for **stage latencies** along the Sandbox path to Ready, plus **child-resource / template reconcile error** counters.

| Metric | Type | Labels | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `agent_sandbox_stage_latency_ms` | Histogram | `namespace`, `launch_type`, `sandbox_template`, `owned_by`, `stage` ∈ {`pod_created`,`pod_scheduled`,`pod_running`,`pod_ready`,`pvc_bound`,`service_ready`} | First observation of each stage per sandbox (guard against double-count, same idea as first-ready annotation) |
| `agent_sandbox_child_reconcile_errors_total` | Counter | `namespace`, `resource` ∈ {`pod`,`pvc`,`service`,`networkpolicy`}, `reason` (allowlisted) | Child reconcile failures (`create_failed`, `update_conflict`, `ownership_conflict`, `adopt_refused`, `delete_failed`, `forbidden`, `other`) |
| `agent_sandbox_template_reconcile_errors_total` | Counter | `namespace`, `reason` (allowlisted) | SandboxTemplate controller / NetworkPolicy reconcile failures |

Notes:
- Use high-precision anchors where possible (controller first-observed annotations), not only second-granularity `CreationTimestamp`.
- `reason` allowlist only — no raw API error strings.
- Can be implemented incrementally (stages first, then error counters).
- Related: [#781](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/781), [#403](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/403), [#836](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/836).


### Why is this needed?

Production Ready latency is a single coarse histogram. E2E/benchmarks already break out stages (pod created → scheduled → running → ready), and OpenTelemetry spans cover `reconcilePod` / `reconcilePVCs` and pod status events — but there are **no matching Prometheus metrics**.

When Ready latency spikes, operators cannot tell whether time was spent in scheduling / image pull, PVC bind, service/dependency readiness, or controller child-resource errors (pod/PVC/service/NetworkPolicy). Template NetworkPolicy reconcile failures are similarly silent until claims fail with `TemplateNotFound`.

This pairs with condition-reason / `DependenciesNotReady` detail metrics for “controller vs cluster” incident triage.

Alternatives (insufficient alone): relying only on OTel traces; using only kubelet/pod metrics (miss pre-pod controller failures); expanding Ready latency buckets without stage labels.

title: Helm: optional PrometheusRule for controller metrics alerts

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

An **opt-in `PrometheusRule`** template in the Helm chart (`monitoring.coreos.com/v1`) so prometheus-operator users can get useful alerts on the controller's metrics without writing one by hand — the alerting counterpart to the opt-in `ServiceMonitor` in #1016 .

Proposed shape (off by default):
```yaml
metrics:
  prometheusRule:
    enabled: false          # requires the prometheus-operator CRDs
    additionalLabels: {}    # e.g. release: kube-prometheus-stack, to match the Prometheus ruleSelector
    rules: []               # override/extend; chart ships a curated starter set when enabled
```

The template is gated entirely behind `metrics.prometheusRule.enabled` and rendered only when set, since the `PrometheusRule` kind requires the prometheus-operator CRDs to be installed. Labels from `additionalLabels` should be applied so the rule group matches a Prometheus `ruleSelector` (same pattern as `metrics.serviceMonitor.additionalLabels` for `serviceMonitorSelector`).

Suggested starter alerts (examples for implementers to refine; thresholds configurable via values):

- **Controller metrics target down** — `up` for the controller scrape job is 0 for several minutes (most useful once the ServiceMonitor from #1016 is enabled).
- **Elevated claim / sandbox startup latency** — high quantile on `agent_sandbox_claim_startup_latency_ms` and/or `agent_sandbox_creation_latency_ms` / `agent_sandbox_ready_latency_ms` over a sliding window.
- **Optional: claim creation signal** — unusual rate or sustained `pod_condition="not_ready"` share on `agent_sandbox_claim_creation_total`.


### Why is this needed?

The chart **already ships a metrics `Service` on `:8080`** and the controller already serves `/metrics` (plain HTTP, no auth — `metricsserver.Options{BindAddress: ":8080"}` in `cmd/agent-sandbox-controller/main.go`), registering both the controller-runtime suite and custom metrics: `agent_sandbox_claim_startup_latency_ms`, `agent_sandbox_claim_controller_startup_latency_ms`, `agent_sandbox_creation_latency_ms`, `agent_sandbox_ready_latency_ms`, `agent_sandbox_claim_creation_total`, `agent_sandboxes`, `agent_sandbox_build_info`.

#1016 / #1017 add an opt-in `ServiceMonitor` so prometheus-operator stacks can *scrape* that endpoint. Alerting still has to be authored out-of-band: operators either hand-write `PrometheusRule` CRs or leave the metrics unused for paging/SLO signals. Shipping an opt-in `PrometheusRule` completes the scrape → alert path for kube-prometheus-stack and similar installs, keeps alert definitions next to the chart that owns the metrics surface, and supports the roadmap items **"Additional Prometheus Telemetry"** and **"Controller Custom Metrics."**

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

`dev/tools/push-images` passes only the basename of the Dockerfile to `docker buildx build -f` and runs the command with `cwd=<build context>`. For images whose Dockerfile sits next to their build context that is fine, but the `sandbox-router-go` image overrides its build context to the repo root (it imports the shared Go module) while its Dockerfile stays at `sandbox-router/Dockerfile`. The basename `Dockerfile` then resolves to the repo-root (controller) Dockerfile, so the pushed `sandbox-router-go` image silently ships the controller binary — its entrypoint is `/agent-sandbox-controller` instead of `/sandbox-router`.

This resolves the `-f` argument relative to the build context instead (`os.path.relpath(dockerfile_path, srcdir)`), which is identical to the basename for every per-directory image and the correct relative path for the context-override case.

Verified locally (macOS arm64, Docker 27.4):

- running the unfixed script with `--images sandbox-router-go --image-prefix repro.local/ --kind-cluster-name …` produces an image with `Entrypoint: [/agent-sandbox-controller]`; with this fix the same invocation produces `Entrypoint: [/sandbox-router]`;
- new unit test `dev/tools/push_images_test.py` (importlib pattern from `release_test.py`, subprocess stubbed) asserts the `-f` value for both the per-directory and the context-override cases — the override case fails against the current script and passes with the fix.

Prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code); happy to adjust anything in review.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Fixes Kind cluster creation failures in E2E presubmits caused by a `kubeadm` configuration schema mismatch.

In Kubernetes 1.31+ / 1.36 (`kindest/node:v1.36.1`), `kubeadm` updated `ClusterConfiguration.apiServer.extraArgs` from a map to a list in `kubeadm.k8s.io/v1beta4`. Supplying `apiServer.extraArgs` as a map caused `kubeadm init` inside the Kind control-plane container to fail unmarshaling on startup, leading to systemd boot timeouts and failed cluster creation in Prow.

This PR updates `create-kind-cluster` to use the `v1beta4`-compliant list format for `apiServer.extraArgs`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

fixes https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/1125
