  * Plain HTTP in encrypted-capable modes now emits a warning to help prevent misconfiguration.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Follow-up to #828, which added the `metav1.IsControlledBy` ownership check to the SandboxTemplate controller's NetworkPolicy management. This PR addresses the leftover review feedback on #828 and adds a few related robustness/observability improvements:

- **Avoid noisy requeues on delete races (#828 review):** in the unmanaged-cleanup path, treat `IsNotFound` on the `Delete` as success. A NetworkPolicy deleted out-of-band between the `Get` and the `Delete` no longer fails the reconcile.
- **Record a Warning event on ownership conflicts:** both the unmanaged-skip and managed-refuse paths now emit a `NetworkPolicyOwnershipConflict` Warning event via the recorder, so the refusal is visible on the object instead of only in controller logs.
- **Wrap client errors with resource identity:** the NetworkPolicy `Get`/`Delete`/`Update`/`Create` errors now include the `namespace/name` for actionable logs and callers.
- **Tighten the security regression test (#828 review):** `TestSandboxTemplateReconcile_Vulnerability` now asserts that Reconcile returns an error (and verifies the message) for an unowned NetworkPolicy in Managed mode, instead of only logging it; both subtests also assert the Warning event is recorded.

Behavioral note: this keeps #828's deliberate asymmetry — Unmanaged mode *skips* (no error) when the existing NetworkPolicy is unowned, while Managed mode *refuses with an error*. The new Warning event is recorded in both cases.

title: Python SDK initialization fails when default kubeconfig is missing

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What happened?

The Python SDK's `K8sHelper` and `SandboxClient` can only be configured via `KUBECONFIG` env variable or if that is absent, a `~/.kube/config`.  The assumption is that for multi-cluster, there will be different contexts within a single file.  This can be ok, but it prevents library users from dynamically setting up their own clients or passing custom configuration files directly (such as in multi-cluster or test setups like notebooks using `pytest-kind`). 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The best way to see this limitation is to try to create a sandbox client to a cluster via a kubeconfig file without setting the KUBECONFIG env var.  There isn't a way to do this that I came across so it's hard to reproduce via code. 

### Version

72e751d80a660f8b1270e3693bf26a5a2da94310

### Anything else we need to know?

#### Suggested Fix: Accept optional `api_client` parameter in constructors

To resolve this issue and make the client SDK robust, we should allow passing a pre-configured `ApiClient` directly to the constructors of both `K8sHelper` and `SandboxClient`. If an `api_client` is provided, we skip the default auto-loading of the configuration.

##### A. Update `K8sHelper` constructor
Modify [K8sHelper.__init__](clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/k8s_helper.py#L36) to accept `api_client`:

```python
class K8sHelper:
    def __init__(self, api_client: client.ApiClient | None = None):
        if api_client is not None:
            self.custom_objects_api = client.CustomObjectsApi(api_client)
            self.core_v1_api = client.CoreV1Api(api_client)
        else:
            try:
                config.load_incluster_config()
            except config.ConfigException:
                config.load_kube_config()
            self.custom_objects_api = client.CustomObjectsApi()
            self.core_v1_api = client.CoreV1Api()
```

##### B. Update `SandboxClient` constructor
Modify [SandboxClient.__init__](clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/sandbox_client.py#L39) to accept `api_client` and forward it:

```python
class SandboxClient:
    def __init__(self, connection_config=None, tracer_config=None, cleanup=False, api_client: client.ApiClient | None = None):
        ...
        # Downstream Kubernetes Configuration
        self.k8s_helper = K8sHelper(api_client=api_client)
```

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The managed NetworkPolicy created by the SandboxTemplate controller selects pods via `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-template-ref-hash`. However, the core Sandbox controller's `isSystemLabel()` filter strips all `agents.x-k8s.io/*` labels from PodTemplate before creating Pods. The label never reaches any Pod, causing managed NetworkPolicies to match no pods and leaving sandboxes without network isolation.

This adds explicit propagation of the label from `Sandbox.Labels` to the Pod, gated on extensions-group ownership (the Sandbox must be owned by a SandboxClaim or SandboxWarmPool). This follows the same trust model used for `warm-pool-sandbox`: extension controllers write the label onto the Sandbox CR, and the core controller propagates it to the Pod only when ownership is verified.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1044

#### How has it been tested end-to-end:

- [x] The Pod should carry the label `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-template-ref-hash`

body:
## What

Adds `MAX_KEEPALIVE_CONNECTIONS` environment variable to control the [httpx connection pool](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/resource-limits/) size in the sandbox router.

## Why

In environments with strict network policies, pooled connections can trigger unexpected drops when the target pod is deleted in meantime without the router being aware. Setting `MAX_KEEPALIVE_CONNECTIONS=0` disables pooling entirely, forcing a fresh connection (and DNS re-resolution) on every request.

## Changes

- `sandbox_router.py`: adds `DEFAULT_MAX_KEEPALIVE_CONNECTIONS = 20` constant, `_get_max_keepalive_connections()` helper (mirrors `_get_proxy_timeout` pattern), and wires the value into `httpx.Limits` on the shared `AsyncClient`.
- `test_sandbox_router.py`: adds `TestMaxKeepaliveConnections` class (6 test cases) mirroring `TestProxyTimeout`.
- `README.md`: adds `MAX_KEEPALIVE_CONNECTIONS` row to the configuration table.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `MAX_KEEPALIVE_CONNECTIONS` | `20` | Set to `0` to disable pooling |

Non-negative integers are accepted; negative values and non-integers fall back to the default with a `WARNING` log line.

title: fix(examples): cross-compile chrome-sandbox entrypoint to avoid QEMU Go crash

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

labels.name: size/S
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 10-29 lines, ignoring generated files.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The `examples/chrome-sandbox` builder stage ran `go build` *inside* the
target-architecture stage. Under a multi-arch `docker buildx` build
(`linux/amd64,linux/arm64`), this compiled the arm64 binary by running the Go
toolchain **under QEMU emulation**. Go 1.26.4's garbage collector can abort with
`fatal error: found pointer to free object` when running emulated, which breaks
the `linux/arm64` image build — and any CI job that builds it (observed in
`presubmit-agent-sandbox-benchmarks-kops-gcp`).

This pins the builder to `--platform=$BUILDPLATFORM` and cross-compiles with
`GOOS=${TARGETOS} GOARCH=${TARGETARCH}`, exactly matching the controller
`Dockerfile` (which already references golang/go#69255 for the same reason). The
Go toolchain now always runs natively on the build platform; only the produced
binary targets arm64.

This is a pre-existing build-infra bug, independent of any example/feature
change. The emulated parts that are not Go (e.g. arm64 `apt-get install
chromium`) are unaffected.

**Verification:** reproduced the multi-arch build on Cloud Build (amd64 host,
QEMU for arm64). Before: the arm64 `go build` step aborts with `found pointer to
free object`. After this change: the `linux/amd64,linux/arm64` build completes
successfully (the arm64 builder step runs as a native `amd64->arm64`
cross-compile in ~11s).

See https://github.com/golang/go/issues/69255#issuecomment-2523276831

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

NONE

#### Release Note
```release-note
Fixed the chrome-sandbox example image build failing for linux/arm64 under emulation by cross-compiling the Go entrypoint instead of building it under QEMU.
```

title: Proposal: Configurable Warm Pool Adoption Retry Count in SandboxClaim

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
## Summary

This proposal introduces a configurable retry mechanism for warm pool sandbox adoption in SandboxClaim, replacing the current hardcoded retry limit of 3 attempts. The new `warmpoolMaxRetries` field will allow users to tune retry behavior based on their specific concurrency requirements and environment characteristics.

## Motivation

### Current Problem
The warm pool adoption mechanism in `adoptSandboxFromCandidates` currently uses a hardcoded retry count of 3 attempts. This approach has several limitations:

1. **Insufficient for High-Concurrency Environments**: In environments with many concurrent claims competing for warm pool sandboxes, 3 retries may be insufficient to handle patch conflicts and race conditions.

2. **No Tunability**: Different deployment environments have varying levels of concurrency and conflict rates. A one-size-fits-all approach doesn't accommodate these differences.

3. **Code Change Required**: Adjusting the retry count currently requires modifying the source code and redeploying the controller, which is not practical for production adjustments.

### Use Cases
- **High-Concurrency Clusters**: Environments with hundreds of concurrent SandboxClaims may need 5-10 retries
- **Low-Latency Requirements**: Environments prioritizing fast failure may prefer 1-2 retries
- **Standard Workloads**: Default of 3 retries remains suitable for most use cases

## Proposal

### API Changes

Add a new optional field `warmpoolMaxRetries` to `SandboxClaimSpec`:

```go
// warmpoolMaxRetries is the number of retry attempts when adopting a sandbox
// from the warm pool fails due to conflicts or not-found errors.
// +kubebuilder:validation:Minimum=1
// +kubebuilder:validation:Maximum=10
// +kubebuilder:default=3
// +optional
WarmPoolMaxRetries *int32 `json:"warmpoolMaxRetries,omitempty"`
```

### Validation Constraints
- **Minimum**: 1 (must attempt at least once)
- **Maximum**: 10 (prevent excessive retry loops)
- **Default**: 3 (maintains backward compatibility)

### Controller Logic Changes

1. Add helper function `getWarmPoolMaxRetries(claim *SandboxClaim) int`:
   - Returns `claim.Spec.WarmPoolMaxRetries` if set
   - Returns `DefaultWarmPoolAdoptionRetries` (3) otherwise

2. Update `adoptSandboxFromCandidates` method:
   - Replace hardcoded `for range 3` with `for range maxRetries`
   - Use the configurable value from the helper function

### CRD Schema Update

The CRD will be automatically updated with the new field validation:

```yaml
warmpoolMaxRetries:
  default: 3
  format: int32
  maximum: 10
  minimum: 1
  type: integer
```

## Implementation Details

### Files to Modify

1. **extensions/api/v1alpha1/sandboxclaim_types.go**
   - Add `WarmPoolMaxRetries` field to `SandboxClaimSpec`
   - Add kubebuilder validation markers

2. **extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go**
   - Add `DefaultWarmPoolAdoptionRetries` constant
   - Add `getWarmPoolMaxRetries()` helper function
   - Update `adoptSandboxFromCandidates()` to use configurable retries

3. **extensions/api/v1alpha1/zz_generated.deepcopy.go**
   - Auto-generated deep copy methods for the new field

4. **k8s/crds/extensions.agents.x-k8s.io_sandboxclaims.yaml**
   - Auto-generated CRD schema update

### Testing Strategy

Comprehensive test coverage including:

1. **Default Behavior**: Verify default of 3 retries when field is not set
2. **Custom Retry Counts**: Test values across the valid range (1-10)
3. **Conflict Scenarios**: 
   - Exhaust retries with fewer candidates than retries
   - Succeed after conflicts with sufficient candidates
4. **Edge Cases**: 
   - Boundary values (1, 10)
   - Zero value (should use default)

### Example Usage

```yaml
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: SandboxClaim
metadata:
  name: high-concurrency-claim
spec:
  sandboxTemplateRef:
    name: my-template
  warmpool: default
  warmPoolMaxRetries: 5  # Increase for high-concurrency environment
```

## Backward Compatibility

✅ **Fully Backward Compatible**
- Existing SandboxClaims without the field will use the default value of 3
- No breaking changes to existing behavior
- Optional field with sensible default

## Benefits

1. **Operational Flexibility**: Operators can tune retry behavior without code changes
2. **Improved Reliability**: High-concurrency environments can increase retries to reduce failures
3. **Performance Optimization**: Low-latency requirements can decrease retries for faster failure detection
4. **Production Ready**: Maintains backward compatibility while enabling customization

## Alternatives Considered

### Alternative 1: Global Controller Configuration
- **Pros**: Single configuration point
- **Cons**: Less granular control, requires controller restart, one-size-fits-all approach
- **Rejected**: Per-claim configuration provides better flexibility

### Alternative 2: Exponential Backoff
- **Pros**: More sophisticated retry strategy
- **Cons**: Increased complexity, may not be necessary for this use case
- **Rejected**: Simple retry count is sufficient; can be added later if needed

### Alternative 3: Remove Retry Limit
- **Pros**: Guarantees adoption if candidates exist
- **Cons**: Potential for infinite loops, unpredictable latency
- **Rejected**: Bounded retries provide predictable behavior

## Migration Path

No migration required - the feature is fully backward compatible. Existing deployments will continue to function with the default retry count of 3.

## Success Metrics

1. **Reduced Adoption Failures**: High-concurrency deployments should see fewer warm pool adoption failures
2. **Operational Flexibility**: Users can adjust retry counts based on their environment without redeployment
3. **Maintained Reliability**: Default behavior remains unchanged for existing deployments

## References

- Implementation PR: #704
- Related Components: SandboxClaim, SandboxWarmPool, Warm Pool Adoption Logic

title: SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig fails with misleading "services sandbox-router-svc not found" when router is not in default router_namespace

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: help wanted
labels.description: Denotes an issue that needs help from a contributor. Must meet "help wanted" guidelines.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What happened?

`SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig` fails with a misleading error when the router service
is deployed in a namespace other than `agent-sandbox-system`.

Following the documented **Developer Mode (Local Tunnel)** quickstart with the router
deployed in the `default` namespace, `sandbox.commands.run(...)` crashes with:

```
k8s_agent_sandbox.exceptions.SandboxPortForwardError: Tunnel crashed: Error from server (NotFound): services sandbox-router-svc not found
```

The error is misleading: the service **does** exist - `kubectl get svc -A` clearly shows
`sandbox-router-svc` running in `default`. The SDK port-forwards to the router in the
**`agent-sandbox-system`** namespace by default (`SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig.router_namespace`),
so `kubectl port-forward` genuinely can't find the service in that namespace - but the
surfaced error never mentions *which* namespace was searched.

`SandboxDirectConnectionConfig` works for the same workload because it bypasses the router
entirely, which masks the real cause and makes the tunnel failure especially confusing.

**Expected:** either the tunnel connects when the router service exists and is reachable, or
the error states which namespace was searched and hints to set `router_namespace`, e.g.
*"service `sandbox-router-svc` not found in namespace `agent-sandbox-system`; set
`router_namespace` if the router runs elsewhere."*

**Root cause** - the default is `agent-sandbox-system`:

```python
# k8s_agent_sandbox/models.py
class SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig(BaseModel):
    port_forward_ready_timeout: int = 30
    server_port: int = 8888
    router_namespace: str = "agent-sandbox-system"  # <-- silent default
```

```python
# k8s_agent_sandbox/connector.py
ROUTER_SERVICE_NAME = "svc/sandbox-router-svc"
...
self.port_forward_process = subprocess.Popen(
    ["kubectl", "port-forward", ROUTER_SERVICE_NAME,
     f"{local_port}:8080", "-n", self.config.router_namespace],
    ...
)
...
raise SandboxPortForwardError(f"Tunnel crashed: {stderr.decode(errors='replace')}")
```

This is largely a UX/docs footgun. The published docs make it easy to hit:

1. The Local Tunnel quickstart uses bare `SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig()` with the
   comment `# Automatically tunnels to svc/sandbox-router-svc` and never mentions a namespace.
2. The Advanced / Internal Mode example hardcodes
   `http://sandbox-router-svc.agent-sandbox-system.svc.cluster.local:8080`, confirming
   `agent-sandbox-system` is the assumed router home - yet the tunnel quickstart neither
   deploys the router there nor tells the user to set `router_namespace`.
3. `router_namespace` (where the router Service lives) is easily conflated with the
   `create_sandbox(namespace=...)` arg (where the sandbox pod runs). Every example pairs the
   tunnel with `namespace="default"`, making it natural but wrong to assume the tunnel also
   looks for the router in `default`.

**Suggested fixes:**
- Improve the error to include the searched namespace + service and a hint to set
  `router_namespace`; ideally pre-flight/validate the service at `connect()` time before
  launching `kubectl port-forward`.
- Align the Local Tunnel quickstart docs: either deploy the router to `agent-sandbox-system`
  in setup, or show `SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig(router_namespace=...)` and clarify it
  is distinct from `create_sandbox(namespace=...)`.

---

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Deploy `sandbox-router-svc` into the `default` namespace:

   ```yaml
   apiVersion: v1
   kind: Service
   metadata:
     name: sandbox-router-svc
     namespace: default
   spec:
     type: ClusterIP
     selector:
       app: sandbox-router
     ports:
     - name: http
       protocol: TCP
       port: 8080
       targetPort: 8080
   ```

2. Confirm it is running:

   ```
   $ kubectl get svc -A | grep sandbox-router
   default   sandbox-router-svc   ClusterIP   34.118.235.84   <none>   8080/TCP   59m
   ```

3. Run the client using the **verbatim** documented Developer Mode (Local Tunnel) example:

   ```python
   from k8s_agent_sandbox import SandboxClient
   from k8s_agent_sandbox.models import SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig

   # Automatically tunnels to svc/sandbox-router-svc
   client = SandboxClient(
       connection_config=SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig()
   )
   sandbox = client.create_sandbox(
       warmpool="python-sandbox-warmpool",
       namespace="default",
   )
   sandbox.commands.run("echo hello")  # raises SandboxPortForwardError
   ```

   Result: `SandboxPortForwardError: Tunnel crashed: Error from server (NotFound):
   services sandbox-router-svc not found`.

**Workaround** - explicitly set the namespace where the router actually runs:

```python
client = SandboxClient(
    connection_config=SandboxLocalTunnelConnectionConfig(router_namespace="default"),
)
```


### Version

k8s-agent-sandbox 0.5.0 (PyPI, requires-python >=3.10); agent-sandbox v0.5.0. Reproduced on Python 3.14.

### Anything else we need to know?

- Environment: GKE cluster with a gVisor node pool; router deployed as a `ClusterIP` on port 8080 in the `default` namespace.
- `SandboxDirectConnectionConfig(api_url="http://localhost:8080")` works against the same setup, which is what first pointed to the namespace mismatch rather than a missing service.
- Full traceback:

  ```
  Traceback (most recent call last):
    File ".../demo.py", line 33, in <module>
      result = sandbox.commands.run(...)
    File ".../k8s_agent_sandbox/commands/command_executor.py", line 49, in run
      response = self.connector.send_request("POST", "execute", json=payload, timeout=timeout)
    File ".../k8s_agent_sandbox/connector.py", line 374, in send_request
      base_url = self.connect()
    File ".../k8s_agent_sandbox/connector.py", line 330, in connect
      return self.strategy.connect()
    File ".../k8s_agent_sandbox/connector.py", line 188, in connect
      raise SandboxPortForwardError(f"Tunnel crashed: {stderr.decode(errors='replace')}")
  k8s_agent_sandbox.exceptions.SandboxPortForwardError: Tunnel crashed: Error from server (NotFound): services sandbox-router-svc not found
  ```

title: opt-in resource resize policy for running Sandboxes

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/awaiting-more-evidence
labels.description: Lowest priority. Possibly useful, but not yet enough support to actually get it done.

body:
## What would you like to be added?

Add a narrow, opt-in policy for reconciling CPU/memory resource changes on a running Sandbox backing Pod, using Kubernetes Pod `/resize`.

This is a focused follow-up to #581 and #612. Those issues discuss the broader question of `podTemplate.spec` drift and whether Sandbox should ever recreate active Pods. This issue is intentionally narrower: it only covers CPU/memory requests and limits, and it should not imply any general PodTemplate rollout or replacement behavior.

One possible API shape is:

```yaml
spec:
  resourceResizePolicy:
    type: Disabled | InPlace
```

`Disabled` would be the default. The controller may report resource drift, but it does not mutate the running Pod.

`InPlace` would allow the controller to use Pod `/resize` for eligible CPU/memory changes. In this mode, "in place" should mean live resize only: no Pod replacement and no container restart. If the requested resize would require `RestartContainer` under the target container's `resizePolicy`, the controller should report failure instead of proceeding.

This implies a creation-time requirement as well. Pods that may later use this policy need to be created with a compatible `resizePolicy`, for example `NotRequired` for the resources managed by this policy. Otherwise memory changes can unexpectedly restart the container, which would violate the meaning of `InPlace`.

Some unsupported cases can be known before attempting resize from startup discovery, the current Pod shape, and the selected container. The controller should report those cases through status instead of repeatedly attempting a resize that cannot succeed.

Other failures are only known after the API server accepts the resize. The controller should project Pod resize conditions into Sandbox status so users can understand whether the resize is still pending/in progress, has completed, or has failed.

Pod `/resize` only updates the current Pod. The PodTemplate resources still need to remain the source of truth for future Pod creation. If resize is driven by a change to `Sandbox.Spec.PodTemplate.Spec`, that is already true: the updated template is the desired state and the running Pod is catching up. If a future API starts resize from somewhere else, it should also persist the target CPU/memory resources back to the Sandbox PodTemplate, otherwise Suspend/Resume, node loss, or a later Pod replacement could recreate the Pod with stale resources.

This policy should not cover image, command, env, volumes, scheduling fields, security context, or other non-resource PodTemplate drift. If CPU/memory drift is mixed with non-resource drift, the controller may still apply the resource-only `/resize`, but it should not claim that the full PodTemplate has converged. Any remaining non-resource drift should be reported separately.

Related previous work:

- #581 describes the broad PodTemplate drift problem.
- #612 discusses auto-recreate vs safe in-place changes.
- #459 adds claim-time workspace resource overrides, but not resize-after-creation.
- #487, #691, and #706 were earlier attempts around in-place resize or update strategy.

## Why is this needed?

Today, changing CPU/memory resources in `Sandbox.Spec.PodTemplate.Spec` after the backing Pod already exists does not affect that running Pod. Users either have to operate directly on the Pod or delete/recreate the Sandbox.

Deleting and recreating an active Sandbox is too disruptive for many session-style workloads. At the same time, treating all PodTemplate changes as mutable would be unsafe. CPU/memory resource changes are a smaller category because Kubernetes has a dedicated `/resize` subresource and status model for them.

The missing piece is a Sandbox-level contract around when the controller may use `/resize`, what "in place" means, and how failures are reported. Keeping this policy strict avoids mixing resource resize with a broader Pod recreation strategy, while still giving users a way to request live resource adjustment where the cluster supports it.

title: Go Client SDK - Sandbox List - path encoding and  HTTP redirect

labels.name: kind/bug

labels.name: priority/important-longterm

body:
### What happened?

List Files example (_clients/go/examples/basic/main.go_)

```
// List files.
entries, err := sb.List(ctx, ".")
if err != nil {
	log.Fatal(err)
}
```

Go SDK URL encoding leaves `.` unescaped. When passed as a path segment, this produces a request `/list/.`, resulting in a 307 Temporary Redirect.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Set up an Environment following _examples/quickstart/README.md_

2. Use Go Client SDK Code from _clients/go/examples/basic/main.go_ to create an Sandbox using an SandboxWarmPool. (Make sure that `sb.List()` uses `.` as the path argument)

3. execution clients/go/examples/basic/main.go:

```
go run clients/go/examples/basic/main.go
"ts"="2026-06-20 23:47:33.257085" "level"=0 "msg"="claim created" "claim"="sandbox-claim-f86qh" "namespace"="agent-sandbox-demo"
"ts"="2026-06-20 23:47:33.280609" "level"=0 "msg"="sandbox name resolved" "claim"="sandbox-claim-f86qh" "sandbox"="python-warmpool-96tkm"
"ts"="2026-06-20 23:47:33.311934" "level"=0 "msg"="port-forward established" "localPort"=50130 "pod"="sandbox-router-deployment-7445877d74-76vsk"
"ts"="2026-06-20 23:47:33.311963" "level"=0 "msg"="API URL discovered" "url"="http://127.0.0.1:50130" "mode"="port-forward"

stdout: Hello from Go!

```

4. kubectl logs sandbox-router-deployment:

```

### Version

This issue does not occur when using `./` as path in `sb.List()` function.

title: cleanup: Remove sandbox_template label from SandboxClaim startup latency metrics

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### Description

During the review of [PR #1050](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/1050), a question was raised about whether the `sandbox_template` label is still necessary for `SandboxClaim` metrics. Since claims now rely primarily on warm pools rather than direct sandbox templates, we should consider removing the `sandbox_template` label to reduce metric cardinality and clean up our telemetry design.

### Why we should do this

Currently, both `ClaimStartupLatency` and `ClaimControllerStartupLatency` record the `sandbox_template` label along with the newly added `warmpool_name` label. 

As the project shifted towards using `warmPoolRef` within the `SandboxClaim` spec, keeping both labels is redundant since a `SandboxWarmPool` already determines or encapsulates the underlying `sandboxTemplate`. Dropping `sandbox_template` simplifies the metrics, minimizes label footprint (cardinality), and keeps the telemetry focused on the primary scaling/warm-pool mechanisms.

### Proposed Changes

1. **Metrics Definition (`internal/metrics/metrics.go`)**:
   - Remove `"sandbox_template"` from the label keys of `ClaimStartupLatency` and `ClaimControllerStartupLatency` vector histograms.
2. **Controller Instrumentation (`extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go`)**:
   - Update the recording helpers (like `recordClaimStartupLatency` and `recordControllerStartupLatency`) to stop passing the template name parameter.
3. **Test Validation (`internal/metrics/metrics_test.go` and `extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller_test.go`)**:
   - Adjust metric expectations and assertions in the controller and metric tests to match the simplified label structure.
4. **Update monitoring dashboards(internal)**

### Related Pull Requests

- #1050 (where the `warmpool_name` label was introduced)

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
<!-- Provide a clear and concise description of the changes in this PR. -->

**Why we need it:**
When a `SandboxClaim` references a `warmPoolRef` instead of a direct `sandboxTemplate`(#899), the metric labels are expected to be updated accordingly to reflect the targeted warm pool. 

This is currently a critical blocker for using KEDA (Kubernetes Event-driven Autoscaling) to scale warm pools down to zero:
1. When KEDA scales a `SandboxWarmPool` to 0 replicas, any incoming `SandboxClaim` will naturally trigger a cold-start since no ready sandboxes are available.
2. Previously, the controller recorded all cold-start events with a hardcoded `"none"` value for the `warmpool_name` label([code](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/bce2dda61294744b764ed87ec0f085450d808568/extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go#L1267)).
3. Because the metric counter was registered under `"none"`, any KEDA scaling queries filtering by a specific `warmpool_name` (such as `warmpool_name="python-sdk-warmpool"`) would return 0.
4. Consequently, KEDA would fail to detect the incoming claim activity, the activation threshold would never be crossed, and the warm pool would remain stuck at 0 replicas.

By replacing `"none"` with the actual referenced warm pool name (`claim.Spec.WarmPoolRef.Name`), we ensure that cold starts are correctly accounted for under the corresponding warm pool metric label. This enables KEDA to successfully monitor the claim rate from zero and wake the pool up on demand.


**What this PR does:**
1. **Controller Metrics Propagation** (`extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go`):
   - Updates the cold-start metric recording call to pass the actual referenced warm pool name from `claim.Spec.WarmPoolRef.Name` instead of the hardcoded `"none"` value.

title: examples/agent-sandbox-rl: performance, scale, and RL instant-claim sizing

labels.name: size/XXL
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 1000+ lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: lgtm
labels.description: "Looks good to me", indicates that a PR is ready to be merged.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
Follow-on to #1000 (the base `agent-sandbox-rl` package). This PR adds the
**performance & scale** work, all scoped to `examples/agent-sandbox-rl/` — no
changes elsewhere in the repo.

## What this adds

**Throughput / pull amortization**
- **`pipelined` strategy** — double-buffered sliding window: prefetch window N+1's
  pools while window N's tasks run, so image pull overlaps execution (bounded ≤ 2
  windows). New `prefetch` phase in the `RunReport`.
- **Cross-epoch warm cache** — `run(..., epochs=N)` keeps pools resident across
  passes (re-pulls hit the node layer cache), `keep_warm=True` for a caller-driven
  loop; reuse guard so warming never re-creates / double-reserves.
- **Parallel pool warming** — `start_warmpools` warms pools concurrently (bounded
  by `max_concurrent`) instead of one-at-a-time.
- **`TemplateSpec.image_pull_policy`** (default `IfNotPresent`) so the node layer
  cache is reused across runs/epochs.

**Correctness / scale**
- **Dedicated thread pool for `AsyncSandboxFleet`** — runs blocking k8s calls on its
  own `ThreadPoolExecutor` instead of `asyncio.to_thread`'s shared default pool,
  which is sized to the driver's CPU count, not concurrency. Under `pipelined` it
  starved teardown and **deadlocked** at scale; this fixes it (live-validated
  100/100 where it previously hung).
- **Disk-aware window sizing** — `recommend_window_disk` / `recommend_window_pipelined`
  + `FleetConfig.avg_image_gb` / `node_ephemeral_gb` / `disk_headroom` cap the auto
  window so resident images fit node disk.
- **Image rewriting** (`registry_rewrite.py`) — `rewrite_image` / `make_rewriter` +
  a `load_tasks(image_rewrite=...)` hook to redirect images at an in-region mirror /
  pull-through cache.

**RL instant-claim sizing** (both opt-in, default off — eval behavior unchanged)
- **`FleetConfig.warm_per_task`** — size each pool to one replica per task so every
  rollout claims a sandbox immediately.
- **`TemplateSpec.colocate_replicas`** — soft `podAffinity` so a pool's replicas
  prefer one node (only the first pulls the image; the rest hit the node layer
  cache); composes with a user-supplied `extra_pod_spec` affinity.

### Eval vs RL (when to use what)
- **Eval** (1:1 image:task, pull-bound): `pipelined` + node cache
  (`epochs`/`keep_warm` + `IfNotPresent`) + in-region mirror. `warm_per_task` is a
  no-op (one task per image).
- **RL** (G rollouts per problem, claim-bound): `naive`/`sliding` + `warm_per_task`
  + `colocate_replicas`. Cuts the per-rollout claim *tail* (the synchronous
  straggler), not batch wall. Not `pipelined` (deep replicas shrink its window and
  serialize problems — guarded with a runtime warning).

Full rationale + measurements are in the README "Eval vs RL" section and `docs/gke.md`.

## Tooling & docs
- **Load-test harness** (`tests/loadtest.py`) — parameterized SWE-bench-style load
  test emitting a self-explanatory report (methodology, cluster/nodes, warm-pool
  plan, per-stage benchmark incl. **claim latency = time-to-sandbox**, a metric
  glossary, and the full RunReport). One redacted sample is checked in.
- README, `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/gke.md`, `docs/design.md`, and
  `examples/rl_integration.md` updated with the new levers and eval-vs-RL guidance.

## Testing
- **188 mocked unit tests** (`pytest -q -W error::RuntimeWarning`), no cluster needed.
- Live-validated on GKE (Agent Sandbox v1beta1): all strategies, including the
  `pipelined` deadlock fix and the instant-claim claim-latency win.

## Follow-up (deferred)
- The sync/async `_run_pipelined` / `_run_windowed` / epochs-loop share structure
  that could be de-duplicated (noted in the earlier #1000 review). Left as a separate
  refactor to keep this PR's diff focused on behavior.

title: Support warm pool staleness detection for VolumeClaimTemplates and Service

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Expand warm pool staleness detection to also evaluate VolumeClaimTemplates and Service. 

Staleness evaluation must remain strictly scoped to unadopted pool sandboxes. Once a sandbox is claimed and owned by a `SandboxClaim`, it must remain protected from pool replenishment rules to prevent data loss on active workloads.

### Why is this needed?

After SandboxWarmPool's rollout feature is implemented (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/347), additional fields in Sandbox spec, including `VolumeClaimTemplates`, and `Service` are introduced to SandboxTemplate, without changing the rollout feature. 

This means `SandboxWarmPool` staleness detection currently only evaluates changes to the pod spec. 

As a result, if an administrator updates `.spec.volumeClaimTemplates` (e.g., attaching a new cache PVC) or `.spec.service` on an active `SandboxTemplate`, existing idle sandboxes in a `Recreate` warm pool are not marked as stale. Incoming claims will continue receiving pre-warmed sandboxes with outdated storage or networking configurations.

title: feat: credential vault proxy to prevent AI agents from reading secrets directly

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
## Summary

agent-sandbox currently injects credentials into sandbox containers via Kubernetes Secrets referenced with `secretKeyRef`. While this avoids hardcoding secrets in pod specs, **the AI agent process itself can still read those environment variables at runtime** — which means a compromised or malicious agent could exfiltrate credentials by leaking them through tool calls, prompts, or outbound API requests.

## The security concern

When an AI agent has direct access to environment variables like `OPENAI_API_KEY` or similar tokens, it can:

- Intentionally or unintentionally include them in generated text or responses
- Exfiltrate them via an outbound HTTP request (e.g., as a query param or request body)
- Expose them through prompt injection attacks where an adversarial payload instructs the agent to reveal its environment

The current pattern in agent-sandbox ([`sandboxtemplate.yaml`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/extensions/examples/kata-aks/sandboxtemplate.yaml)):

```yaml
env:
  - name: OPENAI_API_KEY
    valueFrom:
      secretKeyRef:
        name: azure-foundry
        key: OPENAI_API_KEY
```

...makes the key directly readable by the agent via `os.environ["OPENAI_API_KEY"]` or equivalent. The secret is protected at rest, but not from the agent process itself.

## Prior art

Projects like [OpenSandbox](https://github.com/opensandbox-group/OpenSandbox) tackle this threat model specifically with a MITM proxy approach: all outbound requests from the sandbox are routed through an egress sidecar that injects credentials in transit, so the agent process never has access to the real credential values. [Infisical Agent Vault](https://github.com/Infisical/agent-vault) takes the same approach, bootstrapping agents to route through an `HTTPS_PROXY` that brokers credentials transparently.

It would be worth considering whether agent-sandbox should offer a similar mechanism, given that credential leakage is a realistic threat in agentic workloads.

title: NetworkPolicy podSelector doesn't match pods created by warm pool

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: kind/regression
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a regression from a prior release.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
## Problem

When a `SandboxTemplate` has `networkPolicyManagement: Managed` (default), the controller creates a `NetworkPolicy` with:

```yaml
podSelector:
  matchLabels:
    agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-template-ref-hash: da1fd924
```

However, pods created via a `SandboxWarmPool` referencing that template only receive these labels:

```yaml
agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash: <hash>
agents.x-k8s.io/warm-pool-sandbox: 3884c4c9
app: sandbox  # from podTemplate.metadata.labels
```

The `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-template-ref-hash` label is never applied to the pods. As a result, the managed NetworkPolicy matches no pods. In namespaces with a default-deny policy, this blocks all ingress to sandbox pods.

## Reproduction

1. Create a `SandboxTemplate` named "sandbox" with a `networkPolicy.ingress` section
2. Create a `SandboxWarmPool` referencing that template
3. Observe the controller creates a NetworkPolicy with `podSelector: {agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-template-ref-hash: da1fd924}` (FNV-32a of "sandbox")
4. Observe the warm pool pods do NOT have that label
5. With a default-deny NetworkPolicy in the namespace, pods are unreachable

## Expected behavior

Either:
- The controller should add `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-template-ref-hash: <hash>` to pods it creates, or
- The managed NetworkPolicy should use a podSelector that matches the labels actually present on pods (e.g. `agents.x-k8s.io/warm-pool-sandbox: <hash>` or user-specified labels from `podTemplate.metadata.labels`)

## Environment

- Controller version: v0.5.0
- Previously worked with: v0.4.6 (v1alpha1 API)

## Workaround

Set `networkPolicyManagement: Unmanaged` in the SandboxTemplate and create a NetworkPolicy manually using a label from `podTemplate.metadata.labels` as the podSelector.

title: Claim controller: createSandbox treats AlreadyExists as fatal (cold-start create race)

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### What happened?

In the SandboxClaim controller, `createSandbox` returns a `Create` `AlreadyExists` error as fatal, which fails the reconcile and requeues. On cold-start (non-warmpool) claims this surfaces as recurring `sandbox create error: sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io "<name>" already exists` followed by `Reconciler error`, even though the Sandbox was in fact created successfully and is owned by the claim. The claim converges once the informer cache catches up, so it isn't user-visible, but every occurrence is a failed reconcile for an already-successful create.

**Root cause** — a stale informer-cache race. The fast path (`getOrCreateSandbox`) does a *cached* name-based `Get`. When the cache lags a Sandbox created by a previous reconcile, that `Get` returns `NotFound`, the controller falls through to the cold path, and `Create` then loses the race against the API server → `AlreadyExists`, which is treated as fatal.

The Sandbox controller already tolerates the equivalent situation for Pods — [`controllers/sandbox_controller.go#L919`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/bce2dda61294744b764ed87ec0f085450d808568/controllers/sandbox_controller.go#L919) handles `IsAlreadyExists` on Pod creation by fetching and reconciling the existing Pod. The claim controller's `createSandbox` has no equivalent.

Relevant code (`main` @ `bce2dda`):
- fatal create: [`extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go#L1255-L1259`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/bce2dda61294744b764ed87ec0f085450d808568/extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go#L1255-L1259)

```go
if err := r.Create(ctx, sandbox); err != nil {
    err = fmt.Errorf("sandbox create error: %w", err)
    logger.Error(err, "Error creating sandbox for claim", "claimName", claim.Name)
    return nil, err
}
```

This was previously attempted in #679 (self-closed by the author as "went down the wrong path"). Since it still reproduces on current `main`, we wanted to file a tracking issue and ask which fix direction is preferred. It is the create-side analog of the status-update conflict churn tracked in #527.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

The race is timing-dependent (informer cache lag), so it surfaces most readily under rapid claim churn:

1. Apply a `SandboxTemplate` with the warm pool disabled (forces the cold-start path).
2. Create a `SandboxClaim`, let its `Sandbox` be created, then delete and recreate the claim under the same name on a tight loop — or run many such claims concurrently — so a recreate's fast-path cached `Get` can fire before the informer observes the prior `Sandbox`.
3. Observe in the claim controller logs: `sandbox create error: sandboxes.agents.x-k8s.io "<name>" already exists` and `Reconciler error`, on claims whose `Sandbox` is actually present and owned by the claim.

We also reproduce it deterministically in a unit test with a fake client that returns `AlreadyExists` on `Create` while the (cached) `Get` misses; the reconcile fails where it should adopt the existing, claim-owned Sandbox.

### Version

`v0.4.6` (the affected code path is unchanged on `main` @ `bce2dda`).

### Anything else we need to know?

Two plausible fixes:

1. **Tolerate `AlreadyExists` in `createSandbox`**, mirroring the Pod handling at `sandbox_controller.go#L919`: on `IsAlreadyExists`, `Get` the existing Sandbox, verify it is controlled by this claim, and return it instead of failing. Small and local, and consistent with existing code.
2. **Avoid the miss in the fast path**, e.g. an uncached/`APIReader` `Get` before falling through to the cold create path, closing the cache-lag window.

Given #679 (which implemented approximately option 1) was abandoned, we wanted to ask whether the intended "right path" is option 2, or folding this into #527. We have a unit-tested implementation of option 1 and would be happy to open a PR against `main` if that approach is acceptable.

---

*Filed by an AI assistant (Claude) and human-verified before filing by the reporter, who runs agent-sandbox in production. The code references and reproduction were reviewed by a human.*


/kind bug

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Adds `examples/demo-cilium-egress/`, a self-contained, end-to-end example that demonstrates **per-identity network egress control** for Agent Sandbox using Cilium.

Two sandboxes are given distinct Kubernetes identities (a dedicated ServiceAccount plus a `demo.identity` pod label). A `CiliumNetworkPolicy` with `toFQDNs` grants one identity egress to `github.com` while the other is denied — proven by `git clone` succeeding in the first sandbox and failing (timeout) in the second. A second policy then allowlists the second identity and its clone starts working too, showing additive, per-identity domain egress.

The example is fully programmatic and includes:
- Provisioning scripts: GKE Standard cluster (no Dataplane V2), self-managed upstream Cilium (with the L7 DNS proxy `toFQDNs` requires), and the agent-sandbox controller.
- Manifests: namespace + identities, baseline default-deny + DNS `CiliumNetworkPolicy`, per-identity `toFQDNs` github allow policies, and the two Sandboxes.
- An asserting test script (`test.sh`) that verifies allow/deny/allowlist.
- An optional "gateway routing" ingress add-on: GKE Gateway API + the sandbox-router + a small exec-server sandbox image (built via Cloud Build), plus `test-ingress.sh` that drives `git clone` through the gateway and asserts the same per-identity outcome.
- Architecture and phase-flow Mermaid diagrams, and a teardown script.

Why: upstream Kubernetes `NetworkPolicy` cannot match domains, so domain-level, identity-scoped egress needs a CNI extension. No existing example shows this — the repo only mentions `CiliumNetworkPolicy` as an option for `Unmanaged` NetworkPolicy mode. This provides a concrete, tested realization and ties into the roadmap's "Network Policy Attach at Claim Time" and "Sandbox / Pod Identity Association" themes.

Distinguish sandboxes created programmatically via client SDKs (Go/Python) from those created manually using raw Kubernetes resource manifests (YAML/Helm).

We classify these patterns based on the presence of the `agents.x-k8s.io/created-by` label key:

### 1. SDKs Stamping
* **Go SDK**: Configured `K8sHelper` to automatically label created `SandboxClaims` with `agents.x-k8s.io/created-by: go-client`.
* **Python SDK**: Configured sync and async `K8sHelper` to automatically label created `SandboxClaims` with `agents.x-k8s.io/created-by: python-client` (renamed `PYTHON_CLIENT_LABEL` to `CREATED_BY_LABEL` to align with the core API specification).
### 2. Label Propagation (Controllers)
* **SandboxClaim Controller**: 
  * Propagates the `created-by` label value from `SandboxClaim` resources to `Sandbox` resources and backing Pod templates during creation, update, and warm pool adoption.
  * When adopting a warm-pool Sandbox (which defaults to `created-by: controller`), the label on the adopted `Sandbox` is dynamically overwritten to match the SDK client that claimed it.

title: 🐛 flip AsyncSandboxClient cleanup default to True

labels.name: size/M
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 30-99 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: lgtm

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Flips the default value of `AsyncSandboxClient(..., cleanup=...)` from `False` to `True`, so the async client registers its `atexit` cleanup hook out of the box and tracked sandboxes are deleted on program termination unless the caller explicitly opts out with `cleanup=False`. The `cleanup=True` capability itself already landed in #859; this PR only changes the default.

Why this matters: in the #859 review, @barney-s asked whether `AsyncSandboxClient` should default to `cleanup=True` for a better out-of-the-box experience, and @aditya-shantanu agreed and invited a PR (#930). Without this, a caller who forgets to use the `async with` context manager or to call `delete_all()` / `close()` leaks sandbox claims when the program exits. Defaulting to `True` makes the safe behavior the default while keeping `cleanup=False` available for callers that manage lifecycles themselves.

Design note for reviewers: this intentionally makes the async client diverge from the synchronous `SandboxClient`, which stays `cleanup=False`. The issue title says "Consider", so the asymmetry is the reviewable decision; the docstrings now call it out explicitly. Happy to align the sync client instead if you'd prefer symmetry.

Tests updated/added in `test_async_sandboxclient.py`:
- new `test_cleanup_default_registers_atexit` — bare construction now registers the hook,
- `test_cleanup_true_registers_atexit` / `test_cleanup_false_does_not_register_atexit` retained as regression guards,
- setUp/helper constructions that don't exercise cleanup now pass `cleanup=False` to stay hermetic (the new default would otherwise register a real global `atexit` hook per test).

All 58 unit tests in the module pass locally.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #930

#### Release Note

```release-note
The async `AsyncSandboxClient` now defaults to `cleanup=True`, registering an atexit hook that deletes tracked sandboxes on program termination. Pass `cleanup=False` to opt out. (This differs from the synchronous `SandboxClient`, which still defaults to `cleanup=False`.)
```

AI was used for assistance.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Removes the `use_pod_ip` option from the Python in-cluster connection config.

The current in-cluster client behavior is to use the Sandbox status pod IP when it is available and fall back to the stable Kubernetes DNS endpoint otherwise. Keeping a separate `use_pod_ip` toggle made the public API and docs disagree with that behavior.

This updates the sync and async clients, README, and unit tests around the pod-IP-first, DNS-fallback path.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #1029

## Title
`fix: resolve discovery cache lag and correct documentation typo in migration guide`

## Summary
This PR resolves the final transient E2E failure in the migration upgrade tests and fixes a minor typo in the migration guide documentation.

### 1. API Server Cache Retry Loop
* **Problem:** In the migration E2E test, when resources are queried immediately after being created (`kubectl apply`), the local `kubectl` discovery cache or the API server's REST mapper can hit a transient lag/discrepancy. This causes the test to fail with a `NotFound` / `the server could not find the requested resource` error.
* **Fix:** We replaced the direct `kubectl get` query with a retry loop (up to 10 attempts with a 1-second delay) using the fully qualified resource name (`sandboxclaims.extensions.agents.x-k8s.io`). This allows the local cache and API server REST mapper to successfully sync and guarantees test stability under load.

### 2. Documentation Correction
* **Fix:** Corrected a minor typo in `docs/api-migration-guide.md` specifying there are two migration flows instead of three.

title: Measuring code coverage and optimizing unit and E2E tests

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Wire up code coverage measurement across the repo, surface it on PRs, and use the resulting reports to 

- (a) identify gaps in the existing test suite and 

- (b) optimize the e2e suite where possible.

Coverage tooling isn't wired into the test or CI flow yet, so there's a clean opportunity to introduce it.The repo has two languages
that need coverage:

  - Go — controllers/, extensions/controllers/, cmd/, internal/, and the e2e suite in test/e2e/.
  - Python — clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/ (incl. sandbox-router/), dev/tools/shared/, and the example apps under examples/ (agent-sandbox-rl, gemini-cu-sandbox, hermes-agent).

  Concrete proposal to kick off discussion:

  - Go unit: go test -cover via the existing test-unit target.
  - Go e2e: go build -cover (Go 1.20+) to instrument the controller binary so the e2e suite contributes coverage too, not just unit tests.
  - Python: pytest-cov (every Python suite here already runs under pytest).
  - Aggregation/reporting: a single uploader so Go + Python land in one report with a PR comment + diff coverage. Open to options — Codecov is the most common pick in the k8s ecosystem; Coveralls and SonarCloud are alternatives.

  Follow-up work this enables:

  - Add targeted tests for the gaps the first report exposes.
  - Audit the e2e suite for redundancy / runtime once we can see what each test actually covers.

### Why is this needed?

- Reviewer signal: coverage deltas on PRs help reviewers spot untested paths in new features and bug fixes before merge.
- Repo health: as commit volume grows, an objective coverage signal makes it easier to keep quality from quietly regressing.
- Developer experience: a faster, leaner e2e suite (informed by what's actually covered vs. duplicated) shortens the feedback loop locally and in CI.
- Safer scaling: a well-instrumented test suite is what lets the project absorb more contributors without each change becoming a manual-review bottleneck.

# PR Description

## Title
`test: resolve race conditions and enable active extensions in test-migration E2E upgrade tests`

## Summary
This PR resolves race conditions in the migration E2E tests (`dev/tools/test-migration.py`) and aligns the Helm test path to match the Kubectl test path.

### 1. Robust Warm-started Claim Binding via Dynamic ownerReference
* **Problem:** If we let the controller naturally bind the claim, it often falls back to a cold-start because the warmpool sandbox is not yet Ready when the claim is reconciled. However, if we manually patch the status using a mock sandbox, the old controller manager clears it because of a missing owner reference (since claim UIDs are dynamic).

title: [Python SDK] use_pod_ip flag is ignored — Sandbox/AsyncSandbox always pass get_pod_ip, defeating DNS-by-default

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### Description

`SandboxInClusterConnectionConfig.use_pod_ip` (default `False`) is documented as: *"By default, connects via stable K8s DNS … When `use_pod_ip=True`, connects directly to the pod IP."* (`models.py`).

As of 636e032 (#800), both `Sandbox` and `AsyncSandbox` unconditionally pass `get_pod_ip` to `SandboxConnector`:

```python
# sandbox.py:65 / async_sandbox.py:68
get_pod_ip=self.get_pod_ip,   # was: self.get_pod_ip if use_pod_ip else None
```

`InClusterConnectionStrategy.connect()` then always attempts pod-IP routing first and silently falls back to cluster DNS. Net effect: the `use_pod_ip` flag is dead — setting it to `False` (the documented default) does **not** force DNS routing.

### Impact

- Doc/behavior mismatch: the default is now pod-IP-first, not "stable K8s DNS".
- Environments that *require* DNS/Service routing (strict NetworkPolicy, service mesh, secure overlay) can't opt out — the same scenario #916 raises for the Go SDK. #916's premise that the Python SDK can toggle this via `use_pod_ip` no longer holds at HEAD.
- Stale tests: `test/unit/test_async_sandboxclient.py` asserts `use_pod_ip` is "derived from connection_config", a derivation the wiring no longer performs.

### Suggested fix

Restore the gating — `get_pod_ip=self.get_pod_ip if use_pod_ip else None` in both `Sandbox` and `AsyncSandbox` — or make `connect()` honor `config.use_pod_ip` directly.

### Note

Introduced in #800; present at HEAD. Released `0.4.5` still has the correct gating, so consumers pinned to `0.4.5` are unaffected.

body: This PR introduces the load testing suite, optimized manifests, and execution guidelines for validating agent-sandbox WarmPool performance under Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) and GKE Standby Capacity Buffers. The primary objective is to prove that a standby capacity buffer-backed, cost-optimized cluster can achieve the same claim adoption latency as a statically over-provisioned cluster, at a fraction of the node cost. A small always-on base coupled with a standby capacity buffer should match the latency of a large static fleet while costing a fraction of it. The baseline target SLO is to sustain claimed adoption latency with $P_{50}$ and $P_{90}$ under 500ms, and $P_{99}$ under 1s throughout the test. To meet these goals, this PR incorporates testing configurations and optimized parameters across three critical infrastructure layers: #### 1. Cluster-Level Parameters - **Pod Capacity Optimization**: Standard GKE limits (110 pods/node) leave significant CPU cores stranded when running small sandbox pods. To achieve correct sizing and resource allocation, raising the max pods limit per node to ~160 allows a 32-core node to utilize its capacity fully and hold roughly 50% more pods. - **NAP & Quota Bounds**: Adjustments to Node Auto-Provisioning (NAP) max-CPU settings to prevent resource limits from capping node growth and generating `NotTriggerScaleUp: exceeded quota` failures during scale-up. - **Uniform Provisioning**: Custom ComputeClass configuration to pin machine selection (e.g., e2-standard-32 instances), making dynamic autoscaling predictable and uniform. #### 2. Controller-Level Parameters - **API Server Rate Limiting & Concurrency**: Highly concurrent workloads saturate default controller queue settings and K8s API client limits. The controller configuration has been updated to use `--kube-api-qps=3000` and `--kube-api-burst=4000` to prevent client-side rate limiting and keep pace at 50/s churn. - **Warmpool Size Optimization**: Correct sizing of max replicas in the warmpool to prevent excessive LIST and reconciliation operational overhead on the API server. #### 3. Capacity Buffer & Scaling Parameters (standby capacity buffer + active capacity buffer + HPA) - **Fixed Standby Core Sizing**: Fixed capacity limits should always be utilized rather than percentages, deriving core limits directly from arrival rates. This prevents lagging reactions from HPA adjustments and unintended quota blowups. The sizing metrics follow these formulas: $$ \text{Active_Capacity_Buffer}_{\text{cores}} = \text{rate} \times 30\text{s} \times \text{CPU per pod} $$ $$ \text{Standby_Capacity_Buffer}_{\text{cores}} = \text{rate} \times 120\text{s} \times \text{CPU per pod} - \text{ASN}_{\text{cores}} $$ - **Active Standby Buffer Integration**: Implements always-on Active Standby (ASN) capacity alongside cheaper, suspendable standby capacity. The strategy leverages a large, highly cost-effective Cold Standby Node buffer for sustained traffic, paired with a small Active Standby Node buffer to handle initial spikes (bridging the ~30s resume-time gap). - **HPA Tuning**: Configures HorizontalPodAutoscaler targeting the external `agent_sandbox_claim_creation_total` metric with an aggressive scale-up policy (up to 900% per 15s sync) to avoid staircase staging delays. #### Sample Run: ``` WARMPOOL_SIZE=300 ENABLE_HPA=true HPA_MIN_REPLICAS=300 HPA_MAX_REPLICAS=1000 \ SHUTDOWN_TTL=120 \ ENABLE_CSN_BUFFER=true CSN_BUFFER_CORES=520 CSN_INIT_TIME=2m \ ENABLE_ASN_BUFFER=true ASN_BUFFER_CORES=200 \ PROFILE="5:150,10:150,15:150,20:150,25:150,30:300,25:150,20:150,15:150,10:150,5:150,2:150,0:1200" ./run_churn_test.sh csn-asn-hpa-test ``` Temp folder created under `dev/load-test/test-recipes/csn-load-test/tmp` recording all the events: --- ### Which issue(s) this PR is related to Relates to GKE Standby Capacity Buffers validation for cost-optimized agent warmpools. --- ### Release Note ```release-note Introduced a comprehensive load testing suite, metrics collection parameters, and optimized manifests for agent-sandbox WarmPools utilizing GKE Standby Capacity Buffers and Horizontal Pod Autoscalers (HPA). ``` ## Summary by CodeRabbit * **New Features** * Added an end-to-end standby capacity buffer churn/load-testing workflow, including a phase-based churn driver, a node suspension readiness gate, and a single orchestration script with optional monitoring and teardown. * Added continuous monitoring/artifact capture for warm-pool readiness, HPA behavior, capacity buffers, pod/node states, autoscaler events, and GCE instance status. * Added cost/efficiency comparison tooling (including optional graph output) and new Kubernetes manifests for ComputeClass, Sandbox template, warm pool, capacity buffers, and HPA. * **Documentation** * Added a detailed README for long-running standby capacity buffer load & cost tests, including prerequisites, example commands, expected outputs, and a validation checklist.

body:
# PR Description
`test: resolve race condition in test-migration by using separate template for cold-start claims`


## Summary
This PR resolves a flaky/deterministic test failure in the migration E2E tests (`dev/tools/test-migration.py`).


### The Problem
During the `v1alpha1` phase of the migration test:
1. The test defines a warm pool (`upgrade-pool-warm` with `replicas: 1`) and a warm-started claim (`upgrade-claim-warm`) bound to its only replica (`upgrade-pool-warm-a1b2c`).
2. The test also defines a cold-start claim `upgrade-claim` with `warmpool: "default"`.
3. When the old `v0.4.6` controller manager reconciles these resources, it notices that `upgrade-pool-warm-a1b2c` is bound. To maintain the warmpool replica target of `1` idle sandbox, it scales up the warmpool by spinning up a new sandbox (e.g., `upgrade-pool-warm-zhnhp`).
4. Since `upgrade-claim` is unbound and configured to use the `"default"` warmpool policy (which matches any pool for the template `upgrade-template`), the running controller binds `upgrade-claim` to the newly created warm sandbox.
5. Once bound, `upgrade-claim` becomes warm-started. When converted during migration, the conversion webhook resolves its target warmpool to `upgrade-pool-warm` instead of `shadow-pool-upgrade-template`. This causes the test assertion to fail:

### The Solution
We introduce a separate template named `upgrade-template-cold` specifically for the cold-start claims (`upgrade-claim` and `upgrade-claim-none`).
- Because `upgrade-pool-warm` only matches `upgrade-template`, the controller cannot bind `upgrade-claim` or `upgrade-claim-none` to any warm sandbox.
- Both claims remain unbound (cold-started) throughout the test as intended, and are correctly migrated to `shadow-pool-upgrade-template-cold`.
- Update assertions and verification checks in `test-migration.py` to expect `shadow-pool-upgrade-template-cold` instead of `shadow-pool-upgrade-template` for these claims.


## Verification / Testing
Successfully verified the fix by running:

```bash
for i in {1..10}; do
  echo "=== Running Full Iteration $i ==="
  dev/ci/periodics/test-migration
  
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo "=== Failed at Iteration $i ==="
    break
  fi
done
```

* **Tests**
  * Updated migration coverage to verify the newer warm-pool template naming during upgrade checks.
  * Adjusted expected warm-pool references in conversion validation to match the updated shadow pool behavior.

title: Helm: optional ServiceMonitor for scraping the controller metrics endpoint

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

An **opt-in `ServiceMonitor`** template in the Helm chart (`monitoring.coreos.com/v1`) so prometheus-operator users can scrape the controller's metrics endpoint without writing one by hand.

Proposed shape (off by default):
```yaml
metrics:
  serviceMonitor:
    enabled: false          # requires the prometheus-operator CRDs
    additionalLabels: {}    # e.g. release: kube-prometheus-stack, to match the Prometheus serviceMonitorSelector
    interval: 30s
    scrapeTimeout: ""
```
The template selects the existing controller `Service` (`templates/service.yaml`, named port `metrics` on `:8080`) and scrapes `path: /metrics` over `scheme: http`. It is gated entirely behind `metrics.serviceMonitor.enabled` and rendered only when set, since the `ServiceMonitor` kind requires the prometheus-operator CRDs to be installed.

### Why is this needed?

The chart **already ships a metrics `Service` on `:8080`** and the controller already serves `/metrics` (plain HTTP, no auth — `metricsserver.Options{BindAddress: ":8080"}` in `cmd/agent-sandbox-controller/main.go`), registering both the controller-runtime suite and custom metrics: `agent_sandbox_claim_startup_latency_ms`, `agent_sandbox_claim_controller_startup_latency_ms`, `agent_sandbox_creation_latency_ms`, `agent_sandbox_claim_creation_total`, `agent_sandboxes`, `agent_sandbox_build_info`.

However, prometheus-operator-based stacks (kube-prometheus-stack, etc.) discover scrape targets via `ServiceMonitor` resources. Today users must author and maintain that resource out-of-band, even though the chart owns the Service and knows the port/labels. Shipping an opt-in `ServiceMonitor` completes the existing-but-unscrapable metrics surface and supports the roadmap items **"Additional Prometheus Telemetry"** and **"Controller Custom Metrics."**

title: python-runtime-sandbox: long-running /execute can block HTTP readiness and make pods NotReady

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### What happened?

The official Python runtime sandbox example appears to be vulnerable to event-loop blocking during long-running `/execute` calls.

The current upstream runtime defines `/execute` as an async FastAPI handler, but calls blocking `subprocess.run()` inside it:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/examples/python-runtime-sandbox/main.py

At the same time, the official quickstart points users to the ready-made SandboxTemplate:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/examples/quickstart/README.md

which uses the `python-runtime-sandbox:latest-main` image and configures HTTP readiness against `/` every 1 second:

https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/python-sandbox-template.yaml

Because `/execute` and `/` are served by the same FastAPI/Uvicorn process, a long-running `/execute` command can block the event loop and delay the readiness handler. Kubernetes may then mark the sandbox pod as `NotReady`, even though the user command is still running successfully and the container is not actually unhealthy.

This surfaced for us during pandas / CSV data processing workloads, but the issue seems to come from the upstream example runtime design itself: blocking subprocess execution inside an async endpoint, combined with HTTP readiness served by the same event loop.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Using the upstream quickstart/runtime path:

1. Apply the official Python SandboxTemplate from:
   `clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/python-sandbox-template.yaml`

   This template uses:
   - `python-runtime-sandbox:latest-main`
   - HTTP readiness probe: `GET /`
   - `periodSeconds: 1`
   - no explicit `timeoutSeconds`, so Kubernetes defaults to 1 second

2. Create a sandbox using that template.

3. Run a long-running command through `/execute`, for example:
```bash
python3 -c "import time; time.sleep(30); print('done')"
```
or any data processing(for example, pandas CSV-processing) command that runs for long enough.

4. Watch pod events while /execute is still running:
```bash
kubectl describe pod <sandbox-pod>
kubectl get events --field-selector involvedObject.name=<sandbox-pod>
```
Observed event pattern:
```bash
Readiness probe failed: context deadline exceeded
Client.Timeout exceeded while awaiting headers
```
In runtime logs, readiness GET / requests are delayed until the /execute request completes.

### Version

main @ 262aa41

### Anything else we need to know?

I may be missing intended usage guidance here. If long-running `/execute` commands are expected, should the example runtime avoid blocking the event loop, or should the sample readiness probe be documented differently?

Possible fixes:

1. Use `asyncio.create_subprocess_exec()` in `/execute` instead of blocking `subprocess.run()`.

   Example shape:

   ```python
   process = await asyncio.create_subprocess_exec(
       *args,
       stdout=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
       stderr=asyncio.subprocess.PIPE,
       cwd="/app",
   )
   stdout, stderr = await process.communicate()```
Alternatively, make /execute a sync FastAPI endpoint (def, not async def) so FastAPI runs it in a threadpool rather than blocking the event loop.

Optionally keep a single-command lock if the intended runtime semantics are one command at a time per sandbox.

Add a regression test where GET / remains responsive while /execute is running.

Our local workaround was to replace the runtime server with an API-compatible version that uses asyncio.create_subprocess_exec() for /execute. With that change, a pandas workload completed successfully while HTTP readiness remained healthy:
```text
not_ready_samples: 0
restart_count: 0
unhealthy_events_since_workload: 0
```

title: fix(python): bracket IPv6 addresses in HTTP URLs per RFC 3986

labels.name: size/L

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

RFC 3986 requires IPv6 literal addresses in URLs to be enclosed in square brackets (e.g `http://[2001:db8::1]:8888/path`). Some code sites in the Python SDK and sandbox router construct URLs from raw pod/gateway IPs without bracketing, producing malformed URLs like `http://2600::16:8888/path` where the port is misinterpreted as part of the IPv6 address. This causes breakage on IPv6-only clusters: HTTP 500 on every proxied request through the router, and invalid base URLs from the SDK's InCluster and Gateway connection strategy.

The fix applies a conditional bracket at each URL-construction site:
- [sandbox_router.py](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/sandbox-router/sandbox_router.py): use `isinstance(ip, ipaddress.IPv6Address)` since the parsed object is already available.
- [connector.py](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/connector.py): bracket in GatewayConnectionStrategy and InClusterConnectionStrategy.
- [async_connector.py](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/async_connector.py): same two strategies as async counterpart.

This matches the pattern the Go SDK already uses (`strings.Contains(addr, ":")`). IPv4 paths are unaffected, the `":"` in ip check is false for all IPv4 strings. New unit tests cover IPv6 bracketing and include IPv4 non-bracketing regression guards across all three components.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #988 

#### How has it been tested end-to-end:

Deploy router to the IPv6 cluster and start port-forward. Send request with IPv6 pod IP:

```bash
curl -s -w "\n>>> HTTP Status: %{http_code}\n" \
  -X POST http://127.0.0.1:18080/execute \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "X-Sandbox-ID: test-sandbox" \
  -H "X-Sandbox-Namespace: ipv6-test" \
  -H "X-Sandbox-Port: 8888" \
  -H "X-Sandbox-Pod-IP: 2001:db8::1" \
  -d '{"command": "echo hello"}'
```

Before the fix:
```
{"detail":"An internal error occurred in the proxy."}
>>> HTTP Status: 500
```

Checking router logs confirm the malformed URL:
```
An unexpected error occurred: Invalid port: 'db8::1:8888'
INFO:     ::1:45570 - "POST /execute HTTP/1.1" 500 Internal Server Error
```

With the fix:
```
{"detail":"Timed out waiting for the backend sandbox: test-sandbox"}
>>> HTTP Status: 504
```

Checking router logs confirm correctly formed URL

```
ERROR: Request to sandbox at http://[2001:db8::1]:8888/execute timed out. Error:
```

IPv6 address correctly enclosed in brackets per RFC 3986. The 504 is expected because no sandbox exists at that address; the URL construction bug is gone.

#### Release Note

```release-note
Fixed Python SDK and sandbox router producing malformed HTTP URLs for IPv6 pod and gateway addresses. IPv6 literals are now correctly enclosed in square brackets per RFC 3986, restoring connectivity on IPv6-only clusters.
```

<!-- This is an auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * IPv6 addresses in URLs are now properly formatted using RFC 3986 bracket notation standards. This ensures correct handling across different routing configurations.

* **Tests**
  * Added comprehensive unit tests validating IPv6 address handling and URL formatting across routing scenarios.

<!-- end of auto-generated comment: release notes by coderabbit.ai -->

title: Add collision-free all-in-one install asset (sandbox-with-extensions.yaml) for kustomize/GitOps

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.
