labels.description: Indicates a non-member PR verified by an org member that is safe to test.

labels.name: approved
labels.description: Indicates a PR has been approved by an approver from all required OWNERS files.

body:
## What this does

Publishes a single, collision-free **all-in-one** release asset (core + extensions) so the project can be consumed by kustomize / GitOps engines, and — following maintainer discussion in this PR — renames the release assets for clarity:

| Asset | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| `sandbox.yaml` | core controller + base CRDs + webhook Service (was `manifest.yaml`) |
| `extensions.yaml` | extensions API group only (unchanged; opt-in / additive) |
| `sandbox-with-extensions.yaml` | all-in-one, collision-free (new; core + extensions) |

## Why

The documented install uses two flat assets applied sequentially:

```sh
kubectl apply -f sandbox.yaml -f extensions.yaml
```

That works because `kubectl apply` is last-write-wins. But **both files declare the `agent-sandbox-controller` Deployment** (`extensions.yaml`'s copy adds `--extensions`), which is a duplicate resource id. kustomize, Config Sync and Argo CD all reject that:

```
may not add resource with an already registered id: apps_v1_Deployment|agent-sandbox-system|agent-sandbox-controller
```

So GitOps consumers today have to strip one Deployment when vendoring the release artifacts. This is the same pain reported in #192 (closed) and came up again in #844.

Separately, `manifest.yaml` / `install.yaml` were ambiguous ("which do I apply?"), so the assets are renamed to say what they contain.

## Approach

- Add `k8s/kustomization.yaml` that assembles core + extensions with the controller declared **exactly once** and `--extensions` (plus the optional `agent-sandbox-config` mount) applied via a **patch** instead of a second Deployment doc.
- Teach `dev/tools/release` to render it into a single `sandbox-with-extensions.yaml` asset (same `ko://` image substitution as the other assets) and publish it alongside `sandbox.yaml` and `extensions.yaml`.
- Add a stdlib-only **drift guard** so a new file dropped into `k8s/` can't be silently missing from the all-in-one asset: the release fails if `kustomization.yaml`'s hand-maintained `resources:` list diverges from the glob the flat assets are built from. Covered by unit tests in `dev/tools/release_test.py` (run by `make test-unit`).
- `kustomization.yaml` is excluded from the flat-asset globs so it is not concatenated into them.

The two-step `kubectl apply -f sandbox.yaml -f extensions.yaml` flow is preserved, and `kubectl kustomize k8s/` renders the same all-in-one locally.

## Naming (resolved)

Per discussion with @barney-s, @aditya-shantanu and @janetkuo: `sandbox.yaml` (core only), `extensions.yaml` (extensions only, kept separate since it is opt-in/additive), `sandbox-with-extensions.yaml` (all-in-one).

## Backwards compatibility

The rename applies to assets produced going forward; already-published releases keep their existing asset names. References pinned to historical releases (the API migration guide's `v0.5.0` install, `dev/tools/test-migration.py`) are intentionally left on the old names.

## Validation

```
$ kubectl kustomize k8s/ | grep '^kind:' | sort | uniq -c
   2 kind: ClusterRole
   2 kind: ClusterRoleBinding
   4 kind: CustomResourceDefinition
   1 kind: Deployment          # single controller, args: [--leader-elect=true, --extensions]
   1 kind: Namespace
   2 kind: Service
   1 kind: ServiceAccount
```

`dev/tools/release --tag vX.Y.Z` emits `sandbox.yaml`, `extensions.yaml`, and `sandbox-with-extensions.yaml`. `make test-unit` runs the new release drift-detection tests.

Relates to #844, #192.

/kind feature

* **New Features**
  * Added GitOps-friendly one-time install via `sandbox-with-extensions.yaml`, with separate `sandbox.yaml` (core) and `extensions.yaml` (extensions) options.
  * Release tooling now generates kustomize-based all-in-one manifests with install drift detection; controller exposes the webhook port (TCP 9443).
* **Bug Fixes**
  * Manifest collection now ignores `kustomization.yaml`/`kustomization.yml` so kustomize descriptors aren’t applied.
* **Documentation**
  * Updated install instructions and examples/scripts to use `sandbox.yaml`/`extensions.yaml` instead of `manifest.yaml`, including GitOps recommendations.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Adds **`rl-sandbox-scripts`**: the original, dependency-light **script-based
prototype** for running SWE-bench-style tasks on Agent Sandbox **warm pools**.
This is the work that the `agent-sandbox-rl` package (#1000) productizes — kept as
a readable, standalone reference that shows the core warm-pool flow with minimal
moving parts.

It offers two parallel takes on the same lifecycle (provision pools → claim a
sandbox per task → exec a probe → tear down):
- **Python driver** — `run_swebench.py` → `strategies.py` → `sizing.py` /
  `warmpool.py` (uses `kubernetes` + the `k8s-agent-sandbox` SDK). Implements the
  `none` / `naive` / `sliding` warm-pool strategies and concurrency-aware sizing.
- **Bash e2e** — `e2e_test.sh`: self-contained (`kubectl`/`curl`/`jq`, no
  Python/SDK), with a menu, per-phase **benchmark timers**, and a printout of
  every created object (`SandboxTemplate`/`SandboxWarmPool`/`SandboxClaim`/
  `Sandbox`/`Pod`). Plus `prepull.sh` — a DaemonSet that pre-pulls task images so
  warm pods skip the multi-GB pull.

Also includes an interactive demo notebook (`rl-tunix-swebench-demo.ipynb`),
example manifests (a `SandboxTemplate`+`SandboxWarmPool`, a v1alpha1 reference for
comparison, and per-image warmpools), and the measured working notes
(`optimizations.md`, `performance.md`, `image-analysis.md`) that the package's
strategies/sizing are based on.

There is **no model in the loop** — a lightweight probe command stands in for the
agent rollout, so the warm-pool infrastructure can be developed and benchmarked
cheaply. The example is self-contained.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

NONE

#### Release Note
```release-note
Add the rl-sandbox-scripts example: a script-based (Python + bash) prototype for running SWE-bench warm-pool RL/eval on Agent Sandbox (none/naive/sliding strategies, concurrency-aware sizing, image pre-pull, and an end-to-end benchmark harness).
```

body:
## What this does

Adds a Helm chart registry hosted on GitHub Pages so users can install released chart versions with `helm repo add` instead of cloning the repo. This mirrors the approach used by [cluster-proportional-autoscaler](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cluster-proportional-autoscaler).

### Changes
- **`.github/workflows/helm-chart-release.yml`** — On push to `main` touching `helm/**` (plus manual `workflow_dispatch`), runs [`chart-releaser-action`](https://github.com/helm/chart-releaser-action) to package the chart and publish it to the `gh-pages` branch. `charts_dir: .` is used because the chart lives at `helm/` rather than the action's default `charts/<name>/` layout. Actions are SHA-pinned to match the repo's ratchet convention.
- **`.github/cr.yaml`** — Sets `release-name-template: helm-chart-{{ .Name }}-{{ .Version }}` so chart releases (`helm-chart-agent-sandbox-<version>`) stay distinct from the project's existing `v*` releases produced by `release.yml`.
- **`helm/README.md`** — Documents installing from the repository and a maintainer "Publishing new chart versions" section.

### Usage once published
```bash
helm repo add agent-sandbox https://kubernetes-sigs.github.io/agent-sandbox
helm repo update
helm install agent-sandbox agent-sandbox/agent-sandbox \
  --namespace agent-sandbox-system --create-namespace \
  --set image.tag=<version>
```

## Notes for maintainers
- **One-time setup required:** GitHub Pages must be enabled with the source set to the `gh-pages` branch (Settings → Pages). The docs site is served separately via Netlify, so this branch is free for the Helm repository index.
- **Each release needs a `version` bump** in `helm/Chart.yaml` — the action skips versions that already have a corresponding release.

  * Added guidance on the chart release workflow and GitHub Pages setup requirements.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

**Run reinforcement learning at scale on Agent Sandbox — straight from Python.**
`agent-sandbox-rl` is a batteries-included package that lets an RL/eval pipeline
spin up a swarm of isolated sandboxes across one or many clusters, keep them
**warm** so each task claims a ready environment in well under a second (instead
of waiting on a multi-GB image pull), run the rollout inside it, score, and tear
everything down — all behind a few lines of Python. It turns "give my learner a
fresh, isolated machine for every trajectory, and don't make me babysit the
Kubernetes" into a one-liner: `fleet.run(rollout, strategy="sliding")`.

Adds a new example, **`agent-sandbox-rl`**: a generic, **multi-cluster** Python
package that turns the full SWE-bench-style RL/eval run lifecycle on Agent Sandbox

Today every consumer that wants to run batches of tasks against warm pools
re-implements pool sizing, placement, claim/exec orchestration, and cleanup. This
example provides that once, generically, so RL/eval stacks (R2E-Gym, tunix,
TorchRL, SkyRL, …) can plug in via a single `SandboxHandle`.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Fixes a TOCTOU race in the Go client's handle registry. `GetSandbox`/`CreateSandbox` read `c.registry` under `c.mu`, release the lock, do network I/O (`verifyClaimExists`, `resolveSandboxName`, `Open`), then write `c.registry[key] = sb` **unconditionally**. Two concurrent calls for the same key each build a `*Sandbox`, and the second write clobbers the first without `Close()`-ing it. The displaced handle stays connected but becomes unreachable through the `Client`, so `DeleteAll`/`DeleteSandbox`/`ListActiveSandboxes` can never reach it — leaking its port-forward goroutines (`ForwardPorts` + `monitorPortForward`), SPDY connection, and owned `http.Transport` for the lifetime of the process. (A reproduction on kind with 12 concurrent callers leaked 11 handles and ~205 goroutines; with the fix, 0 orphans.)

The fix re-checks the registry under the final lock (compare-and-set): if a ready handle is already tracked for the key, it returns that one and tears down the redundant handle it just built — `Disconnect` in `GetSandbox` (the claim is shared) / `Close` in `CreateSandbox` (the claim is freshly created). The stale-handle eviction becomes a compare-and-delete so it can't remove a handle a concurrent caller just installed.

Two tests attached (to be run inside `clients/go/sandbox`).

[repro_kind_test.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29152545/repro_kind_test.txt)
[client_race_test.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29152544/client_race_test.txt)

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
<!-- Provide a clear and concise description of the changes in this PR. -->

Introduces a shared `SandboxBlueprint` struct holding the fields common to a live`Sandbox` and a `SandboxTemplate` (`podTemplate`, `volumeClaimTemplates`,`service`), and inlines it (`json:",inline"`) into both `SandboxSpec` and`SandboxTemplateSpec`.

`SandboxTemplateSpec` embedded a bare `PodTemplate` and then re-declared `volumeClaimTemplates` and `service` independently, so every shared field had to be duplicated across the specs and hand-copied field-by-field in the warm-pool and claim controllers. New shared fields meant N copies and silent drift between the specs.

With the blueprint inlined, the shared fields live in one place and flow through to both specs automatically; the controllers collapse to a single
`dst.Spec.SandboxBlueprint = *src...SandboxBlueprint.DeepCopy()`.

**Design: inlined blueprint, not a nested SandboxSpec**
Per the discussion in #969, this uses an **inlined** shared struct rather than embedding the whole `SandboxSpec` as a nested field:
  - **No wire/OpenAPI change** — `json:",inline"` keeps the CRD schema flat, so `spec.podTemplate` stays exactly where it is. No CRD/manifest/client migration.
  - **No runtime-only leakage** — `operatingMode` and `lifecycle` (and their defaults) stay on `SandboxSpec` and are deliberately *not* exposed on templates, where they aren't meaningful.
  - **Template-only fields** (`networkPolicy`, `networkPolicyManagement`, `envVarsInjectionPolicy`, `volumeClaimTemplatesPolicy`) stay on `SandboxTemplateSpec`.

 **Changes**
  - `api/v1beta1`: add `SandboxBlueprint`; inline into `SandboxSpec`.
  - `extensions/api/v1beta1`: inline `SandboxBlueprint` into `SandboxTemplateSpec`; drop the duplicated `podTemplate`/`volumeClaimTemplates`/`service` fields.
  - Regenerated `zz_generated.deepcopy.go` for both packages.
  - `sandboxwarmpool_controller` / `sandboxclaim_controller`: replace per-field copies with a single blueprint deep-copy. 
  - Updated composite literals in controllers, examples, and tests for the embedded field.

# PR Description
`fix: resolve Python 3.11 compatibility in migration test runner`

## Description
This PR resolves a syntax compatibility issue with Python 3.11 in the migration test runner. 

The migration test runner script introduced nested double quotes within an f-string at `dev/tools/test-migration.py:510`:
```python
f"Expected warmpool default, got {c1_v1alpha1["spec"]["warmpool"]}"
```

While this is valid in `Python 3.12+` (due to PEP 701), the Kubernetes Prow CI environment uses Debian Bookworm, which runs `Python 3.11` by default. Since `Python 3.11` is the standard runtime environment for all Kubernetes CI jobs, the standard and most robust solution is to change the nested double quotes to single quotes in the `agent-sandbox` script.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
<!-- Provide a clear and concise description of the changes in this PR. -->
This PR addresses a bug, where the `EnvVarsInjectionPolicy: Allowed` could be bypassed due to Kubernetes' environment variable precedence logic. Because Kubernetes evaluates `Env` variables after `EnvFrom` sources, a user could override protected variables by specifying a variable with the same name in the `SandboxClaim.Spec.Env` field.

The fix implements a validation check that rejects environment variable injection when the `SandboxTemplate` uses `EnvFrom` sources and the injection policy is set to `Allowed`. This is handled by a new sentinel error, `ErrEnvVarsInjectionRejected`, and a helper function, `hasEnvFrom`, which scans both init containers and standard containers for `EnvFrom` definitions. Additionally, the `SandboxClaim` status logic has been updated to report this rejection clearly in the Ready condition.

Working on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/959

# [v1beta1-migration]: Make the migration upgrade tests automated

## Overview
This PR automates the E2E storage migration tests validating the upgrade path from `v1alpha1` (older version `v0.4.6`) to the new `v1beta1` API version. It introduces a periodic test runner for KinD clusters, configures local testing datasets to support offline/network-free execution, and updates the shared CI runner setup.


## Detailed Changes
### 1. Automation Test Runner Script
* **File**: `dev/ci/periodics/test-migration` (New)
* **Description**: Initiates a clean KinD cluster, installs/deploys the `v0.4.6` version, generates active resources, upgrades the controller/CRDs to the `v1beta1` dev build, runs storage migration hooks, validates resources are correctly upgraded, and verifies rollback capability.
* **Optimizations**: Configured `setup_cluster` to only build and load the controller image (`--controller-only`), speeding up Kind loading times significantly.
### 2. CI Shared Test Runner Enhancements
* **File**: `dev/ci/shared/runner.py`
* **Description**: Added support for a `--skip-initial-deploy` flag to allow custom setup routines (e.g., installing a previous release first) to bypass the default controller installation.
### 3. Local Migration Test Data (v0.4.6)
* **Files**: 
  - `test/migration/testdata/v0.4.6/extensions.yaml`
  - `test/migration/testdata/v0.4.6/manifest.yaml`
  - `test/migration/testdata/v0.4.6/helm-v0.4.6.tar.gz`
* **Description**: Added local manifests, extensions, and Helm package tarballs for version `v0.4.6`. This enables offline test execution and avoids rate-limiting/network dependencies on GitHub.
### 4. Migration Test Script Improvements
* **File**: `dev/tools/test-migration.py`
* **Description**: 
  - Added logic to automatically fallback to local manifests/chart tarballs if they exist under the testdata directory.
  - Reset default values for `--image-prefix` back to `"kind.local/"` for local testing environments.

---
## Verification Results
Verified both `kubectl` and `helm` upgrade-and-rollback suites pass successfully inside a clean Kind cluster on the workstation:

```

ALL ROLLBACK VALIDATIONS PASSED SUCCESSFULLY!
```

title: Sandbox Router fails to bracket IPv6 pod IPs causing Invalid port / HTTP 500 on IPv6 clusters

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
## Summary

On an IPv6-only cluster, every SDK request through the Sandbox Router fails with HTTP 500. The Python SDK routes by pod IP via the `X-Sandbox-Pod-IP` header, and the router builds the upstream URL without bracketing the IPv6 literal, producing an invalid host:port netloc.

## What happens

The SDK (SandboxClient in Tunnel mode) sends the sandbox pod IP in X-Sandbox-Pod-IP. On an IPv6 cluster this is a bare IPv6 address (e.g. 2600:1f18:252b:c07:27::16). The router does:

pod_ip = request.headers.get("X-Sandbox-Pod-IP")
if pod_ip:
    target_host = pod_ip            # <-- bare IPv6, not bracketed
...
target_url = str(
    request.url.replace(scheme="http", hostname=target_host, port=port)
)

URL.replace(hostname=..., port=...) concatenates host and port as <host>:<port>, yielding http://2600:1f18:252b:c07:27::16:8888/execute. The trailing …::16:8888 is then parsed as part of the address, and the proxied request fails.

## Observed router log

Proxying request for sandbox 'sandbox-claim-...' to URL: http://2600:1f18:252b:c07:27::16:8888/execute
An unexpected error occurred: Invalid port: '1f18:252b:c07:27::16:8888'
INFO:     ::1:36042 - "POST /execute HTTP/1.1" 500 Internal Server Error

## SDK side:

SandboxRequestError: Failed to communicate with the sandbox at http://127.0.0.1:<port>/execute.
... ResponseError('too many 500 error responses')

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Run the controller + router + SDK on an IPv6-only (or IPv6-primary) cluster.
2. client.create_sandbox(template="python-sandbox-template", namespace=...).
3. sandbox.commands.run("echo hi") → HTTP 500.

### Version

v0.4.6

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

Working on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/740 
# Implement manual API Upgrade E2E Tests (`v1alpha1` → `v1beta1`)
## Description
This PR restructures the `v1alpha1` -> `v1beta1` storage migration path. The primary focus of this change is stabilizing and simplifying our upgrade test validation suite, which now exercises manual script-driven migrations, dry-runs, and emergency rollback validation. In addition, the complex, error-prone automated Helm-hook Jobs (which frequently ran into sequencing and RBAC issues) have been removed from the Helm chart in favor of a manual operational workflow.
### Key Changes
### 1. E2E Migration Test Suite
* **Unified Script-Driven Tests**: Updated `dev/tools/test-migration.py` to drive manual migration phases (`migrate.sh --phase=bootstrap` and `migrate.sh --phase=migrate`) for both the `kubectl` and `helm` upgrade test methods.
* **Added Dry-Run Validations**: Programmatically verifies that `--dry-run` modes work correctly (bootstrap creates no shadow warm pools, and migrate writes no storage migration annotations).
* **Robust E2E Rollback Validation**: Added a `--test-rollback` testing flag. It asserts that resources can be safely rolled back to `v1alpha1` after an upgrade.

### 2. Removal of Automated Helm Hooks & Chart Refactoring
* **Removed Automated Helm Hooks**: Cleared template files `migration-job-bootstrap.yaml`, `migration-job-migrate.yaml`, `migration-rbac.yaml`, and `migration-configmap.yaml` and removed the `migration:` configuration block from `values.yaml`.
* **Decoupled Webhook Service Name**: Promoted `webhookServiceName` to a top-level property (`webhookServiceName: agent-sandbox-webhook-service`) in `values.yaml` and updated `webhook-service.yaml` to use it, preventing template compilation failures when the `migration` block is omitted.
### 3. Documentation
* **Updated Guide & README**: Revised `docs/api-migration-guide.md` and `helm/README.md` to document the manual migration script-driven approach instead of the automated jobs.
* **Added Managed/Private Cluster Firewall Tip**: Documented the GKE control plane to node VPC firewall requirement (TCP port `9443`) for conversion webhooks to resolve connection timeout issues.
* **Emergency Rescue / Rollback Guide**: Added instructions to temporarily disable conversion webhooks on the CRDs (`strategy: None`) to restore write access to the cluster if a migration fails or needs to be aborted, and scaled down/deleted resources in the correct sequence.
---


## Verification Results
Both migration and emergency rollback/restore flows were validated successfully on a GKE cluster:
### 1. Kubectl Upgrade & Rollback Method
```bash
python3 dev/tools/test-migration.py \
  --image-prefix=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/shrutinair-gke-dev/agent-sandbox-controller/ \
  --image-tag=v20260616-v0.5.0rc1-8-g9b7f98c-dirty \
  --method=kubectl \
  --test-rollback
```

```bash
python3 dev/tools/test-migration.py \
  --image-prefix=us-central1-docker.pkg.dev/shrutinair-gke-dev/agent-sandbox-controller/ \
  --image-tag=v20260616-v0.5.0rc1-8-g9b7f98c-dirty \
  --method=helm \
  --test-rollback
```

## Summary

- assign explicit UUIDv7-based names for warm-pool Sandbox objects
- stop relying on Kubernetes `generateName` short suffixes for warm-pool allocations
- sanitize the warm-pool name prefix to DNS-1123 label characters and trim to the 63-character label limit
- add controller tests for explicit names, uniqueness, no `GenerateName`, long-name compliance, and invalid-prefix sanitization

## Why

Short provider-generated suffixes make warm-pool sandbox name reuse possible over time. UUIDv7 names make provider identity collisions effectively disappear at the GAS layer, while tn-api separately owns durable lifecycle identity.

## Validation

- `go test ./extensions/controllers`
- `gofmt -l extensions/controllers/sandboxwarmpool_controller.go extensions/controllers/sandboxwarmpool_controller_test.go`
- `git diff --check`

## Review Notes

- This complements the tn-api runtime lifecycle identity PR. GAS naming reduces collision probability; tn-api lifecycle ids remove our dependency on provider-name permanence.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The `SandboxClaim` CRD already supports `spec.additionalPodMetadata`, and the
claim controller propagates its `labels` and `annotations` onto the running
Sandbox **Pod**. Until now the Python client had no way to set it: the existing
`labels` argument on `create_sandbox` only wires the *claim object's own*
`metadata.labels`, which lands on the `SandboxClaim` resource and never reaches
the Pod.

This PR adds two new optional, keyword-only parameters to both the sync
(`SandboxClient`) and async (`AsyncSandboxClient`) `create_sandbox`:

- `pod_labels` -> `spec.additionalPodMetadata.labels`
- `pod_annotations` -> `spec.additionalPodMetadata.annotations`

They flow from the public client through `_create_claim` into the
`create_sandbox_claim` manifest builders (`k8s_helper` / `async_k8s_helper`),
mirroring the existing `labels` / `lifecycle` plumbing rather than introducing a
new pattern. With this, a caller can stamp a tenant / client identifier onto the
Pod and the running sandbox can read its own identity via the Downward API.

Details:

- Additive and keyword-only, so existing callers are unaffected.
- `pod_labels` reuse the existing `_validate_labels` RFC-1123 validation so bad
  keys/values fail fast client-side (the controller validates server-side too).
- Empty sections are omitted; no empty `additionalPodMetadata` is written when
  neither `pod_labels` nor `pod_annotations` is provided.
- README documents the distinction between claim-level `labels` and Pod-level
  `pod_labels` / `pod_annotations`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #914
Ref https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/914

#### Testing

- Added unit tests for the sync and async k8s helpers (manifest emits
  `spec.additionalPodMetadata`; key omitted when unset).
- Added unit tests for the sync and async clients (parameters thread through to
  `_create_claim` / `create_sandbox_claim` as the expected `pod_metadata` dict;
  invalid pod-label keys raise the same validation error as claim labels).
- Updated existing client tests that assert the exact `_create_claim` /
  `create_sandbox_claim` call signature.
- `python -m pytest k8s_agent_sandbox/test/unit` passes (223 passed).

AI was used for assistance.

#### Release Note
```release-note
The Python `SandboxClient` and `AsyncSandboxClient` now accept `pod_labels` and `pod_annotations` on `create_sandbox`, which are propagated to the Sandbox Pod via `spec.additionalPodMetadata`.
```

  * Supported in both synchronous and asynchronous clients, with client-side validation for pod label formatting.

* **Documentation**
  * Expanded the client README with a “Labels and Pod Metadata” section and new usage snippets, including Kubernetes validation expectations.

title: TypeScript SDK: follow-ups after the resource layer

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

#976 landed the **Kubernetes resource layer** of the TypeScript SDK (`agentic-sandbox-client`, under `clients/typescript/`) — the third supported client alongside Go and Python. It covers `SandboxClaim` provisioning, watch-to-ready, list, and teardown via `SandboxClient` / `Sandbox`, with `enableAutoCleanup()` and optional OpenTelemetry tracing over the claim lifecycle. Node.js >=22, ESM-only, Vitest unit tests.

This issue tracks the remaining work:

1. the **sandboxd protocol layer** (sandbox runtime connectivity — commands, files) as a dedicated follow-up PR;
2. **review follow-ups** from #976 (non-blocking notes);
3. **publishing** (npm package name decision + release pipeline);
4. an **API-parity / hardening backlog** measured against the Python SDK.

### Why is this needed?

TypeScript/JavaScript is widely used in AI agent runtimes and tooling. A first-class SDK makes agent-sandbox accessible without hand-rolled wrappers or manual Kubernetes API calls. #976 shipped the resource layer on its own so it could be reviewed and land quickly; the runtime layer is a larger, separable design.

The lists below are triaged against merged `main` (the squash commit for #976), not just PR discussion.

### Completed (landed in #976)

- [x] Kubernetes resource layer: `SandboxClient` / `Sandbox` (claim / sandbox / pod identity + `close()` / `closeLocal()`), warm/cold pool provisioning, watch-to-ready, `listActiveSandboxes` / `listAllSandboxes` / `deleteAll`, `enableAutoCleanup()`
- [x] Reduced the initial PR to the resource layer — dropped the HTTP transport (`connect()`, gateway resolution, port-forward, `request()`), `src/commands`, `src/files`, `src/extensions`, `src/response-utils`, and the `SandboxClient<T extends Sandbox>` generic seam
- [x] `close()` surfaces a non-404 claim-deletion failure (including the cleanup timeout) as `SandboxError` instead of only logging it, so `close()` / `deleteSandbox()` are retryable — matches Go/Python and AGENTS.md's no-swallowing rule (Python's equivalent fix: #978)
- [x] Kubernetes 404 detection is based on the numeric status code only (no message-string fallback)
- [x] Local resource-leak fixes in the resource layer: stale-handle cleanup on `getSandbox` re-attach, `close()` cleanup-timer races
- [x] OpenTelemetry JS SDK 2.x compatibility — `trace-manager.ts` moved off the removed `new Resource(...)` / `provider.addSpanProcessor(...)` APIs onto `resourceFromAttributes(...)` + the `spanProcessors` constructor option. Tracing now covers only the claim lifecycle span (`<service>.lifecycle`, attribute `sandbox.claim.name`); the command-line-sanitization concern moves with the runtime spans to the protocol-layer note below
- [x] Dependency major bumps while the package has no consumers: `@kubernetes/client-node` 2.x, OpenTelemetry SDK 2.x, TypeScript 7

### Follow-up work

#### Sandboxd protocol layer (dedicated follow-up PR)

The sandbox runtime connectivity that #976 removed, built on sandboxd (KEP-539.2). sandboxd exposes a **hybrid API** over two ports, both reached by a port-forward to the sandbox pod:

- gRPC `:9090` — `ProcessService` (`Execute` unary, `Start` server-stream, `WriteStdin`, `SendSignal`, `ResizeTTY`; optional PTY)
- REST `:8080` — filesystem (`GET` / `HEAD` / `PUT` / `DELETE /v1/files/{path}`, raw `application/octet-stream`) plus `/v1/health` and `/v1/metadata`

Work items:

#1596 & ...

- [ ] Port-forward to the sandbox pod on both `:8080` and `:9090`
- [ ] gRPC client for `ProcessService`, from `packages/sandboxd/spec/process/v1/process.proto` — no TS codegen is wired up yet (`buf.gen.yaml` emits Go only, `buf.gen.python.yaml` Python); a TS `buf` template or hand-written stubs are needed
- [ ] REST client for the filesystem API, hand-written or generated against `packages/sandboxd/spec/filesystem/v1/filesystem.yaml` (OpenAPI 3.0.3; plain HTTP, no stubs required)
- [ ] Command execution: `Execute` at minimum; `Start` streaming, PTY, and `SendSignal` are new surface beyond the old `commands.run`
- [ ] File operations: `read` (GET), `write` (PUT, atomic, `mode`), `exists` (HEAD), `list` (GET on a directory → `DirectoryListing`), `delete` (DELETE, `recursive`)
- [ ] Optional grpc dependency gating, mirroring the Python SDK's `[grpc]` extra and `SandboxdPodTunnelConnectionConfig`
- [ ] Tracing spans over the runtime calls
- [ ] E2E: fill in the `describe.skip("... sandbox runtime operations (#977)")` placeholders in `test/e2e/clients/typescript/`
- [ ] Carry over the hardening from the original draft, adapted to this API:
  - client-side timeout / `AbortSignal` cancellation for both the gRPC calls (context deadline) and the REST calls (`fetch` abort) — note sandboxd defines no `X-Sandbox-Timeout` header (that was python-runtime-only)
  - response-size limits and bounded error-message previews on the REST reads (`GET /v1/files/{path}` streams raw bytes)
  - client-side path checks on the file operations — sandboxd already does symlink-aware sanitization and returns `403 PERMISSION_DENIED`, so this is defense-in-depth / better errors, not the security boundary
  - span-attribute sanitization for `Execute` / `Start` — record the binary name only, never the full command line (mirrors Python #895)
  - pod-IP selection from `status.podIPs`: prefer IPv4, normalize IPv4-mapped IPv6 (mirrors Python's `select_pod_ip`, #917)

The old HTTP `request()` layer, the Gateway/router connection mode, and the computer-use extension are not part of the sandboxd design and are out of scope here; each would need its own proposal. Endpoint discovery via `SANDBOXD_GRPC_ADDR` / `SANDBOXD_REST_ADDR` is for in-pod code and pairs with an in-cluster connection mode (already listed out of scope).

#### Review follow-ups from #976 (non-blocking)
#1535

- [ ] `src/sandbox-client.ts` — `getSandboxClaimWarmpoolName` returns `warmPoolRef.name as string`, which is `undefined` at runtime for a claim without a `warmPoolRef` while the signature promises `string`; type it `string | undefined` or throw `SandboxMetadataError` (real type-safety bug — do this first)
- [ ] `dev/tools/test-e2e` — `kubectl` calls use the ambient current-context while the Go/TS frameworks fall back to `bin/KUBECONFIG`, and one of them patches the controller Deployment. Pass `--kubeconfig` (`KUBECONFIG` env or `<repo>/bin/KUBECONFIG`)
- [ ] `test/e2e/clients/typescript/framework/context.ts` — pass `--kubeconfig` (`this.kubeconfigPath`) to the `kubectl` subprocess calls (here and the timeout diagnostic dumps) so they target the same cluster as `TestContext`
- [ ] `dev/tools/test-e2e` — drop the unused `shutil` and `time` imports
- [ ] `test/e2e/clients/typescript/package.json` — the `allowScripts` key has a 5-segment `../` path vs 4 in the dependency spec, and nothing consumes `allowScripts` (no lavamoat); fix the path or drop the block

#### Publishing

- [ ] **Decide the final npm package name and unblock publishing.** `package.json` sets `"name": "agentic-sandbox-client"` and `"private": true` (the `private` flag keeps a stray `npm publish` from claiming a non-final name). The Python SDK's directory (`agentic-sandbox-client`) diverges from its PyPI name (`k8s-agent-sandbox`); decide whether npm follows the same pattern or keeps `agentic-sandbox-client`, then drop `private: true` and wire up the release pipeline.

#### API parity with the Python SDK (resource layer)

- [ ] `shutdownAfterSeconds` support — a client-side convenience that sets `spec.lifecycle.shutdownTime` to `now + N` (the API field is an absolute `date-time`, not a relative TTL); no equivalent to Python's `create_sandbox(..., shutdown_after_seconds=...)` #1605 
- [ ] `podLabels` / `podAnnotations` support (`spec.additionalPodMetadata`; Python added this in #979) — stamped onto the running Pod, distinct from claim-level `labels`
- [ ] `volumeClaimTemplates` support (`spec.volumeClaimTemplates`; Python added this in #961) — custom PVC requests merged with the SandboxTemplate's own
- [ ] `listAllSandboxes` label-selector support #1606 
- [ ] `Sandbox.status()` — Ready / NotReady / NotFound introspection
- [ ] `getSandbox` re-attach: shorter resolve timeout instead of waiting the full Ready timeout, and an option to skip waiting for Ready (Python does resolve + existence check only)
- [ ] Throw `SandboxError` (not plain `Error`) consistently — `validateLabels`, the empty-warmpool-name check, and other validation paths still throw `Error`, breaking `err instanceof SandboxError` handling
- [ ] Public `getPodIp()` (uncached, per-call — matches Python), if a pod-IP accessor is still wanted at the resource layer

#### Deferred (needs maintainer / issue agreement before starting)

- [ ] Whether `enableAutoCleanup()` should default to on, mirroring Python's `AsyncSandboxClient` flipping `cleanup` to `True` in #1035 — registering process signal handlers by default has side effects; this is a design decision, not a parity fix

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

Make `spec.replicas` optional in `SandboxWarmPool` with a default of `1`. The CRD schema now defaults `replicas` to `1` when omitted, matching how Kubernetes native workloads (Deployment, StatefulSet) handle this field. Explicitly setting `replicas: 0` remains valid and creates an empty pool.

Previously the field was required, which caused friction for users who:

- Use HPA or KEDA to manage replica counts via the `/scale` subresource and don't want to specify a static `replicas` value in their manifest
- Use GitOps tools like Argo CD where omitting replica counts from the declared baseline prevents the syncer from fighting the autoscaler
- Hit admission failures when submitting manifests without `replicas`

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:

Fixes #738

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR refactors `SandboxTemplateSpec` to embed `SandboxSpec` as the single source of truth, aligning its design with how `Deployment.spec.template` embeds a `PodTemplate`. 
Previously, `SandboxTemplateSpec` wrapped a bare `PodTemplate` directly. This meant any non-pod fields added to `SandboxSpec` had to be manually duplicated into the template and claim specs, and mapped manually in the controllers. This limitation also left useful fields like `lifecycle` and `operatingMode` completely unreachable from templates.
**Key Changes:**
- Replaces `podTemplate`, `volumeClaimTemplates`, and `service` in `SandboxTemplateSpec` with a unified, embedded `sandboxSpec` (`sandboxv1beta1.SandboxSpec`).
- Updates `SandboxClaimSpec` to support per-claim overrides for `service` and `volumeClaimTemplates` (applied at cold-start).
- Updates the warmpool and claim controllers to deep-copy the embedded spec and only overlay the specific controller-managed fields (identity labels, secure defaults, etc.). New `SandboxSpec` fields will now flow through automatically.
- Migrates all examples, templates, documentation, and e2e tests to the new `spec.sandboxSpec` structure.
- Includes the latest regenerated CRDs (`k8s/crds`, `helm/crds`) and API docs (`docs/api.md`).

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

  Implements tasks **# 4 (Bootstrap & Storage Migration Script)** and **# 5 (Automated Helm Hook Integration)** of #959, combined into a single PR per @janetkuo's suggestion that we ship one script driven by two Helm hook Jobs (rather than
  separate bootstrap and rewrite scripts).

  - **One script** at `helm/files/migrate.sh` with two phases (`--phase=bootstrap`, `--phase=migrate`), both idempotent and re-runnable.
  - **Wrapper** at `dev/tools/migrate.sh` so operators can invoke the same script manually outside of `helm upgrade`.
  - **Two Helm hook Jobs**:
    - `agent-sandbox-migration-bootstrap` (`pre-upgrade`) — scans v1alpha1 `SandboxClaim`s and, for each unique `(namespace, template)` pair referenced by a cold-start claim, creates a `shadow-pool-<template>` `SandboxWarmPool` (replicas=0)
  in that claim's namespace. Matches the naming convention used by the conversion webhook in #966 (`extensions/api/v1alpha1/sandboxclaim_conversion.go`). Warm-started claims (where `status.sandboxStatus.name` differs from the claim name) are
  skipped — the webhook derives their pool from the bound `Sandbox`, no shadow needed. Claims that reference a specific pool that doesn't exist are surfaced in a final `OPERATOR ACTION REQUIRED` summary.
    - `agent-sandbox-migration-rewrite` (`post-upgrade`) — patches every existing `Sandbox` / `SandboxClaim` / `SandboxTemplate` / `SandboxWarmPool` with a `agents.x-k8s.io/storage-migrated-at` annotation, forcing the API server to rewrite
  each record in v1beta1 storage format.
  - **Shared infra** (`agent-sandbox-migration` ServiceAccount, 2 ClusterRoles, 2 ClusterRoleBindings, ConfigMap embedding the script) annotated `pre-upgrade,post-upgrade` with weight `-10` and `before-hook-creation` delete policy so they
  persist across both phases of the upgrade.
  - The post-upgrade Job has a `wait-for-webhook` initContainer that polls the conversion webhook Service's endpoints for up to 120s (24 × 5s), accepts IPv4/IPv6/dual-stack, surfaces RBAC/API errors in the Job log, and fails fast with a
  clear error if the webhook never becomes Ready. The rewrite Job pod is also hardened to be admitted under restricted Pod Security Admission (pod-level `runAsNonRoot` + `RuntimeDefault` seccomp; container-level drop-ALL caps +
  `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`).
  - The webhook Service name is configurable via `migration.webhookServiceName` (defaults to `agent-sandbox-webhook-service`, matching the Service added in #966).
  - Opt-out via `--set migration.enabled=false` for operators who want to run `dev/tools/migrate.sh` manually (e.g. phased rollout, custom resource limits, large clusters, or a non-Helm install path).
  - `docs/api-migration-guide.md` documents three explicit operator flows (Helm-automatic, manual kubectl, Helm-with-hooks-disabled), shadow-pool lifecycle, re-pointing warm-started claims post-migration, verification commands, and
  troubleshooting.

…ndboxes

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
  Adds KEP-968: Auto Suspend/Resume Lifecycle for Claw-like Sandboxes (docs/keps/968-openclaw-sandbox-lifecycle/). Documentation only — no code or API changes.

  A Claw-like agent gateway (OpenClaw is the reference) running in a Sandbox has no client babysitting it: left idle it keeps burning resources, and once suspended nothing brings it back for traffic or for its own scheduled work. This KEP proposes server-side lifecycle management
  that automatically suspends inactive sandboxes and resumes them on traffic, API invocation, or just before a scheduled cron — without modifying the agent.

  Design highlights:
  - Treats the agent as a black box. No new endpoints, config changes, or forks. Idle is inferred externally from Wakeup Proxy activity + a pod CPU floor; the next cron time is read from the agent's persisted schedule on the PVC via a small read-only schedule-reader sidecar.
  - No new controller. Lifecycle lives in two independently deployable components from the existing architecture — an always-on Wakeup Proxy and an informer-backed Sandbox Lifecycle Daemon (SharedInformer + delaying workqueue, not a controller-manager reconciler and not periodic
  List(all)).
  - State-preserving resume. Resume only patches the existing suspended Sandbox operatingMode: Running so the same PVC remounts. It explicitly never leases from a SandboxWarmPool (pools yield fresh instances, not a restored gateway).
  - Builds on [KEP-119] (Suspended condition) and [KEP-694] (suspend/resume for beta); includes a phased PR breakdown (1–6) and a Future Work section researching an opt-in, higher-fidelity idle signal via the agent's own hook system.

  Out of scope: CRIU/memory checkpointing, warm-pool fast provisioning, a JS/TS SDK, and large-fleet (100k) optimization.

title: SandboxTemplateSpec wraps PodTemplate instead of SandboxSpec, forcing field duplication

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: kind/api-change
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to adding, removing, or otherwise changing an API

labels.name: kind/cleanup
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to cleaning up code, process, or technical debt.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

When the WarmPool flow was changed from creating a **Pod** directly to creating a **Sandbox** (the WarmPool controller now stamps out `Sandbox` objects — see [`extensions/controllers/sandboxwarmpool_controller.go#L382-L407`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/extensions/controllers/sandboxwarmpool_controller.go#L382)), `SandboxTemplateSpec` was **not** updated to follow. It still embeds a bare `PodTemplate`:

```go
// extensions/api/v1beta1/sandboxtemplate_types.go
type SandboxTemplateSpec struct {
    PodTemplate          sandboxv1beta1.PodTemplate                       `json:"podTemplate"`          // <- references a Pod, not a Sandbox
    VolumeClaimTemplates []sandboxv1beta1.PersistentVolumeClaimTemplate   `json:"volumeClaimTemplates,omitempty"`  // duplicated from SandboxSpec
    NetworkPolicy        *NetworkPolicySpec                               `json:"networkPolicy,omitempty"`
    NetworkPolicyManagement NetworkPolicyManagement                       `json:"networkPolicyManagement,omitempty"`
    EnvVarsInjectionPolicy  EnvVarsInjectionPolicy                        `json:"envVarsInjectionPolicy,omitempty"`
    Service              *bool                                            `json:"service,omitempty"`    // duplicated from SandboxSpec
}
```

Because the template describes a *Pod* rather than a *Sandbox*, every non-PodTemplate field added to `SandboxSpec` has to be **manually duplicated** into `SandboxTemplateSpec` (and/or `SandboxClaimSpec`) **and** hand-mapped in the WarmPool controller. This has already happened for `volumeClaimTemplates` and `service`, and it means several `SandboxSpec` fields are simply **not reachable** through a template/claim today.

#### Field drift between `SandboxSpec` and `SandboxTemplateSpec`/`SandboxClaimSpec`

`SandboxSpec` ([`api/v1beta1/sandbox_types.go`](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/api/v1beta1/sandbox_types.go)) currently has:

| `SandboxSpec` field | In `SandboxTemplateSpec`? | In `SandboxClaimSpec`? |
|---|---|---|
| `podTemplate` | ✅ (as `podTemplate`) | partial (via `additionalPodMetadata` / `env`) |
| `volumeClaimTemplates` | ✅ (manually duplicated) | ❌ |
| `service` | ✅ (manually duplicated) | ❌ |
| `lifecycle` (`shutdownTime`, `shutdownPolicy`) | ❌ | ✅ (`lifecycle`) but **not** on the template |
| `operatingMode` | ❌ | ❌ |

The hand-mapping in the controller makes the coupling explicit (each field must be copied one-by-one):

```go
// sandboxwarmpool_controller.go
sandbox := &sandboxv1beta1.Sandbox{
    ...
    Spec: sandboxv1beta1.SandboxSpec{
        Service:     template.Spec.Service,                 // manual
        PodTemplate: sandboxv1beta1.PodTemplate{ ... },     // manual
    },
}
if len(template.Spec.VolumeClaimTemplates) > 0 {            // manual
    ...
}
```

### Why is this needed?

This is API-design debt that will keep getting worse:

- **Every new `SandboxSpec` field needs N copies.** Adding a field to `Sandbox` requires also adding it to `SandboxTemplateSpec`, possibly `SandboxClaimSpec`, regenerating CRDs, and wiring the copy in the WarmPool (and claim) controller. Easy to forget, and the three specs silently drift.
- **Feature gaps today.** Fields that exist on `Sandbox` cannot be configured via a template/claim — e.g. `lifecycle` (`shutdownTime`/`shutdownPolicy`) and `operatingMode` are absent from `SandboxTemplateSpec`, so WarmPool-provisioned sandboxes can't set them.
- **Inconsistency surface.** `lifecycle` lives on `SandboxClaimSpec` but not `SandboxTemplateSpec`; `service`/`volumeClaimTemplates` live on the template but not the claim. There's no single source of truth for "what a Sandbox looks like."

### Proposal / options to discuss

The core idea: have the template describe a **Sandbox** rather than a **Pod**, so `SandboxSpec` is the single source of truth and template/claim inherit fields automatically.

1. **Embed a `SandboxSpec` (or `SandboxTemplate`-of-Sandbox) in `SandboxTemplateSpec`** instead of a `PodTemplate`, analogous to how `Deployment.spec.template` embeds a Pod template. The controller then deep-copies the embedded `SandboxSpec` and overlays only the controller-managed bits, so new `SandboxSpec` fields flow through for free.
2. If a full embed is too broad, at minimum **define the template/claim ↔ sandbox field set deliberately** (which fields are template-level vs claim-level vs controller-owned) and close the current gaps (`lifecycle`, `operatingMode`).

Either way we should decide the intended layering before adding more fields, since this is still `v1beta1` and changing the template shape later is a breaking change.

### Additional context

- `SandboxTemplateSpec`: `extensions/api/v1beta1/sandboxtemplate_types.go`
- `SandboxSpec` / `Lifecycle`: `api/v1beta1/sandbox_types.go`
- `SandboxClaimSpec`: `extensions/api/v1beta1/sandboxclaim_types.go`
- WarmPool → Sandbox construction: `extensions/controllers/sandboxwarmpool_controller.go` (~L382–L407)

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
<!-- Provide a clear and concise description of the changes in this PR. -->

Adds a new example under `examples/policy/cilium/` demonstrating how to provide managed outbound internet access for Agent Sandboxes on GKE Dataplane v2.

Combines:
  - Standard `NetworkPolicy` for L3/L4 default-deny floor (with an optional`CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` variant for cluster-wide enforcement)
  - GKE `FQDNNetworkPolicy` for external hostname allowlists
  - A custom Squid forward proxy (built from a small `Dockerfile` shipped under `gateway/`) for HTTPS interception (`ssl_bump`), URL/path filtering, and per-request credential injection
  - A companion `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy` added to `examples/policy/vap/` that rejects `SandboxTemplate`s with overly broad egress

Validated end-to-end on both GKE Standard and GKE Autopilot.
  
The existing `examples/policy/network-policy-management/` documents the shared NetworkPolicy model but doesn't cover the patterns sandboxes need for safe outbound internet egress to model APIs, package registries, and internal services. This example fills that gap with a runnable demo, and also documents the practical gaps GKE's managed Cilium has compared to upstream Cilium (no L7 HTTP rules on CNP, no `CiliumEgressGatewayPolicy`, FQDN handling differs) so future readers don't repeat the discovery effort.

body:
Working on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/959

# PR Description: Implement Two-Way CRD Conversion Webhook Logic 

## Summary

This PR implements **Step 3: Implement Conversion Webhook Logic** of the *Agent Sandbox OSS API Versioning & Migration Initiative*. It establishes the core Hub-and-Spoke conversion logic to seamlessly translate between `v1alpha1` and `v1beta1` versions of the `Sandbox`, `SandboxClaim`, `SandboxTemplate`, and `SandboxWarmPool` APIs. 

This enables older `v1alpha1` clients and controllers to interact seamlessly with a cluster that stores resources under the new `v1beta1` storage version, guaranteeing complete backward compatibility and facilitating a zero-downtime migration.

## Detailed Changes

### 1. Hub and Spoke Interface Registrations
* **Hub (`v1beta1`):** Marked `v1beta1.Sandbox`, `v1beta1.SandboxClaim`, `v1beta1.SandboxTemplate`, and `v1beta1.SandboxWarmPool` as the **Hub** versions by implementing the `sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/conversion.Hub` interface (adding the marker `Hub()` method).
* **Spoke (`v1alpha1`):** Made `v1alpha1.Sandbox`, `v1alpha1.SandboxClaim`, `v1alpha1.SandboxTemplate`, and `v1alpha1.SandboxWarmPool` implement the `sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/conversion.Spoke` interface by writing `ConvertTo(Hub)` and `ConvertFrom(Hub)` methods.

### 2. Lossless State Restoration Pattern

* When converting `v1alpha1 -> v1beta1`, the original `v1alpha1` resource is serialized to JSON and stored in a special transient annotation (e.g., `api.agents.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1-sandbox-state`).
* When converting `v1beta1 -> v1alpha1`, if the state annotation is present, it is deserialized and used to restore any version-specific fields (like `Replicas` or `Status.Replicas`), while still overlaying any modifications made by the `v1beta1` client.

### 3. Structural API Translations
* **`Sandbox` Spec Conversion:**
  * Maps `v1alpha1.Spec.Replicas` (`*int32`) to `v1beta1.Spec.OperatingMode` (`Running`/`Suspended`), and vice versa.
  * Translates package-specific sub-structures (`PodTemplate`, `PersistentVolumeClaimTemplate`, `Lifecycle`) field-by-field.
* **`SandboxClaim` Spec Conversion:**
  * Elegantly maps `v1alpha1`'s combination of `TemplateRef` and `WarmPool` policy to `v1beta1`'s required `WarmPoolRef`.
  * Implements smart resolution:
    * If `WarmPool` is a specific pool name, it uses it.
    * If `WarmPool` is `"none"` or `"default"`, it resolves a cold-start to a shadow pool name (`shadow-pool-<template-name>`) and a warm-start by parsing the adopted sandbox name from `Status.SandboxStatus.Name`.
* **`SandboxTemplate` & `SandboxWarmPool` Conversion:**
  * Translates all spec and status fields 1:1 using package-specific conversion helpers.

---

## Verification & Testing
 * Comprehensive unit-test
 * Manual round trip test via `EXTENSIONS=true CONTROLLER_ONLY=true make deploy-kind`.

title: Enhance SandboxStatus for better observability

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add printer columns to `kubectl get sandbox` output similar to how `kubectl get po` output is. 

### Why is this needed?

Currently, the `Sandbox` resource provides very limited information in its status. When you run `kubectl get sandbox`, you only see the age of the resource:

```
  $ kubectl get sandbox my-sandbox
  NAME          AGE
  my-sandbox      45s
```
This makes it difficult to monitor health, quickly check stuck sandboxes without inspecting the  resource `describe`.

### Proposed Solution

Add printer columns to `kubectl get sandbox` output similar to how `kubectl get po` output is. 

The `SandboxStatus` already tracks enough information to surface useful columns. The output should look like:
```
 $ kubectl get sandbox
  NAME         READY   PHASE       AGE
  my-sandbox-1   True    Running     5m
  my-sandbox-2   False   Pending     10s
  my-sandbox-3   False   Suspended   2m
  my-sandbox-4   False   Succeeded   30m
```

Proposed Columns:
| Field | Source | Description |
|--------|--------|--------|
| READY |  `status.conditions[type=Ready].status` | True or False |
| PHASE |  `status.phase`  - New Field  |  Description below    |
| AGE | Standard | - |

Here, since the column `PHASE` is quite descriptive, there is no necessity for a `REASON` field. 

The controller needs to compute and set a phase field in `SandboxStatus`, exactly like `Pod.status.phase`:
 ```
type SandboxPhase string

  const (
      SandboxPhasePending   SandboxPhase = "Pending"
      SandboxPhaseRunning   SandboxPhase = "Running"
      SandboxPhaseSuspending SandboxPhase = "Suspending"  // pod not yet terminated
      SandboxPhaseSuspended SandboxPhase = "Suspended"    // pod terminated
      SandboxPhaseExpired   SandboxPhase = "Expired"
      SandboxPhaseSucceeded SandboxPhase = "Succeeded"
      SandboxPhaseFailed    SandboxPhase = "Failed"
  )
```
The phase can be computed as follows:
| Case | Phase |
|--------|--------|
| Finished condition exists AND True, reason=PodSucceeded| Succeeded |
| Finished condition exists AND True, reason=PodFailed  | Failed |
| Ready reason=SandboxExpired  | Expired |
| Suspended condition EXISTS AND True | Suspended |
| Suspended condition EXISTS AND False | Suspending | 
| Ready=True | Running | 
| Otherwise | Pending | 

 All the condition data to derive this already exists - https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/api/v1beta1/sandbox_types.go#L29-L54

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Add printer columns to `kubectl get sandboxclaim` output.

### Why is this needed?

Currently, the `SandboxClaim` resource provides very limited information in its status. When you run `kubectl get sandboxclaim`, you only see the age of the resource:

```
  $ kubectl get sandboxclaim my-claim
  NAME          AGE
  my-claim      45s
```
This makes it difficult to monitor claim health, quickly check stuck claims without inspecting the  resource `describe`.

### Proposed Solution

Add printer columns to `kubectl get sandboxclaim` output.

The `SandboxClaimStatus` already tracks enough information to surface useful columns. The output should look like:

```
 $ kubectl get sandboxclaim 
 NAME        READY   SANDBOX         REASON                                     AGE
 my-claim-1    False    my-claim-xk9z        WarmpoolNotFound              3s
 my-claim-2    True    my-claim-xk9y                                      3s
```

Proposed Columns:
| Field | Source | Description |
|--------|--------|--------|
| READY |  `status.conditions[type=Ready].status` | True or False |
| SANDBOX | `status.sandbox.name`   |  Name of the underlying `Sandbox` resource     |
| REASON | `status.conditions[type=Ready].reason`  | Reason for current ready state |
| AGE | Standard | - |

The `REASON` column is a valuable addition — it surfaces the condition reason directly in the list view, eliminating the need to run `kubectl describe` to diagnose a stuck or failed claim.

Working on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/959

# PR: Implement Webhook Bootstrap, In-Memory Self-Signed TLS (with Multi-Replica Safety), and CRD Patcher

## Summary

This PR introduces a **lightweight, in-controller TLS bootstrap and CRD patching mechanism** to support webhook-based resource conversion between `v1alpha1` and `v1beta1` for `Sandbox` and extensions CRDs. 

To ensure **multi-replica safety (scaled Deployment support)**, the controller manager implements a shared Kubernetes Secret mechanism. The first starting replica (or the leader) automatically generates a self-signed CA and server certificate, stores them in a shared Kubernetes Secret (`agent-sandbox-webhook-certs`), and patches the CRDs' `caBundle` in-cluster. All other starting replicas dynamically load the exact same certificates from this Secret, preventing TLS breakages and mismatch issues across load-balanced pods.

---

## Key Changes

### 1. In-Memory TLS, Shared Secret & Patcher 
* **`generateWebhookCerts`**: Implements the dual-mode TLS bootstrap:
  * Attempts to get the existing `agent-sandbox-webhook-certs` Secret in the namespace. If found, it loads the certificates directly from the Secret (handling scale-up and restart scenarios).
  * If not found, it generates a new self-signed CA and server certificate (ECDSA P-256) with correct DNS SANs, writes them locally, and creates the shared Secret.
  * Gracefully handles concurrent creation race conditions (split-brain) by falling back to reading the Secret if another replica created it first.
* **`patchCRDs`**: Runs synchronously at startup before the manager begins. It fetches the four CRDs (`sandboxes`, `sandboxclaims`, `sandboxtemplates`, `sandboxwarmpools`), filters for those using the `Webhook` conversion strategy, and dynamically patches their `caBundle` and service endpoints in-cluster.

### 2. Controller Manager Integration 
* Added command-line flags for webhook customization: `--webhook-port`, `--webhook-cert-dir`, `--webhook-service-name`, and `--webhook-namespace`.
* Registered the `apiextensions.k8s.io/v1` API group to the manager's scheme.
* Reordered the startup sequence to initialize the temporary client first, enabling the TLS generator to communicate with the Kubernetes API to check/create the shared Secret before launching the manager's `WebhookServer` (`ClientAuth = tls.NoClientCert`).

### 3. Automated CRD Post-Processing 
* Enhanced the post-processing script to automatically inject the complete `spec.conversion` webhook configuration block (pointing to the controller's service on `/convert` and setting `conversionReviewVersions: ["v1", "v1beta1"]` and a dummy `caBundle`) for all CustomResourceDefinitions with multiple versions.

### 4. RBAC Permissions 
* Added kubebuilder RBAC markers to grant the controller manager ServiceAccount the necessary cluster-scoped permissions (`get`, `update`, `patch`) on `customresourcedefinitions`, as well as namespace-scoped permissions (`get`, `list`, `watch`, `create`, `update`, `patch`) on `secrets`.

### 5. Build & Test Suite 
* Updated the `Makefile` to build the entire `./cmd/agent-sandbox-controller` package.
* Added comprehensive unit test coverage in `tls_test.go`:
  * `successfully_generates_new_certs_when_Secret_does_not_exist`: Verifies key generation, SAN DNS name configurations, and Secret creation in the cluster.
  * `successfully_loads_existing_certs_from_Secret_when_it_exists`: Verifies that certificates are correctly loaded and written to disk from pre-existing Secrets (preventing mismatch on scale).
  * `successfully_patches_CRDs_with_Webhook_strategy`: Verifies that CRDs are correctly fetched and patched.

## Testing

* Manual Testing via `deploy-kind` and verified that the CRD now have the CA bundle.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
<!-- Provide a clear and concise description of the changes in this PR. -->

This PR introduces support for volume claim templates within Sandbox Claims, allowing users to customize persistent volumes for their sandboxes. To maintain control over these specifications, we have implemented a Volume Claim Templates Policy on the Sandbox Template, which supports three distinct modes:
- **Disallowed (Default)**: Rejects any volume claim templates (VCTs) provided by the claim.
- **Allowed**: Appends claim-provided VCTs to those in the template, provided there are no name collisions.
- **Overrides**: Replaces template VCTs with claim VCTs by name and appends any new ones.

Additionally, to ensure proper volume provisioning, sandboxes that specify volume claim templates will now bypass warm-pool reuse and start fresh.

Note: `VolumeClaimTemplates` in a `SandboxClaim` is strictly a **cold-start feature,** allowing users to parameterize storage (e.g., custom workspace sizes) at runtime.

**Test Cases:**
- VCTPolicy=`Disallowed` and claim has specified the volume claim templates =>Error 
- VCTPolicy=`Allowed` and claim has specified volume claim template with matching names =>Error 
- VCTPolicy=`Allowed` and claim has additional volume claim template => Success
- VCTPolicy=`Override` and claim has volume claim template => Success (with claim VCT specifications)

title: Alpha (`v1alpha1`) to Beta (`v1beta1`) Versioning & Storage migration

labels.name: kind/feature

body:
## Summary / Goal


The **Agent Sandbox OSS API Versioning & Migration Initiative** is a core stability and reliability effort focused on transitioning the project's APIs (`Sandbox`, `SandboxClaim`, `SandboxTemplate`, `SandboxWarmPool`) from `v1alpha1` (experimental/alpha) to `v1beta1` (production/beta). 
As the project matures and sees broader adoption, we must guarantee API stability, backward compatibility, and a safe upgrade path. This initiative will deliver the necessary Kubernetes conversion webhook infrastructure, update CRD storage schemas, establish automated and manual database (etcd) migration utilities, and build a robust upgrade-testing harness. By establishing this foundation, we ensure that future upgrades are entirely non-disruptive, protecting running user workloads and preventing data loss.

## Target Milestone / Release

v0.5.0

## Motivation

### 1. API Maturity and Stability Guarantees
Transitioning our APIs (`Sandbox`, `SandboxClaim`, `SandboxTemplate`, `SandboxWarmPool`) from `v1alpha1` to `v1beta1` is a major milestone signifying that the project is maturing beyond experimental phases. Under Kubernetes API conventions:
* **`v1alpha1` (Alpha)**: APIs are subject to change at any time without notice. Schema layouts can be modified, fields removed, and backward compatibility is not guaranteed.
* **`v1beta1` (Beta)**: The schema is stable, well-tested, and ready for production use. Crucially, it guarantees that no breaking schema changes will be made without a clear deprecation cycle. This provides enterprise adopters and cloud operators with the confidence needed to run `agent-sandbox` in mission-critical environments.
### 2. Ensuring Zero-Downtime Upgrades for Existing Users
We already have active users running workloads using the `v1alpha1` API schema. When they upgrade to the new version of the controller:
* We cannot simply drop support for `v1alpha1` as it would immediately break all running sandboxes, claims, and automation pipelines.
* A **Conversion Webhook** is required to act as an on-the-fly translator. It allows older clients/controllers to continue requesting and writing `v1alpha1` resources, while the Kubernetes API server seamlessly converts and stores them under the new `v1beta1` schema (and vice-versa).
### 3. Preventing Data Loss and "Stale" etcd Records
In Kubernetes, CRD objects are stored in `etcd` in a single designated "storage version." 
* When we declare `v1beta1` as the new storage version, any new or updated resources will be written to `etcd` as `v1beta1`.
* However, existing resources created before the upgrade will **remain stored as `v1alpha1`** in `etcd` until they are explicitly modified or rewritten.
* If we eventually deprecate and completely remove the `v1alpha1` version in a future release (e.g., when moving to `v1`), **any remaining `v1alpha1` records in etcd will become completely unreadable**, leading to permanent resource corruption and data loss.
* Therefore, providing **Storage Migration Tools (both manual and automated)** is a critical operational requirement to safely rewrite all existing records in `etcd` to the `v1beta1` storage format immediately post-upgrade.
### 4. Operational Excellence and Automation
Manually migrating Kubernetes resources is error-prone, labor-intensive, and poses a risk to cluster stability. By implementing:
1. An automated **Migration Job** (packaged as a post-upgrade hook).
2. A comprehensive **E2E Upgrade Test Suite** that simulates real-world upgrade paths.
We guarantee a reliable, automated, and fully-validated upgrade path for all cluster administrators, removing the burden of manual database manipulation.

## Work Breakdown / Tasks

### 1. Resurrect & Stabilize `v1alpha1` (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/955)
Owner: @SHRUTI6991 
- [x] **Define and Register v1alpha1 APIs**: Ensure both core and extension `v1alpha1` APIs are fully registered and active alongside `v1beta1`.
  - Core API: `api/v1alpha1/`
  - Extensions API: `extensions/api/v1alpha1/`
- [x] **Kubebuilder Markers**:
  - Update `+kubebuilder:storageversion` markers. The marker must be moved from `v1alpha1` to `v1beta1` types.
  - Verify that `v1alpha1` is marked as `served: true` but `storage: false`.
  - Verify that `v1beta1` is marked as `served: true` and `storage: true`.
- [x] **Code Generation**:
  - Run `make all` to regenerate CRDs, deepcopy helpers, and typed clients.
  - Ensure `k8s/crds/` are updated correctly.
---
### 2. Create Infrastructure for Conversion Webhook (Simplified TLS) https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/962
Owner: @SHRUTI6991 
- [x] **Bootstrap Webhook Server**:
  - Configure the controller manager in `cmd/agent-sandbox-controller/` to start the webhook server.
  - Add flags for webhook port, cert directory, and service names.
- [x] **Lightweight Self-Signed TLS (In-Controller)**:
  - Implement an in-memory/runtime self-signed certificate generation routine in Go at controller startup.
  - Configure the webhook server's `tls.Config` with `ClientAuth: tls.NoClientCert` (as it is a throwaway migration controller).
  - Implement a simple startup patcher that dynamically writes the generated CA certificate (`caBundle`) into the CRDs' `spec.conversion.webhook.clientConfig.caBundle`.
- [x] **CRD Manifest Updates**:
  - Update CRD definitions to configure `spec.conversion.strategy: Webhook`.
  - Define the `conversionReviewVersions: ["v1", "v1beta1"]` and point the webhook client config to the controller's webhook service.
---
### 3. Implement Conversion Webhook Logic (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/966)
ref https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/extend-kubernetes/custom-resources/custom-resource-definition-versioning/#write-a-conversion-webhook-server
Owner: @SHRUTI6991 
- [x] **Implement `Hub` and `Spoke` Interfaces**:
  - Implement `pkg/apis/conversion` or inline conversion methods.
  - Make `v1beta1` types implement `sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/conversion.Hub`.
  - Make `v1alpha1` types implement `sigs.k8s.io/controller-runtime/pkg/conversion.Spoke`.
- [x] **Write Conversion Logic**:
  - **Core**: Convert `Sandbox` (`api/v1alpha1/sandbox_types.go` <-> `api/v1beta1/sandbox_types.go`).
  - **Extensions**: Convert `SandboxClaim`, `SandboxTemplate`, and `SandboxWarmPool` between `v1alpha1` and `v1beta1` in `extensions/api/`.
- [x] **Unit Tests**:
  - Write comprehensive unit tests using fuzzing/round-trip validation (e.g., `v1alpha1 -> v1beta1 -> v1alpha1`) to ensure zero data loss or corruption during conversion.
---
### 4. Develop Bootstrap & Storage Migration Script (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/971)
Owner: @vicentefb 
- [x] **Create Migration Script**:
  - Write a robust, parameter-driven bash script (e.g., `dev/tools/migrate.sh`) that supports two execution phases: `--phase=bootstrap` and `--phase=migrate`.
  - **Bootstrap Phase (`--phase=bootstrap`)**: Scans all `SandboxClaim` resources, identifies cold-started claims (`claim name != sandbox name`), and creates a shadow `SandboxWarmPool` with size `0`.
  - **Migrate Phase (`--phase=migrate`)**: Patches all existing resources (touching a migration annotation) to force the API server to rewrite them to `etcd` as `v1beta1`.
- [x] **Documentation**: Document how operators can run this script manually if needed.
---
### 5. Automated Helm Hook Integration (ConfigMap Mounted) https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/971
Owner: @vicentefb 
- [x] **Define ConfigMap**: Wrap the `migrate.sh` script inside a Kubernetes `ConfigMap` manifest.
- [x] **Define Pre-Upgrade Job (`helm.sh/hook: pre-upgrade`)**:
  - Write a `Job` manifest configured as a Helm pre-upgrade hook.
  - Mount the `ConfigMap` and run the script with `--phase=bootstrap`.
  - Configure RBAC: Create a `ServiceAccount` and `ClusterRole` with `create` access for `SandboxWarmPool` resources.
- [x] **Define Post-Upgrade Job (`helm.sh/hook: post-upgrade`)**:
  - Write a second `Job` manifest configured as a Helm post-upgrade hook.
  - Mount the `ConfigMap` and run the script with `--phase=migrate`.
  - Configure RBAC: Create a `ServiceAccount` and `ClusterRole` with `get`, `list`, and `patch` access for `Sandbox`, `SandboxClaim`, `SandboxTemplate`, and `SandboxWarmPool` resources.
---
### 6. Implement Upgrade & Compatibility Tests (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/986)

Owner: @SHRUTI6991 
- [x] **Design E2E Upgrade Test Suite**:
  - Create a new E2E test scenario.
- [x] **Execution Flow**:
  1. **Phase 1 (Old State)**: Install the previous version of `agent-sandbox` (using `v1alpha1` as the storage version). Create several `v1alpha1` resources.
  2. **Phase 2**: Trigger the automated bootstrap job. 
  3. **Phase 3 (Upgrade)**: Apply the new CRDs and deploy the new controller manager (with the conversion webhook active).
  4. **Phase 4 (Migration)**: Trigger the automated migration job.
  5. **Phase 5 (Validation)**:     - Verify that the old resources can still be fetched successfully (validating the conversion webhook).
     - Verify that the resources in `etcd` are now stored as `v1beta1`.
     - Create new `v1beta1` resources and verify they coexist seamlessly.

### 7. Publish Migration Guide (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/848 +  https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/971)
- [x] **Publish Guide**:
- Provide steps for the user to run scripts and upgrade controller + CRD.
- [x] **Update `site/`**
- Add banner at the top about the APi migration with the doc link and make changes in site documentation to reflect `v1beta1`.
---

## What Success Looks Like (Definition of Done)
We will consider this initiative successful when the following outcomes are achieved:
### 1. Seamless Backward Compatibility
* Existing workloads and pipelines using the `v1alpha1` API schema continue to function perfectly without modification or errors.
* The Kubernetes API server can serve both `v1alpha1` and `v1beta1` clients concurrently, executing transparent, lossless, two-way conversions via our webhook.
### 2. Zero-Disruption Controller Upgrades
* Bumping the controller manager version on a running cluster does not cause any disruption to active Sandboxes or client claims.
* The state of the system remains consistent and stable throughout the upgrade window.
### 3. Clean and Complete Storage Migration

* 100% of existing `v1alpha1` serialized records stored in `etcd` are successfully rewritten to the `v1beta1` storage format.
* No stale or unconvertible `v1alpha1` resources remain in `etcd`, completely eliminating the risk of data loss when `v1alpha1` is eventually deprecated and removed from the codebase.

### 5. Automated CI/CD Regression Protection
* A robust, repeatable upgrade test suite is integrated into our continuous integration (CI) pipeline. 
* Any changes to the API schemas or conversion logic are automatically validated against the upgrade path, preventing future regressions.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR refactors the automated release notes generation script (`dev/tools/generate-release-notes`) to support production-ready markdown formatting, dedicated pre-release warnings, proactive breaking change scanning, robust installation block inclusion, and strict PR number traceability guardrails.

Specifically, this PR introduces the following enhancements:
1. **Robust Pre-Release Handling:** Uses regex (`^v?\d+\.\d+\.\d+(?:\.)?rc\d+$`) to identify release candidates (`rc`) with optional leading `v` or dot, and dynamically injects a `### ⚠️ Pre-Release Notice` section with GitHub alert syntax (`> [!WARNING]`). Uses an HTML comment placeholder (`<!-- Insert specific testing guidance... -->`) in the prompt example to prevent visible placeholder leakage in rendered markdown.
2. **Proactive Breaking Change Scanning:** Updates prompt instructions to actively scan commit messages and PR descriptions for unlabelled breaking changes, API upgrades, or modified defaults as a resilient fallback when PR authors omit the `release-note-action-required` label.
3. **Correct Installation Placement & Fallback:** Passes the `installation_notes` block directly into the Gemini prompt to guarantee it is rendered cleanly between `Key Highlights` and `Contributors`. Enhances the script's post-generation fallback check using regex (`not re.search(r"^#+\s+Installation", gemini_notes, re.MULTILINE | re.IGNORECASE)`) to prevent duplicate sections regardless of emitted markdown heading levels.
4. **Removed New Contributors Section:** Eliminates `get_new_authors()` and all New Contributor prompt instructions/examples entirely, as GitHub automatically appends a verified `## New Contributors` block to published releases.
5. **Code Clarity & Self-Documenting Names:** Renames the core generation function from `generate_highlights()` to `generate_release_notes()` to accurately reflect that the entire markdown document is generated by Gemini.

```release-note
NONE
```

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
Explicitly close the client-side connector during the sandbox suspend operation.
When a sandbox is suspended, its pod is terminated. If the client-side connection is not explicitly closed, the local port-forwarding tunnel remains open pointing to a stale IP. Upon a subsequent resume, any command execution or file operation would experience up to 60 seconds of retries before a new tunnel is established.
Tearing down the connector during suspend ensures that the stale tunnel is immediately terminated. The next SDK operation post-resume will then automatically spin up a fresh tunnel to the correct, updated pod IP.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes #585

body:
Working on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/959

## Summary

This PR re-introduces (resurrects) the `v1alpha1` API group version for both core resources and extension CRDs alongside the current `v1beta1` version. This change ensures backward compatibility for older clients, manifests, and integrations that still target the `v1alpha1` API, while establishing a smooth migration path forward.
`v1beta1` remains the designated **storage version** in `etcd`, meaning all resources will be serialized and stored as `v1beta1`. Kubernetes will automatically handle schema-compatible conversion/serving for clients requesting `v1alpha1`.

## Detailed Changes

1. API Definitions Re-introduced (`v1alpha1`)
2. Storage Version Configuration
3. Scheme Registration

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **New Features**
  * Added v1alpha1 API versions for Sandbox, SandboxClaim, SandboxTemplate, and SandboxWarmPool; v1alpha1 is now served alongside v1beta1.
* **Documentation**
  * Updated API reference to include v1alpha1 entries and schemas for extension resources.
* **Chores**
  * Updated generation tooling to handle multi-version APIs and added a tool to consistently sort CRD version lists.

title: Correct time at which we can mark a resume pod as ready.

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
### What would you like to be added?

Mark a Resume Operation completed as soon as the Pod becomes Ready in the Agent Sandbox Python SDK Client
The GKE Pod Snapshots leverages the gVisor [background restore](https://g3doc.corp.google.com/cloud/gvisor/g3doc/features/hibernate.md?cl=head#background-restore) feature, which allows the application to start execution as soon as the kernel state and memory metadata are loaded. The remaining application memory is restored asynchronously in the background while the application is running. If the application accesses a memory page that has not yet been restored, gVisor prioritizes loading that page immediately to unblock the application thread. This can dramatically reduce the "Time to First Instruction" for large applications.

The GKE Pod Snapshot Agent only sets the PodRestored condition after the gVisor [background restore](https://g3doc.corp.google.com/cloud/gvisor/g3doc/features/hibernate.md?cl=head#background-restore) is completed. 

The Agent Sandbox Python SDK client ([code](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/b222ae129bada240cba45f2b264ff6ce8c46d169/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/k8s_agent_sandbox/gke_extensions/snapshots/sandbox_with_snapshot_support.py#L309)) checks the PodRestored condition of the Pod to verify the stateful integrity of the resume operation and detect cold-start fallbacks. Therefore, the SDK client waits until the gVisor [background restore](https://g3doc.corp.google.com/cloud/gvisor/g3doc/features/hibernate.md?cl=head#background-restore) is completed in a Sandbox resume operation. 

Alternatively, the SDK client could mark a resume operation as completed as soon as the Sandbox object becomes ready.

### Why is this needed?

optimize the time a sandbox is marked as ready.
