body:
**Status:** draft / RFC. Posted for discussion alongside #838 (from-scratch Go router). Not asking for review-to-merge — looking for a steer on whether the Envoy + ext_proc shape is interesting enough to pursue as v2 or post-v1 evolution.

## What this is

An alternative implementation of [KEP-NNNN](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/758) that keeps the KEP's three core mechanisms (informer-backed UID→PodIP map, direct Pod IP dispatch, drift handling) in Go but delegates **everything else** (TLS, mTLS, rate limit, circuit breaker, retries, access logs, tracing, WAF, JWT) to Envoy.

The Go service is a single ext_proc gRPC server (~300 lines + cache) that owns the K8s-aware state. Envoy handles the data plane.

## Architecture

```
client ──► Envoy listener (:8080)
            │
            ├── HTTP filter: ext_proc
            │     │
            │     │  gRPC ProcessingRequest (RequestHeaders)
            │     ▼
            │   ext-proc-sandbox-router service
            │     │  - K8s Pod informer (labeled sandbox-name-hash)
            │     │  - In-memory UID → PodIP map
            │     │  - Reads X-Sandbox-UID + X-Sandbox-ID etc.
            │     │  - Returns header mutation:
            │     │    x-envoy-original-dst-host = <PodIP>:<port>
            │     │    (or DNS form on cache miss)
            │     ▼
            │   gRPC ProcessingResponse (HeaderMutation + ClearRouteCache)
            │
            └── HTTP filter: router → ORIGINAL_DST cluster
                                       (reads x-envoy-original-dst-host)
                ─────► sandbox Pod
```

Per-request cost: one in-cluster gRPC round-trip (~sub-ms) plus the Pod-IP dispatch.

## KEP requirements → status

| KEP item | Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Informer watching sandbox Pods | ✅ | Same `cache` code as the from-scratch router |
| UID → PodIP in-memory map | ✅ | Shared between both prototypes |
| Direct dispatch, bypass Service | ✅ | Envoy ORIGINAL_DST cluster reads `x-envoy-original-dst-host` |
| `X-Sandbox-UID` request shape | ✅ | |
| Active cache invalidation on connection error | ✅ | Envoy outlier detection ejects 5xx-returning Pod IPs |
| Hybrid DNS fallback (cache miss) | ✅ | ext_proc returns DNS form when UID isn't cached |
| Sync period | ✅ | Standard 10m informer resync |
| Strict input validation | ✅ | Performed in ext_proc handler |
| TokenReview integration | ❌ | Deferred — drops in as an `ext_authz` filter or sibling ext_proc, not yet wired |
| TLS termination / mTLS | ✅✅ | Envoy native (the from-scratch router has to implement this) |

## Comparison with the from-scratch Go router (#838)

| Concern | From-scratch Go (#838) | Envoy + ext_proc (this) |
|---|---|---|
| TLS / mTLS | Custom (~400 LOC + fsnotify hot-reload) | Envoy native |
| Rate limit | Not implemented | `local_ratelimit` filter (config-only) |
| Circuit breaker | Not implemented | Envoy outlier detection (built in) |
| Retries | Custom retry transport (~150 LOC) | Envoy retry policy + hedged retries |
| Access logs | Custom middleware (~150 LOC) | Envoy access log (config-only) |
| Tracing | Custom OTel middleware (~100 LOC) | Envoy OTel native |
| Custom Go LOC | ~5,000 | ~300 |
| K8s API surface | Same informer | Same informer |
| Operational footprint | One Go binary | Envoy + Go service (two Deployments) |
| TokenReview | Implemented (#838) | Deferred |

## Validated

- Unit tests for cache + ext_proc handler.
- Standalone load harness at `cmd/load-test/` exercising real `Server` + real `Cache` (fake K8s client) — single replica sustains **~38k req/s** at 5k sandboxes with 80% cache hit, no errors, p50 1.4ms / p99 6.0ms. Bottleneck is gRPC machinery, not the cache.
- End-to-end run on kind: Envoy + ext_proc Deployments come up, `/healthz` returns 200, real sandbox Pods get routed via the cache, deleting a sandbox triggers outlier ejection within a few requests.

## Open questions

1. **Is the two-process operational model acceptable?** Trades ~5k LOC of Go for ~200 lines of Envoy YAML, but adds Envoy as a hard runtime dep. For OSS Kubernetes users without an existing Envoy footprint, this may be the wrong default. For users running a service mesh, it's nearly free.
2. **Should this replace #838 or coexist?** Two natural positions: (a) #838 ships as v1 (simpler operational story, no Envoy dep), this ships as v2 / opt-in for users who want the enterprise feature set; (b) this is the long-term answer and #838 is the bridge while Envoy adoption catches up.
3. **TokenReview path.** Two options here: an `ext_authz` filter pointing at a small authn extension of this same service (clean, separates concerns), or a second ext_proc filter sharing the same Go process (one fewer Deployment). Either works; preferences welcome.
4. **UID source.** Same question as #838 — the KEP says "Sandbox CRD UID (read from Pod labels)" but the controller doesn't stamp UID as a label. Both prototypes read it from `Pod.metadata.ownerReferences`. Want me to file a small controller change to also stamp `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-uid`?

Happy to close this out if the direction is clearly "stay all-Go" — the work was worth it as a comparison data point either way.

title: [Feature Request] Support Idle Lifecycle Policy for Sandboxes

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
## Summary

I would like `agent-sandbox` to support an idle lifecycle policy for long-lived interactive workspaces.

The goal is to let active workspaces remain available while in use, automatically stop idle workspaces while retaining their recoverable state, and eventually delete abandoned retained workspaces.

This is useful for browser IDEs, notebooks, and agent workspaces where rebuilding the environment is expensive, but keeping pods running indefinitely is wasteful.

For this proposal, `Suspend` and `Retain` are effectively the same user-facing outcome for this use case: stop active compute, keep enough state to resume the workspace later, and avoid deleting the workspace immediately.

## Desired Lifecycle

A workspace should be able to follow this lifecycle:

1. A `Sandbox` is created in `operationMode: Running` with an active TTL, for example 24 hours.
2. If the active TTL expires, the `Sandbox` transitions to a retained non-running state. In `v1beta1`, this may be represented as `operationMode: Suspended`, but the important behavior is retention.
3. When retained, a new retention TTL is stamped, for example 30 days, with expiration action `Delete`.
4. If the user resumes the workspace before the retention TTL expires, the `Sandbox` returns to `operationMode: Running`.
5. On resume, the active TTL is reset to 24 hours and the active expiration action becomes retain/suspend again.
6. If the workspace is never resumed and the retention TTL expires, the `Sandbox` is deleted.
7. Ideally, active TTL renewal should happen when a client connection is created or renewed, such as a browser IDE WebSocket connection.

```text
Created
  -> operationMode: Running
  -> active TTL: 24h
  -> active expiration action: Retain/Suspend

Active TTL expires
  -> retained non-running state
  -> operationMode: Suspended, if that is the canonical v1beta1 representation
  -> retention TTL: 30d
  -> retained expiration action: Delete

User resumes before 30d
  -> operationMode: Running
  -> active TTL reset to 24h
  -> active expiration action: Retain/Suspend

No resume before 30d
  -> Deleted
```

## API Scope and Ownership

This lifecycle policy should be supported directly on the core `Sandbox` API and enforced by the core `Sandbox` controller.

`SandboxClaim` should be able to accept the same lifecycle policy for template-driven workflows, but it should mirror/pass that policy through to the generated `Sandbox` rather than independently enforcing a separate lifecycle state machine.

Desired ownership model:

- `Sandbox.spec.lifecycle` defines the actual runtime lifecycle policy.
- The `Sandbox` controller enforces active TTL, retained non-running transitions, resume behavior, retention TTL, and deletion.
- `SandboxClaim.spec.lifecycle` may expose the same fields for convenience.
- The `SandboxClaim` controller passes those lifecycle fields through when creating or reconciling the backing `Sandbox`.
- Direct `Sandbox` users get the same lifecycle behavior without needing `SandboxClaim`.

## Why Existing Lifecycle Support Is Not Enough

Current lifecycle support appears centered on absolute `shutdownTime` and `shutdownPolicy`. `Retain` is close to the desired first-stage idle behavior, and `operationMode: Suspended` may be the right v1beta1 representation for the non-running retained state. However, the lifecycle policy cannot yet express:

- Active TTL expiration should retain the workspace state and stop active compute rather than delete immediately.
- Retained non-running resources should have a separate retention TTL.
- Resume should reset the active TTL.
- Connection/activity renewal should extend the active TTL.
- The controller should own the state transition between running, suspended, resumed, and deleted.

## Possible API Shape

This is one possible shape, not a fixed proposal:

```yaml
apiVersion: agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Sandbox
spec:
  operationMode: Running
  lifecycle:
    activeTTLSeconds: 86400
    activeExpirationPolicy: Retain
    retainedTTLSeconds: 2592000
    retainedExpirationPolicy: Delete
```

For `SandboxClaim`, the same policy could be accepted and mirrored to the generated `Sandbox`:

```yaml
apiVersion: extensions.agents.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: SandboxClaim
spec:
  lifecycle:
    activeTTLSeconds: 86400
    activeExpirationPolicy: Retain
    retainedTTLSeconds: 2592000
    retainedExpirationPolicy: Delete
```

The generated `Sandbox` would receive the lifecycle policy and the `Sandbox` controller would enforce it.

## Activity Renewal

For browser workspaces, activity could come from the gateway/router/client layer.

A Kubernetes-native option might be a `Lease` associated with the `Sandbox`. The router or client could renew the Lease periodically while a WebSocket/session is active. The controller could use the Lease renewal time as the source of activity without requiring frequent writes to the `Sandbox` object.

This would allow active workspaces to remain running while a user is connected, without causing high write volume on the `Sandbox` object.

## Open Questions

- Should this extend the existing lifecycle fields or introduce a new lifecycle policy struct?
- Should this build on existing `Retain` semantics, or introduce separate active/retained expiration policies?
- If `operationMode: Suspended` is the representation for the retained non-running state, should the retention TTL start when `operationMode` is set to `Suspended`, or when the `Suspended=True` condition is observed?
- Should activity be represented by a Lease, annotation, status field, or subresource?
- Should activity renewal be optional, gated by a field such as `renewOnActivity: true`?
- How should this interact with future suspend implementations such as freeze or hibernate?

## Desired Outcome

Users can define a lifecycle policy where active workspaces remain running while in use, idle workspaces automatically stop active compute while retaining recoverable state, and abandoned retained workspaces are eventually deleted without manual cleanup.

title: Propagate template-ref-hash label to Sandbox and SandboxTemplate for client-side discovery

labels.name: priority/backlog
labels.description: Higher priority than priority/awaiting-more-evidence.

body:
> [!NOTE]
> This issue is created based on the discussion in [issue #342 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/342#issuecomment-4491820556).

Client applications and UIs need to map a `SandboxTemplate` name to its corresponding `sandbox-template-ref-hash` to query associated Sandboxes and Pods that are labeled with the template hash. A `Sandbox` cannot be labeled with the `SandboxTemplate` name because of a difference in character limitations, noted in the issue linked above.

Currently, this mapping cannot be performed directly using API resources:
1. `SandboxTemplate` does not expose its hash in its metadata labels.
2. `Sandbox` has the `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-template-ref-hash` label deleted during SandboxClaim adoption.

This forces clients to write custom hashing code to resolve the relationship between template and sandbox.

**Proposed Changes**

1. Keep the `sandbox-template-ref-hash` label on adopted/active `Sandbox` resources
2. Add the `sandbox-template-ref-hash` label to `SandboxTemplate` resources.
3. Create the hash label when creating the `SandboxTemplate` and propagate to `Sandbox` and `Pod` during both warm and cold starts instead of recalculating the hash.

**Note for Reviewer**

During Sandbox adoption from a warm pool, it's safe to stop deleting the `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-template-ref-hash` label.

- **Why it was removed in the first place:** To ensure that adopted sandboxes do not appear in warm pool queries.
- **Why it is safe to keep:** Warm pool queries filter using the `agents.x-k8s.io/warm-pool-sandbox` label. Keeping the template ref hash label (while still deleting the warm pool label) will not cause adopted sandboxes to be matched by warm pool queries.
- **Cold starts:** Also stamp this label on the `Sandbox` resource during cold starts.

body:
This PR adds a Go reimplementation of the sandbox-router at
  `clients/go/sandbox-router/`, as a drop-in alternative to the existing
  Python router at
  `clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/sandbox-router/`.

  ### Why

  The Python router is a small reverse proxy that fans HTTP traffic out to
  sandbox pods by reading `X-Sandbox-*` headers and constructing the
  internal Kubernetes DNS name. It works, but for enterprise deployments it
  has gaps: no TLS, no mTLS, no metrics, no structured access logging, no
  tracing, no per-request retry on dial failures.

  This Go version closes those gaps while keeping the contract identical
  so existing callers (the Go and Python SDKs, plus any direct HTTP clients)
  keep working unchanged.

  ### Scope

  **Drop-in protocol contract preserved:**
  - Service name `sandbox-router-svc` on port 8080
  - `X-Sandbox-ID` / `X-Sandbox-Namespace` / `X-Sandbox-Port` /
    `X-Sandbox-Pod-IP` headers with the same defaults and validation rules
  - `{"detail": "..."}` JSON error shape
  - `PROXY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` and `CLUSTER_DOMAIN` env-var support
  - `GET /healthz` returning `{"status":"ok"}` (used by Gateway
    HealthCheckPolicy)

  **Production controls added:**
  - TLS termination with hot-reloading server certificate (fsnotify on the
    parent directory, safe under K8s Secret atomic-rename rotation)
  - Optional or required mTLS for clients
  - Structured access log per request (skips health/metrics endpoints)
  - Trace ↔ log correlation: `trace_id` and `span_id` baked into every
    per-request log line
  - Exponential-backoff dial retries for sandbox startup races
    (`--upstream-max-retries`; only dial-class failures are retried so
    request bodies are never replayed)
  - Prometheus metrics on `/metrics` and optional OTLP push via the
    OpenTelemetry → Prometheus bridge (`--enable-otel-metrics`)
  - OpenTelemetry tracing via OTLP gRPC (`--enable-tracing`); trace context
    propagated to the upstream sandbox
  - YAML config file (`--config` / `SANDBOX_ROUTER_CONFIG`); precedence is
    CLI > file > env > defaults
  - Graceful shutdown with readiness flip + parallel listener drain
  - Configurable request-body size limit (`--max-request-body-bytes`)
  - Built as a multi-arch distroless static image
    (`gcr.io/distroless/static:nonroot`)

  **Tested:** unit tests across every package, integration tests
  (`-tags=integration`) covering end-to-end proxy round-trip with body
  streaming, healthz, all three mTLS modes with real handshakes, retry
  success when backend comes up mid-window, retry give-up within budget.
  All 14 cases from the Python router's `test_sandbox_router.py` have Go
  equivalents.

  ### Compatibility

  The Python router source stays in the tree; the Go router builds as a
  **separate image named `sandbox-router-go`** to avoid colliding with the
  Python `sandbox-router` image (this required a small patch to
  `dev/tools/push-images`). Operators opt in by switching their workload's
  image. Existing Gateway / HTTPRoute / Service manifests don't change.

  Example Kubernetes manifests are in
  `clients/go/sandbox-router/deploy/` (Deployment, Service, PDB,
  NetworkPolicy, ServiceAccount) with a README walking through what to
  tighten for production.

  A local load-test harness is in `dev/load-test/router/`; reference
  throughput / latency numbers are captured in the package README's
  "Scaling guidance" section.

### Files

  New code under `clients/go/sandbox-router/` (config, proxy, tlsutil,
  observability, server packages + main + Dockerfile + deploy/), plus a
  load-test harness under `dev/load-test/router/`. The `Makefile` gets a
  `build-sandbox-router` target. `go.mod` promotes `fsnotify` and
  `golang.org/x/sync` from indirect, and adds the OTLP metric exporter,
  the OTel SDK metric package, and the OTel-to-Prometheus bridge.

  Release Note

  ```release-note
  Added a Go implementation of the `sandbox-router` as a drop-in replacement for the Python router. The new image is
  `sandbox-router-go` and preserves the `X-Sandbox-*` header contract and `sandbox-router-svc` Service name. Adds TLS termination
  with hot-reloading certificates, optional or required mTLS, structured access logging, exponential-backoff dial retries for
  upstream startup races, OpenTelemetry tracing and metrics export (alongside the existing Prometheus `/metrics` endpoint), an
  optional YAML config file, and graceful shutdown. Example Kubernetes manifests are in `clients/go/sandbox-router/deploy/`. The
  Python router remains available; operators opt in by switching their workload's image.
  ```

title: Optimize Network Identity Performance via Metadata Refactoring and Installation Presets

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-soon
labels.description: Must be staffed and worked on either currently, or very soon, ideally in time for the next release.

body:
#### **Background**
We identified a significant bottleneck where Pod startup latency (P99) reached over 20 seconds. This is caused by Cilium generating a unique Identity for every Pod due to high-cardinality labels like `sandbox-name-hash`. To resolve this, we propose refactoring how metadata is handled and providing better installation defaults.

#### **Proposed Changes**

**1. Metadata Refactoring ("Healthy Core")**
We aim to separate "identifying" data from "functional" data by migrating high-cardinality fields to Annotations while retaining low-cardinality Labels for policy enforcement.
*   **Migrate to Annotations**: Move fields like `sandbox-name-hash` and `claim-uid` from Labels to Annotations to prevent "one-identity-per-pod" mapping.
*   **Add Management Label**: Introduce `app.kubernetes.io/managed-by: sandbox-controller` as a low-cardinality label to enable efficient controller watch filtering without triggering identity explosion.
*   **Retain Category Labels**: Keep the low-cardinality `sandbox-pod-template-hash` label for cluster-wide network policy enforcement.
*   **Controller Optimization**: Optimize Pod retrieval by switching from label-based listing to precise `Get` operations or dedicated indexers for annotations.

**2. Enhanced Installation Configuration**
Provide out-of-the-box optimization templates for users using Cilium.
*   **Documentation**: Explicitly notify Cilium users in the README to add high-cardinality `agents.x-k8s.io/` labels to their `label-filter` ignore list.
*   **Helm Chart Presets**: Include an optional `CiliumConfig` or `ConfigMap` template in the Helm Chart to allow users to apply these exclusion rules easily.

**3. IP-based Direct Connection via Selector-less Services** 
To maintain 1:1 connectivity in the Service Opt-in scenario without relying on high-cardinality labels, we will transition the architecture toward selector-less discovery.

*   **Decoupled Discovery**: Provision Services without a spec.selector.
*   **Manual Endpoint Management**: The controller will manually manage `Endpoints` or `EndpointSlices` to point directly to the Pod IP. This eliminates the need for unique labels on the Pod while maintaining standard K8s DNS resolution (e.g., my-sandbox.svc.cluster.local).

#### **Note on Customization**
Customers requiring unique network identities for specific use cases can still add their own custom labels, which will function normally with standard selectors.

title: feat(python-client): allow injecting K8sHelper / AsyncK8sHelper into client factories

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: ok-to-test
labels.description: Indicates a non-member PR verified by an org member that is safe to test.

body:
## What this PR does / why we need it

Adds out-of-cluster authentication support to the Python SDK's factory classes (`SandboxClient`, `AsyncSandboxClient`) and helper classes (`K8sHelper`, `AsyncK8sHelper`). Today the SDK hard-codes `load_incluster_config()` → `load_kube_config()` discovery with no in-process escape hatch, which blocks callers running outside the cluster (Cloud Run, AWS Lambda, peer-cluster workloads) from passing pre-configured credentials (e.g. from `google.auth.default()`) without writing a kubeconfig file to disk or monkey-patching the `kubernetes` config module.

**Why:** the current workaround requires building a `kubernetes.client.Configuration` from ADC, then monkey-patching `load_incluster_config` / `load_kube_config` globally to prevent the SDK from overwriting it — fragile, side-effecting, and unacceptable as a long-term pattern.

Sync and async siblings are patched in lockstep per the project's sync/async parity rule. Tests in `test/unit/` cover both the injection path and the default path, asserting the default is unchanged.

**Backward compatibility:** all new kwargs default to `None`. No existing callers are affected.

---

## Two approaches — pick one

This PR has **three commits**. The first two implement **Approach A**; the third (on top) implements **Approach B** as an alternative. Either can be the landing point — the third commit can be reverted cleanly if Approach A is preferred.

### Approach A — `k8s_helper` injection on factory classes (commits ef5b994, 08635b5)

Adds an optional `k8s_helper: K8sHelper | None` kwarg to `SandboxClient.__init__` and `AsyncSandboxClient.__init__`, plus an optional `api_client` kwarg to `K8sHelper.__init__` and `AsyncK8sHelper.__init__`.

```python
import kubernetes.client as k8s
from k8s_agent_sandbox import SandboxClient
from k8s_agent_sandbox.k8s_helper import K8sHelper

cfg = k8s.Configuration()
cfg.host = "https://my-cluster"
# ... populate from google.auth.default() etc

client = SandboxClient(
    connection_config=SandboxGatewayConnectionConfig(...),
    k8s_helper=K8sHelper(api_client=k8s.ApiClient(cfg)),
)
```

**Rationale:** brings factory classes to parity with the existing `k8s_helper` kwarg on `Sandbox`/`AsyncSandbox` handles, and enables lifecycle-sharing (one helper across multiple clients/handles).

### Approach B — `KubernetesConfig` pydantic model on factory classes (commit cfb4d36)

Adds a `KubernetesConfig(api_client=..., namespace=...)` model to `models.py` and accepts it as `kubernetes_config: KubernetesConfig | None` on both factory classes. The client constructs `K8sHelper` internally from the config — callers never touch the helper directly.

```python
import kubernetes.client as k8s
from k8s_agent_sandbox import SandboxClient
from k8s_agent_sandbox.models import KubernetesConfig, SandboxGatewayConnectionConfig

cfg = k8s.Configuration()
cfg.host = "https://my-cluster"
# ... populate from google.auth.default() etc

client = SandboxClient(
    connection_config=SandboxGatewayConnectionConfig(...),
    kubernetes_config=KubernetesConfig(api_client=k8s.ApiClient(cfg)),
)
```

**Rationale:** auth configuration belongs at the client boundary, consistent with the existing `SandboxConnectionConfig` / `SandboxTracerConfig` pattern. Extensible (QPS, retries, namespace defaults can be added to `KubernetesConfig` later). The `k8s_helper` kwarg is removed from factory classes — `K8sHelper.api_client` injection is kept as an internal seam only.

**To revert to Approach A:** `git revert cfb4d36`

---

## Which issue(s) this PR is related to

none filed; happy to open one if maintainers prefer the issue-first flow

## Release Note

```
The Python client's SandboxClient and AsyncSandboxClient constructors now
accept an optional kubernetes_config kwarg (KubernetesConfig model) for
injecting a pre-configured Kubernetes API client. This unblocks
out-of-cluster authentication patterns (Cloud Run, AWS Lambda,
peer-cluster workloads) without requiring a kubeconfig file on disk.
K8sHelper and AsyncK8sHelper also accept api_client= directly as an
internal seam.
```

body:
# What this PR does / why we need it:

We want to propose a model where the controller manages more parts of the sandbox, and the user has less control over the sandbox implementation.

In this model, the pod we create contains our base image with our pod agent. The user's image is mounted as a volume. The pod agent then handles the sandbox lifecycle inside the pod.

A new extension CRD is created for this purpose - ManagedSandbox.

# Goals

This model can enable the following roadmap items:
- Scale-down / Resume PVC based - Pause resume preserving PVC only, when replicas scale to 0, PVC is saved, when sandbox scales back PVC is restored
- API Support for Multi-Sandbox per Pod - Extend API to support multiple sandboxes in a Pod
- API Support for other isolation technologies - Continue extending the support to QEMU, Firecracker and other technologies
- Auto-deletion of (bursty) sandboxes (RL training typical usage)

In addition, we think that this model can:
- Increase the density of sandboxes, especially for conversational agents, where most of the time, the agent is idle.
- Provide means for L7 policy
- Allow for ssh access (for users using cli agents)

To achieve these goals, the controller needs to have more control over the shape of the sandbox. An agent in the pod is needed to manage the sandboxes in it. This means the API cannot be the pod spec, and needs to be more limited to allow for different backends and for the controller to manage the sandbox lifecycle.

# Changes proposed
- More limited user facing API to move more control to the runtime.
- Allow each pod to have a configurable number (default 10) of sandbox slots.
- A sandbox pod will now have an agent that manages the sandboxes in the pods
  - The controller contacts the agent via gRPC
  - When sandbox is created, it can be quickly scheduled to an existing pod via gRPC call (if no pod available new one will be created).
  - Users can ssh into their sandboxes (Working on a PoC with gateway-api; will update the PR with it soon)
- Use smaller API surface (i.e. not the pod spec)
  - ManagedSandbox can have many backends, and not all will support the entire pod spec.
  - We don't want to give each sandbox control over the volume types. Controlling the volume types allows us to do advanced features, like quick snapshotting, forking, etc. And it will also make it easier to support other backends.

- Create Pool pods based on base image
  - This allows us to use OCI volumes and let k8s handle image pulling.

## Potential follow ups this will allow:
- Integration with Sandbox{Claim, WarmPool}.
- Update sandbox scheduling to pool pod based on requested resources instead of slots.
- TLS MITM proxying (by injecting a CA. enables automatic telemetry and policy)
- Auto drain (sandbox worker can signal when it is idle, and pod will exit)
- Multiple backends
  - Firecracker backend
  - Local experience - allow for users to try the sandbox on their laptops without k8s
- Snapshots for sandboxes (allows for forking, remote backup)
- Network identity (via metadata service)
- Routing can done via gateway-api (controller adds route to pod, pod agent routes to the sandbox)

# NOTE:
This PR has no tests (though i did test it manually), and there are some rough edges to clean and i will be continuing to iterate on it.
I posted it early to see if there's community interest in the use-cases it enables, and if there are any objections with the approach proposed.

I'm looking for early feedback on the major decisions:
- The shape of the ManagedSandbox CRD
- Is Multiple sandbox per Pod desired?
- A sandbox pod having an agent, with gRPC interface

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:

This document addition provides concrete, reproducible GKE cluster manifests and commands to demonstrate how GKE NodeLocal DNSCache (169.254.20.10) operates under GKE Sandbox (gVisor) security isolation:

1. The gVisor eBPF Socket Bypass gotcha: On standard GKE pods (without gVisor), DNS queries targeting 169.254.20.10 are intercepted and redirected in-memory by host-level eBPF socket hooks (cgroup/connect), completely bypassing the virtual network interface (eth0) and any egress NetworkPolicy rules.
2. Egress Policy Dependency: Because gVisor isolates all socket operations inside its virtualized user-space netstack (gonet), host-level socket hooks are bypassed. The query is forced out as a standard L3 packet over eth0, making it strictly subject to your egress rules.
3. Reproducible Scenarios: Includes step-by-step configurations illustrating how strict default egress blocks (which include link-local 169.254.0.0/16 ranges) drop DNS cache traffic, and how explicitly unblocking the link-local range natively enables instant ~10ms DNS resolution without hostAliases or custom external servers.

title: [Bug] Pod adoption silently loses OwnerReference if labels/annotations are already up to date
body:
There is a bug in the SandboxReconciler's pod adoption flow where a newly set OwnerReference is silently lost and never persisted to the Kubernetes API server.

During pod adoption in reconcileExistingPod, when the pod's ownership is resourceUnowned:

1. The controller calls `ctrl.SetControllerReference(sandbox, pod, r.Scheme)` which successfully appends the OwnerReference to the local pod object's in-memory structure.
2. The controller then checks if the pod's labels/annotations need propagation/updating via `r.updatePodMetadata(pod, sandbox, nameHash)`.
3. If the pod's labels/annotations are already fully up to date (e.g., when adopting a pod that was already pre-created correctly by the WarmPool controller), updatePodMetadata returns false.
4. Because updated is false, the controller skips calling `r.Update(ctx, pod)` and the reconcile loop finishes without ever persisting the new OwnerReference to the API server.

Relevant code: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/controllers/sandbox_controller.go#L753-L767 , in contrast Service adoption correctly update the resource immediately upon setting the controller reference https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/controllers/sandbox_controller.go#L558-L563

As a result, the adopted pod remains unowned on the Kubernetes API server.

**Steps to Reproduce:**

1. Have a pre-existing, unowned Pod with labels that match a Sandbox's name hash (such as one created in a warm pool) and with labels/annotations that are already identical to what is specified in the Sandbox.Spec.PodTemplate.
2. Create the Sandbox CR.
3. The reconciler runs `reconcilePod`, fetches the existing pod, and determines its ownership is `resourceUnowned`.
4. The `ctrl.SetControllerReference` executes, but `r.Update(ctx, pod)` is skipped because updatePodMetadata returns false.
5. Describe/inspect the pod and observe that its `metadata.ownerReferences` field is empty/unset.

title: [sdk] Support Dynamic Timeout Propagation in Sandbox Router

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
In local development and multi-tenant setups, the client SDKs route HTTP requests through the sandbox-router proxy. Currently, the sandbox-router enforces a hardcoded [proxy timeout:](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/sandbox-router/sandbox_router.py#L28) and [here](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/sandbox-router/sandbox_router.yaml#L44-L45)

```python
DEFAULT_PROXY_TIMEOUT = 180.0  # 3 minutes
```

If a user runs a long-running process in the sandbox (such as code evaluation or a heavy prompt task using the Gemini CLI) that takes longer than 3 minutes, the router proxy aborts the connection and returns an `HTTP 504 Gateway Timeout`. Even if the user overrides the timeout in their SDK call (e.g., `sandbox.commands.run(cmd, timeout=600)`), that timeout is only enforced client-side and is not propagated to the proxy. 

To allow dynamic, request-level timeouts without manual infrastructure changes, we should propagate the client's timeout to the sandbox-router:

- Introduce support for an X-Sandbox-Timeout HTTP header: If present, parse it as a float and use it as the request-level timeout for proxying that specific connection. Fall back to the default 180-second limit if absent or invalid.
- Python SDK Changes: Update sync and async connectors to automatically extract the client-provided timeout parameter and inject it into the X-Sandbox-Timeout header.
- Go SDK Changes: Update the connector to calculate the remaining context deadline (time.Until(deadline)) and inject it into the X-Sandbox-Timeout header.

title: Agentic Networking Identity and Controls (beyond L4) for Agent Sandboxes

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
We are looking to collect user journeys and use cases to help shape the networking governance model for agent-sandbox. Specifically, we want to understand requirements for network control that goes beyond traditional L4 (IP and Port) filtering, moving towards L7, protocol-aware (e.g MCP), and sandbox identities aware governance.

Traditional Kubernetes network policies operate at L4, which is often insufficient for agentic workloads:

1. Agents often need access to broad domains (e.g., `github.com` or cloud APIs), but we may want to restrict them to specific repositories or endpoints.
2. Agents increasingly communicate using agent-specific protocols like the MCP. We need governance that understands these protocols and have the ability to enforce tool allowlists or inspect tool call arguments.
3. The network policies applied to a sandbox should be dynamically tied to the sandbox's identity. (or something more granular than that?)

We want to explore how agent-sandbox can provide or integrate with advanced networking controls (collaborating with projects like kube-agentic-networking) to address these challenges.

### We welcome User Journeys!

We want to gather real-world scenarios. Please share your use cases by replying to this issue. 

Here is one to start the conversation:

#### 1. Tool & MCP Governance
*   **Scenario**: An agent runs in a sandbox and connects to an external MCP server to access tools.
*   **Requirement**: We want to define policy rules that allow the agent to call `read_file` but block `write_file` or `run_command` on that MCP server

## Description
This PR officially graduates the `agent-sandbox` API from `v1alpha1` to `v1beta1` directly on `main` for the upcoming release cycle. 

Per the maintainer consensus in our [API alignment and community discussion](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1o9w0rlwo1lKO2zcfX7Kp8E7sIt1L-Z8frScLj30kpRw/edit?tab=t.0), we have opted to bypass the introduction of complex conversion web-hooks and their associated roundtrip logic debt and going forward with the **Drop and Adopt** strategy for API graduation. Since alpha APIs carry no structural compatibility or graduation guarantees under official Kubernetes API Deprecation Policy, this PR completely drops support for `v1alpha1` and establishes `v1beta1` as a clean-slate schema.

To maintain a healthy CI pipeline, this PR combines the API structural changes with the necessary controller reconciliation logic refactoring.

### Breaking Changes (`v1beta1`)
- **Directory Migration:** Removed `pkg/api/v1alpha1/` and introduced `pkg/api/v1beta1/`.
- **Controller Update** - The controller is based off of the latest `v1beta1` API.
- **Test files** - Upgraded E2E and unit test files.
- **API document** - had to upgrade `generate-api-docs` to prevent CI failure.
- **Client set** - New client set generation from v1beta1

### Release notes

```release-note
This commit initiates the v1beta1 graduation by dropping the legacy alpha schemas and updating the core and extension controllers to maintain compilation and functional parity. 
```

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR disables automatic HTTP redirects in the `agentic-sandbox-client` Python SDK to prevent a **High-severity Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)** vulnerability. 

Currently, the SDK's `SandboxConnector` and `AsyncSandboxConnector` use default HTTP client settings that automatically follow 3xx redirects. Since the sandbox environment is inherently untrusted, an attacker with execution capabilities can force the orchestrator to perform unauthorized `GET` requests against internal infrastructure—such as cloud IMDS metadata (e.g., `169.254.169.254`) or private internal APIs—by issuing a malicious redirect. 

This fix explicitly sets `allow_redirects=False` (for `requests`) and `follow_redirects=False` (for `httpx`) to ensure the security boundary between the untrusted sandbox and the orchestrator's network is strictly enforced.

#### Release Note
```release-note
SECURITY: Disables automatic HTTP redirects in the Python SDK's SandboxConnector to mitigate potential Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) attacks from compromised sandboxes.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR adds Example 3: GCP Workload Identity & Google Cloud Services (Vertex AI, GCS, etc.) to the network-policy-management documentation.

When using custom egress network policies on GKE clusters with dual-stack enabled, two major gotchas can arise that break Google Cloud SDKs or cause them to experience 2-minute delays:

1. Workload Identity Egress Block: The GCP Metadata Server (`169.254.169.254`) is blocked by the default egress block list. Custom network policies must explicitly omit it from the excluded subnets to enable token exchange.
2. IPv6 Timeout: Runtimes such as Node.js or Python HTTP clients concurrently attempt to resolve Google API subdomains via both IPv4 and IPv6. Because standard Kubernetes network policies operate on a default-deny posture, omitting the IPv6 egress catch-all (`::/0`) causes outbound IPv6 SYN packets to be dropped. This forces the application to wait for the full 127-second TCP SYN retransmission timeout before falling back to IPv4.

This addition provides a robust, dual-stack template example showing how to safely authorize both IPv4 and IPv6 external egress while preserving strict namespace and internal network boundaries.

labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: do-not-merge/hold
labels.description: Indicates that a PR should not merge because someone has issued a /hold command.

body:
Working on https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/740

## 📖 Description / Motivation
Previously, the `SandboxClaim` API used an overloaded string (`WarmPoolPolicy`) to dictate warm pool adoption behavior. A value could represent "None", "Default", or be implicitly treated as a specific pool name. 

To align with Kubernetes API design best practices, this PR refactors the warm pool configuration into a strictly typed, structured object (`WarmPoolConfig`). This change drastically improves API clarity, allows for strict declarative validation (via OpenAPI schema and CEL), and prevents invalid configurations from ever reaching the controller.

## 🛠️ Changes Made
* **API Schema Refactor**: Replaced `WarmPool *WarmPoolPolicy` (string) with `WarmPool *WarmPoolConfig` (struct) in `SandboxClaimSpec`. The JSON key is now strictly `warmPool`.
* **New Strategy Enum**: Introduced `WarmPoolStrategy` with explicit, validated enum values: `Auto`, `Disabled`, and `PoolName`.
* **API Server Validation (CEL)**: Added `XValidation` markers to enforce cross-field logic. The `poolName` field is now strictly required if the strategy is `PoolName`, and forbidden otherwise.
* **Resource Name Compliance**: Added `MaxLength=63` and regex `Pattern` Kubebuilder markers to `poolName` to enforce RFC 1123 DNS Label compliance directly at the Kubernetes API server level.
* **Controller Updates**: Refactored `SandboxClaimReconciler` and `getWarmPoolConfig` to evaluate the new struct fields instead of parsing a raw string.
* **Go Test Coverage**: 
  * Updated existing controller unit tests to reflect the new `Auto`/`Disabled`/`PoolName` terminology and struct formatting.
* **Python SDK Updates**: 
  * Updated `SandboxClient` and `AsyncSandboxClient` (along with their `K8sHelper` classes) to accept a `dict` for the `warmpool` parameter instead of a `str`.
  * Updated the Python manifests builder to serialize the payload using the new camelCase `warmPool` JSON key.
  * Fixed Python unit tests to assert against the updated `warmPool` key.

## ⚠️ Backward Compatibility
**This is a breaking change for the `SandboxClaim` API (`v1beta1`) and the Python SDK.**

Because the data type for `spec.warmPool` changed from a `string` to an `object`, existing `SandboxClaim` manifests will fail validation upon application. 

**Manifest Migration Path:**
* Previously: `warmPool: "None"` 
  ➡️ Now: `warmPool: { strategy: Disabled }`
* Previously: `warmPool: "Default"` (or omitted) 
  ➡️ Now: `warmPool: { strategy: Auto }` (or omitted)
* Previously: `warmPool: "my-fast-pool"` 
  ➡️ Now: `warmPool: { strategy: PoolName, poolName: "my-fast-pool" }`

**Python SDK Migration Path:**
* Previously: `client.create_sandbox(..., warmpool="my-fast-pool")`
  ➡️ Now: `client.create_sandbox(..., warmpool={"strategy": "PoolName", "poolName": "my-fast-pool"})`

Active claims already running in the cluster will need to be recreated or manually migrated if they used a non-default `warmPool` value.

## 📝 Release Note
```release-note
ACTION REQUIRED: The `spec.warmPool` field in `SandboxClaim` has been refactored from a string to a structured object to improve API safety and validation. Existing manifests must be updated. For example, to use a specific pool, change `warmPool: "my-pool"` to `warmPool: { strategy: "PoolName", poolName: "my-pool" }`. To disable warm pools, use `warmPool: { strategy: "Disabled" }`. The Python SDK's `create_sandbox` method has also been updated to accept a dictionary for the `warmpool` parameter to match this new schema.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
SandboxWarmPool status updates are broken when `replicas` or
`readyReplicas` transition from a non-zero value to `0`.

The controller uses server-side apply for status updates. Because
these fields are `int32` with `omitempty`, zero values are omitted
from the apply payload, leaving stale non-zero values in status
after a warmpool scales down.

Switch the warmpool status write path to `Status().Update()` with
conflict retries so zero-valued fields are explicitly cleared.
Also adds a regression test verifying both `status.replicas` and
`status.readyReplicas` can be cleared to `0`.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
None

#### Release Note
```release-note
Fixed SandboxWarmPool status fields `replicas` and `readyReplicas` 
not being cleared to zero when a warmpool scales down.

title: [Feature Request] Add SandboxClaim.spec.lifecycle.ttlAfterCreatedSeconds for auto-deletion of unbound claims

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
### Motivation

  The [2026 roadmap](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/main/roadmap.md) lists *"Auto-deletion of (bursty) sandboxes (RL training typical usage)"*. This issue proposes the pre-bind half of that story.

  Issue #481 (closed by #583) covers cleanup of `SandboxClaim`s after the bound Pod terminates. However, claims that are created but never reach `status.sandbox.name` is still uncovered. Concrete causes we have observed:

  - The client process exits after `CreateSandboxClaim` but before binding completes.
  - The warm pool is empty and on-demand provisioning fails (image pull, scheduling, quota).
  - The referenced `SandboxTemplate` does not exist or is misconfigured.

  In each case the `SandboxClaim` sits indefinitely. At scale this leaks warm-pool capacity and slot count.

  ### Proposed API

  Add an optional field on `SandboxClaim.spec.lifecycle`:

  ```yaml
  spec:
    lifecycle:
      ttlAfterCreatedSeconds: 300   # optional; if unset, no pre-bind cleanup
  ```

  Semantics: if `status.sandbox.name` is not set within `ttlAfterCreatedSeconds` of `metadata.creationTimestamp`, the controller deletes the `SandboxClaim`. Once the claim is bound, this field is inert; the existing `lifecycle.shutdownTime` governs post-bind cleanup.

  ### Alternatives considered

  - **External cleanup controller**: a separate Deployment that lists and deletes stale claims. Works, but pushes responsibility to every deployment. Less idiomatic than Kubernetes' `Job.spec.ttlSecondsAfterFinished` pattern.
  - **Default the timeout in the client SDK**: convenient but leaks past client process failures, since the SDK is not running when the client has crashed.
  - **Reuse `lifecycle.shutdownTime` for both pre- and post-bind**: conflates two semantics. Clients computing a deadline at claim creation do not yet know when the bind will happen, so they cannot pick a meaningful absolute time.

  ### Backward compatibility

  Additive optional field. Omitting it preserves current behavior.

Happy to write a small KEP and the implementation PR if the direction is endorsed.

body:
Working on: https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/issues/740

### Description
* Remove `spec.replicas` and introduce `spec.operatingMode` to represent suspension and resume behavior in Sandbox.

* The Suspension and Resume will now be represented as a new field `spec.operatingMode` which will have `Running` and `Suspended` modes. This is solidified in https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/pull/762/changes. A new KEP is added in this PR which documents the decisions for `spec.operatingMode`. 
The reconciler, extension controllers, generated CRDs, Python SDK suspend/resume logic, e2e tests, docs, and the roadmap are all updated to use the new mode-based vocabulary. 


### Changes
* Introduce `SandboxMode` type with Running/Suspended constants; remove `Replicas`and the `scale `subresource from the Sandbox API and generated CRDs. 
* Update the Sandbox controller, SandboxClaim controller, SandboxWarmPool controller, and their tests to set/check `Spec.OperatingMode` instead of `Spec.Replicas`.
* Update the Python gke_extensions snapshot support (is_suspended, suspend, resume and tests/README) to patch spec.operatingMode instead of spec.replicas, and refresh comments in sandbox.py / async_sandbox.py and the roadmap.

### Release Notes [Breaking Changes]

```
Removing the scale subresource is a breaking change that breaks kubectl scale commands and HorizontalPodAutoscalers (HPA). It also affect PodDisruptionBudget.
```

### Backward Compatibility

We don't have full backward compatibility at this stage, however we do support handling the management of existing Sandboxes via "Defaulting" behavior. The `spec.operatingMode` default behavior is "Running".

- `sandboxclaim_controller.go` & `sandboxwarmpool_controller.go`: Removed hardcoded `Service: new(true)` assignments. Replaced them with dynamic propagation: `sandbox.Spec.Service = template.Spec.Service`.
- Scalability Impact: Warm pools and claims now default to zero Kubernetes Service creation overhead, scaling to thousands of pods without iptables/IPVS bottlenecks.

3. Python SDK (`clients/python/agentic-sandbox-client/`)
- `sandbox.py` & `async_sandbox.py`: Configured the SDK to unconditionally pass get_pod_ip resolution engines to the underlying connectors.
- `connector.py` & `async_connector.py`: Added resolution, caching, and injection of the X-Sandbox-Pod-IP header. Wrapped get_pod_ip() in a safe try/except block to gracefully recover from transient API server timeouts.
- Implemented safety mechanism: if `get_pod_ip()` fails with a 401 or 403 permission error (e.g., for out-of-cluster Gateway clients lacking K8s credentials), the connector `sets _pod_ip_auth_failed = True`. This permanently disables direct Pod IP routing for that client instance, immediately falling back to Service routing for all future requests without throwing errors or wasting K8s API calls.

4. Proxy & Test Suites (`sandbox-router/`, `test/unit/`)
- `sandbox_router.py`: Updated dynamic routing to inspect the `X-Sandbox-Pod-IP` header. When present, the proxy routes HTTP streams directly to the Pod IP, completely bypassing Kubernetes DNS and kube-proxy. When omitted, it falls back to `<sandbox>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local`.
- Unit Tests: Updated mock initialization assertions in `test_sandbox.py` and added `test_target_url_pod_ip_construction` in `test_sandbox_router.py`

Before this PR: 
- For both creations/deletion we have a simple for loop and we do all operations sequentially.

- We are able to do the creations and deletions of sandboxes in the warmpool in parallel.

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
  This PR avoids inferring Sandbox launch type from the Pod tracking annotation.

  Previously, `agent_sandboxes` and SandboxClaim startup latency metrics inferred warm launches from `SandboxPodNameAnnotation`. That annotation tracks the Pod bound to a
  Sandbox and is also set for cold-started Sandboxes after their Pod is created, so cold launches could be reported as warm.

  This PR adds a dedicated `agents.x-k8s.io/launch-type` Sandbox label with `cold` and `warm` values. Cold-created Sandboxes are labeled `cold`, warm pool Sandboxes and
  adopted warm Sandboxes are labeled `warm`, and metrics now use this label instead of the Pod tracking annotation.

  Unit tests cover:
  - cold Sandboxes with `SandboxPodNameAnnotation` still reporting `cold`
  - warm Sandboxes reporting `warm`
  - cold create and warm adoption setting the launch type label
  - warm pool Sandbox creation setting the launch type label

#### What this PR does / why we need it:

The generated fake Kubernetes clients deprecate `NewSimpleClientset` in favor of `NewClientset`, but this repository did not generate the applyconfiguration packages and OpenAPI schema required by the newer constructor. Downstream tests therefore could not migrate to the field-managed fake object tracker or exercise server-side-apply behavior.

This PR wires the complete applyconfiguration pipeline into `dev/tools/client-gen-go.sh` for both core and extension APIs:

- Generates a temporary OpenAPI schema for all served core and extension resources.
- Generates core and extension applyconfiguration packages.
- Passes those packages to `client-gen`, producing `NewClientset` for both fake clientsets.
- Maps every shared core type referenced by extension APIs to its core applyconfiguration type, including v1alpha1 `PodMetadata`, `PodTemplate`, and `PersistentVolumeClaimTemplate`, and v1beta1 `SandboxBlueprint`, `PodMetadata`, `PodTemplate`, and `PersistentVolumeClaimTemplate`. This prevents apply objects from embedding raw API structs and claiming unset zero-value subtrees during SSA.
- Regenerates all affected clients and records the existing structured-merge-diff dependency as direct.

The generated extension APIs now expose `*PodMetadataApplyConfiguration`, `*PodTemplateApplyConfiguration`, and `*PersistentVolumeClaimTemplateApplyConfiguration` consistently for both versions. Getting these exported `With*` signatures correct before release avoids a later breaking Go API change.

title: Improve system label validation and name hashing robustness

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.name: needs-rebase
labels.description: Indicates a PR cannot be merged because it has merge conflicts with HEAD.

labels.name: cncf-cla: yes
labels.description: Indicates the PR's author has signed the CNCF CLA.

labels.name: priority/critical-urgent
labels.description: Highest priority. Must be actively worked on as someone's top priority right now.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR fixes a critical vulnerability where a malicious Sandbox tenant can bypass the internal network boundary. In the original code, user-provided labels inside `Spec.PodTemplate.ObjectMeta.Labels` were copied onto the Pod's metadata without verification, allowing them to overwrite the security-critical `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-name-hash` label. By explicitly injecting a victim's name hash into their own Pod labels, an attacker could hijack network traffic routed via the Headless Service selector.

**Core Fixes:**
1. **System Labels & Annotations Protection**: Added helper checks (`isSystemLabel` and `isSystemAnnotation`) in [sandbox_controller.go](file:///usr/local/google/home/glottman/dev/agent-sandbox-vulEq3/controllers/sandbox_controller.go) to prevent user templates from copying over system-reserved keys. The system labels are now safely assigned *after* merging user inputs.
2. **Cryptographically Secure Naming Hash**: Swapped the predictable FNV-1a 32-bit name-hash with **SHA-256** (first 32 hex characters) for cryptographic collision resistance.
3. **High-Performance Hashing Optimization**: Uses a memory-efficient slice encoding of SHA-256 (`hex.EncodeToString(hash[:16])`) that runs **2.7x faster** than standard string formatting. Micro-benchmarks run on AMD EPYC 7B12 show that the optimized hash executes in **`197.9 ns/op`** (virtually identical to FNV-1a's `151.7 ns/op`), ensuring zero scale overhead.
4. **Seamless Live Upgrade Migration**: Because the controller retrieves backing Pods and Services directly by name, the new controller will **automatically patch and migrate existing child resources** to the new SHA-256 label during their first reconcile loop. No manual migration or sandbox recreation is required.


#### Release Note
```release-note
FIX: Upgraded Sandbox NameHash to cryptographically secure SHA-256 with optimized slice encoding and added verification checks to prevent user-supplied templates from overriding security-critical system labels and annotations.

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR addresses a Remote Code Execution (RCE) vulnerability in the repository's CI presubmits (detailed in Google Buganizer issue #511321600). 

The helper library under `dev/tools/shared/` lacked an `__init__.py` file, meaning Python resolved it as a *namespace package*. Because Python gives higher import precedence to modules (single `.py` files) than to namespace packages in the same directory, an attacker could shadow the entire package and execute arbitrary code in the CI runner by submitting a Pull Request that introduces a malicious file at `dev/tools/shared.py`.

This PR creates `dev/tools/shared/__init__.py` with the standard license header, establishing `dev/tools/shared` as a **regular Python package**. Because regular packages take precedence over single-file modules, this permanently prevents any shadowing/RCE exploit from executing when running tools like `dev/tools/fix-gomod`.

This change has been verified locally to successfully block the shadowing exploit. In addition, we ran `make test-unit` and verified that all 231 Go and Python unit tests passed cleanly, showing no regression or incompatibility across any other dev tools.

#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Ref (Google Buganizer issue #511321600)

Fix Python module shadowing vulnerability in CI presubmit scripts.

Updates the requirements on [opentelemetry-api](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python), [opentelemetry-sdk](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python) and [opentelemetry-exporter-otlp](https://github.com/open-telemetry/opentelemetry-python) to permit the latest version. Updates `opentelemetry-api` to 1.41.1
Changelog

Sourced from opentelemetry-api's changelog.

Version 1.41.1/0.62b1 (2026-04-24)

Version 1.41.0/0.62b0 (2026-04-09)

  • opentelemetry-sdk: Add host resource detector support to declarative file configuration via detection_development.detectors[].host (#5002)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Add container resource detector support to declarative file configuration via detection_development.detectors[].container, using entry point loading of the opentelemetry-resource-detector-containerid contrib package (#5004)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Add create_tracer_provider/configure_tracer_provider to declarative file configuration, enabling TracerProvider instantiation from config files without reading env vars (#4985)
  • Enabled the flake8-tidy-import plugins rules for the ruff linter. These rules throw warnings for relative imports in the modules. (#5019)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Fix AttributeError in ExplicitBucketHistogramAggregation when applied to non-Histogram instruments without explicit boundaries (#5034)
  • Fix BatchLogRecordProcessor default schedule_delay_millis from 5000ms to 1000ms to comply with the OTel specification. Note: logs may be exported 5x more frequently by default (e.g. for users who don't explicitly set the OTEL_BLRP_SCHEDULE_DELAY env var). (#4998)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Add process resource detector support to declarative file configuration via detection_development.detectors[].process (#5001)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Add shared _parse_headers helper for declarative config OTLP exporters (#5021)
  • opentelemetry-api: Replace a broad exception in attribute cleaning tests to satisfy pylint in the lint-opentelemetry-api CI job
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Add create_meter_provider/configure_meter_provider to declarative file configuration, enabling MeterProvider instantiation from config files without reading env vars (#4987)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Add create_resource and create_propagator/configure_propagator to declarative file configuration, enabling Resource and propagator instantiation from config files without reading env vars (#4979)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Map Python CRITICAL log level to OTel FATAL severity text per the specification (#4984)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: Add file configuration support with YAML/JSON loading, environment variable substitution, and schema validation against the vendored OTel config JSON schema (#4898)
  • Fix intermittent CI failures in getting-started and tracecontext jobs caused by GitHub git CDN SHA propagation lag by installing contrib packages from the already-checked-out local copy instead of a second git clone (#4958)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: fix type annotations on MetricReader and related types (#4938)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: implement log creation metric (#4935)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: implement metric reader metrics (#4970)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: implement processor metrics (#5012)
  • opentelemetry-sdk: upgrade vendored OTel configuration schema from v1.0.0-rc.3 to v1.0.0 (#4965)
  • improve check-links ci job (#4978)
  • Resolve some Pyright type errors in Span/ReadableSpan and utility stubs (#4973)
  • opentelemetry-exporter-prometheus: Fix metric name prefix (#4895)
  • opentelemetry-api, opentelemetry-sdk: Add deepcopy support for BoundedAttributes and BoundedList (#4934)
  • opentelemetry-proto-json, opentelemetry-codegen-json: Implement custom protoc plugin to generate OTLP JSON class definitions

... (truncated)

Commits
  • 760e024 Prepare release 1.41.1/0.62b1 (#5138)
  • 90e06bc Unreleased changelog for 1.41.1 (#5137)
  • 1a178fc [release/v1.41.x-0.62bx] Prepare release 1.41.0/0.62b0 (#5064)
  • 37dea4b feat: add experimental logger configurator (#4980)
  • 7c860ca misc: update version for codegen-json and proto-json packages (#5061)
  • b3d98b3 [chore]: update readme (#5060)
  • dbbd1bc feat(config): Add MeterProvider support for declarative config (#4987)
  • 6faa58c feat(config): add host resource detector support for declarative config (#5002)
  • c0cbfbd feat(config): wire container resource detector via entry point loading (#5004)
  • f764e45 feat(config): Add TracerProvider support for declarative config (#4985)
  • Additional commits viewable in compare view

Bumps the github-actions group with 2 updates: [actions/checkout](https://github.com/actions/checkout) and [actions/setup-go](https://github.com/actions/setup-go). Updates `actions/checkout` from 4.3.1 to 6.0.2

v6.0.2

What's Changed

  • Add orchestration_id to git user-agent when ACTIONS_ORCHESTRATION_ID is set by @​TingluoHuang in actions/checkout#2355

Full Changelog: https://github.com/actions/checkout/compare/v6.0.1...v6.0.2

v6.0.1

v6-beta

What's Changed

Updated persist-credentials to store the credentials under $RUNNER_TEMP instead of directly in the local git config.

This requires a minimum Actions Runner version of v2.329.0 to access the persisted credentials for Docker container action scenarios.

title: Fix PVC and Pod Hijacking vulnerability

labels.name: size/L
labels.description: Denotes a PR that changes 100-499 lines, ignoring generated files.

labels.description: Highest priority. Must be actively worked on as someone's top priority right now.

labels.name: approved

body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR fixes a critical security vulnerability  in `controllers/sandbox_controller.go` that allows restricted RBAC users to hijack, mutate, or cascade-delete arbitrary unowned resources (`Pods`, `Services`, and `PersistentVolumeClaims`) in the namespace.
##### **Root Cause**
During reconciliation of Sandbox child resources, if an unowned namespace resource (lacking `OwnerReferences`) exists with a matching name (calculated as `volumeClaimTemplate.Name + "-" + sandbox.Name` for PVCs, or `sandbox.Name` for Pods/Services), the Sandbox controller automatically adopted it by injecting a controller reference to the parent Sandbox. When the attacker deletes their Sandbox CR, Kubernetes garbage collection cascade-deletes the adopted resource, permanently destroying the victim's data (e.g., a StatefulSet's volume `data-mysql-0`).
##### **Solution**
This PR restricts automatic resource adoption to only resources that carry an explicit administrative pool label:
- Defines a new constant `SandboxAdoptableLabel` in `api/v1beta1` with the key `"agents.x-k8s.io/adoptable"`.
- Modifies the `resourceUnowned` case in `reconcileService`, `reconcilePod`, and `reconcilePVCs` in `controllers/sandbox_controller.go`. Adoption is strictly refused, and an error is returned, unless the resource labels map contains `agents.x-k8s.io/adoptable: "true"`.
- Updates all mock resources in existing adoption tests in `sandbox_controller_test.go` to include the pool label so they continue to pass.
- Adds three new negative test cases (`refuses to adopt unowned pod/service/PVC that lacks pool authorization label`) to assert that unowned resources without the label are safely rejected and never adopted.
##### **Performance & Scale Metrics (Code & Security Review)**
- **Memory/CPU Overhead**: Zero additional heap allocations and negligible CPU impact. Checked via static in-memory Go map lookups ($O(1)$ average-time complexity, ~100ns) on objects already retrieved from the API server.
- **API Server Load**: Utilizes metadata of objects already fetched during standard reconciler GET operations, introducing **zero additional API server read/write QPS**.
- **Warm Pool Latency**: Warm pool pre-allocated sandboxes manage owned resources, and sandbox claims do not trigger child resource re-adoptions. Consequently, this check is **entirely bypassed** during the claim path, guaranteeing **0% throughput/latency overhead** on critical warm pool pod leases.
---
#### Which issue(s) this PR is related to:
Fixes Ref: (Google Buganizer #511323083)
---
#### Release Note
```release-note
Fix PVC and Pod Hijacking vulnerability by enforcing explicit pool label authorization (agents.x-k8s.io/adoptable="true") before setting sandbox controller references on unowned namespace resources.

title: [Bug] agent_sandbox_creation_latency_ms lacks millisecond precision due to use of CreationTimestamp

labels.name: kind/bug
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a bug.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
The `agent_sandbox_creation_latency_ms` metric currently measures the duration from a Sandbox's `CreationTimestamp` to when it becomes Ready.
https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox/blob/a8de4e57dcc4c523b31e25438afb86869a331d8b/extensions/controllers/sandboxclaim_controller.go#L1381

However, Kubernetes `CreationTimestamp` only provides second-level precision. This makes it unsuitable for tracking accurate millisecond-level latency, which is the intended resolution for this metric.

Tangentially, this metric is recorded in the SandboxClaim controller, delaying metrics for warm launches until they are claimed instead of when the resource actually becomes ready. This is likely to maintain the separation of the core Sandbox controller and the Extensions controllers.

**Proposed Solution:**

We should fix both issues with a two-part solution that maintains clean architectural boundaries:

* Add a high-precision creation annotation like `agents.x-k8s.io/created-at` or `agents.x-k8s.io/sandbox-created-at` with a creation timestamp `time.RFC3339Nano` annotation to the Sandbox resource when the Sandbox is created.
* Move the calculation and recording of `agent_sandbox_creation_latency_ms` to the Sandbox controller, triggered when the Sandbox transitions to the Ready state.
  * To maintain the (assumed) rule that the Sandbox controller must not depend on the extensions package, the controller will extract the necessary metric labels (`sandbox_template` and `launch_type`) as strings directly from the Sandbox's existing annotations and labels.

title: [Question] Python client support for creating Sandboxes without a SandboxTemplate

labels.name: kind/support
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as a support question.

labels.name: priority/awaiting-more-evidence
labels.description: Lowest priority. Possibly useful, but not yet enough support to actually get it done.

body:
Hi!

A question about the intended scope of the Python client (agentic-sandbox-client / k8s-agent-sandbox):

The Sandbox CRD itself supports an inline spec.podTemplate - we can create a Sandbox directly via the Kubernetes API and the
controller reconciles it without any SandboxTemplate involved. But the Python client doesn't seem to expose that path:
 - SandboxClient.create_sandbox(template, ...) requires a SandboxTemplate name.
 - Under the hood it creates a SandboxClaim, which can override env vars + labels but not the pod spec / image.
 - k8s_helper only exposes create_sandbox_claim — there's no create_sandbox_from_spec or similar.

This means workloads that need per-task variation in the pod spec (e.g. a different image per task) fall outside the client's surface.

Is the Template + Claim model intended to be the only client-supported path, with raw Sandbox creation explicitly out of scope?
Is there a path we missed?

Thanks!

body:
Hey everyone 👋

I've been following agent-sandbox for a while and I'm really excited about how fast this project is growing. As more people adopt it, I think it would be great for us as a community to share how we're using agent-sandbox — so we can learn from each other, discover new patterns, and help the maintainers understand what matters most to real users.

## Why share?

- **Learn from each other** — Maybe someone has already solved the problem you're stuck on.
- **Inspire new use cases** — Your setup might spark ideas for others.
- **Help shape the roadmap** — Maintainers can prioritize features based on real-world needs.
- **Build connections** — Find other teams working on similar problems.

## How to participate

Drop a comment below with whatever you're comfortable sharing:

| Field | Example |
|-------|---------|
| **Organization** | Your company, school, or open-source project |
| **Location** | City, Country |
| **Contact** | GitHub handle, blog, email, or Twitter/X |
| **Scale** *(optional)* | Cluster size, sandboxes/day, etc. |
| **Use Case** | What are you building with agent-sandbox? |
| **Lessons Learned** *(optional)* | Tips, gotchas, or things you wish you knew earlier |

### Example

> **Organization:** Acme AI Labs  
> **Location:** San Francisco, USA  
> **Contact:** @acme-eng  
> **Scale:** ~200 nodes, 50k sandboxes/day  
> **Use Case:** We use agent-sandbox as the code execution backend for our AI coding assistant. SandboxWarmPool gives us sub-second startup, and gVisor isolation lets us safely run arbitrary user-generated code.  
> **Lessons Learned:** Setting `TTL` aggressively (5min) on SandboxClaims helped us avoid resource leaks during peak traffic. Also, pairing with Prometheus metrics (#711, #712) made capacity planning much easier.

### Another example

> **Organization:** University of Example  
> **Location:** London, UK  
> **Contact:** researcher@example.edu  
> **Scale:** 20 nodes, ~500 sandboxes/day  
> **Use Case:** Running Code RL training loops — LLM generates code, agent-sandbox executes it in isolation, we compute reward from stdout/exit_code and feed it back to PPO. Integrated with Ray cluster via the Python SDK.  
> **Lessons Learned:** Warm pool size should be at least 2x your rollout parallelism to avoid claim queuing.

---

No pressure on format — even a one-liner like *"We use it for X at Y"* is valuable. The more we share, the stronger this community gets. 🚀

Looking forward to hearing your stories!

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
This PR introduces a new `spec.service` field to make automatic headless Service creation **opt-in** instead of the default behavior, while preserving backward compatibility for existing Sandboxes.

`spec.service` is a` *bool` so the controller can distinguish three states:

- `unset (nil)`: default, backward-compatible — preserves existing owned Service but does not create new ones.

- `false`: explicitly disables Service management — deletes any existing owned Service.

- `true`: explicitly enables Service management — creates or reconciles the headless Service.

- Added `spec.service `as `*bool` with `//nolint:kubeapilinter `to bypass the nobools linter rule.

- Updated `computeReadyCondition`.

title: [Feature Request] Multi-path persistent storage for Sandbox (filesystem-layer companion to #694)

labels.name: kind/feature
labels.description: Categorizes issue or PR as related to a new feature.

labels.name: priority/important-longterm
labels.description: Important over the long term, but may not be staffed and/or may need multiple releases to complete.

body:
## Problem

`Sandbox.Spec.VolumeClaimTemplates` (added in #52, released recently via `73d40a8`) lets a caller attach one or more PVCs to a Sandbox and mount them at arbitrary paths — in practice, the vast majority of deployments land on a single PVC mounted at a well-known user-data directory (commonly `/workspace`, `/data`, or `$HOME`).

This covers "the user's own files", but **not** the broader filesystem state that users routinely accumulate outside the user-data directory and lose on every pod restart (hibernate, PodFailed, node eviction):

- `apt install <pkg>` → `/usr/bin`, `/usr/lib`, `/var/lib/dpkg` — lost.
- `pip install --user <pkg>` → `~/.local/lib/python*/site-packages` — lost unless `$HOME` happens to be the single mounted PVC.
- `npm install -g` → `/usr/local/lib/node_modules` — lost.
- `~/.bashrc`, `~/.zshrc`, `~/.vimrc`, `~/.ssh/known_hosts`, shell history — lost.
- `oh-my-zsh`, `pyenv`, `nvm`, `rustup` and friends — whatever they install to `$HOME` is lost.

Downstream platforms today work around this by telling users "only work under `/workspace`" and baking every tool into custom images, which leads to image-explosion and a UX that's surprising to anyone who's used a persistent dev environment before (Codespaces / Gitpod / a regular VM).

## Proposal (summary)

A new declarative field `persistentStorage` on `SandboxSpec` and `SandboxTemplateSpec` that:

1. Provisions **one** PVC per Sandbox (cost-efficient; RWO is sufficient).
2. Lets the caller declare N paths (`Mounts []PersistentMount`) to be preserved; each backed by a `subPath` on the shared PVC.
3. On **first boot**, an init container seeds each declared path from the image's original filesystem at that path — so the user immediately sees `.bashrc`, system binaries, etc. as shipped in the image.
4. On **subsequent boots**, the init container short-circuits (subpath non-empty) and the main container sees the user's accumulated state.

```yaml
spec:
  persistentStorage:
    size: 20Gi
    mounts:
      - path: /root
        bootstrapFromImage: true
      - path: /usr/local
        bootstrapFromImage: true
      - path: /workspace
        bootstrapFromImage: false
```

This is **fully backward compatible** with existing `volumeClaimTemplates` — callers can use either, both, or neither. `persistentStorage` is the higher-level, opinionated API for the common "just keep these paths across restarts" use case; `volumeClaimTemplates` remains the lower-level escape hatch for AccessMode control, RWX, VolumeAttributesClass, etc.

## Why this, why not something else?

| Option | Why not |
|---|---|
| Multiple `volumeClaimTemplates` entries | Forces users to manage N PVCs and hand-author N × init containers for first-boot seeding — the feature is possible today but too tedious for the common case. |
| Annotation-based (`agents.x-k8s.io/persist: "/root,..."`) | No type safety, awkward per-path configuration, silently ignored by older controllers. |
| Full rootfs persistence (OverlayFS upperdir on PVC) | Requires CRI modifications; breaks "works on any k8s" guarantee; operationally complex. |
| GKE PodSnapshot | Complementary, not substitute — requires gVisor + GKE, preserves memory state (superset), but can't run on a vanilla cluster. |

## Relationship to #694 ("Support for Suspend API and notion of Snapshot provider")

`persistentStorage` is the **filesystem-layer provider** in a broader Suspend/Snapshot provider taxonomy:

- Filesystem provider (this KEP) — universally available, no runtime dependency.
- Pod-snapshot provider (#694) — optional, opt-in, rich (memory included) when runtime supports it.

This issue is **not** competing with #694 — it delivers one concrete provider that every cluster can use today and makes #694 easier to realize later by establishing at least one working implementation under that conceptual umbrella.

## Non-goals

- Memory / process state preservation (that's PodSnapshot / CRIU territory).
- Cross-sandbox data sharing (PVCs stay RWO).
- Fully generic "persist the entire rootfs" (too high operational cost; targeted paths give ~90% of the value).

## Current state

A KEP draft covering API surface, controller behavior, first-boot bootstrap semantics, safety (path validation), scalability, and alternatives is available here:

**→ https://github.com/Gamattention/agent-sandbox/blob/kep/persistent-mounts/docs/keps/773-persistent-mounts/README.md**

The draft closely follows KEP-174's format and links to the `reconcilePVCs` reuse pattern for implementation.

## Feedback sought

1. Does `persistentStorage` belong as a sibling to `volumeClaimTemplates`, or should it land under an umbrella `suspendStrategy` / `snapshotProvider` field to align with #694's direction?
2. Is the "image-content frozen after first boot" semantic acceptable, or should there be an opt-in "re-seed on image change" knob?
3. Should the path validation block list (`/dev`, `/proc`, `/sys`, `/etc/shadow`, …) be in the webhook or in a separate OPA/Kyverno policy library?
4. Warmpool interaction — happy to extend the KEP if reviewers want more detail on pre-warmed Sandbox inheritance.

Happy to drive the implementation once the design is accepted. Preliminary implementation plan is in the KEP draft's "Path to Acceptance" section.
